They removed the unfair/nightmare difficulty from the
. This is indeed stupid to us Unfair players who would challenge ourselves on levels over and over, raging until we won, or if you were like me, soloing without using any relics whatsoever. They killed the fun there, I agree. But you know what? The main campaign is like.. 5% of the game now.
I played NoX way before I played Gauntlet. In NoX, there was a main campaign which, like Gauntlet, was underwhelming. Then there was a "Quest mode", that started you off at a very low difficulty that kept gradually increasing until the game was damn near impossible. The first teleport floor you find is on level 19.
If you missed Unfair mode, missing things like gilded hams and turkeys, oh well, it's not in the campaign. Make it to floor 37 on Endless and now you're in Unfair mode again, except the maps are random and can be absolutely brutal. They darken the maps, make ghosts black instead of white to hide in the shade, will spawn four obelisks
two necromancers on you (this happened to me in a ♥♥♥♥ing Reaper map), and best of all, relics don't feel game-breaking anymore. You don't have to feel like a scrub for using them!

One of the most overrated games in the past 10 years. This review is disregarding the already apparent issues the game has on PC and Windows Live and will be reviewing the game as if it just came out recently (i.e. ignoring graphics). Bethesda did not do the Fallout franchise justice with the horrid writing, and shallow choices. The illusion of choice is there but it's usually either one of two outcomes in questlines. Although there is room for roleplaying, and different playthroughs, the main quest suffers from the same issues the rest of the quests in the game suffers from; it was too linear and barely allows for different paths and choices. The ending was so hated, Bethesda had to address it in one of their DLCs. Speaking of DLCs, while they do their job as your typical Bethesda DLC♥♥♥♥♥♥ Mothership Zeta infurated me and♥♥♥♥♥♥on the lore. Aliens were supposed to be just a funny easter egg in the game but "nah let's make it canon lol". Anchorage was just a boring stealthfest but provided some neat insight on the war. There are a few good things Fallout 3 does such as the memorable intro, which I loved, the Mechanist vs Antagonizer quest, Little Lamp Light, the followers and Megaton, but otherwise the rest of the game was bland and not up to par with the past Fallouts and New Vegas.
The game is mostly a questing theme park and really just feels like a reskinned Oblivion which really all that spectacular either.
To anyone looking into buying Fallout 3, I recommend New Vegas first, and if you just came out of playing the travesty that was Fallout 4, I guess you could play Fallout 3 after NV with the mod that allows travel between both games. Unlike Fallout 4, Fallout 3 excels in allowing players to build their own character, and their perks and S.P.E.C.I.A.L. points actually feel well invested through skill checks, but at the end of the day New Vegas does everything 3 did well but better. This is objective fact.
Just because there's a lot of quests spread out over a large landmass does not mean you're getting your money's worth, it's quantity over quality with Bethesda which is funny since New Vegas has nearly over double the amount of quests 3 has but they all manage to be better written and executed than the quests in 3.
I give Fallout 3 a 6 or 7 out of 10. Not spectacular but it does the job if you have time to kill.

This is a top-notch localization of a dating sim, one of the best I've ever played, fan translations included.  The choice of language is natural and smooth, using English slang and context in a coherently and fluently, without losing the nuances of the original meaning.  So huge props to this localization!
As for the game itself, despite the shoddy premise (5 dolls come to life and become the HOT5 at your high school, etc), it feel surprisingly natural.  The game plays a lot like a Korean Drama, and for anyone who has watched Kdramas before, they flow more naturally/casually than JDramas, using healthy splashes of humor and humanistic dialogue, despite outlandish or just plain unlikely premises/plots.  Nameless follows a similar trend-- crazy story, but great characterization and dialogue.  I laughed so much playing this game and the humor is funny, without being cheesy.
I look forward to playing all the routes, this is a really fulfilling game!

I really enjoyed Nameless. It's a visual novel, so if stat raising etc is your cuppa, you'll be disappointed. But if you want the equivalent of a choose-your-own adventure book with beautiful art and music, fantastic voice acting, and an engaging slice-of-life-style story, then this one's for you. The romance is sweet and the bad endings are, for the most part, marvelously creepy. The boys all start out as what appear to be one-note otome game stereotypes, but as Eri gets to know them, they become so much more. I enjoyed all the routes, which is a rarity for me, even with the characters that I initially thought I wouldn't care for. Eri herself is a flawed, very human, and very likeable protagonist. She's not immune to the "blushes and shyness" trope with her suitors, a pretty standard feature in this style of game, but her sense of humor and other reactions (not to mention her "o srsly?" face) manage to set her apart. All in all, a great game that's worth its price point.

I there was one thing I could say about this game, is that it is pretty much if the Toy Story movies were a dark romantic thriller focusing on dolls and not the popular preschool toys we know. That being said, it's a fun ride that will tear your heartstrings and leave you asking for more.

***Warning, potential spoilers***
TL;DR: One of the best visual novel games that exists, Well worth the price. I cannot thumbs up this enough, wall of text below if you're wondering why.
-----
I don't even know where to begin with this game.
You play as the heroine of the story, Eri as she falls in love with her dolls to reveal two bonus endings at the very end of the game. This game is deep, dark, heartwrenching, funny, sad, and makes you think about material possessions in a different light, as it thorougly draws you into the mystery and intrigue of the plot line.
First off, the artwork is amazing in this game, bright colors, very painted shading, the backgrounds in the game are mediocre but the character art and the CG's are phenomenally good. Much like Cheritz' other game, Dandelion, all of the characters are broad and deep with good and bad in them. The bad endings are disturbing at times and can be very dark even bordering on violent, but - overall this will keep you interested all the way through. The greatest thing about this visual novel is that you really get a different experience when you're playing all of the paths because while even the first three revolve around a common path, there are still little blurbs that don't just involve the skip button which add depth and a bit of confusion for the first time playthrough anyways.
Once the steam-keys were added, I finished completing the game for the second time (Literally finished 5 minutes ago) and after months of not playing I could still remember the depth of the characters and how amazing they were. What I love about this VN, is that some of the bad endings are so disturbing yet alluring that I would save and choose the right options for the bad ends anyways, and that's phenomenal. All i wanna say is "Oma Tei" is pretty funny in a disturbing way and I had to go through and literally go "Tei, oh my god stop." because he makes an appearance in a bunch of the bad ends. Sorry for any potential spoilers there. Someone should really count the amounts of times Tei shows up unexpectedly.
My favorite path on the first playthrough was Tei, because at first glance his concept was so interesting and I usually play for the princely, usually blonde character first. He's such a broad character however once you get into it, that it is downright scary at times once you realise just how disturbed the character is under the mask he plays most of the time. My second playthrough of it however, I think Lance takes my favorite spot. The reason being is after you've gotten the whole story, Lance really is a deep character. The journal entries are really intense, and it makes me think after playing through it that Lance really doesn't want to give up on the MC with the other characters routes.
The only thing I would actually wish for would be a fully playable path with the bonus character, as after you get the second bonus ending with him, it's heartwrenching and makes me want to actually play a full path with the character. He's so disturbed and depressed that my heart was practically exploding with pain, and the bonus cg. Oh my god. way to tear my heart out Cheritz! hahaha. Seriously though, phenomenal Visual novel. I cannot say that enough.
This VN. It's amazing. If you want a tear jerking, deep, visceral, heart wrenching story with enough content to keep you reading through it for at least a few days, get this. It's well worth the price. The game's voicing is in Korean but all of the text can be read in english, if like me you cannot actually -read- korean. There are a few bugs here and there but honestly they don't break the game, they just could take a little fixing.
Bugs I can remember: MC's name being listed as %$ Or some symbol, during certain cutscenes, or Young %$ due to a scripting error.
Spelling/grammar errors as well: Lance refers to himself as MC's "fist" doll, which made me laugh but I don't think was the intended message. And I believe there were a few typos on Yeon-ho's route as well.
There were also a few issues with grammar/translation Tei-ahjumma is better meant as "Old lady Tei" instead of momma-tei, so it's not exactly accurate, but then again Korean isn't exactly straight-forward interpretation wise... Also there were some down-right difficult to read sentences in the bonus ending that required some re-reading due to how they were worded.
That said for me, overall this game is a serious 9.8/10. If you're into visual novels, and or are looking for a good romantic visual novel as a female character, this one is hands down amazing. Unlike Dandelion, this game does not rely on stat building and is entirely dependent on choices made through reading, as such it's more like this deep heartwrenching story with pretty pictures and pretty characters. MC does act a little stupid/ditsy at times/ignorant, but aside from that all of the characters are fantastic. It's well worth the price.

This game is definitely more of an experience than a game, and is not for everyone. When it comes to gameplay, you walk around, collect items, and witness what is happening around you. If you are more of an action-oriented gamer, this is not the game for you.  But, if you like games with excellent stories, you are definitely in the right place.
The story of this game is highly engaging and interesting, and the characters feel like actual people with motives and flaws. The game can be really funny at times, but can also be really sad and dark- although I will mention that outside of the occasional cuss word, this game has nothing that would be inappropriate for kids. It tackles mature themes of death and morality in an elegant way. The pixel graphics are also pleasing to look at.
I also would like to mention, however, that this game will make you cry. The story does have people dying- but there's no  blood, don't worry- and the game does have a heart-breaking scene where a chharacter talks about autism. If you are very sensitive to crying, are unconfortable with death, or just don't want an emotional experience, this game is not for you.
But, if you love emotional experiences, art games, or want a fresh, though-provoking experience, then I completely recommend this game. It is beautifully crafted, and a wholesome experience that will stick with you long after the credits roll (especially because of the bittersweet ending- and the after-credits scene ;) ). The game also comes with two Christmas "mini-sodes" that are fun to play and definitely are a great free addition to the game lore. Plus, there's more wiseecracks by Dr. Watts, so you will be grinning the whole way through.
My advice would be to wait until a Steam sale, during which the game is only 2 dollars- definitely a huge bargain. However, it is worth the normal price of 10 dollars if you enjoy games like these.

To The Moon is a game developed in RPG Maker that controls terribly, has a poor aesthetic, clunky menus, and little in terms of gameplay. The game is comprised entirely of walking, dialogue, and the occasional flip puzzle. The game itself is poorly designed, lacks polish, and at the beginning feels like a chore.
It's brilliance however shines in the writing and storytelling. To The Moon tells an amazing and unique story of two scientists who delve into a dying man's memories to change his earliest impressionable memories in order to fulfill his lifelong desire to fly "to the moon." It has great dialogue, very emotional characters and scenes, and several plot twists that will have you wanting to finish this game in one sitting. The ending was fantastic and left me with something of a minor life crisis of self-questioning.
Gameplay, Visuals, Controls: 2/10
Story, Writing, Characters: 9/10 (10 w/o memes sprinkled in)
Definitely pick this up if it's on sale and play it in one sitting - you won't regret it.

I can honestly say To the Moon offers one of the most visceral experiences I have ever gotten out of a game. Definitely the most emotional ride I've ever had with any form of media. I've played countless games and seen even more movies, but never before have I actually shed genuine tears from a story. This game does a phenomenal job of making you care about the characters, and the more you get to know them the more you fall in love with them. Even the more minor characters are incredibly lovable. Watching these characters grow will no doubt have you bawling by the end and not just out of sadness, tears of joy will be shed as well.

Shao Jun is an assassin and her mind is set on revenge after the Templars destroyed the Chinese Brotherhood she belonged to: you'll be relying on your superior training, athletics and a small array of different weapons and gadgets to travel through levels and make sure the Templars pay for what they've done, one assassination at a time.
What follows is a game similar to Mark of the Ninja in gameplay, but less engaging overall: there's enough to enjoy in the great art style and fluid stealth but the bland story and so-so combat drag Chronicles down a bit.
-gorgeous art style looks like an antique watercolour
-good soundtrack
-fluid controls paired with a satisfying moveset
-bland and cliched story even for Assassin's Creed standards
-flat characters
-open combat feels a bit too awkward to be enjoyable
Chronicles: China is a pretty decent experience, after all there's no denying that pulling out a perfect stealth section or even just assassinating a few guards unseen is satisfying. The great art style makes levels truly gorgeous and they'd fit well in an antique piece of art: level backgrounds, rooms and character models are all very nice to look at.
The actual overall gameplay is, well, decent but nothing more: you get a few new gadgets along the way and some new enemy types will make your life more difficult but the level design and small number of actual reliable tactics make the experience a bit repetitive in the long run. Open combat is pretty meh and basically boils down to parry and then either riposte or jump over an enemy to try and hit their backs, it works but it's pretty awkward and unsatisfying.
The actual story and narrative are pretty yawn inducing even for the series and it's difficult to feel engaged when all the characters-Shao Jun included- are paper thin. The game is only 6 hours long though, so that helps it not overstay its welcome.
Chronicles: China is a decent game overall and not a bad purchase if you're looking for more Assassin's Creed and/ or some decently done stealth action: just be mindful of its shortcomings.

Europa 3, like its predecessors and its cousins Hearts of Iron and Victoria (Crusader Kings as well, but that isn't as hard to learn), is an extremely complex game that is notoriously difficult to learn, not helped by crappy tutorials. I had an edge having been playing this series since its first installment, but it still took some time to get used to everything. So right from the start expect a significant time investment on learning how to play the game, and learning to do well at it. War, Diplomacy, Trade, Exploration, and more. It's all here.
But it is worth it. Oh yes is it worth it. EU3 is a -gigantic- game with near-endless replayability and a player-driven storytelling ability (creating a story from your own experience of playing the game) in the same league as the Civilization and Sims games. You can play as any country in the world, though the game is a bit euro-centric considering the time period it covers (1399-1821) is the period in history when Europe came to dominate most of the rest of the world. Those who know their history also know that there is a MASSIVE amount of stuff contained in this time period: The fall of Byzantium and the rise of the Ottoman Turks, Columbus' voyage to America and the mass colonizing that followed, The Protestant Reformation and the horde of religious wars that came with it, Independence movements in the "settler colonies" of the Americas, and finally the French Revolution that leads to a gigantic war at the end of the game.
However, little to nothing is set in stone. Byzantium might not fall. The Spanish may not be the ones to build a massive American colonial empire. The Protestant Reformation might just be a tiny local event, and the French Revolution might not even happen in France or at all. In other words, there is considerable variation, and much of that can be the result of the player's actions. Events can follow history or lead to an entirely different result. I've seen just about everything happen while playing this game from the Aztecs never being conquered, the Ottomans being extinguished early on (or built into the kind of monster empire you can see in my screenshots), Spain never being united as a single country, and so much more. And if you are a masochist of the highest order, you can try to take over the world as the Ryukyu Kingdom (Okinawa).
How will things go? It is up to you to see. :)

BY POWER OR THREE HEROES...
In Trine, player controls three different characters. The Wizard, who can create boxes and levitate things in the air. The Thief, who can shoot arrows and use her crabling hook. Using these three different characters in puzzle solving and platforming player must make his way to several different gorgeus looking levels.

Game's story in other hand, is kinda cliche. Three main character are by accident been connected to the magical artefact, Trine. Story won't seems like much first, but feels like it was rip off from bedtime storybook and sucks player into himself by it's charm and music.

Trine mixes in it's gameplay puzzle solving, platforming and hack 'n slash. Especially in puzzle solving game shines. Mixing all three characters player can find several different solutions in puzzles, but was those solved by own way, progressing feels satisfying. Levels are full of secrets like exp-bottles and special items which give game small RPG-feeling.
VERDICT:
Trine is a beautiful and personal looking puzzle platformer with it's couple annoying parts and not having online co-op. I suggest everyone who have any kinda interest to puzzle games and/or platform games.

This game is as zen as zen can be. That's the best I will ever be able to describe this game.
The developer, a one man crew, is planning to release the game with a single player mode, as well as a 4 co-op player mode. Eternal Winter is a survival game where you've to make sure you survive, but you also have to make sure your dogs survive, or else you can be damn sure you'll be the next in line.
Graphics wise, the game is very cartoonish, but the movement are very fluid. There's a possible tweak here and there, but not even close to being a game breaker.
The soundtrack will make you feel isolated, with only your four best friends around, and no one else in the whole wide world.
To resume all of the above, Eternal Winter is a great game, and an even greater one when considering the one man team, which keeps pumping out updates, and good updates I must say (/points to the dogs coming out of the sled to help hunt).
You'll either love, or like this game, there's no hating, unless you've serious problems, or simply don't like survival games. There are no zombies, there are no sharks and there is also no one else around (at least for now), but you'll never feel alone.

With a couple of exceptions, Gameforge's games line-up is all about fantasy titles, however the publisher took a distance from their usual environment by offering you a brutal and competitive military-themed online FPS: S.K.I.L.L.S. - Special Force 2. With a lot of well established free MMOFPS out there, offering something capable to stand out and gather a consistent pool of players is certainly a tough challenge; and of course we couldn't miss the chance to see what Gameforge managed to do in a field that for them is totally new and unexplored, so follow us in this review and check out if the game is worth trying or not!
The first impression upon entering into the game is somewhat both good and bad. It is good because everything is kind of familiar if you've ever played any other f2p MMOFPS, and you will basically know how to play and navigate in the different menus, but at the same time you will probably feel a sense of déjà vu as the developers' intention clearly wasn't to innovate or change the genre, but to offer their personal interpretation of a well-known and working formula.
Speaking about menus, after the log-in you will be brought to a pretty standard home screen containing all the classic tabs that you would expect from a game like this: capsule market, shop, inventory, mini-game, career and clan. While shop, inventory and clan are pretty much self explanatory, the others may need a word or two about them. The capsule market is a place where you can buy different kinds of sealed boxes which contain a random item and give you the chance to obtain special and unique gear pieces. However, most of them are temporary, and you could end up with an item that you don't need at all, so choose wisely if it's worth to gamble or not. Regarding the mini-game tab, don't be too excited; the game offers some interesting and unique game modes, but in this tab the only thing you will find is only a free training mode where you can spawn dummies and do other stuff in order to get confident with controls and mechanics. In the career tab you can find all the information and statistics about your in-game performance and more.
The game features a shop that offers a wide selection of digital reproductions of real firearms, which are usually available for both cash and in-game currency. Of course there are unique VIP weapons which are only available to VIP players, but from what I could see the differences are mainly cosmetic and intended to let you show off your VIP status. One thing that I appreciated a lot is the possibility to buy permanent weapons. They still need to be repaired, but this is a whole different thing compared to a lot of other free MMOFPS where you can only buy temporary weapons and you are forced to constantly play the game in order to buy them again when they expire. With this system, on the other hand, you can buy a new weapon, take a break from the game for some time and then come back without the fear of having wasted your precious weapon.
The control system is standard and identical to almost every other modern FPS. However, I have to say that the jump feels a little strange. There are a lot of objects in the arena that seems to be there just to be climbed and that are not very tall, but you can't actually jump on them. As I said it's a little strange and sometimes kind of frustrating, but it is absolutely not a game-breaker. However, the point where the S.K.I.L.L . - Special Force 2 gameplay tries to differentiate itself from the masses, is probably the featured game modes: Deathmatch,Team Deathmatch, Seizure, Escape, Blasting, Manhunt, Glass, Hero, Sniper battle...there's a lot of them.
Speaking about graphics, S.K.I.L.L. feels like a raw gem; they are not bad, instead, they are actually pretty good, but they just can't stand comparison with the latest free-to-play online FPS. S.K.I.L.L.'s graphics, while clean and enjoyable, lack in details and this makes the maps' design to look a little empty and too simple. The same deal goes with the sounds; they are not bad, but I think that the developers could have made a way better job with just a little more effort. The steps sounds are often a little unnatural, while the shooting and weapons sounds are average.
S.K.I.L.L. - Special Force 2 is a valid free-to-play shooter which puts a lot of emphasis on community and clans. Even if it's not the best shooter around regarding graphics and sounds, it manages to offer a complete and fun overall gameplay experience and some pretty unique and fun game modes.

There are so many games out there that fit into one formula or another, one is tempted to assign numbers to them and say, "For a Number 9, that's not bad." This game utterly defies such cynical pigeonholing...it is its own category. And I say that affectionately and a bit sad that it is over.
Unless you can divide your attention and type like a whirlwind, you will struggle with this game. That's not a criticism, that's just a fact. The game starts easily enough, but each new level builds on all that came before, and all too soon you'll find yourself trying to switch modes during a melee.
That aside, the lyrical and fresh qualities of this game are engaging and I can't recommend it enough for originality, playabiliity, empathy, and challenge. When it ended I felt good about my skill, but I also felt good about the whole premise of the game and its sympathetic protagonists.

This game is amazing on many fronts. It is stunningly beautiful, the story is interesting and written elegantly, the puzzles are challenging and the typing game mechanic is unique, compelling and refreshing. Switching between elements adds an extra layer of strategic planning to the game mechanic and the leveling system provides you with a lot of freedom of choice. It is very, very rewarding.
This is probably one of the best PC games I've played... ever. The dungeons remind me of old school, top down Zelda games. This is creativity and design at its finest. The only complaint I have is that character movement is clunky and isn't all that intuitive. But it makes sense given the game is designed so that you keep your hands in qwerty position 95% of the time (besides in menu). Eventually, you get used to it but it is still very tank-like, rigid, grid movement and just doesn't feel all that natural.
Buy this game. It is well worth the money.
P.S. +1 for Linux support.

This is a re-review of Lego worlds and let me tell you this is a very cautious recommendation.
First of all, the good. The game is extremely fun and the developers have added minor tweaks and differences to how the game works since I last played it. I find myself hooked in just exploring the worlds and collecting new characters and items. I often find myself roleplaying a werewolf character during the night and a human during the day when he turns back. The game is basically super fun for people no matter how old they are and I would certainly recommend if you enjoy open world sandboxes and lego.
Nonetheless this is a very cautious review because of the amount of things which are still glaringly wrong with it. Last time I commented that the camera angles of the games worked terribly with a controller and it had multithreading CPU issues, happily these things seem to have been ameded. The framerate is a little dodgy however and I won't tell you my specs but let's just say I'm running the best of the best at the moment so the issue certainly isn't hardware. I'm not a massive framerate snob but I think anything lower than 60 can be a little jarring for people who get simulation sickness. One more huge caveat emptor is that splitscreen multiplayer is glaringly broken. When I played this yesterday with my girlfriend I found the framerate to be poorer than usual and whenever either of us got into a vehicle it dipped to 10-15fps which is unplayable even by those who don't notice framerate dips as I do.
I'll be keeping a close eye on this game because the devs seem to listen to the community in regards to controller support and performance issues, but I think this game has a bright future.

This game is definitely more of an experience than a game, and is not for everyone. When it comes to gameplay, you walk around, collect items, and witness what is happening around you. If you are more of an action-oriented gamer, this is not the game for you.  But, if you like games with excellent stories, you are definitely in the right place.
The story of this game is highly engaging and interesting, and the characters feel like actual people with motives and flaws. The game can be really funny at times, but can also be really sad and dark- although I will mention that outside of the occasional cuss word, this game has nothing that would be inappropriate for kids. It tackles mature themes of death and morality in an elegant way. The pixel graphics are also pleasing to look at.
I also would like to mention, however, that this game will make you cry. The story does have people dying- but there's no  blood, don't worry- and the game does have a heart-breaking scene where a chharacter talks about autism. If you are very sensitive to crying, are unconfortable with death, or just don't want an emotional experience, this game is not for you.
But, if you love emotional experiences, art games, or want a fresh, though-provoking experience, then I completely recommend this game. It is beautifully crafted, and a wholesome experience that will stick with you long after the credits roll (especially because of the bittersweet ending- and the after-credits scene ;) ). The game also comes with two Christmas "mini-sodes" that are fun to play and definitely are a great free addition to the game lore. Plus, there's more wiseecracks by Dr. Watts, so you will be grinning the whole way through.
My advice would be to wait until a Steam sale, during which the game is only 2 dollars- definitely a huge bargain. However, it is worth the normal price of 10 dollars if you enjoy games like these.

To The Moon is a game developed in RPG Maker that controls terribly, has a poor aesthetic, clunky menus, and little in terms of gameplay. The game is comprised entirely of walking, dialogue, and the occasional flip puzzle. The game itself is poorly designed, lacks polish, and at the beginning feels like a chore.
It's brilliance however shines in the writing and storytelling. To The Moon tells an amazing and unique story of two scientists who delve into a dying man's memories to change his earliest impressionable memories in order to fulfill his lifelong desire to fly "to the moon." It has great dialogue, very emotional characters and scenes, and several plot twists that will have you wanting to finish this game in one sitting. The ending was fantastic and left me with something of a minor life crisis of self-questioning.
Gameplay, Visuals, Controls: 2/10
Story, Writing, Characters: 9/10 (10 w/o memes sprinkled in)
Definitely pick this up if it's on sale and play it in one sitting - you won't regret it.

I can honestly say To the Moon offers one of the most visceral experiences I have ever gotten out of a game. Definitely the most emotional ride I've ever had with any form of media. I've played countless games and seen even more movies, but never before have I actually shed genuine tears from a story. This game does a phenomenal job of making you care about the characters, and the more you get to know them the more you fall in love with them. Even the more minor characters are incredibly lovable. Watching these characters grow will no doubt have you bawling by the end and not just out of sadness, tears of joy will be shed as well.

*UPDATE 3 AND (hopefully!) FINAL* Upon the release of the latest patch and Nvidia's 388.13 drivers, this game now appears GENUINELY playable. As in, you can launch the game and it will run perfectly, no matter if you tab out, alt+f4, or any other nonesense. Outrageous though it is that we had to essentially wait a month for this game to be properly playable, I am changing this review to positive, as the game is truly a wonderful experience when it runs correctly. Keeping the previous updates tagged on for posterity however. Next time, can you just not release it until it's ready? Delay it by a month rather than repeat a launch like that.
*UPDATE 2* I still think this should have launched in a far, far better state than was delivered, HOWEVER, I would recommend that anyone who experiences the bugs I did stick with it; this game is worth it. It's a fantastically fun experience with a masterful narrative made all the more poignant by the chaos in our current politic environment.
*UPDATE* Upon re-installing the game, I was - finally - able to begin playing the campaign in earnest. I have since suffered only one blue screen, caused by alt+tabbing (I have heard that running the game in windowed-borderless may be a workaround for this issue however). Whilst I still cannot, for one moment, justify recommending a game that launches in this state, I will add that once you do run the gauntlet of trials necessary to get it working, this is a truly enjoyable gaming experience. The narrative is compelling and well written throughout, the gameplay is visceral and entertaining, with enough challenge to keep veterans happy on the higher diffculties, whilst not proving too punishing for newbies on the lower settings. Had this launched in an even remotely acceptable state, I would happily put it amongst "game of the year" contenders. Alas, whilst it may very well be welcome in such lofty heights on consoles, assuming their launch was smoother than ours, I'm afraid the damage is somwhat done here. In summary: great game *if* you can get it running, but still doesn't justify the state of the launch.

Cons:
Nvidia really dropped the ball on this and realesed bad drivers. For those having crashes at the menu screen there is a hotfix available on Nvidia's website:
This did not fully reslove my issue, but doing the following additionally did:
- Run the game as administrator.
- In advanced settings, turn off Async Compute (it is towards the very bottom of all the options).
- Hit apply settings as quickly as possible before the game crashes.
- Click New Game.
I had to do this 2 times because I wasn't fast enough. However, once I did the game runs buttery smooth and I have had no crashes.
Personally, I would give this game a 8/10 so far.
However, if you have an nvidia card and you are patient to play this game, I would wait until this coming week when Nvidia relases an official patch. Because of the circumstances which I don't know whether to pin on the devs or Nvidia, I would give this game a 6/10 until patched.

Firstly let me say, if you don't like strategy games and you don't feel like spending a bit of time feeling like a lost puppy whilst attempting to learn one, this game is NOT for you.  Go play Pac Man or Streetfighter or some other button masher, because this game will just hurt your wittle feelings.
It's old.  The graphics are mediocre at best and god help whatever tonedeaf goober composed the soundtrack.  None of which takes one iota of shine off the proverbial apple that is this game.  Simply put it is a masterpiece of strategic gaming.  To date this is Paradox's definitive opus.  It somehow manages to maintain beguiling simplicity side-by-side with byzantine depth.
When you first start playing around with it you will probably fumble around like a weetodd on a trampoline(no offence to all you 'todds out there), but you'll STILL be able to make satisfying headway.  And once you have a firm grasp of the mechanics you'll be orchestrating Machiavellian plots that will bring massive swathes of the world under your evil (let's just face it you warmongering bastage) grasp.
If you can master the mechanics of this baby you're well on your way to being a fully qualified field marshall of strategic gaming.  I highly recommend this game to anyone just getting into Paradox's line of strategy games.  It's a far more refined product than it's successor game EU 4 is at this point.

This is not the Gauntlet you used to know.  It is not Gauntlet Legends.  Nor is it Gauntlet for the arcade.
It's something... else entirely.  It isn't enjoyable and is no longer an RPG.
It isn't even worth your time unless you're willing to sink hundreds of hours into the Call-of-Duty esque perk system that is based on achievements rather than experience.
Your character doesn't grow more powerful unless you unlock these achievements, and you don't get the 3-tiered special ability system that Gauntlet Legends had.
Not to mention that Potions now act as AMMUNITION for the "relics" that you have to buy throughout the game.  The potions that originally IN THE ARCADE VERSION that this game so egotistically proclaims that it is a callback to, no longer do a full-screen wipe of all enemies, or the awesome AoE effect of Gauntlet Legends.

While I do recommend this game, that recommendation comes prefaced with a gigantic "Your mileage may vary".
First off this game is more of a puzzle game/ walking simulator than a 3rd person hack n slash. Combat is a significant part of the game but if you're looking for button mashing, combo breaking, mook killing hack n slash, this isn't really that kind of game. The Combat system is basic but fleshed out enough to be satisfying to those who master it. You've got your standard light attack, heavy attack, and counter-attack-on-perfect block system. There's no upgrade or level ups, at certain points in the game you gain the ability to slow time as well as a charge attack but that's it. At the end of the day combat is there to punctuate the game with a sense of peril rather than provide the meat of the experience.
Most of the puzzles in the game fit into 2 broad categories: Perspective Puzzles and World Swapping. Throughout the game you will need to find runes hidden in the environment to unlock doors which bar your progress. Finding said runes usually involves looking at the environment from a certain angle so that certain objects line up to form the correct shape. This can sometimes be frustrating but the game gives you little hints by indicating when you are in the general area of the thing you need to find. Savvy players will eventually be able to intuit where the game wants them to go based on level design.
World swapping puzzles involve looking at the world through arches or portals to see a slight difference in the environment that opens the path forwards. Stepping through the arches makes this change real, allowing you to progress. Some of the more complex puzzles require you to change the world, open a short cut in the environment then change back to make use of a previously inaccessible path.
Mechanically speaking the game is not very complex and can almost be described as easy. This is not a bad thing. The crux of Hellblade is not to provide a mechanical challenge but to immerse the player in the story of Senua and her struggle with her inner demons. The game does a very good job of this with it's beautiful, haunting environments and the voices in Senua's head. All the dialogue in the game is between voices in Senuas head whether they be her own or her memories of other people and it does a very good job of setting the tone of the game.
Another reason that the game being easy is a good thing is that there is a permadeath mechanic. Senua is afllicted with black rot which creeps up her arm everytime she dies in game. If the rot reaches her head then the game is over permanently and you will have to start again. By the end of my play through the rot had spread up to her shoulder. This might be a bit of a turn off as players who fail to figure out the games more lethal puzzles may die several times simply because they didn't understand what they had to do next. The game rarely explicitly explains it's systems, often hinting at what to do next through the voices in Sensua's head.
tl;dr If you want a dark story driven walking simulator/puzzle game with a generous topping of Hack n Slash combat then this game is for you.

...is a keyboard practice adventure. Explore a world that unfolds before you as you recall memories of the past while practicing your typewriting skills.
The core goal of the game is to practice your keyboarding skills, having you type words without mistakes as fast as you can. Combat segments usually consists of waves of critters advancing to your position from all sides, each with random words above them you must type to strike, some requiring multiple words to defeat them. The more words you chain in a short time, the more experience you get from the encounter, leveling up to unlock perk points you spend on passive skills.
You expand the world by reaching Reveal locations, each requiring an increasing amount of experience to show more of the world, creating new paths or connecting islands to the main continent. There are also dungeons you can explore to collect fragments for experience, solving puzzles, and learning new powers (using fire burns enemies whose word you type, ice will freeze them, etc.), some creatures and interactive world elements can only be affected by certain powers.
It is an absolutely gorgeous game. Everything is themed around literature, from the story segments that are narrated to you as you progress through the game, to the exploration where pages of text flip open to create the land, trees and rocks. Every world object is built from origami-like art or paper mâché, same goes for the critters you encounter. This fits perfectly into the mechanics that, after all, consists of typing words.
The story is a mystery for you to discover. You’re a girl riding a fox as you recall your memory from exploring the world. You enter an area where fond or eerie segments of the story are told, either by a narrator, or from recalled voices of events from the past. You will spend the whole game not getting closure on what is happening until the end of the game where the credits conclude and reveal exactly what this whimsical adventure was about.
You can’t learn proper keyboarding technique from this, as it only gives you your finger placement once in the early game and never gets back to it. You also jump right into typing entire words, rather than gradually memorizing your keyboard a few additional keys at the time, or using any proven keyboarding learning methods from typewriting edusofts.
Narration and story won’t make sense as you play through the story mode, and may even come out as an obnoxious attempt at being artsy, you actually need to complete the game for you to make out a coherent pattern. But you’re unlikely to replay the story mode a second time to finally understand the narration, as once you’ve reached the level required to complete it, re-doing the story mode will feel too easy so you’ll limit yourself to Arena challenges if you wish to continue perfecting your keyboarding.
I liked
and am happy I played it. If you don’t want to practice keyboarding skills or don’t already know a proper keyboarding technique, this may not be for you. But if you do and are looking to practice, it is undoubtedly the most beautiful keyboarding practice game there’s ever been on the market before, and that’s where this gets my recommendation.

I'd like to start by saying that I bought this game simply because there's a person riding on the back of a giant fox.
I was a little dissapointed to learn that it was a typing game (I of course realized this before buying and stuck it on my wishlist to buy during a sale in case I wouldn't like it), and didn't really know what to expect as far as story was concerned.. I didn't want to delve into something that was too repetative or boring. Typing games are fun and all, but usually I just end up frustrated that my 45 WPM isn't good enough, and usually it's just typing with no real direction behind it.
That being said, I literally have no regrets in purchasing this game.
The graphics are unique and the story unfolds (literally, unfolds) into a deeply and eloquently written mystery. As you play through the levels, you slowly realize that this mystery is about you, as the main character... you are slowly piecing together memories of where you came from and how you ended up where you are now. While that story arch has certainly been over-used in games/movies/books, etc, the ending was delightfully fulfilling, regardless. I can't say that it tugged fully on my heartstrings, but it came awfully close.
One of my favorite things about the game is the narration. As you explore the map and unlock new areas, the unlocked scripts are narrated for you. This not only sets the mood in many instances, but it helps piece together the story of your adventures throughout the map (and your own memories). It felt a little like a fun novelty in the beginning, but by the end of the game I found myself eagerly searching small corners of the map in hopes of finding something I had missed. This feature also helps drive the game without feeling like you are being lead around by the nose (if you ever feel lost, try to follow where you think the next set of text lines will be!).
The graphics are good without being overwhelming. I actually really loved the simple origami style, in which most everything looks like folded paper. There are some areas which felt hard to navigate because certain grasses are not walkable but look like they should be (there are a few "backgound", decorational items like this as well); but overall it did not really negatively affect the gameplay. It was also fun to see the fox's gait change on surfaces such as ice, where instead of walking, he slips around. The controls were easy to understand and use, and I found no issues with any of them (I played on my laptop keyboard and mouse).
I was also fond of how the levels were set up, in that if you did things slightly backwards, it wasn't a big deal. Some areas you can only unlock after unlocking something else (you need to complete this level in order to gain an ability that lets you into the next level, etc), but for the most part it felt fairly free-roam. You can move around the map as you please, discovering new areas and/or defeating nests for experience points, which you can then spend as you'd like. This allows you to build up your character skills in whichever manner you'd prefer (you'll have enough skill points to buy out everything at the end of the game, but choosing how you want to build in the beginning may change difficulty between players). You aren't forced, at any point, to select certain abilities in order to get past a level. This made gameplay feel more natural and less lead, which I enjoyed thoroughly.
Overall, I found the game very relaxing and really wondered why they didn't put games like this into schools to encourage us to WANT to learn to type (and then remembered that I went to school oh-so long ago).
On top of most of the game being a relaxing dive into a great story, it did have some great "boss" battles, which actually had me on the edge of my seat. Some were easier than others, but most really required a great amount of focus and calm (which is difficult when your adrenaline is pumping!). The more you work yourself up, the more blunders you make while typing, the more times you are apt to fail. The trick really is to stay as calm and focused as you can to get through - and boy is it relieving when you finally do!
I think the only thing that I can really say negatively about the game is that one nest in particular is ABSOLUTELY RAGE INDUCING. I rage quit the game a few times, to say the least (and scared my boyfriend with my incessant, top of my lungs swearing). I stumbled upon the particular nest about mid-way through the game, failed a million times, and then decided that I probably needed one of the abilities I had not yet unlocked in order to defeat it. I was wrong. The new abilities really didn't do anything for me, and I finally managed to defeat it using my first two of ice and fire, primarily. Whoever decided that the word "Pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis" should be included can go suck it. I can't even read that thing in my head, let alone try to furiously type it while surrounded by a swarm of other convulutedly named insects. It was this nest in particular that played on my fears that 45 WPM would never be good enough to get me through a typing game (but I made it, so TAKE THAT!).
Overall, I highly recommend it, even though I will likely never play through a 2nd time, if only for that one nest (it seriously ruined the entire mood of the game for me and I never want to feel that level of rage again). I bought it on sale and feel like it was worth the money (40% off, I believe). Couldn't tell you if full-price would be worth it.. I suppose it would depend greatly on your taste in games. But if you like reading, typing, and a fairly laid back play style (with some short, adrenaline rush battles), this game is for you!

After some positive comments and reviews on Steam praising the game, I decided to try this game. I will try to be brief, this is an overrated game, plain and simple. Let's delve into Epistory.
The idea is to combine exploration, typing and a good story, at least that's the impression you get in the first hour of the game. The problem lies that all the promise shown in those first stages quickly evaporates. The typing mechanic is just a gimmick, as such you will find typing the same words over and over and over again for hours. The developers try to spice things up with a series of powerups which don't solve the core problem, you will get bored quickly typing the same words. The core mechanic of the game is simply boring. But that's not the only flaw of the game, the exploration is simple and not rewarding at all, I mean what is the point of looking for chests when the only reward you will get is an image? That's the reward they offer you for exploring the map, EXP points and a portion of an image. After a while you just don't care about those chests. The only thing left is the story, at first it seems like an interesting proposition, soon you will dismay in front of such a bland and dull tale. Besides, it has a very bad ending which doesn't offer the player value for his/her time.
If you are asking yourself why this game has so many good reviews, your guess is as good as mine, I suppose some people really liked the art style but apart from that the rest is average at best. There are better options on Steam.

TL;DR:
If you are wanting an okay typing game, buy Epistory
If you are wanting a game that transcends the genre, look elsewhere.
I enjoyed my time with this game, although I do not think that it deserves the lofty praise that Steam's review structure affords it. There is more good than bad, though the good is more middling than excellent, and the bad is perhaps more personally felt than indicitive of the games appeal. The art direction is its strongpoint, the exploration, collectability, and discovery is enough to create a half-decent hook, and the music is pretty well done. However, while typing is its focus, the gameplay doesn't capture the rythmic movements of typing itself, and while promising a more involved story-driven game, it does not deliver.
First, the typing. It is a strange complaint, I know, but I do believe the control scheme could have been better implemented. When typing a sentence, you rely on the space-bar to string together words. In Epistory, the space-bar initiates typing but it also ceases it. This creates a disconnect with how you type normally and how you type within the world the game has created. This nitpick of mine is just that - a nitpick. But it is the difference of the gameplay feeling natural and familiar rather than stuttered and almost-familiar. For a long while I could not understand why I struggled with reaching my natural typing speed in-game (45WPM vs. 35WPM) and why stringing combos together was more difficult than it should be. If this input had instead been the Enter key, with each new word needing the space-bar to begin, I think it would have resulted in a more free flowing and enjoyable game.
Why Epistory initially appealed to me was through its unique gameplay, art style, and the promise of a narrative that would engage. It is not an engaging story. The narrators vague ruminations were never able to burrow itself deep enough within me to care about what the game was trying to say. I started the game actively trying to piece together what had happened and why, though I quickly gave up on this. Epistory does a poor job of holding the players attention, telling the story in loose, generalised statements rather than with something poetic. We are told early on that something has happened, with the main character struggling to remember what, but the hints offered after are just variations on this first mystery. The environment gives clues but nothing relevatory, no inspired ending - in fact, no story to speak of, just a plot point that sadly does nothing except give the false impression of motivation. I'm all for sparse, emotive storytelling, but Epistory does this in the most forgettable way.
Halfway through I gave up on the story as I did not care, instead enjoying it for what it is - an okay exploration-based typing game. But for a typing game, this seems to be enough to garner what seems to be universal praise. Had the story and the gameplay meshed in a more satisfying way instead of an easy-to-ignore telling of a half-baked premise, it would have been easier to recommend. Instead, the game doesn't offer much more than typing words in an aesthetically pleasing manner. It commits what I think is the cardinal sin of gaming - it becomes boring.
I do recommend it to people that want a decent typing game - it is that. But it is not as good as what the Steam reviews indicate. There is enough here to warrant a purchase if what I have said hasn't put you off, but considering what it could have been, Epistory was a disappointment to me.

What's there not to like?

I know that, like me, many of you may be wondering if you really want to pay $30+ for a visual novel.  Luckily, with Nameless, your incredibly emotional experience will be worth every penny.
It took me 22 hours to get all of the endings (using a spoiler-free guide - if not, it would take a lot longer, of course): there are 5 main pursuable characters, each with one good ending and 3-5 bad endings, plus a secret route.  Unlike many visual novels, each character's route has a wealth of unique content, so you are not just playing the exact same thing over and over again to get one or two extra scenes.
I also found it to be one of the best-written games I have ever played --  I genuinely laughed and cried at the appropriate times.  Although many of the characters initially appear to conform to VN tropes, the game will consistently surprise you by revealing hidden depths to the characters and by tying their backstories very well into their personalities.  The voice acting is absolutely top-notch -- I don't understand a word of Korean, but I could still feel the emotion in each line.  The art is also pretty gorgeous, especially compared to some of the incredibly hideous stuff that has somehow made its way to Steam.
For those of you who played Dandelion (Cheritz's other Steam release), Nameless does away with all of the stat-raising from that game but still manages to be a similar length, meaning there is (I think) a lot more dialogue and actual story content in this one.  As I mentioned above, I found these characters to be generally more interesting than the ones in that game, and each route has more unique content, so playing through all of the routes doesn't feel like a slog at all.  Basically, if you enjoyed Dandelion, pick this up without a second thought.  If you didn't enjoy it, though, you may still end up loving Nameless.
In short: I, too, held off on buying this game for a while due to the price point, but I am ever-so-glad that I finally got it.  Totally worth the money.

Edited version of the review:
For some reason this game is among favorites for many visual novels fans. Why is that so, I have no idea, since "Nameless" has almost all problems that "Dandelion" had with little improvement in terms of story (basically tiring and pointless stat-raising is gone, hurray!), and much more unpolished overall feeling.
I tried to finish every route, I gave up after fourth one and I didn't feel like I've missed anything important. The concept is very similar to "Dandelion". If you like dating your pets, maybe you will like dating dolls too. Good luck, enjoy, oh and backstory is also, almost the same, with extra "dramatic" character from protagonist's past.
And no stat-raising here, so it's actually all story. Bland, boring and not interesting, but story nonetheless.
Gallery, diary, phone, that seems pretty pointless most of the time, but it's there.
Once again, it's not fitting what's going on and it adds absolutely nothing to the atmosphere.
This is a pricey game, that almost never have any discount, yet there is so little going on in terms of graphic. Sure, it looks great, but CGs seems lacking, there are few scenes when it was obvious that CG was intended to be there, but apparently ended up not being created.
Low resolution. Don't even get me started. Unless your game is an old-time classic, there is absolutely no justification for 20$+ price tag with this quality. This is outrageous. Whether you like the story or not is always a subjective thing, but this sort of practice is a pure laziness. Add bugs to that and you'll come to the conclusion that there are many better games out there for much lower price.
Yupp. Player's name isn't always showing correctly, for example, issues with phone, and so on.
It's Dandelion 2.0, just without stat raising and with dolls.
You have your flirty type, your caring guy that
, you have your energetic eats-a-lot character, your cold but with golden heart and your child-looking one. Nothing I haven't seen. And as much as some aspects of their routes were touching, again, it's nothing I haven't seen or expect.
She's a victim. Again. Because her grandfather died, which is tragic and I know that very well, but she really isn't the most suffering girl in the entire world and this game paints her that way.
Besides the thing I will mention right below, there is way too much drama regarding protagonist and her constant being a victim and when you don't buy that and you don't get attached to her, it gets pretty much meaningless. There are no stakes really.
. Dramatic tension is gone, when this game tries to introduce a little bit of humor. Mixing humor with drama can have great effect or can be poor and ruin the mood. In "Nameless" it's the second thing. Humor it typically absurd and anime-ish. I don't remember smiling even once.
Wait. How did I end up with this weird love triangle? Or as this... doll-slave? How did that happen? How is that possible? When we established that this may happen to me or at least hinted at it? Are those purely for shock-value? Because they don't make any sense.

The sequel to Dandelion, Nameless, is a big step up. No more boring, dull point farming. This time the other characters are still part of the story and you get to see them after you’ve chosen which boy to pursue. Unfortunately, it’s still not exactly the dating sim I was looking for. You make choices, sure, but those choices don’t really give depth. They don’t give your character personality that might appeal more to one boy and repel the other. It’s either you make the right or wrong choice. That’s it. I really wish there was a sim dating game where there was no “pursuing”, but rather you grow your character’s personality by making choices the others characters in the game can choose you just as much as you can grow fond of them. Kinda similar-ish to the game Cinders.
All in all, great game and I totally recommend it. The characters are complex and it’s just a whole lot of fun, but it could have been better for me.

"Charming" is probably the single best word to describe this side-scrolling puzzle-platformer. Attractive graphics and a great soundtrack highlight a strong physics system that makes the way you solve its puzzles the focus, rather than the solutions themselves. Fans of super hard platformers a la Meat Boy and those hoping for extremely complex puzzle elements will likely be disappointed with the relatively low level of difficulty. The lack of combat depth and variety of enemies are the game's weakest points, but it knows its limits and doesn't spend too much time on either. If you're looking for a responsive game that allows you to utilize your own creativity in solving its puzzles, this is a must buy.

A relaxing, engaging adventure game where you type words to interact with the world, whether it be regrowing trees, destroying blockades, unveiling lost memories, rebuilding bridges or fending off waves of monsters will magical spells while atop a giant fox.
The layout of the world and all of its puzzles are intuitive. You may get the feeling of being lost but end up exactly where you need to be before you know it. Puzzles have a similar air to them: you're always learning them at a comfortable pace. Its never confusing and obscure. The concept can be clearly deciphered.
Much like the world, the combat and mechanics are also intuitive - not just because everything involves typing either. As you progress, they will gradually introduce you to new mechanics without completely spelling out every little detail for you - they will not baby you. However, you will still learn everything you need to know organically - through play. They strike the balance well.
Its difficulty is not punishing. It is casual and relax but still engaging/challenging. In fact, its difficulty scales with how well you play. Every decision in a battle can be a strategic one. The different spells and settings will demand that you learn its mechanics and execute appropriately, if you wish to succeed, which is done in a fair manner.
This game's mood is not epic or grand. The journey is calm, for the most part, though for the younger crowd, those afraid of insects and those afraid of the dark, it can be unsettling at times (in a good way). Its music is dynamic; ever-changing to fit the scenario you fall into. Whether it be exploring a new landscape, making closer and closer steps toward solving a puzzle or getting swarmed by gigantic bugs and horrors.
All the while, throughout your entire journey, your story will be narrated. Speaking of which, the voice acting is also good. It will never take you out of the moment - what it will do is pull you deeper into the world.
If you still aren't sure, do remember that they have a demo available.

I've been playing for maybe 45 minutes and here are my first reactions-
-A ton of potential! I feel isolated, bewildered and hopeless.

-Some items are just too obviously unavailable. I now have 3 water bottles, some arrows and a match book after drinking a water bottle and eating a power bar. The point - I felt jazzed to pick up the arrows; I would feel better if I could have stabbed that wolf in the eye with one instead of escaping! I know you're going to do it but I think a huge part of making your game solid before you enhance graphics, stabilize everything and create a "feeling / story" will be creating a feeling of driven interaction; every item is exciting because each has the possibility of extending my life in your game. n environment with distinctive characteristics is something that would make this game explode!

Going into this, I expected it to be another typing game with a formula similar to "The Typing of the Dead." But no. This game is a unique breed that is an absolute masterpiece.
Epistory follows an unnamed female protagonist who rides around on her steed (a giant fox). As you walk around, you get narration of what is going on in the girl's head. In order to make progress (defeating enemies, removing obstacles), you must type the words shown on the screen. The game has a "free" mode (where you can walk around), but you can quickly switch to "battle" mode (typing) with the touch of the space bar. It balances adventuring and battling really well, in a fun but marginally stressful way. This game will most likely take you anywhere from 5-8 hours to complete, and features a mix of easy and challenging achievements, as well as a beautiful card set.

Update 1.2 and 1.1 + 40% sale (35,- eur) was the reason why I bought this game.
I had no experience with it before and I avoided the hype and hate around.
The game is worth 20 euros. 30+ is still much.
Here is my experience which I have right now with the game and with Steam:
- Basebuilding part (patch 1.1) comes into normal gameplay after around 5-10 hours. Basically, you cannot test this feature within 2 hours. I.e. you cannot refund on Steam. I was asking for refund after 10 hours (and 7 days) (my first refund) - REJECTED. Well done. Steam is platform for awkward indie games, support for anything more complex is limited. Embarrassing.
- Basebuilding again - After you build a base you should move to next sector towards galaxy center. Weird? Yes it is. Why to stick to one place when I need to go forward ? Nonsense. Moreover, when you build new base on next place, previous base is cancelled, and all refinement you bought is lost, except some material. Yes, it is fun to build the base, but after 30 minutes the point is lost.
- The content is locked in the beginning. You explore abandoned base or space station, but the doors are locked by access key lvl 1,2,3... It feels very unnatural. Like RPG element, but the game is not RPG. It doesn't fit here.
- Crafting is good element for survival games. This game is not survival and the crafting is not done very well. You need to gather resource A. Then create a thing B, add another thing and craft C, add another thing and craft D, and finally craft product E which you need for hyper-jump. Confusing in the beginning, boring afterwards.
- Confusing is also inventory. You have space ship inventory and personal (suit) inventory, both are very limited. It gets full on 1st or 2nd planet. Since then you are always looking into inventory what to purge, but you don't know what thing is important, what to keep and what not. Just pick some trash at random. You can't drop it, you can't store it somewhere else, you have to delete it.
- You cannot craft, buy and usually talk with full inventory. Next ship with 3 more space costs around 300.000 of something. The best ship around 10-40 milions of something. It will be long way to the galanxy center...
- Aliens, common 2 types. Frogs and Lizzards. No movement, just sitting / standing. Stup1d.
- The nice thing is sunset / sunrise on different planets.
The conclusion :
No Man's Sky is something between walking simulator and a game. Barely something can kill you, but the game is not about that. Well, I don't know what is it about after ~20 hours of gameplay :) Main objective is to move towards galaxy center. I feel like someone stole my money.
No Man's Sky (+patch 1.2) - 4/10

I almost never feel compelled to post reviews of video games, but after spending over eight hours in the bleak, disturbed, often hauntingly beautiful landscape of Senua's mind, I can say that Ninja Theory has something special on their hands. Hellblade is totally unlike any other game I've ever played. It has a little bit of fluid but fairly simple combat, a little environmental puzzle solving, a little walking sim through the pantheon of Norse mythology, but it's mostly an intense and emotionally taxing journey with a grieving Celtic warrior on a psychotic break. It's obvious to me that the minds at Ninja Theory had a compelling story they wanted to tell, and that spark of inspiration pervades every single aspect of the game -- from its well-balanced themes of loss and sacrifice, clever use of Nordic lore and gameplay mechanics to immerse the player in Senua's own reality, to a stunningly intimate performance of the main character herself.
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is a harrowing experience that I'm not sure I'll ever want to relive, but I'm grateful that games as gorgeous and strange as this can now boast visuals and production values rivaling even mainstream AAA releases. This is a title I'll be thinking about for a very long time.

This game is well worth the money. It is less a video game and more an interactive movie. If other developers followed this games formula of short yet high quality gameplay the gaming industry as a whole would benefit from it. Hellblade does few things wrong but story telling and immerstion is not two of them.
Pros: high quality story telling, combat, lore, overall game feel and, story resolution.
Cons: Game Camera and mouse speed. (make sure to have a beefy GPU because running it at ultra is the ONLY way to play Hellblade)

I will start with the bad (and I found very little to place in this category).  The combat feels like an afterthought; something added to increase tension and turn what would otherwise be a fantastic piece of interactive media into a game.  I did encounter a few glitches; a ladder that did not transition out of climbing at the correct time (leaving me hanging in mid-air until I climbed back down and tried again), a rune/story stone that would not play the appropriate voice-over until I restarted the game, and some minor fps loss (particularly towards the end of the game, but always above 30fps).
Then there is the good:  The sound quality and  music easily hold their own with any AAA title.  The graphics are generally stunning, perhaps a little bleak at times, but stunning anyway.  The controls are typically tight and responsive enough for a story driven adventure game.  The story line is relatively unique to the gaming setting.
Finally we come to the outstanding: The acting and voicework are near peerless in this medium.  I can only hope that other (larger?) developers take notice of this and someday put the same effort and care into their own production.   Hellblade also delivers an environment and atmosphere often limited to large budget Hollywood productions.  This relies heavily on the sound production, voicework and excellent graphic design.
I spent most of the roughly seven hours on my first playthrough with a brooding sense of dread.  I cared what happened to the character and felt the pain and failure when something didn't work out well (whether though my error or story driven).
I went into this game knowing very little about it.  I did not follow it's development and expected very little from it.  I ended up with one of the most unique and touching (sometimes disturbing) gaming experiences that I have ever had.  I would not recommend this game to anyone looking for an action or hack'n'slah fueled rampage.  I would very strongly recommend the game to anyone looking for an incredible story, some simple but intelligent puzzles or a new gaming experience that doesn't quite have any comparison.
If you meet any of those criteria, then I would say that Hellblade is worth every penny.

Imagine Plants vs. Zombies. You're placing down your peashooters and shooting up those zombies, popping their heads off. Great tower defence game, right? Probably your favorite; it's a lot of peoples favorites. Really good game.
Now, let me explain. Bloons Tower Defence is a long running franchise of flash games where you have a large variety of towers, and you put them down and pop balloons. But this isn't a left to right tower defence. It's full-screen. Each tower has it's own uses, each upgrade for each tower changes how you use it and the way it works. If you want to go on one path, there's a strategy behind it. There's a time and place for everything, and it's really fun training yourself and finding out ways to use every tower and every upgrade path. The maps are great, the modes are fantastics and essentially unlimited; there's just SO MUCH STUFF! I can't possibly fit it all in one paragraph! So let me give you the fast version.
-Wide variety of towers, each with 8 unique upgrades for each one.
-Wonderful map selection which is getting upgraded constantly
-NO IN-APP PURCHASES THAT MAKE THE GAME PAY TO WIN! (I don't see Plants versus Zombies 2 doing that.)
-A lot of modes that are much more than one-off things that you'll never play more than twice.
-Easy to learn, but hard to master. This game is something you can pick up super easily.
-STRATEGY. This game is incredibly complex, and each and everything has ways to use it. You only need to tinker with it long enough and find out what works for you, when, and where.
-Consistently updated
-Great learning curve, and difficulity curve as you progress through rounds
-Money is dispersed well (so you can buy towers and etc).
-The constant bloon popping can get ear-grating at times, but this can be fixed with a simple button pressed.
-Money is not dispersed very well in Co-Op mode. Doesn't make it any less fun, you just need banana farms.
-Susceptible to lagging. The engine is decent. It's not perfect at all.
-It is still a timewaster. It's not meant for incredibly long play sessions.
Such minors cons as opposed to all those pros? You really cannot go wrong with this game. Sure it has a pricetag, but it's a pricetag that every self-respecting tower defense lover needs to get! And even if you don't like tower defense, still get it. This game is a masterpiece, the essential TD game. Plus, there's a new one coming out 2018, so you probably should catch up on it.

Gauntlet (Slayer edition) is a modern remake of the classic hack and slash game many people played in arcades and home systems. Besides being 3d, characters now have gear and special abilities that can be purchased with the gold you find in each dungeon. There are also boss fights and “death” makes a return as a nag character in several levels.
Multiplayer is pretty much the reason to own this game and they managed to carry forward the absolutely ruthless competition from the original. You will be sprinting to steal gold and deny food to other players all the while prioritizing your own survival as Gauntlet is more of a competitive co-op game than a friendly one. It’s kind of like playing Monopoly where all your friends end up hating each other by the end of the game.
The game itself is pretty short and can be completed on normal difficulty in less than 5 hours, leaving the only reason for playing it further to grind for gold to buy all the abilities and cosmetic items. Most useful abilities are very, very expensive which means that during a single playthrough you will be stuck only using a few of them. The dungeons are randomly generated, though, meaning there is at least some replayability to be found. I recommend waiting until the game drops back to it's sale price of around $5 to really get your money's worth.
