The Lady: A Strange Kind Of Love
The Lady is an interesting interactive art project and a game that explores several mental and emotional issues, told through the eyes of the main protagonist, simply called the Lady. It is confusing, obtuse, aggravating, repulsive and bizarre experience that solely uses metaphor to ask questions to the person who is playing this game. These questions are entirely subjective and free to interpretation, but might include thoughts of depression, anxiety, sexual repression and identity, BIID and body dysmorphia and more. The Lady is not a game for everyone as it asks some fairly uncomfortable questions.
Just as it contains muddled and confusing story, The Lady also has action segments and gameplay that also feels as equally as muddled and confusing. It is imprecise and detracts somewhat from the entire experience since it's not that well implemented. Even though there is no music in the game, it more than recompenses with atmospheric sound effects filled with terror and shock, just as visuals do.
Would I recommend this game? Barely... Its price is low enough, but the biggest issue is that in effort to dissect very unpleasant and relevant themes, it dares not plunge deeper into their core. Ideas in the game are explored superficially, thus The Lady provides a short, restrained and sedated experience. Simply put, The Lady tries to tackle some very serious issues, but it does so in an inelegant and dull way. Their creators are however onto something interesting, they just need to approach more bravely and boldly when designing their next game.

The Lady is a really unique and entertaining game. The gameplay is a bit confusing at first but after finding out the controls and learning how things work it becomes a great game that is a bit creepy but a lot of fun. The Lady is... odd, to say the least. In some ways, it throws back to the games of yore, throwing you right into the thick of things without explaining much of anything, and leaving you to figure things out. It also eventually finds its way to vertical shooter "boss" battles, to that effect. Its eerie art style and unique soundtrack seem specifically designed to put the player on edge, which works well enough.
Complaints about the gameplay seem to abound, but while figuring out the timing for certain things takes a certain amount of trial and error, it wasn't overly frustrating. Margin of error was also pretty narrow for some of the combat, but once I recognized the patterns you need to watch out for, it was less frustrating.
The game's narrative seems rather thin and/or muddled, but in some respects, I rather liked that aspect of it. Rather than laying down a clear story, The Lady leaves more than enough room for the player's imagination to run with things. My main takeaway is that the titular Lady was struggling with some personal issue; whether it's body image, her past, depression, or whatever else is up to you. To be fair, she could also have some issue with other women. Like I said, a lot of room to think about things, since nothing's all that clearly laid out.
When all's said and done, The Lady isn't exactly something that's going to change your world, but it was fun enough, and definitely found a little nook in my mind to occupy after I was done, making me wonder what things were all about. I'd say give it a chance.

Skullgirls is a 2D fighting game that is solid for beginners and veterans of fighting games alike. It's a great starting point if you want to learn how to play 2D fighters. The tutorials in Skullgirls are probably one of the best of any fighting game; it teaches you the fundamentals in a simple manner. Gameplay is pretty standard like most fighting games; you have arcade mode, story mode, local and online versus mode. Online is pretty smooth; even against people with 200+ ping, GGPO makes it tolerable. One feature to note is a combo breaker; if a combo extends too long, you can burst out of it. Graphics aren't exactly top notch, but the visuals are great. Backgrounds are detailed and the characters are well drawn. The soundtrack matches the theme, and one of the composers, Michiru Yamane, is notable for having worked on Castlevania games before.
Overall, not a bad game, and it's fairly cheap at US$15(non-sale price). If you happen to get it during a sale, get the DLC characters to expand your playable roster. Keyboard is not recommended, I suggest using a gamepad or arcade stick.
NOTE: You can fight against people who have the DLC characters; you're just locked out from playing them yourself.
Summary:
+ Tutorials are great, teaches you how to play
+ Visually pleasing, but nothing spectacular
+ Soundtrack is appropriate and enjoyable
+ Most cases, no major issues with online multiplayer
= Gameplay is pretty standard for a fighting game; not a bad thing
= When not on sale; the game with all the DLC characters costs around US$30
= As with most fighting games, keyboard is unsuitable; play using a gamepad or fight stick

Assassin's Creed Chronicles is a spin off series of Assassin's Creed (who would've guessed?) that uses the aspect of "2.5D" combined with stealth. This is obviously very different than the original series which uses 3D based worlds. Assassin's Creed Chronicles: China is part of the spin off series set in early china (Ming Dynasty ~1500's).
Just like the original games, the story is based on parts of real history of the Ming Dynasty but different than the original game because it is also based on the past history of the previous Assassin's Creed games. You play as Shao Jun(main female protagonist) who had been taught by Ezio Auditore da Firenze(sound familiar?)
But of course the best part of this game and the whole reason you should get it is because of the concept of 2.5D stealth that his game implemented. It is a very innovative concept that really has not been used by many games and really should be used more.
Another great point in this game is the art style. It is very traditional as it models paintings from old Chinese empires and really brings out beautiful visuals.
The creators of this game also made Shao Jun into a very interesting character having started from nothing as a concubine to becoming one of the coolest assassin's in China. (who can deny that awesome looking red cape she wears?)
Now the biggest problem in this game is the controls. I wouldn't be complaining about this if it was possible to change the controls in the settings, but that is not possible. The controls are not balanced between the right and left hands - the left hand has a lot more buttons to press than the right. And this is especially frustrating on the escaping sequences/levels that are in the game where you have to run(hold shift) while using the WASD keys to move around, as well as jumping(space) and ducking(left control) and killing guards as you do all this parkour (right/left mouse buttons). As you can tell, there is definitely some inbalances here in controls.
Other than that, this game is amazing and beautifully done. The price for this game is a good price and is definitely worth it. And yes there definitely needs to be a full scale Assassin's creed game done in China.

As a fan of space exploration/trading games in general (such as Elite, Freelancer etc.) I find a lot to like in No Man's Sky. However, the gameplay can become limited after a while, particularly since NMS has more in common with Rogue than other space-based games. That said, the updates to NMS, especially the most recent one (Pathfinder update, 1.22 at time of writing) gives me a lot of hope for the future. These are solid updates which expand the base game.
Since the latest update, the PC version suffers somewhat from hard crashes where the game freezes and must be closed. These appear to be pretty random, with neither time spent running the game nor any particular activity (planet exploration, space combat) seeming to cause crashes more often.
In short: If you want a Rogue-like, "lite" exploration game (I play a lot with my seven year-old son) then NMS is enjoyable now and I have confidence it'll get better in the future. If you're looking for something meatier, or more "hard" sci-fi, I'd suggest EVE, Elite Dangerous etc.

If you're looking for the originally advertised game, it's not there - yet. But if you're looking for a fun exploration game, this one is for you.
I love it.

Somehow I have managed to clock more than 600 hours into this game. Does this make me biased?
You would tend say it does, but instead I'd like to think it made me more critical of what the game is, and isn't.
For an exploration game, I'd say it is without a doubt the biggest game I have ever played regarding playing field. It's full of planets and moons which you can explore to your hearts' content, but space is depressingly empty. Once you've seen one asteroid field, you've seen them all.
The adding of freighters in the Foundation patch livened it up a bit, but the game could definitely use some more anomalies, rogue star bases, system wars and space battles.
Planets and moons are awesome. Graphics wise this game can be mind stunningly beautiful. And if you're like me, someone who could just wander around enjoying sights and views, you're in for a great time.
However, play long enough and you'll start to see the same trees, rocks, and even similar creatures, wherever you go. Play a while longer and you'll start wishing they'd add more parts, and be more giving regarding size limitations, and density.
Underground planet exploration is disappointing, you can explore caves upon caves, which are richly generated by the game, but you won't find anything worthwhile in them.
Storylines, quests, npc interactions, are nice, but at one point the storyline becomes a somewhat semi-tedious journey, the quests run dry, and the npc interactions are recycled. There are no repeating quests or jobs with rewards worth spending time on.
The Path Finder patch added one repeating quest which will yield you some credits, but when you're at the point where you can do it you could just shoot a few creatures, create some products, and end up with a bigger monetary reward.
So why you might ask have I given this game a thumbs up, and why did I spend so much time playing it?
Everything is procedural, and I love it. It's a game where you can go and do anything you'd like to do when you want do do it, as long as it's within the game's limitations of course.
I am unsure what to expect from Sean Murray and his team in the future. I do not regret buying this game for the full price, but I did need a long break before the first patch as I was just burned out on the lack of depth and content.
Recent patches made things better, and if they keep this up, I'll definitely keep playing.
Take it for what it is. A time waster.

I pre-ordered this game and have had the luxury of experiencing it evolve over the past year. With the recent release of 1.3 it could be argued this is a different game entirely from what we had at release. I managed to sink about 80 hours into the release version of NMS although much of the game felt aimless and repetitive. The only thing that really kept me going was my appreciation for the technology behind the game (there are some great videos about it on the GDC YouTube channel if you're interested) and the amazing mod community (I honestly don't know if the game would be what it is today if it weren't for you guys. In many ways you showed Hello Games what we wanted out of NMS). The Foundation and Pathfinder updates vastly improved the game but it was never really enough to get me invested in it again. However 1.3 has made NMS my dream game. Every planet looks gorgeous and the new art direction (photo-realism) gives an entirely different atmosphere. Every planet is interesting and most feel unique. The story is incredible (props to the writers at Hello Games) and the fact that they could somehow weave such an interesting story into a procedurally generated universe is mind-blowing. The missions, portal glyphs, economy, and guilds give this game a purpose which it was lacking upon release. I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a near infinite survival game.
My only recommendation to Hello Games would be to build a tool that enables players to create and share their own stories/missions. You guys have created an amazing framework all it needed was more content. Opening that to the community would likely allow for some very interesting possibilities. Also the addition of the "Ambient Gamemode" would be much appreciated ;)
Thank you Hello Games for continuing to develop NMS. While I was certainly disappointed at release, I never lost faith in you guys and I'm glad to see what the game has become. I have so much respect for everyone at Hello Games. You stuck by a game that had received perhaps the worst public reaction to a large scale release I have ever seen. While many developers would have ditched the game and moved onto their next project you stuck by it. Please continue to develop NMS. This patch has made it quickly become one of my favourite games of all time. You guys have something truly unique on your hands and I'm excited for what the future holds.

Absolutely beautiful game - and a great example of show (not tell) storytelling. Amazingly satisfying when you complete it, but also decently hard (I'm bad at platformers, and I made it in ~10 hours). The characters are lovable, the music is AMAZING, and everything is just stunning.

Definitely one of my personal top games of 2015, and definitely the most aesthetically pleasing Metroidvania-style platformer I've ever played. The art direction, character design, animation, and musical score were excellent, able to be both serene and menacing when the scene called for them to be.
Every frame was a painting in itself, and it perfectly captured the feel and sense of lonely melancholy the story presented, providing the most immersive experience possible.
The gameplay, without a doubt, was terrifyingly brutal, even for a platformer. This is the kind of game even experts would get frustrated about, and yes, expect to die A LOT in this game.
I personally ended it with a whooping 547 deaths on my first run!
Don't be fooled by its fantasy/Ghibli-esque environments, this game has the most merciless of difficulty spikes you'll ever find in platformers, requiring quick reflexes, pinpoint accuracy, and the overwhelming urge to ragequit. But somehow, despite all that, you manage to prevent yourself from ragequitting, simply because the aesthetic, the story, and even the challenge and promise of a well-deserved victory all keep you going.
This doesn't mean there aren't any flaws.
I think most critics' biggest complaint is the fact that Ori himself is so small, and can sometimes be lost in all the gorgeous background around him, leading to really annoying segments when you just want to get through an area, but you can't find your own character. Another would be the downright useless lifebar. While it does defend well against weaker enemies, expect to die in a hit or two from several others, not to mention the obstacles and terrain you come across. Everything is a potential deathtrap, making it a very trial-and-error type of game (hence the multiple deaths). The good thing is, they managed to pull off a very smart system on how players can save their game and start over, aka the Soul Link, which allows players to save anywhere they want provided they have the MP for it.
This, on the other hand, does up the challenge as well, since there are certain areas in the game which, upon completion, cannot be revisited thus losing the chance to get some much needed upgrades for Ori.
While I hear they'll be fixing this issue as well as several others in the upcoming "Definitive" edition in 2016, Ori and the Blind Forest was still an amazing experience as it is.
Nowhere else will you find a modern platformer that defines the term "NES Hard".

Ori and the Blind Forest is your standard affair of side scrolling action that can be found on steam, it  just so happens to be very very pretty. As Ori you clammer through maze-like environments with tight controls, avoid enemies (or fight them), and use new abilities to traverse the world. You also find shiny things of varying importance which can appeal to the hoarder kind of player mixed with a hefty lump of rote memory button checks.
Ori's main schtick, besides being very very pretty, is that you can save anywhere. As long as it happens to be on flat ground, not during a boss fight, not near enemies, not during a button check procedures, and you have enough resources. In others word save states with asterisks. Nothing to write home about, but an idea I don't see pop up too often.
When you're not playing cram school with your button checks, Ori and the Blind Forest is of medium difficulty. Most areas have tricky jumps and trigger fast use of abilities. But nothing makes you stop and think or use abilities in novel ways- its just a lazy follow the pattern or die play through. Makes me wonder why there is health at all- as taking multiple hits rarely comes into play. Players who have enjoyed a ton of sidescrollers will find nothing new, find the not-so-secret secrets, and breeze through the puzzle. New players will be treated to 30 odd years of culminated but standard side scrolling know-how.
Ori and Blind Forest is conflicted when it comes to play and aesthetic. Unless you force yourself to slowdown, you may completely miss the beauty of the game- which I believe to be THE selling point of the game. Ori has stunning artwork. I know I've repeated myself many times, but its an absolute treat for the eyes. Sometimes, its kind of downer that the game is so focused on dashing, jumping, and ricocheting through the stages that you never have a chance to absorb where you are. In some sense, I felt like the game may of benefited from a simpler aesthetic. Its got a “run through this stage quickly” feel with a “stay awhile and gawk” look.
Ori and the Blind Forest has a paper thin narrative. Ori does all this running, jumping, and murdering because “nature is dieing because a magic shiny thing was stolen”. Ori just so happens to be lost portion of a big tree's life-substaining magic, and without Ori the forest just doesn't work. The story isn't important, its all about the game play. Beyond the intro and the ending, there are no tender or beautiful moments you might expect from the trailer. You can take the levels, characters, abilities and give them a new coat of paint and it would be all the same. This is perhaps Ori and Blind Forest's biggest downfall- it looks unique but plays generic. If being a forest spirit is pretty darn special, then develop a game to play to that experience. Make me feel like I'm a glowy forest spirit, not an accessory robot with homing lasers, jet boots, and an upgrade kit.
Ori may be nothing new, but it has what you expect from a sidescroller for 20 USD. Its average in my book. Younger players or players new to sidescrollers will have a solid entry into the genre. If you want a lighter exploration experience of the Metroid series mixed with Volgarr the Viking or Super Meat Boy memory-based gameplay, you'll find Ori and the Blind Forest to be an addition to your collection or at least a decent hold-over game until the next big side scrolling adventure comes along. If you're like me and have an absolute need for new, fun, challenging, or innovative sidescrollers, Ori and Blind Forest is unsatisfying because you've played it all before.

This review is for the game ''Trine'',a side-scrolling action platform and puzzle video game,developed by the video game company ''Frozenbyte'' and published by Nobilis(wordwide).It was released in July 3,2009 for Microsoft Windows and since then the game has been released for the PlayStation Network,Mac OS X and for Linux as well.Trine uses the Proprietary engine.
Plot
Trine takes place in a magical but destroyed kingdom.After a brief period of peace,the king died without leaving any heir.So the kingdom descented to anarchy.During this political instability an undead army appears and attacks the kingdom destroying everything that's on its path.
After some time three heroes,unkown to each other,reach the Astral Academy,a magical institution,where they touch a magical object,later said to be the Trine,and their souls bind together.After that incident they search for a way to free themselves of that peculiar effect.The trio must eventually undergoe  an adventure searching for three artifacts that once reunited they could be free.Apparently the Trine is the artifact of souls and without it the other two(the artifact of the body and the artifact of the mind) created the undead making them responsible for all the chaos that polutes the kingdom.
After finding them they face a last ultimate challenge where they combine the Trine with the two lost artifacts,unbinding their souls forever.The game ends with the storyteller informing us that the kingdom has been cleansed from the undead and the three proclaiming it as its heroes.
Characters
You take control of Zoya,the thief,Amadeus,the wizard,and Pontius,the knight.Each of them has special abilities.Zoya is the stealthy one of the group and uses her bow and arrow,making her an exceptional marksman.Amadeus uses the power of magic,allowing him to conjur objects(planks,cubes,pyramids) helping the team to overcome obstacles and reach remote areas with great ease.Last but not least Pontius uses his sword,shield and sledgehammer with great force,making him the group's main damage dealer.The player is supposed to combine the group's power together in order to accomplish difficult stunts and unlock the group's true prowess.
Recap
Incredible game,breathtaking graphics,with exceptional yet simple plot.Enjoyed every bit of it and i definetely recommend it.

A touching, story driven adventure where an old man’s dream is set to come true by going through his memories. This is a non-combat classic styled RPG.
Okay, hold on a sec here. This is a classic styled RPG and therefore it will have “bad” graphics as you might say…and I do say that myself too. For a game that came out in 2011, the graphics are not its strongest point. But I don’t think it would bother you in any way as a game is not always defined by how it looks.
Executed with excellence and a must play for story heavy players. It is absolutely beautiful, unique and astonishing. It made me cry so bad. If that doesn’t sound convincing, I don’t know what is…
All and perfected. The music has been perfectly synced to match each and every scenario the game had to offer. They just sound beautiful to my ears.
I haven’t played many classic styled RPG games so I had to get used to how the game works; and I managed to do so very quickly. I however, did not really like how the character moved in a very ‘square’ like direction, it felt a little out of immersion for me. But it still presented itself in a way in which it wouldn’t be too confusing to understand and it was fine going from there. Nonetheless, the gameplay was very smooth throughout the entire game; I mean it’s not like you need a beefy setup to run the game anyways. Any old computer can probably run this with no issues.
With under 5 hours of total completion time, it’s a relatively short game; and for the price of £6.99, it’s worth getting. You might as well spend some extra cash to get the DLCs as they are short additions to the main game and you can also get the awesome soundtrack and the comic.

Pros:
If you were a fan of Diablo 2, but were disappointed by Diablo 3 because of its lack of stat distribution, its straightforward skill system and its auction house, and were a bit put off by the cartoony art style of Torchlight (it doesn't really fit this genre in my opinion), then you will enjoy Van Helsing, because the mechanics are pretty close to Diablo 2.
Cons:
Once you complete the game, you realize there is no variety in it, and no replay value. There are only 2 types of melee weapons and 2 types of ranged weapons (fast & slow), and the skills are pretty boring and not really apparent, you basically use mana and rage to make your attacks more powerful, and that's about it. At the beginning of the game, it looks like there are many skills to choose from, but then you realize there are only 4 legit builds: tank melee, spellcaster melee, DPS ranged and spellcaster ranged.
So... it's still a great game if you like action RPGs, but don't expect anything near Diablo 2 or you might be disappointed. I'd give it an 8/10.

The Bad Ends, especially, have been a point of discovery — while some, at first, can appear to be “random” or added simply for shock value, over time I’ve recently discovered even the most bizarre of these has a satisfying explanation by digging deeper into the plot’s world building characterization.

This will be a bit more of a mixed bag, simply because there are a few elements of this visual novel’s interface I have a bone to pick with; however, let’s start with the positive elements…which is nearly everything! This game is super lovely.
So let’s get negative instead.
. I despise it.
It is pretty, yes, BUT.
. Not only is it the width of the screen, but it also is leaves just enough space at the bottom for a pixel-high transparent distraction. Ah!! Visual claustrophobia!
Decreasing the box’s opacity in the options menu
lessen the transparent line’s impact; alas, doing so means the name tag and text box will darken wherever they touch, which is nearly as distracting.
Like it or not, the text box is inescapable.
While the controls for the most part are simply point-and-click, there are a number of things that cannot be accessed simply through a left-click of the mouse.
Unfortunately, there is no indication within the game what the controls are; you have to either stumble across them by accident or surf the internet for hopes of a guide — and IMO essentials such as a menu and script should be obvious for even a first timer.
This weakness could be rectified a number of ways.
- a tutorial
- a list of (keyboard or mouse) control shortcuts
- a help button, either on the title menu or on the interface to access a page explaining how the auto text works, skip etc.
- or, if such cannot all be contained or too awkward to insert, a notice
on where to find such information — perhaps Online or in a readme.txt
This is especially important for Steam customers considering most won't have a Cheritz account.

This game is a romance sim with a wonderful story that keeps you wanting to know what happens next. I have played and watched other people play romance games like this before, but most of them are different in that they have a mechanic where you raise a stat (Like intelligence or beauty) in order to progress with your love interest. Even though I liked these games too, that mechanic felt repetitive and tedious at times, because I just wanted to find out what would happen next in the story. Nameless, however, does not use this mechanic. The game progresses based entirely on your dialogue choices. How you choose to speak and act towards the other characters will affect how the story unfolds.
I have only one real negative critique of the game, which is that it could use a patch to fix the spelling and grammatical errors in the translation. If you are someone who absolutely cannot stand misspellings and typos, then you may not want to pick up the game until those are fixed. However, if you can look past the errors (which probably occurred during translation), then you will find a really great story, which is the main reason why I recommend this game.
The story and characters are very strong. The voice acting is done well, and it gives you a sense of each character's personality. The characters feel three-dimensional, and they are very likeable across the board. I was especially happy that the main character has a real personality and sense of humor, unlike some romance sim main characters, who feel rather flat and colorless. The romantic interests also have very interesting personalities, motivations, and stories of their own, which has kept me wanting to play through until I have seen every piece of the story. I have not played through every path yet. However, the stories and characters in Nameless are so intriguing that I plan to try to get every ending, good and bad. The creators of Nameless have made a game that has a story which is sweet, funny, sad, and even sometimes terrifying, and I heartily recommend it.

I'm a sucker for AC, and I often find myself playing the games and aiming for 100% completion despite their flaws.
I was interested when I first heard about this smaller digital games. As a child I remember the magic of playing Prince of Persia with it's precision timing, jumps, and sword fighting. I figured if the game could simply live up to the standard sset by that 30 year old game, then what could go wrong.
And that is the problem with the game. It technically doesn't do anything wrong.... but it doesn't really do anything right either. So I'm having a difficult time deciding whether or not I can reommned the game.
I'll start with comparisons to Prince of Persia (I'm talking the old DOS game here, not the PS2/Xbox era game). While AC Chronicles China is not as unforgiving as PoP, it is also not as accurate. Similar to it's 3D big brothers, your assasin has a bad habit of going in directions you didn't intend. This can lead to countless "restart checkpoints" if you are aiming for higher scores. The running, jumping, sliding, and other movment mechanics are pretty good. My favorite levels often invovled skill runs through a collapsing environment. On the othe rhand, the combat sections are simply not fun, and I think the developers knew that, which is why you are punished very heavily score-wise for getting invovled in sword combat. Considering charatcer upgrades are tied to your level scores, this means you are heavily pushed towards silently moving through levels unseen. And if you have to kill, don't be seen while doing it.
Which leads me to wonder why the bothered with so many combat mechanics. Blocking, countering, rolling over enemines, light attacks, heavy attacks, are all mechanics that, if you play as the game encourgaes you to, will never actually be used. It reminded me of the older splinter cell games that gave you 20 gadgets to kill a man, and then penalized you for killing.
The story itself is fairly shallow. Precursor artifact? check. Crumbling assasin brotherhood? check. Gang of evil templars in a convient order of importance? check. Assassin that doesn't listen to their master and causes trouble? check. This is all familar territory. and it really only serves to set up the flimsiest of reasons as to why we are killing all these guys.
As this is the first game in a 3 part series, it is hard to tell at this point how much lore the series will ultimately add to the AC universe. At this point it very well could be a throwaway story, or the precursor artiofact mentioned might end up being something rather important.
That is honestly where the developers should be focused at this point. The AC universe is dense and can be somewhat convoluted. There are fans who understand everything about the lore and many more who know there are artifacts and ancioents, but aren't really clear on what their deal is.  Smaller games like this are the perfect opportunity to flesh these things out. Define the artifacts. Define the background stories of people who have met or heard about.
So far, these games don't feel like they are going that route. Rather they had a list of lcoations from a brain storm meeting on where the next big AC game should be, and someone took the scraps that got lef ton the table and decided to make this series based on them.
Ultimately, the gameplay is serviceable and I had moments where I felt pretty badass. Sliding from hiding spot to hiding spot with only split seconds to spare is pretty awesome. That is until you go to jump into the next spot and your assassin instead decides to jump on a guards head and then just stare at him while every enemy in the area lights you up.  If the game had a better story, then based on the gameplay as it stands, I would have gone ahead and given a thumbs up. Unfortunately the game could literally have been called anything, because other than name dropping Ezio and mentions of the artifact, there is nothing else Assassin's Creed about the game.  And for that reason, I can't recommend it. There are better action platformers out there. And there are enough other AC games that have more variety, better gameplay, and more substance that are worth your time and money.

It's propably not going to a too popular review, but AC: Chronicles is a huge disappointment for me.
Now that Ubisoft finally woke up saying "oh sh_t we forgot the other two, let's rush them in a month", I think it's time to leave a review. I don't recommend buying it, but not because it's "this" episode specificly, more because of it's core gameplay engine that is not going to change in the other two either.
My expectation was a sidescroller, sometimes 3D stealth based linear game, and having played many great games in this genre I can say Chronicles is a medicore-at-best entry with a selling franchise name burnt on it.
The gameplay is incredibly slow, restrictive and forces your hand to play on predetermined paths and methods. Most of these type of games do the same, but they either do it way more seemlessly or in a much more engaging satisfying way. Perfect example would be Mark of the Ninja, which achieved both and gave some freedom of creativity with the different types of ninja suits allowing different tricks. Here however, your playthrough is set in cement, every centimenter of your movement in the blank level design just constantly makes this thought linger: "the devs want me to hide there. The devs want me to jump over that". Obviously, since it's linear, but the sluggish (definitly feels it was made for handheld consoles), constantly autocorrecting slow glue controls and movement paired up with the incredibly dull level design just pushes this to my face constantly because there is nothing else worth to pay attention to. Almost all of the game is with constant emply, blank rocks and (cave-)walls as a background, which is where 2D sidescroller games usually excel at but Chronicles definitly is the worst at. There are some beautiful ones aswell, but... you know, they had to have something attractive in the trailers. And those are all you'll see (or even less, because one of them isn't even in the game).
Stealth mechanism is dull. Not only compared to Mark of the Ninja, but compared to This War of Mine aswell. Basicly it's "guard shows his back, you are invisible". Noise, shadows, enviromental cover, nothing you can play with. But you can! Liar! You may say. Pay attention to the wording - PLAY WITH. When I have to go through a 50 meter long tunnel with one or two patrolling guards and there is an absolutely GIGANTIC black hole on the wall that from a kilometer away you can tell "yes, the devs want me to hide there and this is the only way to go through", that's not PLAYING. That's something that makes me feel like I'm treated like an idiot. And that's EXACTLY where Chronicles goes wrong in every minute and every second of it, because these types of stealth games shine when they achieve the feeling of "almost comfortable" challange through smart gameplay in creative enviroments. Chronicles... almost writes on the screen for me to "go there, pull that, go there, shoot that, go there, hide there AND ONLY THERE because there is nowhere else to hide - we placed it there only for you so you can pass this part, and go through... and win! Congratulations you are an epic skillful master assassin! I feel like this game is treating me like it's a logic test for babies where they must push the triangle object to the box through the triangle hole, the ball through the circle hole etc, with the smiling devs constantly watching over not to ever possibly harm myself, offering a lollypop for success. Except the lollypop here is "for the brotherhood! For revenge! I'm a shadowy cool assassin now! Because I'm told, not because I feel like one".
This, is not what I'm looking for in Assassin's Creed.
This, is not what I'm looking for in any stealth game.

Epistory - Typing Chronicles is a game in which you play as a girl who rides upon a giant fox.

Somehow I have managed to clock more than 600 hours into this game. Does this make me biased?
You would tend say it does, but instead I'd like to think it made me more critical of what the game is, and isn't.
For an exploration game, I'd say it is without a doubt the biggest game I have ever played regarding playing field. It's full of planets and moons which you can explore to your hearts' content, but space is depressingly empty. Once you've seen one asteroid field, you've seen them all.
The adding of freighters in the Foundation patch livened it up a bit, but the game could definitely use some more anomalies, rogue star bases, system wars and space battles.
Planets and moons are awesome. Graphics wise this game can be mind stunningly beautiful. And if you're like me, someone who could just wander around enjoying sights and views, you're in for a great time.
However, play long enough and you'll start to see the same trees, rocks, and even similar creatures, wherever you go. Play a while longer and you'll start wishing they'd add more parts, and be more giving regarding size limitations, and density.
Underground planet exploration is disappointing, you can explore caves upon caves, which are richly generated by the game, but you won't find anything worthwhile in them.
Storylines, quests, npc interactions, are nice, but at one point the storyline becomes a somewhat semi-tedious journey, the quests run dry, and the npc interactions are recycled. There are no repeating quests or jobs with rewards worth spending time on.
The Path Finder patch added one repeating quest which will yield you some credits, but when you're at the point where you can do it you could just shoot a few creatures, create some products, and end up with a bigger monetary reward.
So why you might ask have I given this game a thumbs up, and why did I spend so much time playing it?
Everything is procedural, and I love it. It's a game where you can go and do anything you'd like to do when you want do do it, as long as it's within the game's limitations of course.
I am unsure what to expect from Sean Murray and his team in the future. I do not regret buying this game for the full price, but I did need a long break before the first patch as I was just burned out on the lack of depth and content.
Recent patches made things better, and if they keep this up, I'll definitely keep playing.
Take it for what it is. A time waster.

I pre-ordered this game and have had the luxury of experiencing it evolve over the past year. With the recent release of 1.3 it could be argued this is a different game entirely from what we had at release. I managed to sink about 80 hours into the release version of NMS although much of the game felt aimless and repetitive. The only thing that really kept me going was my appreciation for the technology behind the game (there are some great videos about it on the GDC YouTube channel if you're interested) and the amazing mod community (I honestly don't know if the game would be what it is today if it weren't for you guys. In many ways you showed Hello Games what we wanted out of NMS). The Foundation and Pathfinder updates vastly improved the game but it was never really enough to get me invested in it again. However 1.3 has made NMS my dream game. Every planet looks gorgeous and the new art direction (photo-realism) gives an entirely different atmosphere. Every planet is interesting and most feel unique. The story is incredible (props to the writers at Hello Games) and the fact that they could somehow weave such an interesting story into a procedurally generated universe is mind-blowing. The missions, portal glyphs, economy, and guilds give this game a purpose which it was lacking upon release. I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a near infinite survival game.
My only recommendation to Hello Games would be to build a tool that enables players to create and share their own stories/missions. You guys have created an amazing framework all it needed was more content. Opening that to the community would likely allow for some very interesting possibilities. Also the addition of the "Ambient Gamemode" would be much appreciated ;)
Thank you Hello Games for continuing to develop NMS. While I was certainly disappointed at release, I never lost faith in you guys and I'm glad to see what the game has become. I have so much respect for everyone at Hello Games. You stuck by a game that had received perhaps the worst public reaction to a large scale release I have ever seen. While many developers would have ditched the game and moved onto their next project you stuck by it. Please continue to develop NMS. This patch has made it quickly become one of my favourite games of all time. You guys have something truly unique on your hands and I'm excited for what the future holds.

As a huge fan of Wolfenstein, I loved this game. The characters are better than ever, the gunplay and stealth are much improved. I feel like the difficulty curve is a little weird. It's not a steady increase, more like a sine wave that randomly zig zags here and there. The world is insanely detailed for a "linear" first person shooter, littered with collectibles that actually add to the world rather than just existing for collection's sake. The hub area, Eva's Hammer, lets you see characters interact and react to you playing the game and it adds a ton of life to the game.
My only complaints is that the first half of the game seems to drag on a bit long due to story reasons, but at least it closes on one of the highest points I've ever experienced in a video game. Like holy♥♥♥♥♥♥the halfway point of this game is crazy good. In addition to that, the weapons are a lot more lackluster than the previous games. They turned the Laserkraftwerk into a generic railgun, while the Dieselkraftwerk is more fun (though less useful in combat). The Fergus timeline is also less interesting as a whole, as Fergus' character arc in the game is basically non-existent while Wyatt gets actual attention. Due to it being the second game in a trilogy, it also suffers from one of those endings where it wants you to wait until the next one for real closure. That's not an issue with the game itself, but trilogies in general. And the weapon wheel is bad!
This is a great game, despite its performance issues the first few days of launch (now fixed for me). The first time I played I got a nasty crash right before the ending that ended up corrupting my save files, but the second time I had almost no real issues. You get to kill Nazis better than you've been able to in any game before, and that's definitely the #1 reason to get this game.
8/10 I will play it some more

I have always been a fan of Gauntlet games since playing a ton of the original 4-player co-op arcade game.  My favorites along the way were Gauntlet IV for the Sega Genesis and Gauntlet: Dark Legacy for the PS2.  I feel that this game is a pretty good entry in the franchise.
I have completed about 10 hours of play so far and I'm enjoying the game quite a bit.  My system struggled a little with some of the graphics settings but, once I turned some things down, it has played very smoothly while still looking quite good.  I believe that Arrowhead did a good job of recreating the spirit of the original in a modernized version of the game.
It's pretty easy to jump right in and start playing because gameplay is quite basic.  The weapon and potion abilities are a nice touch to aid in combat.  Some people have complained about the repetition in environments and enemies but that's been the case with every Gauntlet game - I see that as being true to the franchise.
As for negatives, I find that the system for buying new weapons and stuff is lacking.  It's not immediately apparent what benefits, if any, there are to buying upgrades.  Some things seem to do nothing more than change the character's appearance.  Different weapons have different abilities but there's no indication that the weapons are more powerful.  Relics seem interesting but their use is not totally intuitive.  I plan to experiment more to see how useful they might be.
Another problem I have is Death.  In previous Gauntlet games, you could use potions to kill Death.  However, in this game it appears that potions simply drive Death away for a short time.  Potions are fairly uncommon and you can only carry a few at a time so you really just have to try to avoid Death, which can be really frustrating.
Overall, I find this game to be a lot of fun to play.  I would prefer a better system for buying upgrades and I would like a better way to deal with Death like earlier Gauntlet games but these negatives don't stop the game from being fun.  The $20 full price isn't terrible but I would recommend waiting for a sale if you can.

- Delightfully twisted characters. If you've played Dandelion these characters are definitely darker. However they're not just like that as flavor. Their problems and pasts, and the way it's affect them, flow very well with each of the characters. They're all very distinct.
- The MC's friends actually matter. Her friends Soi and Shinbi actually have their own personalities and matter throughout the course of each route. They plays active roles in helping the MC out, as well as receiving help.
- Compelling story that gets progressively darker the further you get.
- The Art. The character designs, sprites, were all lovely. The backgrounds were nice, but in general I don't pay too much attention to the background art. (Unless it's Cinders, so pretty. *_*).
- I'm in the camp of those that enjoyed the audio, especially the music when things were going wrong. XD
- Typos/Grammar Issues. Honestly my brain tends to auto-correct things to the point I don't always notice small grammar issues or typos when I'm not reading to edit and I'm incapable of editing whatever I'm reading, but I did spot some. I never felt like it ruined the game for me though. I've spotted typos in published books. It happens. It sounds like others have had bigger issues with this in the game than I did, but given the enjoyment I got out of this VN it feels like nitpicking.
- Some of the CGs were admittedly pretty awkward, especially those belonging to Tei.
I understand a lot of people look at the price and wonder WTF? This is one of the higher quality games on the market with 20-40+ hours of gameplay depending on your reading speed. I played this when Cheritz first released the game. I don't know how many hours beating it the first time took, but second gameplays are always faster and it still took me 33.3 hours to complete.
That's not just it though. This game is fully voiced, has many CGs, audio, and has been translated. For its cost you get a lot out of it. Games like this run $60+ in Japan. In America, high quality VNs tend to be around this cost. Hakuoki: Memories of the Shinsengumi, Backstage Pass, Phoenix Wright.
Does that matter? You have a CG gallery, memory gallery, and diary entries all sitting there to collect. Good achievements are one you get for hitting points in the story (Dragon Age: Origins does this) or actual gameplay achievements (like for less story oriented games). Collecting all the CGs, memories, and diary entries are achievements. Yeah they're nice to have, but if the lack of them stops you from buying any game (unless you have already played the game) then you probably weren't very interested in the game to begin with. Having them or not having them has zero impact on the game itself, and to treat the game like it's worse because it doesn't have them doesn't make sense.
Finally, I want to address Voxit's review since it's one of the first reviews you'll come across.
Voxit had a huge issue with the story. Yes, if you're attentive and enjoy figuring endings out before they happen you'll be able to do so. Does that make it any less touching? It did for him. It didn't for me. Unlike him I don't believe the necessarly game runs on trying to surprise you, leaving you unimpressed if it doesn't. If it did it doesn't make sense for the game to be litered with hints about what's going on. The story tries to warn the player. Honestly progressively understanding what's going on makes it as a whole creepier for me because I'm aware of how messed up the situation is. So there's another side to consider.
And then there's Voxit's main complaint. I finished the game twice and I never found Red to be the 'true pairing'. He states this but at no point in the English translation does it support this. (I don't know Korean, and thus haven't played the original.) This is assumed. Due to the personality of the characters and the situation, Red has to come last, but just because he's the game's last route doesn't mean she necessarily ended up with him.
Therefore if you like open endings, it's great. If you don't you're going to have more of a problem with it.
From what I got out of the game, I think the 'true ending' is actually when you meet the secret character. What does this mean for her romantic life for those who read spoilers or already played the game? Open ended. Yes all the dolls end up in the same dimension and in love with the Heroine, but
. Therefore the other endings do matter. It never denies the existence of any of the relationship,
. At the end of the game she regains the memories of all the timelines, therefore she'd most likely be in love with all of them.
Maybe she started a harem and dated them all. Maybe she ultimately did decide on one, or two! Maybe she dated the secret character instead!
Do I think the dolls would have fought for her? Of course. The dolls always fight with each other regardless, but do I really think that it's that much of an issue? Nope. We see endings where dolls share her between them even in their most messed up states. At multiple times do they back down to let another doll pursue her, or even help the doll to this end! To a point they respect the others, even in their fighting, and ultimately they want the MC to be happy. It's even stated at the end by Tei that it required
of them to fill her heart, and they all understand and agree with this. So no, I don't think, whichever ending you decide to go with, that it would have been a problem.
I think it's of use to point out that the dolls are just that: dolls.
dolls. It's shown that dolls pretty much love their owners unconditionally to the point of madness. Even when they become human they're still connected to their doll bodies, shown by the fact that if something happens to the dolls the same thing happens to their human bodies.
As for how the Wizard continued to make new dimensions I have no idea. Lawl. That's a flaw I'll tip my hat to Voxit.
I'll leave off with my impression of the game. Maybe the game is actually more about how the relationships between characters can change people for the better and help all invovled heal. It's about obsession and scars, how they fester, and how they hurt. It's about growing up and how people change in theat process. It about the fight between the private and public self. And it's about real friendships and the unconditional support they bring.

First off, I have played quite a few otome games and Nameless~ The one thing you must recall~ has easily became number one on that lengthy list.  This game is filled with plot twists that you don't expect, beautiful artwork, passionate voice acting, in-depth dialogue, and amazing character development.  If you have played through Cheritz's previous game, Dandelion Wishes Brought to You, then you also had to deal with the whole "bring up the love points until they're human"-bit and while it's fun the first time, it gets old quickly when all you want to do is get to the individual character's story.  Well, that is no longer an issue as you only have to play through the prologue for three out of five of the characters and even though that may still seem tedious, it changes each time and you are given the option to skip through the parts that you have been previously exposed to, so no worries for those of you who are as impatient as me!  Similar to Dandelion, there is a secret character's story that intertwines with each of the main guys' stories...and it gets intense!  When you finally get through every one of the main character's stories, the anticipation you feel will be so incredible that by the time you actually get to playing through that part of the story, your eyes will be glued to the computer screen in suspense!
To briefly summarize the actual background behind this game, main character (player) Eri collects dolls and one day, they come to life.  The first thing that came to mind when I learned of this was that that's actually kind of terrifying (dolls freak me out ^^0).  However, if you put yourself Eri's shoes, you'll realize that this is actually a dream come true for her due to her feelings of extreme loneliness ever since her grandfather passed away.  From the moment that she made each one's purchase, she fell in love with them even if they were simply inanimate objects.  Now it is the player's choice to go with one of the dolls Yeonho, Lance, or Yuri at first and later Tei or Red.  Each character has it's own charm, although my personal favorite was Lance ^^.  When the player encounters all of the boys at the beginning and learns about their personalities, the first impression that the player may get is that these are just your run-of-the-mill, stereotypical otome game guys.  The silent type, the flirty playboy, the cutesy shota boy, the kind and sweet boy, and lastly the innocent/happy-go-lucky boy.  However, the player soon learns that each one is so much more detailed than the orignal first impression that they were given.  Honestly, one of the things that I like most about this game is that all of the characters are so complex, it's so interesting to learn about each one that you just want to keep playing.  Not only are the characters of the boys so interesting, but the art for them is so beautiful that you may even find yourself getting caught up in the beauty of the character's appearance.  The CGs that you get when you pick correct choices are stunning, so much so that I'm sure that we as players are not even able to grasp just how much work and care was put into each individual drawing.  The artwork truly enhances the overall experience of the gameplay just as much as the interesting dialogue and overall story keep you wanting more.  Another enhancer to the game was the voice acting and I can personally tell you that it was amazing because you just want to take your time and listen to the voice actors speak each line.  There is so much passion and emotion within their voices, giving the game a new dimension and making it really come to life.
This game had me laughing outloud, smiling weirdly to myself, making me want to punch a pillow (the bullies >n<), and cry for over an hour.  While all of that may seem a bit exaggerated, trust me when I say that I'm not overdramatizing the emotions I felt when playing this game (espeically when it came to the secret character's story *cries*).  I absolutley adored this game to no end.  Thanks to all of the beautiful artwork, intriguing dialogue, amazing plot-devlopment, and passionate voice acting, this game is easily one of the best otome games I've played in a long time.  Would I recommend this game?  Yes yes and yes.  I have already recommended it to friends who like otome games and will continue to bother them until they buy it >:3.  Was it worth the full price of $33?  Yes, it is worth that and more, without a doubt.  If you read this review and are having mixed feelings about buying this game, you should definitely do it because I will never be able to truly express to you through a simple review just how much I adored this game and you will only really be able to understand it if you play it for yourself!

So! Is this game worth buying? Yes! Does it have issues? ... also yes. Normally I'd recommend this one on sale, except it never seems to be on sale. The game has some very strong points, and as many a reviewer prior to me has pointed out: it has ALL THE FEELS. But for something this pricy, one would think it would be more polished than it is.
The graphics are beautiful, the interface functionality is a step up from Dandelion, and the background music is not intrusive. This is a plus given how often one has to listen to it on a loop. The characters are also very engaging, and for anyone interested in the subject of transhumanism, this game provides some good thought fodder. Some of the routes are hilarious, others are downright disturbing, so buyer beware if you're expecting nothing more than a light hearted wish fullfillment.
As for gameplay itself: the emphasis this time is definitely on the 'novel' end rather than the 'game' end. No stat management, although there are decisions to be made regarding how you respond to the characters that determines how things go.
Although I'm no believer in a "perfect" game, I do think a game should be polished, and there are some issues here that really should've been caught before the release, and haven't been fixed nearly a year later. They really needed someone to check the spelling, grammar, and punctuation for the translation. Sometimes the love interest's names aren't capitalized, things are misspelled, and there's frequent confusion between "you / your / you're."
The skip button sometimes does not work, and this is an important function in a game where the opening sequence is nearly an hour long on its own, and you'll be revisiting it at least three times, or more if you're like me and have an impulse to be nice to everyone and keep getting an accidental game over. It also occasionally forgets what the main character's name is, even if you left said name on default.
Conclusion: It feels a bit odd to say this, since normally I have the opposite problem. But I love the game's characterization and art and plot. I don't have issues with the story. I wish they'd taken more care with the functionality or had at least released fixes for what was wrong. The translation fixes, being text based, one would think would be an easy thing to do.

Nameless ~The one thing you must recall~’s Steam port quickly follows the Steam release of Cheritz’s other Otome game, Dandelion –Wishes Brought to You-
Having played both the original game, and now the Steam port, I can say that the Steam release runs just as well as the original did. Bugs which previously existed for some users were quickly fixed by Cheritz. As for the content of the actual game:
Story: The plot follows Eri, a girl who has been living alone due to the fact that her parents work abroad, and her only other family, her grandfather, passed away. To ease her loneliness, Eri has collected 5 ball-jointed dolls. They all come from a company that’s known for having dolls “with a soul.” Surprisingly, one day she wakes up to find all five of her dolls have turned into human boys. Through a series of misunderstandings, they begin attending school with her in addition to living together. The game follows Eri’s life as she becomes closer to the boys, and of course, the player makes choices to romance one of their choosing.
Nameless may have a very bright exterior and be filled with lots of jokes and fun, but it also isn’t afraid to address darker themes, such as abandonment, the fear of not being accepted for who you are, abuse, and having parents who don’t understand or connect with you. And while I can’t get too far into this without spoiling, Nameless is interesting in that it provides a canon and plot-related reason as to why you can start your game over and over again to romance different characters. This gives extra incentive to keep on playing the game, as even if you’ve finished the route of the boy you are the most interested in, you never know what the next route might reveal about the overarching plot. All this adds up to make the story a fun, engaging, and rewarding experience.
Characters: As far as the five datable boys go, I have no complaints at all. Each boy has a very distinct and unique personality, and Cheritz certainly isn’t afraid to get creative with their character set-ups. Everyone is very well developed throughout their route, and I always ended a route with a much better understanding and appreciation for the character I had finished pursuing. There is nobody who I find dislikable among the boys, as even the one I wasn’t sure I was going to like I had become completely empathetic to over the course of playing his route.
Eri herself is also well developed. She does have enough character of her own to be a well-rounded lead while still being easy to identify with. I appreciate the fact that through the routes she comes to terms with her problems with her own will and effort, and while the boys certainly do help her, none of them magically make everything better just with love. It makes for a more realistic story and character development.
The most notable side characters include Soi and Shinbi. They’re an absolute pleasure to have around. It’s actually somewhat uncommon to see an otome where the heroine has pre-existing female friends who play a large role in the story, but that’s exactly what Cheritz included with Soi and Shinbi. Both are hilarious characters in their own way, while also being wonderful friends who are fiercely protective and supportive of Eri. As well, Soi and Shinbi aren’t lacking their own development, and it was great to see that the two aren’t neglected just for being side characters. All the characters of Nameless are interesting in their own ways, and that just helps the game to shine.
Gameplay: The gameplay of Nameless is really quite straight-forward, as it plays out as a fairly typical visual novel. As the play you will read through character dialogue and descriptions of events, and every now and then be prompted to make a choice for Eri, which can possibly lead you to a bad ending if you are not careful. This takes up the vast majority of the gameplay, and while not done badly at all, it is just fairly standard of otomes. There is one “exam” minigame where you simply answer trivia about the game and character under a time limit, but it only occurs once per character route. If you enjoy visual novels, you’re probably not going to have any issues at all with it and enjoy it quite a bit, but if you’re not, this probably isn’t going to offer much in terms of gameplay that’s different enough for you.
One thing that does stand out is that you are not allowed to pursue any boy of your choice straight from the beginning. Instead, you must pick from “gems” on a menu screen, each of which representing a different boy, and you cannot access certain boys’ routes until you’ve completed other characters’ routes. This is done very purposefully, as each route is written in a certain so as that it adds up to slowly the overall plot and story, so you do not accidentally reveal big plot details early into your playthrough.
In comparison to Dandelion the quality of translation has improved. While Dandelion did not have a bad translation, there were still some distracting typos and grammar mistakes scattered throughout the game. Nameless still has a few, but there are far fewer ones than in Dandelion, and all of the dialogue flows quite nicely in my opinion. I mentioned this in my Dandelion review, but I do think perhaps having a native English-speaker do a “test reading” of the script just to sweep for any simple spelling or grammar mistakes may be beneficial to improving the overall translation quality if it is a viable option for Cheritz.
Art: The art of Nameless is very nice. Pretty well everything in the game is original art, and it’s all very well done. One of the first things that got me excited about Nameless after its announcement was the color palette. The colors of Nameless are rather pastel, almost a little washed out, but it still manages to feel very bright and warm at the same time. It’s very pleasant to look at. The character sprites are all also very nice, and I really don’t have any complaints with the art style they chose to go with. Each character looks very individual and unique, and you can tell each part of their design was chosen to help emphasize their personality.
The CGs are all very nice too. The background are also very nice in my opinion, featuring those same soft colors I enjoy while seeming to be done well from what I can tell. Overall, I find Nameless to be a very visually pleasing game.
Sound: I very much enjoyed the voice-acting. Though I know due to the fact that I do not speak Korean I will not be able to pick up on certain intricacies of the acting, from what I can tell everyone does an amazing job. Each character’s voice suits them very well, and I can easily sense the emotions they are trying to convey.
The music is very enjoyable. Each track has a unique identity, and every character receives their own theme. Other than one track carried over from Dandelion, all of the music is completely original. A nice mix of instruments are used and they complement the overall feeling of the game very well. The opening theme is also very nice, and it’s cute how the lyrics are very specific to the actual plot and is obviously about all of the boys’ feelings towards Eri. Perhaps my favorite track though, is “What’s Your Name” which is a beautiful, melancholic song only for completing the secret character’s ending, and it reflects the entire game quite well. I own the OST, as I find this game’s soundtrack to be a delight and something worth having around.
Overall: Cheritz has created yet another top-quality Otome game with the addition of Nameless to their lineup. It is an enjoyable and memorable experience from beginning to end, and chances are if you’re interested at all in it, you will end up enjoying it thoroughly. I would highly recommend this game as it is worth every dollar, and I excitedly await the arrival of Cheritz’s future games as well.

I only got this game for free because there was something wrong when I was buying this from Chrono.gg a while back. When it was resolved the offer was already gone, so as customer service should do, they gave me this product for free. That's it.
That said, I like this game. I almost 100% it, just two more Nests to go. You can play in under 7 hours.
Pros:
* Beautiful. Goes well with the theme of a journey of a writer, e.g. origami theme, handwritings, etc.
* Challenging, but doable. You may have to type very fast, but I think it's fun. Even if you scored 800 on the SAT, there are still some insanely long words you wouldn't understand (if they are words). There's even some strategy into it as time goes on.
* Very forgiving. There is no health bar; you die if an enemy touches you if you don't type fast enough, but you will spawn almost right where you left off, and the enemies have already took the damage that you dealt. There's even some encouraging text on the black screen, so this really prevented me from burning out.
Cons:
* Controls are hard to control. Because you view it at an 45 degree angle, much of the time you have to hold two arrow keys to go where you like. Don't even try their new letter-navigation method, it's counter-intuitive and takes too long to get used to. It's a nightmare when you have to deal with sliding-on-ice, because you have to be very careful what you press is where you want to go, otherwise you'll slide all the way in the opposite direction.
* Some glitches, but nothing that affects gameplay. e.g. Teleportation devices sometimes lacked the animation.
* Music doesn't repeat smoothly in last stage. For some reason. Doesn't seem to happen in earlier stages.
Some tips for gameplay:
* Don't worry about the points. Points are required to unlock later stages, but you should be fine. There are plenty of combo opportunities. Just type fast.
* Don't worry about the fragments. Fragments provide the life story of your character, but if you don't really care or are patient, you will get to see all of them in the credits (which kind of bugs me).

Epistory is an ingenious mixture of modern game design, beautiful artwork, and educational themes.
The keyboard-only control scheme is elegant beyond the fact that it's a typing game. While the story mode was very appealing, I more often find myself coming back for quick arena runs, to gauge self-improvement (WPM stat, leaderboards). I'll be treasuring this gem for a long time.

It is an awesome game. Great graphics, and excellent for typing. It is one of the best experiences I had with a game, and I really appreciate that is available on Linux.

A genuinely charming, creative, and enjoyable game.
One of the most wonderful things about Epistory is the way in which it uses typing not just as a game mechanic, but as a thematic focus for both the story and the player's actions. Words that you type relate to the tasks you're performing, the emotional tone of the moment, and the metaphorical story playing out in the background of the main game. This is one of those rare examples of a game utilising its mechanics in a way that intertwines perfectly with the narrative experience it's trying to create.
Alongside a cleverly presented and emotionally compelling story, the mechanics are also devised in a charming way that has you rolling your fingers across the keyboard to turn cranks, punching in numbers to open safes, and hammering letters repeatedly to break open padlocks.
My only criticisms of Epistory would be that it's perhaps a little too long given how simple it is. While by no means a lengthy game (the main story taking me around 4-5 hours), the same patterns of puzzles interspersed with enemy gauntlets do become somewhat routine by the end of it, despite some clever gimmicks being thrown in to keep every dungeon fresh. Besides that, the ending also felt to me like it missed an opportunity to utilise the game's themes of writing and creativity in a way that gelled more closely with the story. I was expecting a really satisfying emotional payoff given how clever the game was at integrating its story with its mechanics, and what happened instead was slightly more predictable than what I'd hoped for. That being said, the ending is still very sweet and charming, and I may have shed a tear when the credits rolled.
Whether you're looking for a genuinely great typing tutor or a creative and enjoyable game, Epistory has you covered. It's a real breath of fresh air, and more than a little reminiscent of titles like Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons both in its emotional tone and clever treatment of game mechanics. Definitely worth a buy.

I first saw the trailer for this game back in 2016 and my jaw dropped. It looked so freaking beautiful, I couldn't believe it. The style just clicked with me, so I pre-ordered it. It's the one and only game I have ever pre ordered.
When it released, I didn't get the backlash this game got. I mean, it wasn't how awesome it was advertised, but I knew that. Then, I jumped the stars and found the Atlas path. This was the moment when it became stale for me. Since I had spent so much time in one system, I already had acomplished a lot without realizing it. When I jumped to other systems I was craving adventure and the unknown, but it was pretty much what I had already seen. I still liked the vistas, colors and weird stupid animals, mind you, I still haven't grown tired of the style this game has, but regarding gameplay... yeah, it quickly became "mine more minerals for better upgrades and then go see the Altas". After I had done this like 10 times I decided the game was over for me.
I didn't care for new ships and I knew, since I'm familiar with the narrative style this game tries to evoke, that at the center  of the galaxy there would only be a nihilistic answer to existential questions. So yeah, I didn't care and decided the game was over at 40 hours.
For 60$ I was 2/3rds satisfied, but not so much that I would leave a good review of it in Steam. Since Hello Games said they'd be releasing free updates, I decided to wait until I saw how real they were before writting my review. If they didn't release anything, this would have been negative. If they did, well...
The first update they released was called "Foundation" and it introduced base building and Freighters into the game. I decided to see how it was for myself and I quickly grew to like it. Freighters I didn't care much about, but base building seemed like something with potential. They introduced new npcs and quests, as well as many new elements into the game which allowed for different kind of biomes and planets.
Overall, I liked this update, but still not so much as to grant them a full positive review. Although cleverly implemented, the quest chain was easily achievable in little time and in the end all bases ended up looking pretty alike, so I eventualy grew bored with it.
And then came the second update, "Pathfinder". This one introduced more stuff for the bases, vehicles, classes for ships and vehicles, the ability to have more than one ship and the truly godsend mode this game needed from day 1: PERMADEATH.
In my opinion, this is the only way this game should be played. It's extremely hard and requires you to be constatly aware of your resources and storage capacity. Everything is slower in this mode and everything's quite harder to achieve, hence making every little achievement a huge sucess. I had built an entire base in "normal mode" previously and didn't feel as rewarded as I felt when I finally built my first container in "permadeath mode". Also, yes, this means that if you die once, all you've accomplished is instantly lost. You only have one chance to make it, so the more you advance in this mode, the higher the stakes. I died like 10 times before I learned how to reach my broken-down ship alive through trial and error.
I realize this is not for everyone, but for me, this is what I needed. This makes it feel like you're in a hostile environment all the time and makes every small decision count. I can't tell you how many times I tried to float over a cliff and clenched my butt as I barely made it to the other side. It's great stuff, seriously, and if you don't like it, I guess you still have the option to take it easy in "normal mode".
So, tl;dr:
- Did they lie? Yes, they did. Quite a lot actually. I never cared about what they lied about in the first place, so this didn't factor in at all for me.
- Is this game fun? Yes, yes it is.
- Is it flawed? Yes, in many ways.
- Is it the worse game in Steam? No. People love to hate it though.
- Was it overhyped? Oh yes, beyond belief.
- How much should you pay for this? In my opinion, 40 bucks, tops.
