At this time of writing, I have finished Hellblade on hard. I loved it. But there are a few things you have to understand;
1. The game is first and foremost about story and Senua as a character. Don't expect any riveting gameplay aside from a great but simple and hard-hitting combat system, some exploration, and some simple puzzles about perception, which while easy, will make you say "ooooh clever" on many occasions.
2. The game was made to represent Psychosis, a mental illness. WEAR. HEADPHONES. You won't get the full incredible experience of the voices in your head and the chilling sound unless you do.
3. This game is really ♥♥♥♥ing scary at times. Like I've played through Dead Space and Silent Hill games plenty of times, and this was still way up there in terms of horror. The visuals and atmosphere, and ESPECIALLY the sound will give you violent chills.
So would I recommend this to everyone? No. But I would definetly recommend it to anyone who finds my previous points interesting. Norse mythology is very well told in side bits of audio you find from runes around the game, and if you love that mythos like I do you'll find lots to love. The story in this game is ♥♥♥♥ing incredible, so I don't want to spoil anything. The camera in this game is very close and claustrophobic, but it's like that on purpose, and gives things like combat a very overwhelming feel, even when faced with only two enemies. There is no HUD in this game, so you take visual cues to tell if you're going to die, or even listen to the voices in your head warning you of incoming attacks from behind and berating you for being so♥♥♥♥♥♥at combat. There will be times when the voices shout and argue over things you want to hear, but that's also on purpose, to show how annoying and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ having voices in your head can be. The game gets better the further you get into it, so if you're kind of interested in the beginning, you'll be hooked during the final acts. This game is well worth a play, and I think Ninja Theory have really made something special here. I'm all welcoming of this new AAA indie game sort of setup. There's a ton of creative freedom to be had.

Despite what a lot of people have said about this game, I really enjoyed the combat. The puzzles, I believe, could have been more intriguing, but I am not too worried about that. The story line of this game is worth every penny, even if I completed the game in only 7.6 hours, and that includes enjoying the scenery that this game perfectly executes. The game is very story driven, and you will fall in love with the story, and develop actual feelings for these characters.
I would recommend this to all my friends. It is a must buy, and is one of my favorite games so far this year. Play it with headphones, and in a dark room. You will get fully immersed in the game, and at times you will be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ yourself. I clinched my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ a few times. I also recommend playing on a harder difficulty. I believe it gets you more immersed in the story.
Overall, 9/10 for me. Look forward to the next one. Keep them coming guys!

Disclaimer: I'm still a newb.
If you're worrying about whether you can play on a keyboard, I play on a keyboard and have no problems relating to using it. BnB combos are perfectly capable of being executed on a keyboard.
Feedback is oomphy. Hits are satisfying. Controls are fluid. Oh yeah, there's backdash-canceling, which is pretty damn nice to have. Everything you expect to have from a fighting game is there. Netcode works pretty damn well.
If you want to get into fighting games, this is the most welcoming as it will get out of the box. An excellent tutorial introducing core mechanics is present. Finish it. A more in-depth guide on using the training mode frame data and punishing would be better though.
This game is solid. Find a friend to play with and figure out the mechanics. Be prepared for significant time investment if you want to "git gud", because that's what fighting games are. If you're new to FGs you will struggle at first, but once you get used to the timing and rhythm picking up other moves become considerably easier.
Game has pretty lenient hit-confirm windows, no ridiculous combo input requirements/windows/links unless you're going for the insanely high damage combos, in which case you deserve your damage.
I like the artstyle, the announcer and the music. They all fit together quite well.
Don't expect to launch the game, and be able to go toe-to-toe with people who have put a decent amount of time into learning characters and combos. As is with many other games, you will have to put time into something you want to be good at. Find people who are slightly better than you, or of equal skill level to play with.

This game is hard to review because it has so many faults and yet I still recommend it. The controls are beyond awful, the "puzzle" and "action" sequences are worse than amateur attempts you'd find on Newgrounds and in fact detract from the game itself, and worst of all: the "humor" that is non-stop present in the game is so idiotic and childish that it undermines the rest of the experience. The "humor" is essentially the dumbest smartass comments I've ever heard spewed so nonstop I felt like I couldn't go a minute without it being displayed. I laughed maybe once and I don't believe humor in a story based game that is about something so deep and serious is necessarily a bad thing, just done very poorly in this case. Also as a composer, I feel the music is very tacky "pop art" and poorly composed, as well as repeated nonstop (but I suppose that goes well with the theme of the game) and overall it also undermines the story for me.
However, I feel that this game still has a very deep and interesting story that brought about a lot of emotions in me and I feel the overall writing was superb. It's cheesy in all of the right ways...by actually delving into serious real life issues and being bitterwsweet about it the entire time. And on top of that, it personally struck home with me both because of the story and because of the surrealistic aspect of the entire game. I consider all video games as art but for the sake of categorization, I would call this an "art game" in the sense that it clearly tries to be more than simple mindless entertainment.
I recommend it to anybody but it should probably be played in short stints to avoid frustration at the issues mentioned.

I have always loved the tables that the Russian developer OOO Gameprom has made. Unfortunately, for a very long time, the only way to enjoy these tables was through playing on the tiny screen of a smartphone or on a tablet like an iPad. Thankfully, their best tables have been gathered together and this collection has landed on Steam allowing more people to play them. So the big questions that need answers are how did the move to Steam work out for the game and is it worth the price point that the developers have set?
Did the transfer to Steam go well for this game? Yes. The Steam version's menus and interface first of all are just as easy to use as the mobile menus and interface are but the two versions have differences. All of the tables also have quick guide pages that will give you the basics of what to do on each table which is great.
These tables feature something fun that most pinball tables do not have: the mission system. The table will give you a mission which is a shot that needs to be made or a place the ball has to go and if completed, gives you bonus points. These allow the player to always have something to aim for and try to achieve. There are also side pockets that will catch the ball if going down the left or right outlanes. After use, they must be reactivated by hitting drop targets to prevent future ball drains.
The physics that this title are known for are intact and great. While they might not be as robust as something like Pinball Arcade or Zen Pinball (Pinball FX2 on Steam), they are still silky smooth and very good. They are closer to how Zen Pinball handles physics with less realistic bounces on the flippers. Trying to use bounce-passes and similar techniques won't really work here because the physics system was developed prior to pinball games like Pinball Arcade, and since this title is aimed at a generally more casual audience, they have not changed the physics yet. It is worth mentioning that using the nudge feature does allow the player to perform bang backs to save the ball and it almost always works.
The visuals are in general amazing. Tables like Da Vinci are stunning in their appearance and design. These tables are in general king in one area: creativity in design. Tables like the Arcade table with minigames to play while playing pinball are so original that it changes the whole game of what you're doing. The tables are visually striking and fun to watch with generally bright color schemes. There are a few different view options available with the flyover mode the best in my opinion.
The sounds and voice acting are great. Most of them exceeded my expectations with only a couple being slightly less than expected. One of my favorite tables that I have played is surprisingly the Halloween table which has great voice and effects that are themed very well with the visuals.
The top tables that I have played that I think are stand out examples of their brilliant design are:
1. Da Vinci
2. Arcade
3. Red Planet
4. Halloween
5. Pirates
The fact that most people do not know about this title is that it is not a small collection. It has a whopping 15 tables with a very large variety of themes and designs. Obiviously some tables are lesser quality than the rest like Fantasy for example, but the others that are great make up for the shortcomings of the lesser few. The fact of the matter is that in my opinion, 15 tables all gathered together which are overall great with some tables even reaching awesome status, makes for a package that is well worth the price if you like/love Pinball like me and you want more pinball on Steam. These tables are great additions to the pantheon of tables that are currently available on Steam for players.
The game is not perfect and does have some minor problems. First of all, the game does not have built-in controller support. This can be subverted using a program that converts keyboard keys to gamepad. I recommend the Steam application called Controller Companion. Using something like this makes for a much better experience. It is very much playable on keyboard but the catch is that your controls are left and right arrows for the flippers, holding down the down arrow launches the ball and the up arrow nudges up. These controls are not remappable at the time of this review. It is unknown whether this will be added in the future. If you have a controller and a program that can convert to gamepad like the one mentioned prior, you will have a good time here. There are also some bugs and issues reported but I personally have not encountered any of these reported bugs. It is possible that these reported bugs/issues will not be patched because the developer has not made an appearance on the game's forums here on Steam.
This collection is a great gathering of many original designs that were priviously not available to Steam users. They include many fun to play tables with varying degrees of difficulty and design, with great sounds, voices and visuals. The downsides are that with no built-in controller support, the user must use a third-party application to make up for the shortcomings of the control options on offer here. Still playable on keyboard but not as good as playing with controller.

Basically, if you're a digital pinball collector and/or looking for some variety, you might want to get this. I'm actually finding it fairly enjoyable.
There are 15 tables with a variety of themes for $20. That's a reasonable price per table. Yes, this is a mobile port, and it shows.
The physics are very basic (think Space Cadet, but a bit better), and the designs vary in complexity from very simple to moderately complex.
You'll absolutely need to apply anti-lag tweaks, and you'll probably also want to force AA/AF externally.
The 3D graphics are reasonable, but mostly nothing special. The art is quite good, including some decent animations in places. Textures are somewhat low low res and models are low poly, though. No fancy lighting here, but there are some reflections. The graphics/art of the game look much better when you're using the dynamic camera.
There is no controller support or key rebinding. The game doesn't even tell you what the controls are! But I just use JoyToKey, that's not a deal breaker in this case. Controls are left/right arrow for flippers, down arrow for launcher, space for nudge (just upward), C for camera change. R switches to portrait orientation.
There are 3 camera views - top down, angled, and dynamic.
Nudging, as mentioned, exists, but you can only nudge upward. This is basically enough for a nudge pass. There's a tilt system with warnings on a timer (I think), but it takes more than one nudge to trigger a warning.
Dead bounces somewhat work, but are not terribly reliable. Hold passes work on some tables.
Bang backs also work quite reliably on most tables.
The flipper gap is quite small, making slap saves rather effective.
There is multiball (possibly on all tables). I've seen up to 5 balls.
There are kickbacks that are on by default, can be depleted and re-raised, at least on the tables I've played.
Tables typically will have a mix of passive progressive elements and (simple) goal oriented modes. There are some video modes too. There's a decent variety of playfield elements, including extra flippers and playfields. Extra balls are awarded at certain score thresholds. Some tables have fairly involved progressions that are quite difficult (even for me) to progress through.
Music and sound effects are ok - nothing special.
The developers are not native English Speakers (company is based on Russia). This shows in some awkward grammar in places and accented speech clips.
There are working steam leaderboards as well as local high scores (yes, I set #1 scores on the 3 tables I've played through so far ;).
Each table saves progress automatically, even if you kill the game or if it crashes.
There are various bugs I've encountered, some game breaking, but they're not too common. Some elements of some tables don't seem to work correctly. There's a glitch that causes serious game-breaking graphics issues occasionally if you open the help while in game and then immediately resume.

First and foremost, I LIKE “Pinball HD Collection”. I’ve played fifty years of pinball, literally thousands of hours of computer pinball from numerous companies, and no doubt several tens of thousands of games. Naturally, I’ve enjoyed some more, and others less. Computer pinball developers have in general, chosen for themselves a frustratingly Sisyphean task; to compete against those who “port from reality” tables loved (and played to financial success) for decades. But also to create, out of the blue, new tables that will be compared to every table ever made, computer or real, in both design and function. I believe that OOO Gameprom has generally succeeded. (Certainly to this player’s satisfaction.)
The Pinball HD Collection (PHDC) Store Page doesn’t seem to mention that this game offers FIFTEEN tables, and that might go far toward explaining what otherwise may seem to be a high price. What a player gets for $20US are some of the most interesting, creative and non-derivative tables I’ve yet seen. Admittedly, at this point I’ve only play a single game on most tables, but the need to produce this review weighed heavily on me.
Design wise, these are generally very beautiful tables, most having at least one additional playfield (and some have more than I’ve ever imagined) but used wisely and productively. Pinball is in actuality far more than simply flippers and balls…it’s intelligent, wise, fun design. And as far as I can tell PHDC offers those aspects adequately (or beyond) in most cases. One concern seems to be is that this is a ported phone app. Not having ever played a game on a phone, I can only make the comment…..”Who cares?!” I care about design. fun and playability, and I’m mostly satisfied. Where I’m not, I’ll go to the next table and perhaps lose a very small portion of my “investment”.
It’s said by some that PHDC has poor physics. But it has also been said that computer pinball may never match the physics of actual tables, and no doubt that’s true (at least for now.) While I’m generally loath to mention competing products in reviews, I think this example can be excused, and perhaps this alleged completion is itself a myth for these two games. Most of the community agree that Pro Pinball Ultra’s Timeshock! table has the best physics currently available on any platform. I tend to agree. I’ve played in the neighborhood of 2,500 games of Timeshock!, and when going directly from that table to PHDC, I don’t even remotely experience a “physics funk”. True, they aren’t directly comparable, but TS costs approximately ten times as much per table, and has been in development since 1997! In PHDC the ball acts as I anticipate it should, and when I hit it, it goes where I expect it to, utilizing the “middle flipper sweet spot” extensively. For a game geared less for the elite player, and more for the beginning or average player (99% of the pinball market), it obeys the same laws of physics I do. I think that for the most part, complaints about physics are really more a request for a more realistic (or perhaps faster) speed. Personally, I’d be much happier with PHDC if there were at least two game speed choices available.
While it might be nice to make it clearer somehow that in PHDC, the ball is launched by holding the down arrow button, and flippers are operated with the left and right arrow keys, the game rules and instructions are expressed very nicely with a single (though sometimes complicated) graphic of the table currently chosen. (And it’s available during gameplay.) Also, the instructions unfortunately downplay the versatility of choosing from a variety of camera angles during play simply by pressing the “C” key. A very nice feature that may need to be used regularly as the ball enters various playfields.
At this point it’s not clear exactly how to play the two tables that utilize vertical areas of the gamefield – Pinball Fantasy and Pirates. Hopefully I can obtain clarification so I can edit this review. And I’m currently not in a position to comment on the 3-D glasses aspect of this game, strictly from lack of knowledge. The leaderboards are adequate, but after placing 12th on six tables in a row I realized I needed to reset them manually by toggling between “Local” and “Steam” to get accurate data. (But if you want to get in early with some high ranking scores, now’s the time. After a single game on each I managed at least one #1 score, so it’s likely YOU will too.)
Who might enjoy Pinball HD Collection? Anyone will enjoy the creative layouts and original design. For elite players, on some tables some shots can be just too easy to make, and on some of the tables the games may just last too long. (Heck of a complaint, huh?) It’s not for players that value franchise content over the very basic Zen-ness of pinball. It’s also not for those that place achievements first over content. (At least for now. But as I’ve said before, I played pinball for over fifty years before I even heard of achievements.) For beginners, I’d don’t see how a pinball game could be much more satisfying. I still play, and very much enjoy, Balls of Steel (no longer available on Steam) based on it’s amusing and clever layout and design, and I feel fairly certain that if you too still enjoy earlier computer pinball, you will likely enjoy PHDC even more. I’m an average pinball player, but I WILL be keeping this game, and playing it at least occasionally (possibly much more) for a break from the often “too serious” world of competitive pinball. I think PHDC is the perfect game for those who just wish to enjoy pinball at both its most basic……AND more complex.
Thank you.

Let me preface this by saying I have never written a review for a game before, ever. On top of that my Steam library is not that extensive compared to many game collectors, as my preference in games is somewhat particular. With all that being said, I can safely say this is one of the best indie games I have ever played.
First, the knitty-gritty of it: you're going to die. A lot. This is not an easy platformer by any means, especially if you are looking to collect everything, and it was created with that in mind. Every single obstacle, puzzle, and area is set specifically with certain abilities in mind. Attempting to traverse more 'advanced' areas without progressing properly will result in many many deaths, and the kicker is
Now,
, it is not completely impossible to get around these areas, and that's what makes this game so fun. The story helps you progress in a linear fashion like most platformers, while also allowing you to freely explore as much as you're physically capable of (gaining/upgrading said abilities helps with this). Timing, reflexes, precision, and patience are all keys to successfully getting through this craziness, with gameplay mechanics being responsive and itchy at the same time. But through all the attempts, deaths, expletives, and misery you'll spend trying to get over one specific obstacle, the elation you will feel after overcoming it is
. No matter how many times I died, no matter how many times I wanted to face-smash my keyboard; I was never once put-off or disallusioned; this beautiful world continued to engross me.
you hear and read about this game is true. From the moment you launch the game (especially the opening scene: it was freakin' Marley and Me all over again dammit) to the closing credits, it will all pull you deeper into the game, creating one of the most memorable experiences you could ever imagine. The
is phenomenal, adding yet another detailed layer on top of an already vibrant experience that tugs at your heart-strings. It'll definitely hit you in the feels department. The story is charming while also deep, creating a more immense setting than one might initially expect. The artwork and visuals are
as well, providing a rich, colorful, and unexpectedly layered environment. All the typical platformer tropes; it takes these, deconstructs them, and creates something delightfully new and refreshing, while still channeling and tempering the core platformer values. Everything is so perfectly tied together in this game, and I cannot recommend it enough.

A surprisingly solid action RPG. It reminds me a lot of Path of Exile or Titan Quest, along with the original Diablo 2. The skill trees have a moderate amount of depth, along with a torchlight style companion and reputation system that allows you to select special perks to benefit your character.. Skill trees are basically split into your standard magic, ranged and melee skills, plus 2 active "trick" abilities and 2 passive "tricks". My only gripe about the skill system is that you only really get to use 4 abilities at once (thought you can swap them out on the fly), so that may be dissapointing to those who like long  action bars of skills. The loot variety is fairly good, though you'll be sticking with greatswords, dual swords, pistols and long-barreled guns. Armor/weapon appearences also change as you get different gear, which is always nice. At the moment it sounds like the developers are going to be adding a lot of new content, with a new level 30+ scenario mode added for players who hit the level cap of 30, along with coop (already in) and future content planned such as a New Game +. Overall I was pleasantly surprised with this game, I haven't finished it yet at this time, but I've so far enjoyed the hours I've put into it, both with a ranged character and a a melee build.

Really good atmosphere, really good sound. Playing with headphones is highly recommended. Game bounces between simplistic puzzles, simplistic combat, and being a walking sim. Story is interesting, puzzles aren't difficult while not being immediately obvious either, and combat has some depth despite it's simplicity.
Movement in combat is terrible, though. Dodge only executes across short distances and in 4 directions, and sprint only executes straight toward whatever enemy you are locked onto. For most instances this isn't necessarily a bad thing, but in many late-game combat scenarios you'll find yourself facing off against multi-wave monster closets in very small spaces where enemies will frequently just appear behind you. Coupled with the camera, which can get caught behind scenery and completely obfuscate your view, some later combat sequences can be downright frustrating if you find yourself in a bad position.
Environments are good looking, one in particular about halfway through was hellishly amazing. In one area about halfway though the game the framerate took severe dip (sub-20fps, heavy stutter) and persisted in that area even after dropping res/settings to Low/720p. After spending a few hours editing config files to no avail I ended up just pushing through and dealing with the poor performance, which eventually evened back out (1080p/60fps) in subsequent environments. Sadly, many visual options are all baked into two PP/VE option settings, meaning things like motion blur, film grain, AA, AO, etc cannot be toggled individually.
Overall the atmosphere and presentation alone make this worth a purchase IMO, assuming you have the patience to push forward through some potential frustrations. Definitely a unique, albeit flawed experience.

This is a very pretty & polished game with clever game-play ideas that are well executed.  It's a game where you have to quickly type words to defeat enemies and interact with the environment.
But it's not just mindless typing.  The game adds elemental magic that greatly increases your tactical options.  Do you want to use fire magic that burns enemies faster?  Ice that slows down the enemies bearing down on you?  Lightning that can strike multiple foes if you use it correctly?  And the elemental modes and enemy variation are well balanced so that it's actually worth the trouble to think strategically moment-to-moment about which elemental mode is best depending on which enemies are attacking and which directions they are coming from.
The game has an option to adapt to your typing speed. I played with it on and I found the game  consistently challenging but not frustrating.
The little dungeons have more puzzles than I would have expected - not difficult, but engaging.  And the pop-up book style artwork looks great. I enjoyed it.

Paradox have a fantastic collection of history based Grand Strategy Games. Think 'RISK' with a little bit of politics, and that's what you're going to get from Europa Universalis III. Those going in expecting amazing graphics and detailed animated battles will be disappointed, as it's simply not _that_ game.
Fights are math/dice roll based, which take into account unit type, general, terrain, etc so there is depth in the battles. However, visually they are represented by single unit graphic, numbers, and literally dice rolls. I don't mind this, as it suits the desk top game nature that I've come to admire from the Paradox Clausewitz Engine.
Once you overcome this the games become incredibly indepth, with various scenerios based on history appearing throughout the game. You can either follow them as we know them, or change the course of history.
To give you an idea of the scale the game can potentially last over the course of 400 years (if you have all the expansions) from 1399-1821. So you can start at the end of the 'Hundred Year War' and finish around the time of 'Napoleon' with all the history in between.
The latest DLC 'Divine Wind' adds the Far East to EUIII (Japan & China). I haven't had a chance to fully test out this area of the game yet, but it sounds detailed and exciting.
If you enjoy Empire Building (and a slight Dynasty building element), and don't mind a lack of detailed animations to keep your attention span, then this game might be for you.
There's a good thread on GAF, which has plenty of helpful people to help you understand what's going on -

I'm a newcomer to this game; I get the feeling this will be an ongoing opinion. But It has grown on me the more I play it as I have got more used to the way things work within the game. When I first crash landed on a horrible frozen planet, I had no clue as to what I had to do so that I could to get off this frozen wasteland of a planet, OK there were some prompts but performing simple tasks was a challenge. Things became particularly difficult once the mining beam ran out of power. It took a while to realise (and research) that the good old Neanderthal method of hitting things with the multi-tool worked! Also during my initial stumblings, I kept on incurring the wrath of the Sentinels. I am now much wiser, and they no longer kill me for destroying things.
I couldn't find any Zinc to complete the necessary repairs to get my spaceship flying again. Resulting in a long trudge to a small centre with a Landing Pad where I was able to sell some items which I'd accumulated while aimlessly wandering around and buy some Zinc. Eventually, I managed to take off after all that and end up in another hellish planet that was so hot.
There is some hand holding in the game to get you started but working out hitting plutonium with the multi-tool could be used to recharge it. Albeit very slow.
At the start, this game came off as cold and harsh and didn't immediately pull you in like some other space games I've played such as Empyrion Galactic Survival. But it may be exposure to those types of games that made it feel cold and harsh, or it could simply be that I happened to be stuck on a cold, harsh planet.
I didn't think I was going to stick it out though and came close to stopping. But the game gradually grew on me, and now as I have more possessions such as a ship with bigger slots, an Exo suit with more slots, Numerous Exocraft  it is getting a great deal more interesting
I find I end up looking to trade up to ships with more slots. So consequently I never have any money spare. I need to be patient and save up for that nice 48 slot ship. I so far have not seen an option to trade in my old ship though, as you were able to do in the original version of Elite. (I haven't played Elite Dangerous so don't know if you can in that.)  Upgrading slots in your Exo suit can start getting expensive as each extra slot after the first free expansion costs 10,000 units more.
As you travel through the game while heading to the Galactic Core, you mine and collect relics or other objects for trading or constructing items. The one thing that you need to remember is not to be a hoarder. I keep forgetting and ending up running out of slots as I keep significant amounts of Resources with me. Just in case. So a tip for you, do not horde things on you or in your ship, as you limit your ability to make a profit. My base probably will end up on an episode of hoarders! As I have containers full of resources just sitting there waiting for me to sell for significant profit, but I just can't seem to part with my precious horde.
There is a lot I have still to do and have resorted to reading some beginners guides to get some tips, although most of them are for the original version and the subsequent updates have changed things.
Such as previously you could find signal scanners to find abandoned bases, crashed ships, etc. To use these signal scanners you needed to create a bypass key for them. Now you can build the signal scanner.
I'm playing the Normal game mode which offers what they call a chill experience, but there are other modes:
Creative
Survival
Permadeath
I have played Permadeath and Survival; They are a great challenge to even get to your ship. I've had to make many restarts with those two modes. They feature much more aggressive pirates that the Normal mode and resources are much scarcer
So overall for me, this game so far has been worth the money I paid for it. I admit I did pick it up recently for 40% off when it was on sale for the Pathfinder Update. I had looked at this game,  on and off, since it's release, but the large numbers of negative reviews for it put me off. But Now I'm glad I took the plunge, and for me, it was well worth getting past the first few hours of the game.

Finally got it working! For the message: "Message type not defined problemen" I did the following:
1. Uninstall GeForce Experience
2. In Steam Settings; Disable Cloud sync
3. Close Steam
4. Go to: C:\Users\<user>\Saved Games\
5. Delete directory: MachineGames
Then the second part of my problem; Crashing on chaning Video Settings:
1. Go to: C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\Wolfenstein.II.The.New.Colossus
2. Right klik on NewColossus_x64vk.exe and select properties
3. Go to tab Compatibality
4. Turn on: Override high DPI scaling behaviour. Scaling performed by: Application
5. Disable full-screen optimisations
6. Apply -> OK
Then start the game and you would be able to change settings an go to play.
After your session is done, don't forget to turn on Cloud Syncing again in the Steam Settings.

The Incredible Adventures Of Van Helsing is a decent action RPG experience. I've seen games that were a lot worse in the last couple of months. Van Helsing brings nothing new to the table but is enjoyable nevertheless. If you ever played Diablo or Torchlight, or any other aRPG, you know exactly what to expect. Lots of killing, upgrading, sidequests to complete and loot to collect. This game has tons of loot, by the way. Maybe not all useful, but enough to let you choose your own equipment, creating a character based on your preferences. Same goes for the skills and perks. Plenty of choice here.
The game is pretty challenging, but it's not because of its carefully placed (groups of) enemies, but because of the fact that enemies are on every corner of the road, never alone and always in groups. It feels like the developer just spammed enemies on the map, not knowing it would result in difficulty spikes. These enemies frequently get mixed up with a bunch of elites/uniques as well, making the game even harder than it probably should be.
Please note that I do like a challenge, as long as it's fair.
Graphically it looks pretty and it runs reasonably well, despite its framerate issues.
The voice acting is mediocre, but I guess it gets the job done. There isn't a lot of acting anyway, so it's alright.
Van Helsing doesn't do anything particularly wrong except for the enemy placement, and what's there is mostly good fun so if you'd like to have a cheap but lenghty aRPG give this one a spin.

I've never been so pleasantly surprised by a game before! Top-down RPGs aren't generally my thing, but I'm having a blast. The skill combinations result in some pretty sleek and/or carnage-filled playstyles, and all the easter eggs, references and humour are super entertaining. Be careful about your dialogue choices, and you might find that some clever bonuses or really nifty items come your way. If you're in between more serious/thoughtful/stressful games, The Incredible Adventures of Van Helsing a fun way to fill the time.

The Incredibly Long Title of Van Helsing is a fun 10-12 hour (main campaign) hack and slashy romp. What's there is good, though the melee could use a bit more... oomfph.
The skil tree is a bit shallow and some of the abilities don't scale too well at higher difficulties. While the power up system is a unique gimmick, it boils down either feeling too clunky to use on the fly or becoming an automated left or right click with the auto option turned on.
The humor is very tongue-and-cheek and often breaks the fourth wall. Voice acting is pretty good overall with hilariously stereotypical vampire and mad scientist voices.
Environments are well used. Even though you spend half your time in a forest, each one feels unique.
The inventory management and itemization in this game is one of the best in this genre. A simple thing like automatically reorganizing if you pick up something and logically have the space to do so if not for one stupidly placed sword is a godsend.
Overall if Van Helsing had a deeper and more complex skill tree along with a Newgame+ instead of just a pure endgame, this would be a worthy competitor to the big ARPGs. As it is now, it's still a decent romp for its price.

Gauntlet. The game, the myth the legend. The classic arcade game is reborn anew for a new generation. If youre looking for a game to just delve into with friends, or, something to slaughter hordes of enemies in, look no further. From the warrior with his high health and brutal melee attacks to the fragile yet versatile wizard with his spells, theres a character for every basic fantasy. If you have the 3 friends for it (or are willing to play with new people), you will find the abilites of the base four characters compliment each other well.
While it is a pared down version in comparison to the arcade cabinent, it has been polished to a fine sheen. Quest forth on Campaign mode, test your steel in the arena mode, or battle the horde in endless mode. As you play you complete mini achievements for how you interact with the game, which grant gold. Disclaimer: I've owned this game for quite a long time, well before it became available on steam. I've put literally hundreds of hours into it, so the time shown in my steam profile isn't reflective of my experience with the game.
This is one of, if not the best operational level wargames I've played. It's the next logical step up in complexity for people who are comfortable with games like Panzer Corps, Unity of Command and Commander: The Great War. It is both realistic and complex, yet still accessible with a rather gentle learning curve. That said, Blitzkrieg from Warsaw to Paris is quite deep, and you'll be learning something new about the system with each campaign you play.
Included with the game is the 1939 invasion of Poland, the invasion of France and the Low Countries and a hypothetical invasion of Great Britain. There are other minor scenarios available, and tons of variants to keep things interesting and unpredictable. There are also elements to the gameplay like playing decision cards which make Blitzkrieg from Warsaw to Paris unique among its contemporaries.
I recommend this game to anyone who is interested in wargames and ready for a greater challenge (HQs, supply and logistics, etc.) than what is available in more introductory level wargames. Blitzkrieg from Warsaw to Paris presents these more complex concepts in an approachable and elegant manner, resulting in a rewarding and thoroughly enjoyable wargame experience.

Epistory - Typing Chronicles is an unique action adventure/typing game hybrid. You control a girl riding a strange fox and explore a gorgeous origami world. Since this is a typing game, all your actions (apart from movement) are performed by typing words.
The visuals in Epistory are gorgeous and easily the best aspect of the game. The origami art looks superb, especially when new areas are revealed.
The soundtrack is quite nice and the voice acting is solid too. Unfortunately there are some issues with the ambient sounds as some of them are extremely loud compared to the rest of the sound effects and there's no separate volume adjustment for ambient sounds.
Unfortunately the gameplay is rather shallow. The battles are pretty much a pure test of your typing skills. Picking the right spell adds some limited tactical depth, but overall I feel the game could have done much more with the concept.
There are some simple puzzles to solve too, but overall I didn't find the puzzle and exploration aspects of the game particularly satisfying.
The game offers a number of different difficulty levels, including adaptive difficulty (based on your measured typing speed). These should cover a wide variety of typing speeds.
The controls aren't particularly great and it's rather easy to get stuck in the scenery. In practice this isn't as bad as it sounds since most of your playtime will be spent typing.
The story is rather vague and not particularly enjoyable. The writing is surprisingly weak too considering the subject matter.
While I did not encounter any major issues, the game has lots of small glitches and feels rather unpolished. For example enemies sometimes get stuck in the scenery and some of the puzzles suffer from glitches.
Personally I found Epistory - Typing Chronicles a rather disappointing experience. The presentation is great but the gameplay is quite shallow and overall the game feels unpolished. I didn't find the game particularly fun and I wouldn't recommend it unless you are a big fan of typing games.
I played through the game on normal difficulty (with adaptive difficulty turned off). This took me around 5.5 hours.

(Edit: for some reason, the bullet-formatting doesn't show up in Steam's Review 'quick-view', so if you want to read the review, but also want to avoid large blocks of text mashed together, you can click on the review itself, and the opened page should show the bullets properly!)
Epistory - Typing Chronicles is, not so surprisingly, a typing game at heart, combined with aspects from your typical progression-based RPG, along with some basic puzzle-solving ingredients as well. The world consists of a relatively large, multi-biome hub that connects the game's levels together, though you only have access to a percentage of the hub at the beginning of the game, and unlock access to more of it as you progress.
Since the story revolves around the main character re-learning lost memories as the story goes on, I will do my best not to spoil anything there. In a nutshell, however, you play as a young female antagonist who rides a large pet fox, that serves as your main form of transportation throughout the game, battling insectoid enemies with typing-based combat, and earning 'points / experience' to level up various perks that make the main character faster & more powerful.
As mentioned earlier, you fight the insect enemies you come across in your travels by entering into a typing mini-game when they appear. The insects slowly approach your character, but can be defeated by typing words that will show up above their heads. Again, I don't want to spoil too much here since they are unlocked as you progress with the story, but there are four "elements" that all have some benefit within combat (some enemies can only be damaged by a specific element type). These same elements are also required in order to open up more areas of the main hub.
In my opinion, the Pros largely outweigh the cons in Epistory, so if you like typing games, or unique RPG's, you'd be doing yourself a disservice by not picking this one up! (And even for those new to the genre, I think there are still a number of things that will satisfy -- enough so that the game is still worth a shot!)

Epistory is a beatiful game with a nice narrative for people that want to practice their typing skills in a fun and entertaining way.
The game is split into two separate subgames: One is the story mode where you control a little girl on her fox (with three tails! ;)) that needs to find out who she is and where she belongs and the other is an arena battle that pits you against some monsters in different surroundings with no story and no moving around. You play in a third person isometric perspective.
In the story mode you get to explore a wonderous world that gets introduced by an off screen observer whenever you enter new areas. You have to unlock each area by accumulating enough points and then standing in a marked location and the world will literally unfold in front of your eyes (a very nice effect).
Within that world you will find inanimate objects that you can destroy by just typing the words associated with them but also monsters that will come your way and try to kill you to pose a time challenge. Once in a while you will find a "nest" which is basically a local battle arena where you are locked in one place, monsters come at you from all sides and you have to survive for a few waves to complete an area or find something special.
The game works with a skill system that allows you to spend points whenever you level up. The skills you get to spend your points on have to be unlocked first and will include different ways to eliminate your enemies (and some enemies can only be eliminated by certain skills and some traps will also only be solvable with certain skills). Some of the skillsets are nicely worked into the world by appearing as a foreign language that you can't type when you don't have the skill required.
There is also a combo system that allows you to score more points the longer you manage to eliminate new challenges within a certain time. The timer gets pushed back a little with every enemy or thing you eliminate making really long combo chains possible - it gets a bit hecktick though and you have to time certain attacks in the right way so to not kill your enemies before you know where your next target will be otherwise you will loose your combo waiting for new monsters ;)
Sadly the story mode can be completed within a day if your typing skills are medium to high but the story and the world are going to make it a very entertaining day. For those that are not typing that fast: The game has an adaptive difficulty and battles never feel as difficult if you manage to die in one.
The arena mode is a never ending slugfest of monsters. It can be lots of fun and it will test your typing skills much more than the actual game with waves getting more and more dangerous.
Although I really enjoyed plaing the game there are two things that I didn't like so much:
a) story mode is too short and not really challenging (a minor complaint - there is still enough, I just would have liked more)
b) the character controls. I repeatedly ran into the wrong direction because the controls were so unfamilliar and in my opinion unintuitive. If they would have turned the directions by 45° I would have been so much happier with the game ;)
I recommended the game to the rest of my family and am happy that I bought it.

Long version:
This game alternates between exploratory phases and fighting phases. During exploratory phases you travel a paper world which unfolds as you stride, in a way much reminiscent of Bastion. The narrative follows you and is integrated to this exploration (once more, much like Bastion). As you explore, you are mainly looking for chests which bring more XP and collectibles in some levels (art gallery items). There are also some very light puzzles to solve, and environment items you can interact with by typing (you can make flowers by blossom, or you can make wood log disappear). And you can stumble upon nests, which lead to a fight sequence.
Fight sequences are very enjoyable. Insects (worms, spiders, snakes ; okay none of them are insects, but they are called like this in the game) come from different sides of the arena, on a wave-based pattern (if you didn't finish the wave the next one does not appear). If they reach the center of the arena where you stand, you die and have to start the fight again. You kill the insects by typing the words written above them.
A very nice thing is that you have four elemental powers. Each of them have a different effect on the insects you strike and give you an edge. Fire will burn the next word, ice will freeze your foe, etc. Some insects are also of a certain color and can be killed only if you strike them with the right elemental power. This adds some fun variety, but it feels unexploited somehow. As a general rule, all fights are pretty much alike.
This, I think, is one of the main drawbacks of the game. It is well done, fun to play, but you always repeat the same things over and over. Explore a little but, open some chests, wipe a nest, enter a new area, explore, solve puzzles, wipe another nest. At least, each different level have a distinct graphical touch which breaks a little bit the gameplay monotony.  Also, there are no quests and you have no incentive to revisit an area once you found it. The game would have been much greater in my opinion if there had been some additional tasks to perform, or interesting items to dig up.
Killing insects give you XP. You can then buy some upgrades, but usually, you have bought all available upgrades before unlocking new ones, so there is a limited amount of choice in this. XP become thus useless quite early in the game. Unfortunately, gaining new XP and unlocking new abilities could have been a nice incentive to go on even after the end of the story. The only reason left to do so is to unlock the remaining, tedious achievements (e.g. kill 10,000 insects while the counter would be around 2,000 at the end of the story).
Now let's turn to the other main drawback of the game: the story. The game is really really nice, everything has been well thought out, and yet, there is no actual story. There is some narrative line, half allegorical, which ends with some poor 'revelation' (don't expect anything) which withdraws all meaning from the game. It's just about wiping worms nests, basically. This is quite sad as the game would have greatly benefit from a nice story. It almost calls for a nice story, as the tone of the game is delicate, a little precious, so that a proper narrative seems a requirement. Unfortunately this is not the case.
So, Epistory is a nice little game, carefully polished, with charm and qualities, but it could have been much greater with few additions. It is this kind of game for which I wish there would be a DLC - adding some items inside chests, for instance, some lore in the universe, some mystery, I don't know. For in this state, the game leaves a feeling of disappointment, of something unfulfilled, which is quite sad.

'To the Moon' is intelligent, well written and extremely creative. Two scientists dive into a dying man's mind to alter his memories in order to fulfil his final wish. And yes, the game is just as awesome as it sounds. It has some really cool moments and even though the idea is pretty surreal, it is presented to you in a way that it just sucks you in and the game MAKES you believe it is all actually possible. Not only that, you will feel for these characters. Rarely have there been games that tug on my heart strings the way this game did. Some people seem to finish it in one sitting, take 2 or 3 hours to complete it but it took me 5.2 hours for 1 playthrough from beginning to end. I like to be thorough in my games, especially the story heavy ones that rely on exploration. You will want to take it all in with this game because it is just that good.
It is a very basic point and click game, nothing overly complicated and it doesn't require too much work, there are some minor riddles to solve but in the end, it relies for the most part on its emotion heavy story. The game is story driven and the visuals and soundtrack are both there to intensify the experience. Some songs might come over as repetitive (something actually made fun of within the game itself) but you will hardly notice this because the music is just that good. The graphics are reminiscent of the Super Nintendo era and it works for this game. Finally 'To the Moon' is jam packed with useless nerdy trivia for gamers and people who watch all the good tv shows.
'To the Moon' is dark, atmospheric and you won't leave the game unmarked.

I've been playing for about three hours.
The game is very well-optimized: I'm using GTX 1080 + i7 6700k + 64GB RAM, and the game is able to run very smoothly (~100fps, never noticed any framerate drop so far) under highest graphic settings. Overall, in terms of graphics, the game is a huge improvement over The New Order and The Old Blood.
I did run into several problems which have been very frustrating, when I try to start the game at the beginning. At first the game wouldn't start and gave a message window saying something about cannot write crash dump. After some googling, this issue was solved by
, after which the game could start normally, but at the main menu the screen would go black for several seconds, and go back to normal for about one second, and repeat. After some experiments, I found that this issue was caused by G-Sync. Disabling G-Sync would solve it, but the preferable solution is to update to 388.10 driver, which completely solved the problem for me. Besides these two problems I mentioned above, I never had any other problems. The game runs very smoothly and stably.
There have been a lot of negative reviews from people who cannot get the game working. I understand the feeling when one has pre-ordered the game and waited for months, only to find out that he/she couldn't get the game to work. But I wish they could be more patient. Making a game work smoothly for so many different PC builds and systems are extremely hard, and it is almost impossible for the developer to test the game on all of these builds. When running into problems, do some googling and experiments, which usually solves all the problems. If not solved, report your issues to the developer. Being impatient and angry, giving negative reviews doesn't help anybody.

A lot of people are saying that Hello Games were pushed by Sony to release this game early. If that is true, they would understandably stand to lose a lot of ground with a AAA developer/publisher if they even hinted at this. I think everyone knows they oversold and underdelivered what I think is a game that will likely live up to MOST its promises. Eventually.
If this had released initially with the coveted Early Access tag, this game would have been a shooting star of a game. But the above issue, coupled with what is admittedly TERRIBLE PR on Hello Games' part, did the initial negative reaction no favors (if no communication or patches for literally months after publication could qualify at all to be called PR in the first place).
So why should anyone pick this up now? Well, actions do speak louder than words. And in a world where talk has become increasingly cheaper, what's important is being communicated solidly. The patches that have since started to release are high quality, fix bugs, and address community concerns. The developers seem intent on delivering on their promises, if we can be patient. 20th century patient.
A noteworthy improvement recently has been transportation, which I think everyone would agree is key to a solid exploration game. They have added land vehicles, as well as freighter ships you can store your other, smaller ships in. They all handle rather well, though the game has a built-in purposefulness of actions that will take getting used to. Oh, and learn to Melee + Jump to boost!
And when you're not adventuring you can build a base on any planet and make that your home planet. I even liked the addition of teleporting between your base and any space station throughout the universe. This way of always anchoring you in the great expanse ends up adding a sense of purpose woefully lacking in the initial release. You don't get disoriented and it's fun to "go home" once in a while.
They've also fixed controls and made UI enhancements. There's permadeath and a few other modes as well, but I've decided to stick with my initial save file for now so I can't comment on those, my apologies.
I'd argue at this point, this is worth probably 30 USD if you were thinking about getting it before and put it off due to the bad release. 20 or less on sale otherwise. Honestly, we all kinda know what this game was initially going for. I know what we got wasn't quite... there. It's not going to be all of what was intended, but I think we're going to like what we end up with. They have a LOT of money to use to fix this thing.
EDIT: Almost forgot. Can't play with friends directly still. We won't be able to. We can share bases through Steam Workshop and technically you CAN visit them if you can find the planet. Good luck with that. Your friend won't be home. You can use their stuff though, so that's neat. Skyrim doesn't have multiplayer, but we deal with it I guess.

I adore this game. It is simple but far from mindless.
What I love is that it makes 4 different classes with different skills that play differently. Modern games in the likeness of diablo 3 have many classes with dozens of skills but many are useless. Gauntlet keeps things simple but yet each class is unique and fun in its own way. Playing with 4 friends is a blast and there is a skill curve that the origional titles lacked.
The problems with the game are a lack of content, enemy variety, and overall shortness of the experience. There's only a few bosses, there is very limited gear, and while the relic and talisman system is interesting, generally there is a flat out "best" build for a class that makes the other options a moot point.
Still, Gauntlet isn't great because of it's gear selection or character customization. It's great because it is simple, striped down, and doesn't need any of that stuff to be fun to play with your friends.
I never expected Gauntlet to turn into something so uninspired and flavorless.

Very nice addition to the Assassin's Creed franchise. It's kinda nice to see that the side scrollers are making a re-appearance after they faded out in the late 90s. It works much better than I thought, even if it's 2.5D these days.
The gameplay is very smooth, very precise, and the art style is superb. This 2.5D side scroller is easily as immersive as any of the other 3D free roam titles in the franchise and overall the objectives, weapons and game flow are well realized. You learn abilities as you progress through the game, and although you may not be successful the first time, the game sets fair respawn points.
I do think the proposed system requirements are listed a little high. I believe any high-end Core 2 Duo or QuadCore machine (other gaming components of similar, fitting strength being present) should be able to handle it. I am admittedly towards the lower end of the spectrum, and it runs smooth at HD resolution with some additional enhancements turned on within my GPU's control panel.
One issue I have - and this is something I keep mentioning again and again these days - are the controls. I actually did something I said for the longest time I wouldn't do, and bought a game controller (Logitech F310). Keyboard controls cannot be remapped in-game, and even though I was able to remap them using an external tool (GlovePIE), it's a lot of work for something that should be a
! Especially from a well established developer you should be able to expect customizable controls. I'm left handed on top; WASD never worked for me, and never, ever will.
That aside, and especially for the price tag, this is an awesome addition to the series and anyone who calls themselves an Assassin's Creed fan has to simply get this.

Four and a half hours into the game and I have to say this is not exactly what I was expecting, but I am pleasantly blown away by the immersion that Hellblade brings to my gaming experience.
If you want a game with complex combat, loot from every mob, inventory management and a sense of 'leveling' your character in order to become powerful so you can thrash more mobs, loot more corpses and prove you are a bada$$, then this is definitely NOT the game for you. If you like the kind of games that make you go 'whew!' when you close out from playing a couple hours, immersion in a gritty yet beautiful (and simultaneously horrific) environment, a protaganist that doesn't have b@@bs the size of watermelons or a face that belongs on a supermodel, if you like 'realism' in your games and if you want to get every bit of your money's worth from a game, then this game is for you.
I have played all kinds of games-rts, fps, mmo (rpg etc), platformers, rail shooters, etc and I have to say that while some people may b1tch and moan about this game being linear, being 'more of a movie than a game' and all around NOT being a fps shooter or some kind of Viking Skyrim, it is one of the best games I've played in years. Hats off to Ninja Theory for this masterpiece. Great graphics and incredible, just incredible voice-acting, along with the Norse lore given at stiles throughout the game bring this experience to a level unmatched by most of what Steam has to offer.
Other reviews have gone into detail about the psychological aspects of the game. I won't add to that except to say that it's rather disturbing at times, though it does not distract from the gameplay-it enhances it in spades.
The only negative comment I have about the game is the lack of mouse adjustment. I would like to be able to turn Senua a bit quicker, but I realize that this is part of the realism of the game. I have read books that don't create 1/3 of the sympathy for the protagonist that Hellblade has generated within me for Senua. I've decided not to rush playing through this game because it seems to stick with me after logging out. THAT is the sign of a game that is more than a game. If you are looking for a casual game to piddle away a couple of hours while WoW updates or if you're looking for a game with a stripper in a chainmail bikini fighting orcs and goblins in a Norse setting, look elsewhere.

As someone who lives with serious mental illness and undifferentiated psychosis, this game made me extremely happy. While I do have a few mechanical and design quibbles with the game, they're vastly outweighed by the quality of writing and voice acting on display here, as well as the effort that has gone into seeking out perspectives from mental health professionals and victims of psychosis to create a piece of fiction that accurately reflects the reality of these crippling illnesses.

My thoughts on Trine:
Trine is a beautifully designed 2D action-jumping-fighting-puzzle solving indie game. You get to play three differennt characters at once - a knight, a thief and a wizard. While obviously only controlling one of them at a time, you can switch between those three at any time, using their individual strenghts and abilities to make it to the other side of the map.
As the knight, you're armed with shield and sword and are capable of lifting heavy objects and throw them at your enemies. The shield can be used to block any incoming attack, while the sword is the perfect weapon to deal with the growing numbers of skeletons, bats, and other enemies that you'll encounter.
The thief is armed with a bow and thus able to fight enemies from afar (duh), and can shoot a rope on wooden objects to swing across pits, pull herself out of them in case you still manage to fall and perform cool looking jumps.
As the wizard, you can summon cubes or planks to make yourself an easy way across pits, build stairs to get over high cliffs or drop them on your enemies.
Each ability and spell can be upgraded throughout the game, like letting you shoot several arrows at once, create more cubes to stack on each other or make your sword even deadlier. There are hundrets of casks granting you exp or mana hidden across the game and finding (and reaching!) them all is no easy task!
The graphics are among the best I've seen on a 2D game, only behind this games successor Trine 2. A special praise goes to the awesome person who created this beautiful soundtrack, the music fits this game just perfectly.
I personally didn't like all of the jumping parts that much, just because I'm usually not a big fan of jumping games (and suck at it too), and died several times over. I know I'm criticising a jumping game for its jumping parts, so someone who's into that kind of stuff will have a really good and challenging time with this game. For people like myself, it's still enjoyable, and swining around with the thief is fun, but after a while it can get boring. There could be more different enemies too, since in like the first three chapters or so all you fight are skeletons and bats.
Lots of good things to be said and a few bad too, still I'd recommend anyone to buy this game, especially if it's on sale for like € 1,- or so.
If you like a good platformer then you'll love this game. I highly recommend this game!

Is your Fallout 3 GOTY PC copy always freezing every 5 minutes? Here's an easy fix:
1) Search the fallout.ini file (back it up if you want)
2) Find the line: bUseThreadedAI=0
3) Change the line to: bUseThreadedAI=1
4) Now add another line after it and insert: iNumHWThreads=2
This will limit the game to 2 cores, and prevent the engine from freezing. Ever since I've used this quick solution I've had zero crashes. Have fun!

I've tagged Fallout 3 as one of my top games in my Steam account. I've actually put way more hours into it than my Steam account shows (see note below), and it's one of my favourite games of all time.
I love the post apocalyptic setting - this game really pulls it off. But unlike some of the other Bethesda games such as Skyrim (which I also love!) this one has a really engaging landscape. There is stuff to check out everywhere! I get so sidetracked when doing quests because there's always something that catches my eye and I think "oooh what's that?" and I go check it out. There's so much to do!
In the most part the quests are really good, but I admit I was getting a little bit annoyed near the beginning of the main quest with the constant "looking for Dad".
One thing that is great about FO3 is the very satisfying weapons. Some shooters can be a little weak, and RPGs are usually weaker still with the FPS elements but I found FO3 to be very solid. Yeah the AI is not brilliant but the weapons themselves feel very good. I particularly love taking somebody's head off from half a mile away with a sniper rifle :-)
Also, you can't really talk about a Bethesda game without discussing mods! I'm a big modding fan and I never play these games vanilla for very long. I used FWE, MMM & EVE along with several mods that added new perks and a mod that allowed you to level up more slowly but get several perks per level which I really liked.
Overall, it's a fantastic game and I'm really looking forward to playing New Vegas and then Fallout 4! (Yep, I'm seriously behind on my gaming!)

'To the Moon' is intelligent, well written and extremely creative. Two scientists dive into a dying man's mind to alter his memories in order to fulfil his final wish. And yes, the game is just as awesome as it sounds. It has some really cool moments and even though the idea is pretty surreal, it is presented to you in a way that it just sucks you in and the game MAKES you believe it is all actually possible. Not only that, you will feel for these characters. Rarely have there been games that tug on my heart strings the way this game did. Some people seem to finish it in one sitting, take 2 or 3 hours to complete it but it took me 5.2 hours for 1 playthrough from beginning to end. I like to be thorough in my games, especially the story heavy ones that rely on exploration. You will want to take it all in with this game because it is just that good.
It is a very basic point and click game, nothing overly complicated and it doesn't require too much work, there are some minor riddles to solve but in the end, it relies for the most part on its emotion heavy story. The game is story driven and the visuals and soundtrack are both there to intensify the experience. Some songs might come over as repetitive (something actually made fun of within the game itself) but you will hardly notice this because the music is just that good. The graphics are reminiscent of the Super Nintendo era and it works for this game. Finally 'To the Moon' is jam packed with useless nerdy trivia for gamers and people who watch all the good tv shows.
'To the Moon' is dark, atmospheric and you won't leave the game unmarked.

Literally the best purchase I have made in a very long time.
I have been a gigantic fan of platformers all of my life. It has been depressing that they mostly fell out of style. The only place that you seem to be able to find them now is in the indie scene and when you are getting games there you take a wild chance on whether or not they will be good. This game fulfilled everything that I had been looking for in a platformer.
The story is decent, the talents you get are fun and easy to use, and the art is breathtaking. The game flows seamlessly between cutscenes and gameplay to a point where there were times I was just standing around because I had not realized I got control back. There were quite a few refreshing 'skills' that you can use to navigate the world that made it more than just jumping and the way you can chain moves together makes just running around a blast. There is quite a lot of backtracking, especially if you are a collector, but the later skills you get in the game make it fun instead of a dry and boring trek as is often the case.
I have only one true complaint with it all. The game does have a completionist percentage to each map, which I love. However, there is one section on the map that becomes inaccessible. I took a wrong guess on the right path and locked myself out of ever completing that portion of the map during that run. It was frustrating, to say the least.
Overall, I love this game. If you like platformers I truly encourage you to give it a try. It rekindled my love in platformers and gave me hope that there are people that can resurrect the genre.

Mirrors is a good addition to the puzzle genre. It has enough mechanics that make its gameplay easy to play but difficult to master. There's a surprising number of stages too. At time of writing, I've played two and a half hours and am still unlocking new tombs to be completed. The Curator's Well feature is also well-realised, and decent to use. The game has been regularly updated since launch, with plenty of bug fixes and improvements. They also added Steam Achievements and localisation. This game is good value for money considering the content included for the price.
Summarise:
+ Solid gameplay, easy to play and difficult to master
+ Plentiful levels
+ Haven't encountered any bugs
+ Regular updates in response to user feedback
+ Level creator is fun to experiment with
+ Potential for growth
+ Good value for money
- Level creator UI can be confusing at first. Open menu, select item, close menu, place item.
- Unable to share creative levels via social media or workshop (for now, according to developers)

It’s all very pretty, but not as pretty as I think it ought to be. For some reason the characters appear very scratchy, which I think is a result of having been designed to look much better when seen closer up, and not well surviving the distant camera necessary for letting you see the wor(l)d around you. However, the presentation is undeniably lovely. As you roam around, the esoteric story is told by a narrator, with the words appearing as text on the land. Typed letters go black and then completed words fade away, with additional magical abilities adding further effects to the mix. Fire, for instance, means every other word for an enemy will burn away, allowing you to take on multiple encroaching bads by judiciously typing on one, then another, then another, balancing their deaths before they getcha.
To prevent your travelling too far, too soon (and as such presumably to prevent your seeing the whole of the moon), different coloured words are in different unknown languages – only when you’ve learned the language will they appear in English, meaning you need to solve one area to progress to the others, each sprawling out from the central starting area. There are also sections that will only appear once you’ve scored enough points, which is a lot less elegant, but again ensures the game opens up as you’re ready for it.
Rather brilliantly, this isn’t limited to QWERTY keyboards, either. It supports AZERTY, QWERTZ, DVORAK, COLEMAK, WORKMAN, NEO2 and BEPO, and comes with adaptive difficulty if it recognises you’re banging out the words too quickly. Words are often thematically linked to whatever they’re attached to, sometimes amusingly, giving the game a sense of curation rather than just being a series of random typing tasks.
Whether it actually improves your typing I’m not sure, but it gives you statistics on your speed and so on, which you can compare before and after I guess. I’d not see the game that way at all, though, and instead recognise it as a novel (fnarr) way to play a cute, gentle third-person action RPG.
It really is a lovely thing, offering a good amount of game for a tenner, rising above its own gimmick to be a little bit special.

Four and a half hours into the game and I have to say this is not exactly what I was expecting, but I am pleasantly blown away by the immersion that Hellblade brings to my gaming experience.
If you want a game with complex combat, loot from every mob, inventory management and a sense of 'leveling' your character in order to become powerful so you can thrash more mobs, loot more corpses and prove you are a bada$$, then this is definitely NOT the game for you. If you like the kind of games that make you go 'whew!' when you close out from playing a couple hours, immersion in a gritty yet beautiful (and simultaneously horrific) environment, a protaganist that doesn't have b@@bs the size of watermelons or a face that belongs on a supermodel, if you like 'realism' in your games and if you want to get every bit of your money's worth from a game, then this game is for you.
I have played all kinds of games-rts, fps, mmo (rpg etc), platformers, rail shooters, etc and I have to say that while some people may b1tch and moan about this game being linear, being 'more of a movie than a game' and all around NOT being a fps shooter or some kind of Viking Skyrim, it is one of the best games I've played in years. Hats off to Ninja Theory for this masterpiece. Great graphics and incredible, just incredible voice-acting, along with the Norse lore given at stiles throughout the game bring this experience to a level unmatched by most of what Steam has to offer.
Other reviews have gone into detail about the psychological aspects of the game. I won't add to that except to say that it's rather disturbing at times, though it does not distract from the gameplay-it enhances it in spades.
The only negative comment I have about the game is the lack of mouse adjustment. I would like to be able to turn Senua a bit quicker, but I realize that this is part of the realism of the game. She doesn't sprint like she's attempting to set a record in the 100m, but for some reason she does shuffle sideways a little faster than she runs forward. Weird, huh?
I had one bug/glitch when I was in a ditch (when I should not have been) and fell through the world. Glad to see that some things in games never change. Otherwise, no hitches, stumbles, artifacts or general all-around bugginess in the game so far. Run it on max if your PC will allow, your eyes and your ticker will thank you.
Overall, $30 for a game of this caliber is a great deal. I've got a stable of sorry EA releases which never morphed into anything beyond something to make me want to slap the devs. I have AAA titles I paid almost twice as much for without 20% of the effort Ninja Theory put into this game. I have read books that don't create 1/3 of the sympathy for the protagonist that Hellblade has generated within me for Senua. I've decided not to rush playing through this game because it seems to stick with me after logging out. THAT is the sign of a game that is more than a game. If you are looking for a casual game to piddle away a couple of hours while WoW updates or if you're looking for a game with a stripper in a chainmail bikini fighting orcs and goblins in a Norse setting, look elsewhere.

As someone who lives with serious mental illness and undifferentiated psychosis, this game made me extremely happy.  It's nice (and rare) to see a piece of fiction that handles these issues with the gentle, sympathetic touch that is needed to avoid further stigmatizing mental illness - I was very hopeful for Hellblade, and am thrilled that my trust wasn't misplaced.
While I do have a few mechanical and design quibbles with the game, they're vastly outweighed by the quality of writing and voice acting on display here, as well as the effort that has gone into seeking out perspectives from mental health professionals and victims of psychosis to create a piece of fiction that accurately reflects the reality of these crippling illnesses.

The only game I've ever played that is anywhere close to this is Spec Ops: The Line. Many hated that game but I think they didn't get it.
Hellblade takes the concepts from The Line and blows them out of the water. I've found myself tensed up just by the voices in Senua's head telling me I'd fail, kudos to Ninja Theory for nailing that. Soundbar users will miss out on much in this title due to audio being very important. Headphones or a legit multi channel AVR are required.

Heads up -  This review is pretty much me raving about how great this game is, prostrating myself before it in all its glory.
When I reviewed Hellblade originally, I was 3.5 hours in (out of roughly 7.5), and my mind was utterly blown by how great this game is. Now, having played through the game not once, but twice, my opinion is unchanged. This is easily the best game I've pre-ordered on Steam. It may even be one of my favourite games, period. The character detail, lighting, and motion capture are the best I've ever seen in a game, and coming from a 3D artist, that's saying something.
At this price point I was expecting maybe a 2-hour experience with very simplistic combat. I bought it for the visuals and atmosphere more than the gameplay anyway. However, upon playing through the first couple of fight sequences, I found the combat was a lot more complex than I imagined, with a full combo system including short thrusts, heavy swings, blocks, counters, kicks, punches, sidesteps, combat rolls, and leaping-sprint attacks (all of which flow flawlessly from one pose to the next). While a lot of the combat sequences do become rather samey over time, there are a few different enemy types that help break it up a bit, and the boss fights are epic on a scale that rivals Dark Souls, in my opinion.
If I had to complain about anything in this game, it would be the sluggish out-of-combat player movement, which makes traversing large areas a bit of a chore, especially if you have to go back and forth searching for clues to solve puzzles. Another very minor thing I dislike is the obnoxious glowing runes that float in the air when interacting with lore objects. They tend to break the immersion from the incredible environments and lighting. I would have preferred it if they were just engraved symbols that lit up briefly when you touch them or walked near them.
All-in-all, it's a fanstastic visual experience with surprisingly satisfying combat, great storytelling, epic music, and intelligent puzzles, albeit with slow player movement. At this price I highly recommend it.

Is your Fallout 3 GOTY PC copy always freezing every 5 minutes? Here's an easy fix:
1) Search the fallout.ini file (back it up if you want)
2) Find the line: bUseThreadedAI=0
3) Change the line to: bUseThreadedAI=1
4) Now add another line after it and insert: iNumHWThreads=2
This will limit the game to 2 cores, and prevent the engine from freezing. Ever since I've used this quick solution I've had zero crashes. Have fun!
