To the Moon tells us a wonderfully written, captivating and touching story of life, death and of a very simple - yet the greatest - thing, called: love. The game does this so beautifully that you are guaranteed to cry many times throughout the course of the events. It's the triumph of storytelling that a game built on an ancient japanese rpg engine (first used by Dragon Quest), with text-only dialogue and without any complex puzzles whatsoever can offer such a deep experience. Because contrary what the engine would suggest, To the Moon is an adventure game and could be best compared to a wonderfully good book.
The main concept of the game can be a bit untempting (at least it was for me, even though I do love sci-fi). In the near future people on their deathbeds can order a service with which they can relive their lives in a perfectly ideal way, having artificial memories implanted into their minds. Thus they can pass away peacefully and in happiness. This process requires a specific machine (made by Sigmund Corporation) and skilled technicians who must discover the hidden wish of the patient and fulfill it by taking a different path at certain points of the person's life.
The player takes the role of two such technicians, Dr. Eva Rosalene (Senior memory traversal agent) and Dr. Neil Watts (technician specialist). They both have different personalities: Dr. Rosalene being the more serious one (still she also cracks better jokes) and Dr. Watts being childish (and somewhat subordinated to Dr. Rosalene). They also regulary mock each other.
Strangely enough they aren't the game's main protagonists. but the dying old man, their current patient, Johnny Wyles and the love of his life, River (who has passed away not long ago). Johnny and River were high-school sweethearts and were seemingly made for each other, still, their marriage wasn't as happy as expected. Johnny now lives alone on a cliff near the ocean, with a beautiful view to a lighthouse, with Lily, the housekeeper and her two children. Johnny's dying wish is a journey to the Moon.
The two technicians traverse back through time in Johnny's life via several decisive mementos, that played an important role in his life. With each leap backwards they/we get to know Johnny's life beginning from a few days before to his high school years. In most of these memories, River is also present. When the technicians finally reach Johnny's childhood, they encounter a memory block and therefore unable to travel to the point when Johnny was a small kid. They don't attach great importance to it and begin the installation of his new "memories". However it seems Johnny has absolutley no desire to go to the Moon. At this point Eva and Neil must somehow awaken an interest in him towards the Moon.
The gameplay is very simple: by controlling Eva and Neil the player must explore each memory segment (in the upper section of the screen we can always check which segment of Johnny's life we are in), solve some hidden-picture puzzles and then travel back in time to the next memory. In order to do this however, you'll have to find and unlock mementos by collecting memory orbs. These memory orbs can be acquired by clicking on familiar characters, items, or locations. You can't get stuck, as the solution is often intuitional: for example at the ranch where Johnny and River go horseback riding, you have to catch up with the lively and joyous River and ride alongside her to receive the orbs (this segment contains the loveliest tune in the game by the way: Take Me Anywhere).
Besides Take Me Anywhere the main theme is also amazing as is the rest of the music in the game, always perfectly reflecting the current tone of the given memory segment. These piano themes are fantastic and further facilitate the brilliance of the game.
The ending is lovely but also a bit of a letdown (don't worry, there is a happy ending :)), because it is predictable what Eva is planning to do with River in Johnny's memory. I think it would've been a bit better if it was up to Neil (who actually changes over the course of the story in a positive way) to rearrange Johnny's memory and leave River in the role she deserved to be in.
Still that's only a minor lament from my side and hardly detracts from the game's value. To the Moon points it out how beautiful memories ordinary people can have and is one of those few games that should be played by every single person all around the world.
I'm sure the world could be a better place after that.
PROS
+ superbly written, heartbreaking love story
+ great, loveable characters
+ charming music
+ often sad, often hilarious dialogues
+ some of the sections are so beautiful, they're worth replaying
CONS
- River shouldn't have been removed from Johnny's childhood memory
- Dragonball references
RATING
9.5/10

(edited on 2-8-2017 to reflect recent fixes)
Game Overview
At a glance you may mistake the game for Smite but you’ll soon find its much faster paced and will take much more practice to nail your character’s combinations. The 30 characters come with 4 unique abilities each and are divided into 4 classes: Specialist, Assault, Support, and Defense. Your team’s success will require a balanced combination of choices and a commitment to fulfilling the role of your selected character. The control scheme will play similarly to other 3rd person MOBA titles however abilities are much less telegraphed and require a great deal more precision to master. Tuebor’s game modes are objective driven and draw inspiration from titles like Rocket League and the Unreal Tournament series. Let’s Take a look at the available game modes.
Skull Ball
Think Rocket League on foot with an arsenal of weaponry where killing the other team is just as important as scoring! Your team can boost how far they hit the ball by killing opponents granting a significant edge. Try to score while watching out for the unique environmental hazards that each map has to offer. The new Breath of Fire map is particularly dangerous as fire breathing skulls always seem to be looking your way.

Death and Glory
A group of six attempts to kill off waves of bad guys while defending two reactors that power your Translocators (necessary for respawning you and your friends). As an added bonus, or possibly hazard, keeping the basement free of bad guys will reward you a salvage bonus for every wave you pass without the experiments contained within being released. Flooding the basement with lava is an option but you’ll forgo the extra salvage and have to deal with more baddies targeting the reactors.
Capture the Core
Featuring chaotically large 8 person teams a single core spawns in the middle of the map, capture it and return it to your base. Take over forward spawn locations and turrets to give your team an edge. Keep in mind that you can’t attack while carrying the core, so you’ll have to rely on your teammates ability to defend while you scramble back to your side of the map.
Team Annihilation
Classic team death match, with no other map objective to be a distraction you’ll have to master abilities and hone your killing skills. The team with the most kills at the end of the time limit wins so stay close and watch each other’s back!
Playing in any game mode will reward your account with “salvage”, an in game currency that can be used to purchase skins and upgrades that occupy customization slots on each of the 30 characters. Where you spend your salvage will have a profound impact on your character’s performance. Purchased skins are more than cosmetic with camo skins offering an increased chance of dodging attacks and arctic skins extending ability range. Spending salvage on various modules can boost energy, armor, shield, and other stats. Use these upgrades to build characters that suit your play style, no two players will build their heroes the same with an extreme amount of customization choices.
Criticism
Keep in mind that the game is still in Early Access and FREE while SIN Studios polishes the game. This is refreshing to see in a world where Early Access is too often abused not to improve the game but to accelerate revenue. That being said there are still some bugs to work out! If you put effort into it you will be able to get your character stuck in certain spots or find exploits where NPC bad guys won’t be able to get to you. I have also managed to get myself outside of the normal boundaries of the map a few times. The developer is working on fixing this issue and the others mentioned. We (Infirmary Gaming) have witnessed frequent patches that directly address our concerns and improve the game in general. Do your part! Give Tuebor a try during Early Access and if you do find any bugs or have constructive criticism join the Sin Studios Discord server and let the Devs know yourself!
Infirmary Gaming is a proud supporter of Strength in Numbers Game Studios. Indie Developers are critical to the growth of the gaming industry we appreciate their mutual support for Infirmary Gaming Community and the development work they do!

Not since Sacred (2004) have we seen a Diablo-esq game of this type. What Van Helsing may lack in overall polish or content, it more than makes up for with an incredibly well-designed combat system and genuinely witty banter between the two main characters. The plot, though incomplete right now, ain’t half bad either.
You play as Van Helsing, son of *that* Van Helsing, accompanied by the lovely (and beheaded) Katarina. Even though there’s only one playable class, Van Helsing provides ample customization variety. You toggle between sword-based melee and gun-based ranged attacks on the fly, both styles with their own skill trees and magic spells. All attacks have a kind of “power up” system that lets you add extra oomph to an attack on demand, if you have enough “rage” built up. It would take too long to explain the nuances of the combat here, which is a pity.
Katarina is herself, a functional and very useful companion. You decide which skills she learns, when she should be using health potions, if she should pick up items or not, if she should stay ranged or attack up close, and like the pet in Torchlight II she can be sent off on an errand to sell items and buy potions. She acts as a great counterpoint to Van Helsing’s stoicism, throwing barbed insults at the up-and-coming monster hunter, but tempered with a genuine respect and warmth.
The world being hand-crafted, everything is placed with purpose. There are plenty of secrets to find, and pop-culture references to stumble across. Monsters have a degree of randomness in where they spawn, but only when returning to cleared areas. This does limit the variety when doing subsequent playthroughs some. The upshot: when loading a previous save, you’re placed exactly where you left off instead of at the start of randomly-generated map, like in Diablo III.  Boss encounters deserve special mention for being imaginative and well designed, something quite rare in the genre.
But how is the loot, since that’s what this genre is all about, right? To NeocoreGames credit, they seem to have a firm grasp on the kind of granular itemization games like this need. Items come in all the expected flavours (normal, magical, rare, legendary, set) and house a lot of the kind of stats that assist in build diversity. You might suddenly find an item that makes you consider changing your entire build paradigm, just to benefit from the item’s unique properties. Items may have hidden properties as well, only uncovered once certain criteria are met (damage dealt, enemies killed, etc).
Everything is wrapped up nicely in a powerful game engine with an absurd amount of detail settings. The screenshots don’t do it justice.

Van Helsing is an arpg fantasy game set in the not too distant past. You play as the son of Van Helsing and, like your father, you have a variety of spells, ranged weapons, and blade weapons at your disposal. The story isn’t great, but it’s also no worse than the stories in other arpgs. Van Helsing, the ghostly companion, and a few other notable characters have decent voice work, but the rest of the cast is plagued by lines likely composed by the programmers themselves. Most of the locations are graphically pleasing, but some appear slightly blurry (idk why???). The-game play is smooth and responsive; the enemies vary in aesthetics and behavior; and the progression system is elaborate and rewarding. Overall, the game at its core is great, but bugs, glitches, and oversights (see comment section) compound to drastically ravage the overall experience.
The Incredible Adventures Of Van Helsing: 7.5 / 10.0

Late adopter here: just bought the game during the $35.99 sale. Was very skeptical given the bad reviews, but also curious, because it seems like the kind of game I'd like. It does feel like some things get repetitive - like the space stations - but there is also a lot of interesting variety and depth. It compares favorably to two games I enjoy a lot: I think it out-planet explores Astroneer, and also out-does Everspace for roguelike star system exploration - not bad!  As someone who felt burned by Elite:Dangerous, I'm happy that the developer isn't burning their early supporters by cutting the price and then charging for the DLC that makes the game worthwhile. Good choice! All in all, very much worth the $35.99, and will see many more hours of playing time.

I held off on this game after release, only to buy it now (on sale) and find out that it’s pretty much what I hoped it would be. This is what I wanted from the game, and this is what I got:
1)	Light on story, but heavy on exploration
2)	Scanning, mining, gathering, salvaging, repairing
3)	Survival elements, but nothing so heavy handed that it feels like a survival game
4)	Cool space ships you can build or trade for
5)	Resource management
6)	Interesting creatures and biomes
7)	Impressive land to orbit transitions, with many planets and space stations to land in
This game (as is) is for casual players who simply want to escape into a different world, see crazy things while working on getting a bigger and better space ship. It is not Star Citizen (but good thing that game is coming!) but more of an SC-lite version. I personally did not expect any amount of multiplayer from NMS, so what we get (names, base sharing) is enough for me. I also really enjoy the art style, can’t wait to get back into the worlds and explore some more.
This is definitely a family friendly game, and one of the first I will play with my son.
EDIT: For those who think I'm not allowed to review a game after casual play? Guess what? I am totally allowed to, and this review is for people who will appreciate the game casually as well.
I will never understand someone who puts 400 hours into this (or another) game and then downvotes it. That's far more absurd than my review for obvious reasons. What can I say about Trine? It's pretty good. This is how character switching should be done (I'm looking at you CreaVures!). In Trine you play as three separate characters who are magically bound together, due to the three touching some hokey magical item that apparently does this, and only one of the characters can be active at once in some sort of multiple personality disorder situation where your other personalities can bring weapons along with them. Makes sense? No? Well it doesn't have to because the gameplay is good. Trine doesn't make you go back and walk your other characters through the same level after one has cleared it already because all characters occupy the same space. Good old platforming with skill switching to accomplish certain tasks. That is what Trine offers and it does not fail to disappoint.

The shooting is good. This game feels better than a lot of other shooters out there. Blowing half a dozen Nazis in half with dual wielded fully automatic shotguns will never get old. With that being said the game doesn't feel nearly as good as the New Order. You're too squishy. You're often forced to play the CoD style of pop in and out of cover. The weapons also feel generic.
Problem is you're not shooting as much in this game as in the previous 2 entries. You'll spend literally about half your time watching cutscenes. It's a shame really. Anytime you get into a good groove with the shooting you're pulled out to listen characters vomit their idealogical views at you for 10-20 minutes. There's simply too much story (not even that good tbh).
The ending was also underwhelming; it just kinda stops. Remember how the New Order ended? BJ fighting a 25ft tall Nazi deathbot in the middle of a badass lightning storm in a burning building with a nuclear bomb about to be set off. For those of you who have played that, compare it to this game's ending.
At it's best the game is a lot of fun, at worst it's a mediocre movie. If you haven't played any Wolfenstein games go buy the New Order/Old Blood instead.

LEGO Worlds has come a long way since when I initially bought it in Early Access, around the time of release. However, it was only interesting initially, and a fast growing dissapointment with each late monthly release. I had given up and abandoned watching for updates some time mid to early 2016. When I soon saw that it was releasing with all it's buggy features and small content, I was face palming in that the game was no where near ready yet.
When my friend said I should try it again though, I did so expecting the same old dissapointment from the update posts. I was wrong, LEGO Worlds had changed so much that probably only the base code and the models were the same. Though the two main issues I don't like about this game are the undead, and the bugs.
When it comes to undead I have to first off state what
the obvious, that undead, vampires, zombies, and the like are NOT for children! I don't care how dressed up or silly the animations are, that's going to give someone nightmares. The other part about this is I'm sick to death about zombies in every possible corner you look.
The other reason is that the LEGO Games with the TT engine have started out fine and enjoyable, but as they continued down the production line, I was facing a growing dissapointment with each new LEGO game. Always building up my hopes, to dash them down to dissapointment in say, a few hours. LEGO Worlds at least had a longer time frame and slightly different, but the reasons are roughly the same: LEGO Worlds uses the same engine, and hasn't bothered to fix the same bugs that poke out like a sore thumb since the first LEGO Starwars. You'd think with almots a decade, LEGO could learn something here. However LEGO Worlds adds in new mechanics too, and with new mechanics and features, come new bugs. LEGO Worlds is playable.
I tried to ignore the undead but they pop up so often it's impossible not to. I'm afraid I can't trust LEGO to build a decent game because the issues presented are never fixed, they move on to the next new feature without addressing the issues, and dress up the gameplay to suck you in and move on to the next marketing "scam." Being a LEGO fan it pains me to say this but that's honestly how I feel now. :/

Amazing little game with great art, style, and soundtrack!
The concept (typing-based combat) has a lot more complexity than you'd expect, especially towards the latter part of the game. While the game's difficulty is adaptive by default, if you're a competent touch typist I recommend just setting it to max.
The words aren't chosen at random from a dictionary either - they're linked to the actual things and creatures in the game world, as well as the story in some cases. The entire concept is linked with the story, and just feels really well connected.

When I got this game, I did not know what to expect. Maybe I did expect to play a game where I would have to type, but I did not think I would be this engaged in the story.
First of all, I love the art style. It is absolutely stunning and even the parts that had less things placed around were a wonder to look at. The soundtrack is amazing and very calming and it is even right when you go into battle, it just gets your attention more.
The story is a bit all over the place if you do not stick to something, but that is very hard to do. All the bits collected from the different parts of the world come and mold together into an outstanding story about a female character. The narration is beautifully done and the voice acting is good. What I liked more about it is that even when you hurried through areas and you pass 2 or 3 places where the narrator starts talking, if she is saying the words from the first part, she will not just cut in the middle of the text and jump to the next one. The narration is continued normally and it flows so naturally.
The game is not really for everybody, but it is a nice adventure with somewhat challenging experiences and is very pleasant to look at. If you have any intention to buy this game, as small as it is, just buy it. It will be worth your time and money.

The art style is lovely, a blend of origami and animation styles that I haven’t seen before. As for story, its good, better than I expected from a game like this but it’s overall ending lacked some of the emotional impact I was hoping for. Overall the game is worth your time, especially if you’re looking for something you haven’t seen before.

So, I'm an IRL off-roader and currently my Jeep needs a head gasket and the front end of my pickup was destroyed, and rather than spend my precious days off in the pouring rain, it's more fun for me to race through the sunny maps in this game.
Some things the game does well:
+ Your ruts really messing up at the start of hills and on the second laps...the high-centering emulation is great
+ In-cab cam really emulates that terrifying feeling of not being able to see where you're going next all of the time and having to drive from memory.
+ It captures the sort of time trial challenges of professional competitions with closed circuits and tight corners very well
+ Super off-roaders are fun!
Some things it does poorly:
- It's really hard to use the external camera. I don't have a game pad (RTS/MMO player here) and so must use the keyboard setup. With your right hand on the up/down/left/right controls and bottom row of keys, you have to take your hand off the vehicle controls to move the camera. If you set it up to a more traditional WASD vehicle control setup, your right hand has to be on the bottom row of keys and you're constantly jumping your right hand back and forth between the differential locks and the camera...and the mouse's native sensitivity is such that when you put your hand on it even lightly the camera jumps all around. So, I just use the in-cab camera.
- Only includes super off-road vehicles like "truggies" and what-have-you. I'd prefer a game with some stock vehicles, maybe even ones I've driven in real life. I'd rather struggle in a little Toyota pickup or an F-150 than, honestly, driving these ridiculously expensive competition vehicles. My favorite vehicle in Spintires is the stock UAZ. :)
- It doesn't have that Test Drive: Offroad (I still have the original cardboard box on my game shelf!) feeling of fast and furious fun racing we've sort of come to expect from an arcade viewpoint, and while I think it does time trials very well, I can't help but wish I were racing around a track, knocking over opponents and doing fun jumps.
- As it's a time trial, there's no shortcuts to discover.
- Because it's a time trial, there's no open-world exploration. They could have added some large maps to bumble around and discover your way to the end point as quickly as possible. Imagine if Spintires had a mode where you needed to reach a specific point on the other side of the map as quickly as possible...searching through myriad paths and making myriad mistakes would keep you busy for hours. And if you had competition to observe or deal with, each taking their own route...man, that's be Tops Bloobies (Adventure Time reference, in case you were wondering). Although, considering that this is an older game and Spintires is an anomaly, it might not have even been possible with their development time/budget (or even on their radar as a possibility).
So: Great professional offorad simulator; not an arcade-style fun racer. I'd highly recommend it to any RL off-roaders or people who want something more challenging than your run-of-the-mill arcade racer.
Oh, and I should point out that I've only ever had vehicles with positive-locking rear axles and unlocked transfer cases...I have no idea what that actually feels like to use IRL, and it feels awkward in this game, but maybe that's somewhat realistic and I can get that same feeling without spending $100,000 USD. Having an unlocked rear sounds terrifying, honestly. So far, swapping between the three locks is a little challenging to my brain and I tend to just leave them all locked and swap in and out of 4WD, sometimes unlocking the transfer case if it's getting squirrely and pulling to the left.
Has a lot going for it. Wish there was more development in this genre .

I was a bit skeptical and worried about such AC series spin-off.
I felt that Unity is possibly last of AC game i played for ever (except maybe in future repeatedly playing AC1/2/Brotherhood/Revelations and maybe even Black Flag for its naval gameplay :)).
But beauty of artwork and very positive reviews together with reasonably low price 9€ made my decision.
As a long-term fan of AC i don't regret. This game is absolutely hillarious. I expected nothing beside beautful visual side. Or i expected something like Mark of the Ninja - stealthy assassin in Asia. I was wrong.
I am in middle of the game and i can't wait for another Chronicles game. Forget about victorian London in upcoming Syndicate as it would easily (and probably will :/) end like Unity - beautiful world without any decent story, even without any character to remember, because everyone will die like in Unity long before you can make your own relationship to him or her.
Pros:
- simple story about almost eradicated AC brotherhood in medieval China and following revenge. Easy setting, nothing extra complicated
- beautiful painted in light style and yet very emotional and typical Asian style. I often forgot i play game and felt i play painting :)
- game mechanics are flowy and well managed
- true 3D platformer, i was just stoked when game show me i can go forward and backward in planes, later in game you go around corners, inside buildings through windows etc.
- most of the time you can go as total shadow (unnoticed and without anyone killing)
- definitely and without overreacting - THIS is one of best AC ever made (i played all big installments since AC1 except Rogue)
Cons - most of them aren't a big deal, anyway:
- even game is in UE3 engine there is simply almost nothing to tune in game, like antialiasing or shadows etc.
- un-rrebindable controls, unles you would like to mess with strings and variables in .ini file(s)
- on keyboard and mouse is game sometimes really clumsy, specially in those "action" parts like forced run away and forced fight
- annoying context_key messages, even in middle of story and game, game sometime keeps you telling what to do like to 5-year old child, even if game told you do so hours before (i wish i could turn them off)
- Helix points - nowhere in whole game is told what are those Helix points, what Helix is etc., this traditional part of AC story (i mean Animus, then Helix) is left unexplained and later game pushes you to use those Helix point, which is sort of "reality" hack, you can do some things unnoticed because you somehow "drift" through Helix
- navigation on map could be bit confusing, especially when you hunt for side tasks, i forgot to zoom out in map few times so i missed closest one plane and end up in going back through whole level
Every fan of AC should play it. It gives me feel of Altaír/Ezio times. Straight and nice gameplay with nice atmosphere. After bitter-sweet Unity and sort of waving bye-bye to AC series i am glad i gave this game try.
8.5/10 from long-term AC fan for whom AC2 and everything in pre-AC3 (Connor) era is still best ones and for whom was Unity big disappointment (mostly due to meh story).
P.S.: my gameplay was such long because i repeated often cesrtain parts until i was satisfied with my total stealthy and killing no one if possible. I am sure that some unpatient gamer would have not more than 10 hrs of gameplay, but it is still nice.

Hellblade is such an amazing game in my opinion because of the fact that mental illness is portrayed realistically, specifically psychosis. However I am biased because psychology fascinates me so much so other people may not enjoy this game as much. This game plays more like a puzzle game and a "walking simulator" combined with some combat. If you're thinking about playing the game expecting a hack and slash game then avoid this game. The combat is very basic but gets the job done. You have light attacks, strong attacks, a dodge and block. The combat feels fluid. Your attacks can be canceled into a dodge and you are never stuck in an animation. Despite this, the combat gets repetitive after a while and is only used to drive the story forward. The acting in this game is really well done as well and you can really see the pain in Senua's in expressions.
In my opinion I feel like this game is more about being a learning tool to help understand psychosis and if anyone is interested in the subject they should play this game.

I held off on this game after release, only to buy it now (on sale) and find out that it’s pretty much what I hoped it would be. This is what I wanted from the game, and this is what I got:
1)	Light on story, but heavy on exploration
2)	Scanning, mining, gathering, salvaging, repairing
3)	Survival elements, but nothing so heavy handed that it feels like a survival game
4)	Cool space ships you can build or trade for
5)	Resource management
6)	Interesting creatures and biomes
7)	Impressive land to orbit transitions, with many planets and space stations to land in
This game (as is) is for casual players who simply want to escape into a different world, see crazy things while working on getting a bigger and better space ship. It is not Star Citizen (but good thing that game is coming!) but more of an SC-lite version. I personally did not expect any amount of multiplayer from NMS, so what we get (names, base sharing) is enough for me. I also really enjoy the art style, can’t wait to get back into the worlds and explore some more.
This is definitely a family friendly game, and one of the first I will play with my son.
EDIT: For those who think I'm not allowed to review a game after casual play? Guess what? I am totally allowed to, and this review is for people who will appreciate the game casually as well.
I will never understand someone who puts 400 hours into this (or another) game and then downvotes it. That's far more absurd than my review for obvious reasons. I'm just giving an impression of the things I experienced and enjoyed, and how they are sufficient enough for me to want to continue playing. Even if I stop playing after 15 hours, as long as I'm satisfied with the experience it's enough.

The music is an experience unto itself. The soundtrack is mostly orchestral, and each piece of music is tailored to your surroundings and situation. It helps you feel the serenity of some areas, while also making you feel the urgency and danger of another. In short, the music is brilliant.
As for the game itself, it is visually impressive and is a fantastic platformer. Your jump height will depend on how much pressure you put on the jump button, and some areas require precise control, so a controller is recommended because the game is much easier to play using pressure sensitive buttons and a control stick. The world is quite large, is full of enemies, challenges and upgrades. If you're the type to explore every nook and cranny of the world in search of upgrades, like me, you won't be dissapointed. They also included a leveling system with 3 upgrade trees that add replay value. However, if you're thorough, you will eventually obtain enough levels and extra ability points to max out all 3 upgrade trees regardless of what upgrade path you choose in the beginning.
Overall this game is well worth the full price, and is especially worth the buy if it's on sale. If you like platformers, you'll like this game.

The physics shown in this game were great, and that's what made the flow of controlling Ori so amazing.
Lastly, all the characters were lovable, and I grew attached to them all.
In conclusion, the game's mechanics and structure were pretty much flawless, the gameplay was very fast paced and exhilarating and also brought many great challenges to not make everything tedious, the story was short- but very endearing- and all the characters were well made and unique without even presenting much of any background stories on each one (Except Ori, but it's necessary), and the appearance of the game is stunning and beautiful, and in no way an eye sore.
Whether it's on sale or not the game is worth buying, so please buy the game! It is an amazing experience!

Just decided to pop in and try out the game for hour and was mildly surprised. The game itself is very early access so you’re going to run into bugs and a few things feel unpolished. That being said I feel there is some real meat on this game and possibility to succeed. As it is now try it out, 30 days of free play on the heroes will do nicely to help you find which ones you might enjoy. On that note I would recommend the game. But for the dev's here’s a small list of critique that may help you continue to build the game and the community.
DO's:
Sound:  Keep refining content, the name of the game here is juiciness. If I play Nyd I want that chain gun sound, I want to feel the impact from the character.
Assets: The environments are beautiful so keep building areas with more character and feeling. Create as if they were lived in.
Animation: I’m no animator but I can feel the characters lack some weight in their attacks. This area of the game I feel needs lots of tweaking as there are lots of characters to manage.
UI: Make player health more obvious, if I have to look at my health bar to know I’m close to death. It probably needs reworking
Gameplay: Skull ball is fun but ironically it may be more fun with a normal ball. Perhaps create a large skull design in zbrush on a sphere and see what you get. Other game modes seemed okay but Im sure you could get better feedback on those from other people
DONT's:
Create more maps or heroes: Its too early to be creating new content you have framework set up so utilize it and refine it.
Ignore your user base: This isn’t an issue now but its pretty common in free to play communities. When a game starts to fail its often pretty obvious to the players but not so obvious to the devs.
Overvalue your product: The current cost of heroes seemed a bit high. Mitigate this by allowing players to rent or try out the characters they like. Remember free weekly rotations works as well.
Thats all! I'll be sure to try out the game periodically when i have time.

Edit: Just wanted to give massive props to the developer for replying to pretty much everything anybody posts at the moment. It's rare in my experience for a dev to be quite this courteous, active, and polite. So yeah, I have a lot of faith in this game getting consistently updated over time.

This is an OK game that could have easily been much better.
It's a stealth game. That's really annoying by times, especially if you're the type that feels like you've failed and that you need to redo a stage if you weren't able to stealth through everything. It is what it is - you either enjoy stealth or you don't, and this is really no better or worse than a typical stealth game. Also, it's uplay,
The UI can't be turned off; the information widgits at the four corners of the screen are rarely relevant, but they can neither be turned off nor set to a contextual mode. The story is razor thin; the game gives very little reason to care about any the characters or events without greater knowledge of the Assassin's Creed series or thorough reading of the game's codex. The graphocs options are minimal; this looks to be designed for consoles first, with PC as an afterthought.
Despite that, I had fun. When I was stealthing successfully, I was death incarnate, taking or sparing lives at my whim. The graphics are fantastic, beautifully designed to look hand-painted in a Chinese style. The score may be the best of any Assassin's Creed game yet, a wonderful blend of the familiar themes with a far east influenced style. Some of the levels are truly awesome; one level in particular is one of my favorite moments in video games this year, and after beating it I immediately retried the level so I could so I could do it again.
I cautiously recommend the game. It has big, glaring flaws, but it does some things very well, and I think that it's definitely worth it's current $9.99 price tag.

An Assassin's Creed game set in China?! OH MY!! YES!!!     Oh wait...it's not the usual style of Assassin's Creed game...?
Personally I had been craving for an Assassin's Creed game set in China, and I was very excited to see Chronicles release but it's not the usual AC game style that has previously been released, this is a side scroller, parkour run and jump glorified assault course in effect.  While this was disappointing initially, it was a refreshing change.
The art style, while not the most detailed looking game ever, it does look nice. There are some beautiful background landscapes throughout the story. Character models are very basic; at times it even looked as if some of the enemies didn't even have faces.
Each of the levels are nicely set out, you have various optional objectives to complete in each stage for extra rewards, and I would highly recommend aiming to do these as it pads out some of the story so you can get further immersed in this world.
At times the difficulty of China is very easy; there are no major stumbling blocks to be found along the way, the hardest parts for me were the melee, but since this is a stealthy assassination game, you shouldn't really be aiming to take enemies on in melee fights anyway.
The only thing that let China down would be the game length; I was able to complete the whole story mode in just less than three and a half hours. I would at least expect a five or six hour story mode from Ubisoft here.
Since the only negative point I was able to find was the game length, I would recommend China, since it is still only £7, 99, you could possibly wait for sale season to start to get a bit more of a bargain.

So I'm not great at the whole reviewing thing but I'll give it a shot.
When I got this game, it was in early access, and was essentially Minecraft for the LEGO fan. It was beautiful, played well, was enjoyable, and was worth every penny of the $14-$15 I paid for it back then. But I took a break from it to focus on other games and returned to it reletively recently to find something completely different than what I had left. It now has a campaign(ish) mode where you just run back and forth like an idiot collecting things for people, and a sandbox mode like in the early access version of the game. The campaign provides some passing enjoyment but it quickely becomes tedious as you go through the travel sequence moving from planet to planet continuously looking doing quests, as the items you need seem almost disproportionately on a diffent type of world. In other words, get used to seeing that spaceship of yours, because you'll be spending a lot of time together. Sandbox mode is what you'd expect, a sandbox mode. were you can run around, explore, and just generally screw around. Its the main atrraction of a game like this, though I haven't spent much time in it since the full version was released as I have spent most of my time in the campaign because I'm too stubborn to give up on it until I exhaust what I can do in it so I'll leave the more in depth sandbox mode review to someone who has spent more time in it. I know at this point this reveiw is a bit long and probably seems like I'm rambling so I'll start to wrap it up. I'd love to recomend this game to people for what I've experienced in sandbox as long as you have a friend to play it with. I cannot however, in good conscience, reccomend this game at full price, which has jumped to about $30 since the time I bought the early access version for half that price. This is a game you should pick up while it's on sale because outside of sandbox mode, the game doesnt have much to offer except tedious mediocrity. I don't mind the traveling to other worlds, but I feel that could have been included in the sandbox mode without needing to add in a campaign. The game tried to hard to be more like other LEGO games, such as LEGO Star Wars or LEGO Harry Potter by adding a story mode, but in doing so lost some of the very charm that made it stand out amongst the other LEGO games. In short I reccomend this game, but not at full price and not for the campaign mode. I hope this helps people who are looking at the game and I apologizze for the short essay-esch review I'm leaving here for people to read.

S.K.I.L.L. - Special Force 2 is a first person shooter game that is free to play. Hence the title, it does require skills and talents to be good at this game, the good thing is that this description means no more pay to win content. Another nice feature about this game is it has categorised servers to beginners and specific ones to the professionals following the Kill/Death Ratio (K.D ratio more than 1.2 or has a higher level), which makes this game pretty fair.
The combat system fits any players that have already experienced other FPS games before, it has a perfect accuracy from the hip and adjusts even more when using the scope, so if you are players from counter strike, you won't need to worry much about this and can get the gist quite easily (while it's not really realistic on it's system of recoil...). The graphics looks quite realistic and well made, a feature that albeit is an exception but somehow really useful to the players is the ''quickscope'' action of the sniper rifle, which you will eventually discover while playing as a sniper...
However, there are quite a few hackers and players with bad reputations (which means players that swear a lot), this damages the quality of this game. Notice that there is a little difference between real professionals and hackers, don't judge them to quickly, before calling them hackers when you see them doing a perfect headshot, you should observe him for a few more kills.
Overall, This game is almost a fair game, just lacking some anti-hacking systems, I found this game quite interesting, it's really worth to try as a F2P FPS game.
Positive remarks
+realistic graphics
+combat systems appropriate to either beginners or professionals
+specialised servers to beginners
+''quickscoping'' system on sniper rifles
+no big difference between playing for free or paying
+easy to get into the game, not too difficult to play
Negative remarks
-hackers and unfriendly players
-not many presented game modes

TL;DR Pretty good game if you're into Bethesda games, with typical emphasis on dialogue and exploration. Like any Bethesda game don't look here for particularly good gameplay though I would say it's not that bad, but at this point it may feel rather dated for an FPS.
I quite enjoyed this game, I rarely replay games, and this is one of the few I have, albeit my second playthrough was quite different from first. First being vanilla, no DLC with second being all DLC + a few of the most well known mods for the game.
Story - The main storyline is... Ok. Nothing special but passable for Bethesda main quest. As usual, side quests are where it's at for interesting story chunks. Though the last main mission is pretty epic.
Setting - Awesome world to explore. Chronologically it feels off but ignoring that, the world really gets what it set out to do, a lonesome nuked world. You can have plenty of fun simply walking around the world.
Gameplay - Pretty loose, wonky for an FPS. Personally on vanilla Fallout I just used VATS all the time. I wouldn't praise the game much for the gameplay, personally I find VATS to be decent but it's no top tier shooter or rpg in terms of action gameplay. Late game the game gets really easy, nothing will kill you once you hit higher levels. The dialogue system is great though and allows for choices that seem to matter, unlike fallout 4. The leveling system is great. All in all, the game is an rpg first shooter second.
Audio - The ambient non-radio music is very fitting, probably underrated since few actually listen to it. The radio has got those distinctive oldies retro songs everybody has come to love. Gun sounds are fine. The voices used for characters are pretty good.
Mods - The mod support for this game is top of the line. You can easily mod it to feel very different. Good♥♥♥♥♥♥
Lore - Something worth pointing out, though probably not an impact to many is that this game is NOT lore friendly to Fallout 1 or 2. This one of the biggest criticisms of this game, though many have not played those games (including myself) so you probably don't care, but it is what it is.
Really if you really enjoy Bethesda type games, where you just explore the world, get interesting sidequests, have great dialogue with npcs, then this really does it right. Just don't expect an amazing shooter, or a pretty looking game.

Epistory: Typing Chronicles is one of the most simple yet unique games I have played in quite a while. It puts you in the boots of the muse of a struggling writer, a little girl riding on a fox who has to travel around in an origami world and return the world to its former glory.
The story is surprisingly upbeat and usually starts off with the little girl going into a gloomy world which seems to close around her and her overcoming all odds to come out of the world at the end of each act. The story is told through a narrator with the words appearing on the map itself as the story is being told. There is something so nice and sweet about the story that made me want to progress through it to see what new things the game threw at me.
The gameplay of Epistory revolves around your typing. You move around with WASD or a different combination of keys given by the game to maintain your hand in a good position for typing. You need to switch between movement and typing by a single tap of the space key and then proceed to type the words out given on the screen.
Obstacles like wood and fire pits can be removed from the way by typing. The enemies that come towards you can only defeated by typing. Small enemies require less words to type with some even requiring a single letter while larger enemies can require up to 8 words and big ones at those. As you string together combos and defeat enemies, you get more XP and points. You can use your XP to unlock various perks which help give special abilities like knockback and fire spells to your word attacks or simple ones which increase the intensity of your attacks.
These points are used to unlock new areas which in turn help in progressing through the story. There are a few puzzles through in there for good measure which are simple and require trial and error. The gameplay is simple and effective and the game has a dynamic difficulty setting which changes the difficulty based on your typing speed. There are certain chests scattered around the world which contains bonus or artifacts which also require typing to unlock.
The game does have some confusing parts regarding exploration and you might get stuck after completing certain parts. The game world features a hub called The bridge which has portals which go to different new areas.  The game does not require a mouse and can be played entirely with a keyboard and even navigating through the menu is quite easy due to this.
Epistory can get brutally difficult at times due to the simple reason that enemies can kill you with a single hit if they reach you and sometimes you will miss out seeing an enemy and that will lead to your demise. But the game starts you off back just where you died except in wave battles at the end of any area. Overall, Epistory holds true for the fact that simple gameplay can also lead to effective experiences.
Epistory features an origami world which changes as the story goes on and unfolds before you like a page turner. There is a certain charm in the world that immediately draws you in the game and never lets go. The environments while nothing new, are really well done and have a lot of variety in them. The only problem here is the way the enemies look in the world when the camera zooms out. It becomes quite difficult to pinpoint small enemies and can result in some cheap deaths.
The sound design of Epistory is absolutely fantastic. The game has a stellar soundtrack which goes hand to hand with the overall nature of the game and it has a soothing touch to it. The voice acting and sound effects are also done very well and overall Epistory has a complete sound package you would want from a game like this.
Epistory is one of the few surprising games I have played recently and I absolutely adored it. The game has an incredible feel to it and I am just glad that I got to review this game because it might have easily been gone into my pile of backlogs if I didn’t have to review it. The game is stellar at its price point and a steal if you find it on a sale. You should definitely check Epistory out for its charming nature and stellar world building.

Great game. Difficult to judge or compare.
It's most frequently compared to Diablo and Torchlight, obviously. As it is a top-down  ARPG with Diablo-pioneered mechanics. I'd just try to point out the most striking qualities. (Oh, and when I say Diablo I mean 1 and 2. 3 doesn't exist for yours truly)
In the setting, artwork and ambience it seems much closer to Diablo than Tordhlight.  Monsters, some grittyness et al et cetera. Yet Van Helsing tries its own in having more dialogue, and quite cheesy-yet-aware-of-it humorous based-in-vampire-themed-cultural-stuff style.
In comparison to Torchlights it feels certainly more authentic and serious. Aside style, in the mechanics and stats-things. Yet it does fall a tad boring all in all.
We arrive at a most apparent gripe, lack of stylistic variety. Whilst gameplay has the neatest ideas and mechanics, there's nothing really "wow" in Van Helsing's art direction and design. So aside some neat little mechanics, like trap-placing in Borgova, it doesn't feel too fresh or inspiring.
So in the art, setting and overall originality department it's not as strong as was Diablo. And only a bit preferred over Torchlight. Yet it also falls short in a variety aspect that both Torchlight and Diablo have - classes. There isn't much replayablility and experimenting as there's only one character available for play, albeit with diverse and flexible specializing. Tho thanks to this, it does win some story and dialogue points over Torchlight. (since I wrote this, a DLC was made, now the game has 2 classes :)
Torchlight, however, has a moddibility to it Van Helsing won't dream of achieving. Yet that's not as high in my hierarchy of idealized game aspects. :)
All in all I'd give Van Helsing the same score as Torchlight 2. If objectively speaking. Personally I enjoy Helsing much much more tho. Plus I'd have to take into account that its starting price was 10 euros. There's vast quality for such a small price.
So I'll compromise between the two and write it an 8 in a scoring system where Torchlight 2 would get a 7,5.

Hellblade is frigging amazing. Honestly, I remember quite a few games with good soundtrack or good sound design, but to use it this way? Even that game where you play blind girl in a haunted house was not able to use stereo sound not as a mandatory addition, but as an actual part of the experience. Some say fighting is dull and simple, but, they need to remember, that this is not Devil May Cry. It makes sense. You can feel the impact of each blow through each animation, even though it is repetitive to a point. And the fact, that you do NOT see that there is someone behind you and the only indication of that are the voices in Senua's head... Again, that makes sense. It feels close to Condemned: Criminal Origins, which was a very gritty and brutal experience. And visually while it's not photorealistic or anything, it's still good. Playing with lights and effects... Only one game comes to my mind to compare it, but it was a Far Cry from what Hellblade provides. And this is from just 1 hour of playtime so far. This is what fuels my passion, my desire to be able to make a game by the time I die.
Ninja Theory, thank you for another great experience.
A bit about technical stuff: 4k, very high, on GTX1070 - 30 FPS stable (remember, that it's not FPS that makes it smooth!). In terms of sound, I have Creative Labs Gigaworks T40 Seris II and it plays good, but I need to turn it up a bit more than usual.It's also fine with Sony MDR-ZX770BN. Sound differs, of course, but equally good in both cases. Definitely not recommended with integrated speakers or monitor speakers or whatever.

Hellblade reflects us the psychosis experience in a terrifyingly good way. After the first 45 minutes I had to give a break because the voices were getting to me (with time, I loved them though; they even became my favorite thing in this game). And not just the voices; the dialogue, the story etc. it's clear that they took their time to learn about the plot elements.
Thanks to their advanced mo-cap technology; the animations are unrivaled. It beats most of the AAA blockbusters. Added with the amazing voice acting; characters become alive.
Graphics are great. Senua's model, enemies etc. are very high quality. Some objects like rocks etc. have not-that-high-quality textures; but after lighting and effects they seem fine. Lighting, reflections, particles etc. are great thanks to Unreal Engine 4, so no problem there either.
Graphics are nice, animations are top notch, voice acting is great and there is no HUD in the game. Which makes it very immersive.
Combat was a bit basic but you feel the impact of the hits, so it's nice too. Only problem is rare combat sequences lasts a bit longer than what it should be. With the basic combat, they start to become repetitive.
To sum it up, Ninja Theory had a 100% awesome track record for me, and I was hyped for this game. And boy did it deliver! I don't watch most trailers to not get spoiled up so I was expecting an action/adventure game with mental illness themes as a side note. What we got is way better and I'm already hyped about Ninja Theory's next game.

I'll update this once I complete the game but since it just released today, I thought it fit to release a review now that I am done with the first two missions.
First off if you haven't played the first wolfenstein, do so now it's worth every penny.
Now, the story is even more inviting than the first game and the cutscenes are even more mezmerizing. Dialogue is much more thoughtful. Everytime Blazkovich thinks or speaks his words leave you with plenty to ponder as you mow down Nazi scum.
The Ai are more intelligent than ever, actively protecting weaknesses, attempting to flush you out from your last known position, chucking in a nade then breaching a room, it all makes the gunfights much more intense than any cod multiplayer match.
Not to mention that the game is absolutely gorgeous with an artstyle that is just pleasing to look at. I haven't run into any of the bugs I keep hearing about either. I'm running everything at max and getting a silky smooth 60 fps at all times.
Not sure if it's worth $60 quite yet, and if you're one of those people who thinks a $60 game needs 60 hours content then this is probably not your stop as this game's predecessor took me roughly 10 hours to complete. However if you are a quality over quantity person, the first game was definitely worth the money so I'm sure this will pan out to be the same.
So in short, buy it.

I always thought the first review I'd ever write would be for something like Skyrim or the other AC games, but I've come to really love this game and I'm on my second playthrough now and I can play it over and over again. So, for the actual review:
Visuals:
One thing that really stood out for me in this game is the visuals. It looks like an animated Chinese painting, you can see some details really looks like it was hand painted, and some even crudely drawn, but it adds more artistic style to it, I think. The atmosphere of the game reminds me of Child of Light(which I also love), where it's like you're in an interactive storybook so this automatically rose up in my rank of favorite games.
Gameplay:
Never have I seen two guards who are so into their conversation they never notice anything else, like, say, an assassin creeping up behind them, climbing up the wall, up the ceiling, or hell, even dashing from column to column. Not that I don't like that, I just find it hilarious. As for fighting, I really love it when Shao Jun uses the hidden blade in her shoe to finish off an enemy. Also, the fact that avoiding killing and drawing unwanted attention plays a big part in this game is somewhat fresh for me. If you do kill a guard, better hide the body fast or all hell will break loose.
Others:
Music:
Will there be an OST release? Because I definitely want one. The main theme is pretty much a variation of "Ezio's Family" from AC2, but mixed with traditional instruments. I stayed idle for a while during a certain sequence because the music was really nice. If you like traditional/ethnic type of music, then you're gonna love this.
I'd be really happy if this game becomes like the other AC games, or something like Liberation or Freedom Cry. I think it'd be cool to see Shao Jun in full 3D action.

The first entry in the
trilogy is
, and for the sake of all that is good about
, I sincerely hope
and
are as visually satisfying, fun and overall enjoyable as this one is.
China is a fairly befitting setting for the assassins’ style, the only thing is that there’s only one of them (Chinese brotherhood members) left: Shao Jun.
Who is Shao Jun? Well, remember that Chinese girl who went to see Ezio during the last of his days in that short film titled
? Yep! That’s the one. She went to see him to learn how to lead and rebuild her Order. Ezio is probably the best choice for that.
After being trained by none other than the legendary Ezio Auditore da Firenze himself two years prior to the start of the game, she is returning to China in 1526 amidst the crumble of the Ming dynasty and seeks vengeance upon the Templars who annihilated her brotherhood and plans to restore it.
The game is noticeably different than most others in the franchise, instead of being open-world the playable areas are offered in sections. It is also 2.5D (literally 3D but with side-scrolling platform gameplay), with some aspects of 3D gameplay, as one can sometimes access the Z-axis, which makes the gameplay interesting and adds a third dimension to otherwise two-dimensional levels.
there’s free-running, climbing and parkour all over the place, and it all feels extremely fluid. The gameplay is heavily based on platforming, stealth and combat. There are hiding spots almost everywhere, and if there isn’t you can always cause distractions by cutting a rope with a Throwing Knife and dropping hanging objects, or using the Noise Dart to lead a guard away, or stunning them or simply whistling to distract a guard. The hiding spots are cleverly implemented into the level design, and when you’re in a hiding spot close to another one you can switch to and from quickly, avoiding guards and progressing faster.
, things don’t always go as planned so the combat is actually pretty well executed; there aren’t counters like in other games in the franchise, instead you block a lot more and roll over enemies for strategic purposes. There’s a soft but fast hit, and a slow but hard hit. Depending on the weapon your opponent has also results in varied ways of blocking/dodging. The combat is purposely difficult, as the game’s true core gameplay lies in being unnoticed, but one can still carry out assassinations without being noticed,
.
As for the visual aspect of the game, I can’t say that it’s extremely intense or detailed, but that doesn’t mean that it’s not a beautiful looking game in its own right. The world looks like it’s been hand painted, and filters or motion-blurring is in perfect balance with the art-style. Adding NVIDIA Physx also added to the visual fidelity and blending of everything into a seemingly alive environment that grabs you, immerses you and does not let go.
Now, this isn’t as hard-core a game as the rest of the franchise, it’s difficult, and it does require a certain level of skill and awareness, but I can’t help but feel that it’s a bit more on the casual side. That doesn’t mean that it’s not fun and enjoyable though.
In conclusion, it’s a very entertaining game, you play as a character that was barely known but trained by the probably-most-known character in the entire series, which adds a little spice and keeps things fresh. Also, come on, who
wanna
. She used it in the short-film, and she uses it now.

On the plus side, the art style is great, and the stealth gameplay is a good application of traditional AC movement into the 2D setting. However, the bad really outweighs the good here. The controls are terrible and there is no way to rebind them aside from messing with game files. A result of this is that combat feels clunky and overall unpleasant. Now I'd be willing to overlook this, considering the game's focus on stealth, but there are so many bugs - some completely progress halting - that it all snowballs into a really unenjoyable experience of a game. I don't even know how much content there is in this game because I can't progress past a bugged sequence.

A fun mashup of Assassin’s Creed and Mark of the Ninja - basically a side scrolling stealth game with some Assassin’s Creed mechanics sprinkled in (which are well integrated).
Each level (sorry, Sequence!) is split into smaller segments which score you on three categories (finish it without killing anyone, finish it with stealh kills or going in loud and fighting everyone).  There are almost always several paths to reach your goals and the game ramps up the difficulty pretty well by introducing new types of enemies and skills.  The controls are solid and towards the end you will need to be comfortable with them to get through the areas without being detected.  If you are a perfectionist you can restart a segment almost instantly and if you want to switch from stealth to fighting (you got detected for example) its very smooth.
The fighting mechanic is decent, includes timed counters and other Assassin’s Creed flourishes, except you will go down fast so it isn't brain dead easy like in the main games.  With stealth though you can easily avoid all fights, and most of the enemy types only affect combat- people with shields, etc who you can still one shot if you use stealth.
The voice work is rather bland and there are several "run towards the right while being chased" sequences that devolve into memorization.
Technically the game is a bit of a mess - changing resolution requires a restart and anti aliasing has to be set by editing an ini file.
Also the game has Leap of Faith into haystacks.

Did I buy into the hype? Yes. Was I disappointed on release? Yes. In addition, I have been dreaming about this type of game for decades; an endless universe to explore in a far-flung, whimsical, sci fi setting. Upon release, I put in about ten hours or so, and then put it away and resisted jumping on the hate train. So I waited, hoping for news that an update was being worked on. I began to despair when there was no news in the months after release, and started to come to terms with the probability that this was indeed the debacle of the year, if not the decade. Then, all of a sudden, the foundation update dropped....
Ladies and gents, this game deserves a second chance. Hello Games deserves credit for not giving up on there passion project, despite the unprecedented amount of negativity. We, as informed gamers, have to accept the fact that an independent studio got caught up in the massive media hype which doomed them for an inevitable crash. Now with the huge pathfinder update, the game is now a semblance of the game we dreamed about. Is there still work to do? Yes. I believe history will judge in favor of this game and it will attain a sort of cult status. Blade Runner was not popular when it was released, but became beloved over time. This could be true here. This game represents a unique vision and should be supported.

I never write reviews for anything but this game was so bad, so heart wrenchingly dissapointing, that it's going to get a horrible review. As a kid, I loved the original NES Gauntlet. Before this game was released, I was itching to get the game. I bought it only to find out I could not run it on XP. I planned buying an entire new computer just so I could finally play this game. After getting to Windows 10 and finally playing this game, here are the fundamental horrible injustices of the game.
1. It's a grinding game. We finished the campaign on normal difficulty and barely have enough gold to buy 1 relic let alone upgrade it to level 2 (max is 3). There are 8 relics, 5 weapons, 3 talisman. Then there is a bunch of wardrobe stuff that is expensive and does nothing to help you. Of all the relics and weapons and talisman, you can only equip one of each category and the default seems to be the best. The descriptions are terrible so you don't know what you get until after you buy it and it's not refundable. So... fine, let's just play the game like the original... except even the achievements for the game, "Kill 50,000 bad guys" is just unreasonable. We finished the game and I haven't reached 2000 bad guys. And all of this is PER CHARACTER. To put it in sperspective, 9 hours = 2000 bad guys then do that 5 more tmes. I bought the DLC pack to get the new Necromancer and this game is so terrible, I don't want to even try it out.
2. There is a terrible audio bug that completely crashes Windows. Windows 7, 8, and 10 have experienced it. First you lose audio completely in game, then Skype, then completely. Reboot fixes it... if you can reboot... This made everyone I play with rush for the uninstall button which is now totalling 5 players.
3. Gauntlet didn't have much of a plot but the original 8-bit Nintendo had more plot than this game. The commentary is so cringeworthy that NAVI from Zelda 64 seems less annoying and makes problem 2 seem like a blessing.
4. The worst part of the game is the actual game play. Bad guys spawn at a rate faster than you can kill them and you just get swarmed. Cool down abilities are too long, bad guys are over powered, and bad guys can shoot through obstacles and do 90% if not 100% damage in 1 hit. Food and Potions from the original game have really lost their value completely.
This game is so terrible that I honestly would like a refund for the game. I truly regret this purchase.

Simply put, i make my wife to sleep alone (something she hates) to keep typing and discover the story; didn't get dissapointed.
Now if you excuse me, i need to start typing an apology.

-Instead of frantically clicking your mouse when monsters start shambling or skittering your direction, you frantically type words that appear above them.  This is a lot more fun/stressful than it sounds.
-Your character rides a red fox.  Also, the fox has three tails for some reason.
-Instead of dark macabre surroundings, everything here is word/writing-related. The background story reveals itself on the very ground you walk on and new areas to explore unfold like origami.  A pretty and consistent theme.
-You don’t use a mouse.  Or a controller.  Or a joystick.  Or a VR headset.  Or a trackball.  Or a Pong paddle dimmerswitch thingie (what were those called?).  You just use your keyboard.  If you hate typing and don’t ever want to do it or improve then you should probably move on, this game will make you cry.  But who am I to tell you what to do?  Maybe you need a good cry. Whatever you need man.
-Ironically, the loot you find in Epistory consists of paintings that flesh out the storyline, unlike Diablo loot that drops in piles of multicolored words.
-You learn vocabulary, which probably isn’t that surprising since you spend a good portion of time typing in multiple synonyms of things you encounter.  Even the game’s name encourages you to look something up in the dictionary…
Ahh, I see what you did there typing game.  Well played.
-Instead of the obvious goal in Diablo (kill Diablo), here it is much more subtle.  A story is revealed in parts as you explore.  I think you are trying to.… solve a mystery? inspire an author? create a narrative?  I’m not really positive yet.  Like I said, more subtle.
On second thought, I guess the game isn't that much like Diablo.  It is pretty good though.  I had completely forgotten that typing games existed until this one popped up on sale on Steam.  It, somewhat surprisingly, teaches you a skill, and makes you want to get better at it.  Since, in order to get good at most games, you have to practice a bunch of arbitrary keystrokes and mouse clicks, you might as well make one that hones a skill that is helpful outside the game.

So thumbs up Epistory.  You taught me something.

This game is one of a kind experience.
You will not remember Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice for its gameplay, it ranges from average (puzzles) to good (combat), but you will remember the unique setting and story, the way it is told and felt by the player.
In a lot of ways it is an experiment, exploring games as a medium and it is a success.
The game is linear and has very little replayability, so the less you know about it, the better.
And a last note for people like me that hate horror games, that heavily rely on cheap jumpscares, this game is not like that at all. In this game horror comes from the atmosphere and the mind of the main protagonist and it is done very well.

Hellblade:Senua`s Sacrifice is one of the best games i have played in a long time, not only for the beautiful image and the best sound i`ve seen in a game but for a combat dynamic that makes you feel powerful with Seuna`s sword dance. The story tocuhes with very strong emotions and before you realise you are rooting and becoming stronger alongside Senua. I strongly recommend that anybody that likes good story and good combat games to play this game, is an unique experience.

Hellblade reflects us the psychosis experience in a terrifyingly good way. After the first 45 minutes I had to give a break because the voices were getting to me (with time, I loved them though; they even became my favorite thing in this game). And not just the voices; the dialogue, the story etc. it's clear that they took their time to learn about the plot elements.
Thanks to their advanced mo-cap technology; the animations are unrivaled. It beats most of the AAA blockbusters. Added with the amazing voice acting; characters become alive.
Graphics are great. Senua's model, enemies etc. are very high quality. Some objects like rocks etc. have not-that-high-quality textures; but after lighting and effects they seem fine. Lighting, reflections, particles etc. are great thanks to Unreal Engine 4, so no problem there either.
Graphics are nice, animations are top notch, voice acting is great and there is no HUD in the game. Which makes it very immersive.
Combat was a bit basic but you feel the impact of the hits, so it's nice too. Only problem is rare combat sequences lasts a bit longer than what it should be. With the basic combat, they start to become repetitive.
To sum it up, Ninja Theory had a 100% awesome track record for me, and I was hyped for this game. And boy did it deliver! I don't watch most trailers to not get spoiled up so I was expecting an action/adventure game with mental illness themes as a side note. What we got is way better and I'm already hyped about Ninja Theory's next game.

I've never bothered to write a review for a game on here before. Was never really feeling like it was all that important.

It isn't all too much of a gameplay-inspired game but the story has a powerful punch to it. While I would not recommend such a game to someone who plays nothing but FPS, if you enjoy the type which has the ability to emotionally toy with you from start to finish, this is for you.
It is well-written, well-paced, emotionally well-timed, and wonderfully tethered with its touching soundtrack, leaving you guessing all about it until the story all connects to make a beautiful picture of pixels at the very end.
Not going to lie though. The comedy, while there were quite a few perfectly-timed jokes, there was a reacurring presence of it feeling quite forced at times.
Don't hesitate to purchase this game. It will certainly go down as one you wont soon forget.
