Gauntlet is a top down dungeon crawler game that was developed by Arrowhead Game Studios and published by Warner Brothers. Gauntlet was released in September 2014, and was later ported to the PS4 in August 2015.
You take the role of one of four classes of heroes. Each hero has their own unique play style and special abilities. Personally I played the game primarily as the archer, because I just find the range classes more fun to play, but there are warriors and mages included here too. Your character has a regular attack, a special attack and a more situational ability too. The special attack and special ability all change when you upgrade your weapon. You may find that certain weapons/abilities are more suited for certain levels as well. The gameplay reminded me very much of a Diablo style, in that I was actually able to just hold down my left mouse button which is the regular attack and not let go as enemies just surround you most of the time - your other abilities come with a cooldown so you need to time these for when they are going to be most beneficial.  The aim on each of the levels is to reach the end of the stage - there aren't any side quests on any of the stages, it’s purely a dungeon crawler. Throughout each of the levels, you will come across piles and piles of gold. The gold is used in the lobby screen before each level to purchase upgrades, whether it be new weapons, new skins for your character, new relics or new special abilities, and they cost a lot of gold too, so it's a good thing you will come across abundance amount of gold in this game.
The graphics in Gauntlet are OK - they aren't anything special, but they certainly aren't bad by any stretch. The lighting on the darker levels is something I found to be really well done though - you get a sense of being really deep underground and with the helpless lost feeling as you are crawling through empty dark hallways and caves. The lava levels are really pretty too and some of my favourite stages in the game are because of their aesthetic.
Gauntlet is fully voice acted, each of the four heroes has their own individual voice actor; all be it the elf archer can wear very thin on you at times. The narration is done very well too, as it guides you through the plentiful stages on what is happening and keeping the plot going.
We see three levels of difficulty in Gauntlet, Easy, Medium and Hard - easy mode is VERY easy. You should only be playing that if you want to blast through the game for special achievements or just for completion sake. You could also be playing easy if you want to learn a new class. The downside to playing on easy is that you get less gold from drops though - so it is kind of swings and round-a-bouts. The medium difficulty is where you should be spending a lot of your time - this is where you will get a regular amount of gold, and the enemies will be sufficiently challenging. Hard mode should only really be played if you are planning on playing with friends who have a lot of experience in the game, or you have built up a ton of upgrades allowing you to min/max your way through the stages as efficiently as possible.
I touched on playing friends briefly above, Gauntlet is able to be played in a four player co-op environment, each player takes control of one of the four classes and you play the game as a team. The enemies are all scaled up depending on how many people are playing - most people will say that co-op is the only mode you should be playing Gauntlet - whilst I may say that will be true, it is certainly not wise to be playing with PUGs (pick up groups from quick queues). If you do want the multiplayer experience in Gauntlet, then play it with friends and get on Skype together, it will make the entire experience so much more fun and will definitely make it a better play through as opposed to playing with randommers or on your own.
Each of the numerous levels in Gauntlet all have a main dungeon design to them, but a lot of the stages are also procedurally generated, allowing for some stages leaving you lost in the deep depths of caves and forcing you to explore around in order to find the exits. Others which are more objective based, whether it be lowering a gate, or finding keys to open a door, will be more or less the same for each play through. Some of the better levels I found are when you have to outrun "Death", you are not able to kill "Death", you just have to run as far away from him as possible before he catches you up.  As I said above, there is so much gold to be looted in this game, you can go off the beaten path on the hunt for more of it if you desire, with secret rooms and areas just overflowing with gold all to be found. On top of the gold, there are a few other items you can pick up, Health potions, but these come in the form of dinner on the plate - a nice little feature is that you can actually destroy this meat by hitting it, so that makes the close range combat a little bit more on edge, if you know you are going to need to heal up soon after a fight; it also gives the range characters a need to be a little more precise when it comes to where they aim their attacks.  The final item is a potion, this potion is used as a sort of mana crystal for using your special abilities, they can be few and far between so you should try and pick your moments wisely for when you want to use it.
A full run through Gauntlet on medium mode took me just over three hours - even when you finish the whole run, you can still go back and replay previous levels to farm more gold allowing you to purchase more upgrades. I still plan on playing through the game again on hard mode and also playing it with friends. This will easily mean Gauntlet will have a pretty hefty amount of hours/content on offer. I would say you can easily push about twenty hours from it, and that's just with playing with one character! If you want to get fully immersed in this game, you can be at it for weeks and still not experience it all.
Even though the graphics are nothing spectacular, I wasn't able to play Gauntlet on 4k resolutions with max graphics as the frame rate drops down to the region of 30FPS, which for me is unplayable - but I didn't find the graphical differences between 1080 and 4K to be anything massive so I wasn't too bothered about that.  Gauntlet can be played with a controller, and to be honest, I think it is designed with a controller in mind, given the amount of abilities and keys you need to be pressing; it makes perfect sense to plug in your controller and sit back to play this game. I also played Gauntlet with the Steam controller, and was able to map all of the buttons perfectly to how I wanted to play.
I am going to strongly recommend Gauntlet, the price tag of £14,99 is reasonable but the amount of content and gameplay quality really out way the price. The game has been known to go as low as £3 on Steam and other sites, so if you see it on sale anywhere, do not hesitate to pick it up. You will get so much game time out of this game and it is something that all RPG fans should be playing.

A fairly interesting and exciting game for those who like war-themed games. It's great and somewhat entertaining, however it's not without it's flaws. The menu and the instructions really unclear. I ended up accidentally buying two sets of magazines in the beginning because I wasn't sure if I had already bought it. There was no notification whatsoever upon purchase. I'm pretty sure navigating through the main menu was more of a challenge than the first few games itself.
The amount of spelling and grammatical mistakes in the game is also incredibly high for a game that's being sold on Steam. Made me question whether or not this game was proof checked before it was released. I saw that they just added two additional languages (French and Dutch) into the game  a few weeks ago. Perhaps they should start focusing on the base language of the game first instead of adding new ones.
Flaws aside however, the gameplay is actually pretty nice. The graphics are acceptable (could've been better, but I'm not going to complain; each game has their own style), the sound effects are quite on point and the game itself is neither too easy nor it is too hard. Overall I would recommend this game - even more if the minor messes I mentioned above get fixed. But you get roughly what you paid for, if not more.

This would be my first typing game on Steam I've ever played. I picked it up because I've been wanting to try this sort of game for a while to see if I could improve my typing ability and, obviously, because it's friggin' gorgeous! Oh and fox mount, yeah! Oh, oh... oh, AND it was on sale! :D So I though, why not?
The default setting for this game is set as "adaptive difficulty," I believe, which I hadn't realized until things got unbearable. I was "blazing" through Chapter 1. After like, the 2nd to last "boss battle"-thing, I was dreading the next. Haha, I got slaughtered! "No, game! I'm not as good as you THINK I am!" lol (Now playing on a SET difficulty, thank you very much.)
SO, yeah, in the "boss battles" (cuz I'm not sure what else to call them) enemies start to swarm you left and right, and you have to destroy them before they reach your circle. When they do, it's instadeath. The strategy is pretty simple but it's the execution that determines winning or losing. The longer the battle goes on, the faster they spawn and the harder prioritizing targets become. It starts to get pretty overwhelming, especially when your fingers decide they no longer wish to participate and type words/letters that have nothing to do with any word on the screen!!! *sobs*
Another thing I really like, is that this game has introduced several words I have never seen nor heard used before, like "riebeckite," "speleothem," "goyazite..." all some sort of cave rock formations and some others that I can't recall because it all happened so quick!! But, I like seeing new words!
Hopefully, with my new SET difficulty, I'll be able to actually focus on improving my typing "skizzels" while having a blast in this beautiful world. I can't wait to play more when I get the chance. Definitely recommend this game for anyone even remotely interested.
If you like using your keyboard, can type at a fairly decent WPM, and enjoy adventure games such as bastion, I'm certain this game will suit you.

-editable review-
I figured this game was mediocre at best but then simply viewed the trailer, y'know the one that mixes real video with game footage, and I thought to myself of how well made and of high quality that was made. Easily this game could be lost among the so many other off-road/racing/muthatruckers that have been released and fallen either into obscurity or electro-plated for every successive generation until it gets cancelled to let the latest driving/riding/racing/combat trend blaze it's own trail into the aforementioned obscurity.
Is it simulation? I believe so but a simulation that is easily digestible, with corners cut realistically to - play. The vehicle roster is fanatsy based in reality, meaning the trucks are patterned off of real life counterparts only lacking the liscences to use their names.
But the game is slow and hard to control, even without whatever is in place for native controller support amd multiplayer, the FPS drop on a consistent basis, and becomes so sluggish that it is a pain to drive.
As far as tracks go, and they sometimes go far, and sometimes don't go anywhere fast due to rugged terrain, are based upon reality and there is no need to trademark dirt, mud and water. The mud will bog you down more than deep water. You will skid along twisting dirt roads deep in the jungle. Climb vertically over rock precipices. Scramble upon rocks jutting out from deeper waters. Each country has a plethora of tracks to race against the clock and other rider's time and are wating to be unlocked along with vehicles.
Offroad Drive's gameplay can cater to the casual driver - meaning you can get through most tracks not using the tools at your disposal such as onboard tire pressure control, locking and unlocking differentials, 4 wheel drive etc. , allowing the player to enjoy the scenery and bumpy ride at the cost of finishing near the rear of the pack.
For the enthusiast it is recomended to fasten your seat belts, because there is much challenge and learning of the tracks and modification for integration of utilization of skills per individual track, that only the most harcore could fathom gaining 1st place in every track with every vehicle. Basically this equals to much practice.
+first person with head on a swivel
+detailed graphics all around
+simple as you would prefer
+complex as you could imagine
-performance overall is lacking
-Controller support? what? where?
-NO FREE ROAM (stay on or near track or be penalized and teleported  within 5 seconds)
-Does multiplayer even work and what would be the purpose if it did, you only race against the clock and ghost truck
-without good controls, whats the use of trying
If you believe that this is a standard arcade racer - that is fine - it does have somewhat  flexible controls (use what you want, sometimes a hitch is necassary) but lacks true controller support.
The detail is abundant in the environment such as the dust can almost be tasted during the hotter regions and the plunges into the creekbeds feel almost refreshing. The mud actually washes off of your vehicle when plowing through water. The trucks will flip over but not often and there is no explosions or machines breaking down that I saw exception like my windshield smashed out once and parts may fall off of the truck, but it is pretty much a vehicular goreless game. The only thing that ever stopped me was meandering into too deep water and something about my exhaust getting flooded.
There is an incredible depth to the simulation aspects of this title. With many ways to overcome obstacles- such as simply finding another route around, power-winching over it, depressurizing tires to soften your friction, plus more. Therefore each track COULD be mastered by finding what works best with what accessory or truck in the turbulent and primal landscape. And if you don't do it correctly or turn at a point just a little early/late, then possibly it will warrant a restart. Unfortunately a restart is what the controls need and a tune up as much.

To the Ninja Theory; thank you.  Thank you for telling Senua’s story; thank you for approaching the subject matter with the gravity and care that is due it. I hope this game gets the success that I believe it deserves and I look forward to seeing more of your vision in this realm.
First off I would definitely follow the suggestions and wear headphones, ones that simulate surround sound makes it all the more immersive. Beyond that I'm not sure what to say here beyond wow…this is an incredible piece of interactive storytelling that approaches a mature subject matter with great care and to great impact/effect.
The combat gameplay is a bit rudimentary at times, though strikes carry a weight that makes it feel as brutal as it should and it serves to move the story along.
Puzzles range from scavenger hunts, (some feeling a bit tedious,) to some really well designed pieces that I would call 'refractory' puzzles.
The acting is really solid; the leads ability to convey such a range of emotions about the story through her face and eyes is amazing.  This is a real credit to her acting ability as well as the ability for the Unreal engine and the designers/coders to convey her ability to the screen.
In the end yes I would recommend this; if for nothing else than to see through the eyes of a struggle that would as easily translate to an individual’s experiences today as it did to Senua.

Probably this game is the best Tower Defence game for casual players. But strategic players will find this game extremely boring and repetitive.
The rules are simple. You have an army of monkeys (21 tower) with different abilities which stands against.... balloons. Seems funny. Looks pretty funny. Sometimes I have feelings it was designed for children, because graphics is so.. childish, but then I remembered what the gameplay is incredibly simple too, so the graphics and the gameplay perfectly fit.
Let's go back to the gameplay. There are different colour of balloons. For example, red ballon can be popped with 1 hit. Blue releases red balloon if it was pierced, green releases blue and etc. There are also metal balloons, camouflage ballons, anti-freeze, boss and etc.
So this game ballons and monkeys. Place monkeys, pop balloons, buy stronger monkey with bigger weapons. And it's pretty funny until you realise that all maps has the same filling of waves. I mean 15th wave of any map has the same amount and order of ballons as all other maps. Incredible. Have you ever seen a TD game with this awesome feature? Congrats, there is a one.
This "feature" makes the game boring after you passed one of levels. But... suddenly.. I have found that casual players like it. There is a guy with 750h+ in this game. Can you imagine, he played a thousands of times at the same missions (yeah, there are 5 difficulties, which has 15-20 to wave count), passed the same levels with same ballons. Incredible. Actually, this is the main reason why I gave this game a positive review, because a lot of players could like this game. Thank to god, I am not one of them :D
Pros
- 21 tower with different speciality. I liked the upgrade system for towers. Each tower has 2 paths and 4 upgrades in each path. You can take both 2 levels in each path, but after you need to choose a path for 3 and 4 tier upgrades. Also, upgrades are interesting. Some of them are simple (more range, more attack speed) and slightly change visual (blue hat becomes red), but other significantly changes visual of tower and gives huge bonuses. For example, there is a Monkey Buccaneer. You can upgrade it to Battlecruiser with tier 3 upgrade and to aircraft carrier with 4 tier upgrade. So, there are actually much more than 21 towers. Meanwhile, a lot of them are useless :D
- A lot of maps, more than 40. Each has interesting visual and changes a path. There are 5 difficulties and some other modes like Co-op or Odyssey and etc.
- A lot of other stuff. There are upgrade system for tokens, rank system for exp, shop stuff for cash. There is a daily rewards with daily quests and etc, achievements and etc.. Hello from free-to-play past. (game doesn't require any in-purchases)
- No text, no preview, no tutorials. You ll go into the battle on your own. But it's easy to understand, so it's plus
Cons
- Same wave filling and order.
- You need to play/grind a lot to open all towers upgrades
- You can lose suddenly. I mean, you play, defended 40 weeks with no leaks, you play of course on 2x speed. When something happens and you lose in 5 seconds. It is really frustrating
- Even the first level has 50 waves at least. Actually, all maps has 50 waves at least, so is the first. I preferred that the time of first map was less
- Games crashes. I have got 2 game crashes during 3 hours of gameplay. Anyway, there is autosaves, so this is not big deal.
- I have seen a lot of recent negative reviews where people complained about lost progress. I have seen no replies, so I suppose, debs don't care much about their players
- Annoying and repetitive music
So, If you are searching for an interesting TD game with deep strategy, different levels, unique enemies   - don't buy it, I can't recommend this game for you even for 1 dollar.
But if you play TD games because you like watching how your towers kill enemies or because TD games relax you - this is the game for you. There are 200h of watching how balloons pop, I suppose,

Stumbled across this one on the front page and, after a lapse in money sense, nabbed it up. Glad I did though, I've been aching for another dungeon crawler after I beat the pants off Torchlight 2 and the DRM-mess that is Diablo 3. Seriously, to whatever Blizzard exec decided it should be always online... ♥♥♥♥ YOU. By the way I totally mean that.
Anyways, angry rant out of the way, Van Helsing is a neat little gothic dungeon crawler where you play the son of the famous monster hunter himself, sent off to Borgovia with your companion, the lovely and post-humous Lady Katarina, to sort out some trouble there. I haven't gotten very far into it but so far I've fought werewolves, harpies, rulska (a sort of water demon), literal 'tin soldiers', and goat legged spellcasters.
Katarina plays your support a-la the pets from Torchlight in that she helps you fight and can zip back to town to sell unwanted gear, but she's also witty, can learn some very useful defensive and offensive attacks, and can do both close up and ranged fighting. Her dark humor (she is a ghost after all) and the way she and Van Helsing play off each other helps to offset the otherwise gory and dark setting.
So far I'm having a blast with it. If you like the occult and are into stories about vampire hunters (or similar) then this is a game for you.

Initial BSOD issues solved, hardware overview:
Had same BSOD issues that are commonly reported. Nvidia hotfix 388.10 fixed it. Running EVGA 1080ti  SC watercooled at 3840x2160 getting great framerates (60fps at uber quality setting) on 43" Dell P4317Q monitor. Remainder of setup is 4790K at 4ghz, 32gb RAM, two M.2 NVMe 512gb samsung's and a 1tb SATA SSD samsung. Playing w xbox 360 wired controller. Initially I was very frustrated w BSOD, but driver hotfix immediately resolved.  Have not had any other glitches.
GAMEPLAY:
Game is very fun so far after about 6 hours of play on launch day.  I'm playing at "bring it on" difficulty, which seems well balanced for my skill level.  A few areas are challenging enough to require reload a dozen or two times to get through it, which is about right.  Other areas I can walk through pretty easily.  Seems to be plenty of ammo and the weapons and tactics are well implemented and a lot of fun. Graphics and detail are amazing. Sounds and music are perfect. Cutscenes and story are just about right in amount/length/content to keep you interested and knowing why you're doing what you're doing.  My favorite historical titles include the Fallout series (although I haven't been able to get "hooked" on Fallout 4 for some reason, but I completed all of the previous titles back to Wasteland in 1988), Skyrim, Bioshock series, Gears of War series, Halo series, Civ series, and some builders like Factorio and Simcity series.
I did not play the original Wolfenstein New Order (I played W3D back in the day), so I can't compare it to that, but overall I think it is well implemented, although I was quite disturbed initially by the crashing. Once new hotfix driver was loaded all is good.
Overall score: 9/10.  Knocked it a full star for the launch headaches. A new AAA game shouldn't BSOD my machine with a one-week old driver on it and top of the line video card.

I loved this game. It has a great story, and I enjoyed the way the programming aspect fits into the story. If you know Lua and how its translated into bytecode, you'll enjoy this game even more. I loved the editing of multiple nested closures part of the game, and I love the fact that this is an actual meaningful part of the gameplay and story. Its very novel. Code reading is an important part of the game toward the end, when as a player you are trying to determine if the changes you are making may be going too far or don't end up being relevant to the story. Finding this canonical way the game wants to be modified becomes the game. As long as you approach it with that attitude, you'll enjoy this game very much.

A fun and innovative game, that sadly gets a bit boring after a few hours. A really neat concept with occasional brilliant means of execution marred by questionable design choices and a terribly steep difficulty curve.
When you first hop into the game, it throws fairly simple trial-and-error concepts at you with well named variables that allow you to fairly quickly comprehend what you're doing and how it works. Unfortunately, each new concept is tossed at you as a one-off novelty that is quickly replaced with the next step, which really detracts from the exploration of the concepts.
Before long, you are given incredible power to really delve deep into how each thing works... to the point where you can crash the game. Over and over. Trial and error becomes a test in monotony as you sometimes lock-up the game and have to reload. On occasion, it can be hard to tell if it's due to something you caused or a bug in the game (and trust me, there are definitely bugs). And boy oh boy, let's hope you have experience in reading LUA, because I sure didn't and I found some of the puzzles incredibly obtuse to solve (I am an intermediate programmer, otherwise).
I did find that, shortly after the halfway point, my patience for solving some of the puzzles wore thin and my investment did not match the feeling of achievement anymore. I'd end up referring to a walkthrough after a few minutes of skimming over a bunch of confusing syntax. This game is definitely not a tool to learn programming through -- it will only strike fear and apprehension into the hearts of novices.
Also, there are way too many ledges to accidentally walk off in this game. And the game likes respawning you right on the tip of the edge so that you'll almost instantly fall again if you're not pressing in a direction away from the edge. Frustration mounts.
I really wanted to like this game because I love the idea. But this isn't the fun learning experience I was hoping for.

This is maybe the first game with actual design, story, original idea and viable budget that I found absolutely horrendous. While the promise is interesting, the game fails to deliver in all fronts.
The animation is low quality, the map and art design is such that I constantly fallen into water, missed doors, stuck up in environment as the presentation of the 2.5D world failed to distinguish depth many times.
The characters are following the Link-Navi stereo/archetype, but they are annoying and are lacking any kind of personality.
Gameplay is basically combat-less, but at the same time presents quite some puzzles that were made in a weird way ; at some point in the game raises the difficulty from "hack the stone so instead of rolling one forward it will go 4 backwards so I can pass" to logic gates, functions and complex algorythms ; the game made a faint attempt to explain and implement programming (self = comes outside, a real-world fact, not changeable by hacking means) but at the same time it used professional abbreviations of programming, including short forms of functions and types of variables.
It's great that I kinda understand that 10-opening levels will trigger a trap and close the door, but I seriously have no idea how various call functions, comparisons and seemingly random 3-4 letter shortenings mean, and what I need to change in them to work. I know what I need to reach, but the means are nowhere explained ingame.
The game starts with chapter 2 (yes), and ends in chapter 5 ; chapter 2-3 are fine and kind of fun in their low-impact way, but chapter 4 and 5 made that close to unclimbable jump in unexplained difficulty and features. (I finished it with a guide to see what are people talking about)
I absolutely can not recommend this game. It's lackluster in design, originality, (accessible) challenge or "adventuring" throughout the whole game, making an unexplainable change in design, gameplay and completely messing up any difficulty curve in it's second half

And so I begin, Ori and the Blind Forest... Where do I start with such a gem...
I came into this game not expecting much, a bit of fresh perspective mainly. Boy was I wrong.
Now I fear this review will not do this game justice, let me evaluate:
Right off the bat, this game kicks you in the feels, and this vein continues on for the rest of the game, in some parts it legitimately brought me to tears.
The atmosphere is rich with color, vibrancy, expertly crafted and mastered, nothing is bland in this world, some parts are dark, scary, others are bright, happy and bring you joy.
The music is the best I have ever heard, ever, hands down, even now it brings me joy, and sadness, to listen to it, the work that went in to producing it is immense, the talent that brings you to tears time after time... This game has the, best soundtrack, ever scored and played.
The gameplay isn't as important to my view of the game, but it is still amazingly fun, inventive, intuitive and even challenging, some parts play like a puzzle, others are the classic platformer elements that have been tried and tested.
To end my review... This gem of a game set my personal standards for story, atmosphere, and sound design, if it was my choice, this should win game of the year, it is by far my favorite game of 2015 and possibly ever, hands down.
If you enjoy a rich story, a vibrant atmosphere, and an emotional rollercoaster you will remember for ages, then I say, without a single doubt in my mind. GET. THIS. GAME.

You wake up...
You're 82 years old and have been living the last 7 years with lung cancer.
From your nostrils you can no longer breath by yourself; there's a tube that reaches out to an oxygen tank on your left, while on your right, an I.V. pierces your skin.  You no longer go outside, or leave your room.  You're doing nothing more than waiting to die.  If you could relive your life, imagine you did everything the way you wanted in your final moments.  Would you?
10/10. Would cry again.
as a game it's a bit of an unchallenging chore. the story is really nice though. probably would have worked better as a graphic novel or an anime.

Yes, the core game mechanics are pretty bare, and yes, it is more of an interactive story than a game.
But what story !
The only thing I could say is "thank you". Thank you Kan Gao and all people involved in creating such an immersive experience, during which I laughed aloud, cried aloud, and could not stop the tears for hours afterwards. A vivid memory that keeps bringing up those same tears years after playing it, simply at the first notes of soundtrack I keep listening to.
To you, potentially future player, do not take this as a game, but rather as a book. Lower your expectancies, close your curtains, don't allow yourself any break (it is about 3-4 hours long), and just flow in with the story, music and mood.

10/10 the feelings are too much for me.
And now I hope one day people will get it my mind and do some NASA-spam.

Oh god, Trine is one of the most boring and monotonous games I've ever played. It really doesn't get much more trivial than this for a platformer, even Super Mario Bros. has more variety and little unnecessary filler.
The AI is dumb and will constantly fall off ledges and jump back up, only to fall off again. Weapons are slow and inaccurate, the wizard's conjuration ability requires such precision that it becomes useless in any combat situation. Also, why can't I jump and fire arrows or use my conjuration spells in the air? Stupid limitations.
The premise is interesting, the Trine mechanics are innovative, albeit contrived. The story is lacklustre. The narration during the loading screens is so slow and fragmented that I can't be bothered waiting to hear what's being told.
The levels are all too similar in layout and lack inspiration. The puzzle mechanics aren't challenging and are too predictable, they seem to be the only reason for the physics engine to exist in the first place.
Co-op is almost unplayable and seemed tacked on "just because" as both players control one of three characters, but only have access to two of the characters at a time, which slows down gameplay considerably. It also doesn't make sense in context with the Trine itself. The option for three player co-op is there but I'm not certain many people would be able to take advantage of this on PC.

This is offline which means getting two or three players crowding around the PC – another example of the pleasant Amiga-style nostalgia Trine engenders. There a few downsides. The combat becomes a bit of a chore later on, and distracts from the puzzling and sightseeing. Also the game is relatively short at around six-eight hours, which makes the price point feel high. Nevertheless, 2D platform games are practically extinct on all platforms, let alone the PC, and Trine is a gorgeous example of the genre.

HnS is a very short, deeply flawed, pretty creative puzzle game. If the writing is inconsistent but generally terrible, the puzzles can be unfairly obscure, the soundtrack merits a level "meh" if not a disapproving "feh" at some times, and it comes off as a prototype that is exceedingly buggy and sometimes hard-crash prone (e.g. the first room in Act 5), why "buy that for a dollar" even on DEEP sale?
Because the gameplay is pretty unique, and the art is charming (Stacked and this game give a good look at why DoubleFine is kind of like the anti-Kojiman Tarantino of video game limited engagements). You progress from altering a few variables on rocks and turtles (alas, LOGO!) to solving spatial puzzles with non-obvious objects to tugging at a restrictive set of arguments and logical tests directly in a strange room and machine floor metaphor for a program. The final act involves regularly recursing into this "live-debugging" process for objects you really would not ordinarily be expected to try to muck about with, and there is a corny endgame, high-concept way of subverting objects that aren't there. A Git-like branching checkpoint system seems cute and overkill at first but will necessitate itself near the end. The game feels like around 3.5 to 4 hours of those comic interludes in Paper Mario, like where you had to bake a cake that one time.
For all its quirks, what is maddening is this:
* Game is too short to let this wonderful system sink in, but there is also a conspicuous lack of easy-to-have-added polish.
* For all various reviewers yammer on about programming, writing scripts is not a capability you ever get; you are purely a saboteur of low cunning who breaks things from within, as advertised. The old hacker ideal of making something is not here unless you want to munge a burning bush to spawn a turtle breeding ground which hatches an outhouse decal. Play Scribblenauts for those shenanigans.
* It seems like DF dropped this game like a hot rock, which is just dumb given how this game's potential far exceeds that of their other junk. The game and its main menu strongly suggests moddability, and advertises this, but there is *effectively* no support for Steam Workshop and no easy roadmap to how one might decompile the Lua that is still compiled and correctly package mods. Any community seems to have died long ago, and it is laughable in a truly sad way.

Gauntlet: Slayer Edition is a remake of a classic arcade game by Atari from 1985 and was developed by Arrowhead during 2014. Basically a dungeon clawler, hack and slash videogame, Gauntlet's (extremely scarce) premise is about a group of heroes being summoned by a powerful wizard to overcome the challenges of the titular gauntlet to gain acess to a great treasure.
Gauntlet can be played either by a single player or up to four, with each controlling a single hero. The main objective of the game, regardless of the mode chosen, is about to advance through the current dungeon till its end while destroying the enemies thrown at you and dodging the various hazards. The player can choose between five different heroes, each with his/her own strong suit and weaknesses, gear and abilities of choice:
- The warrior is a heavy-hitter melee character capable of a great damage output, but he spots a worse mobility than the other heroes (althought his charge/evade move can knock enemies over)
- The elf is a fast character who specializes into striking enemies from afar with his arrows and has the best evading manuver: his main weakness is however being extremely fragile if the enemies manage to catch up with him
- The valkyrie, much like the warrior, is a melee-oriented character, but she's most effective in defence than in sheer attack power: her shield can block incoming damage and withstand enemy pressure while the other heroes do the damaging
- The wizard is arguably the hardest hero to master properly: he can use a grand total of nine spells by mixing up his three elements. You can use one spell at a time and each has a single purpose: one spell is able to freeze foes in a cone in front of the wizard, while another will help him teleport out of harm's reach. As such, the wizard can bring to the party a lot of utility, but will be a load if misused, given he has poor speed and damage reduction
- The necromancer (which is the content of a paid DLC and not available in the base game) is a hero capable to use both offensive spells and summoned minions to divert enemy attention
While riding Gauntlet's dungeons is important for each hero to watch out for food, which is the only way to replenish one's health. Should a character die, he/she can be brought back with a skull coin: such coins are available after a certain number of enemies has been killed by the party. If there are no coins available, the game is over and the dungeon must be repeated from the very beginning. Another important resource for heroes is gold, which can be used between levels to purchase additional gear for the heroes. Aside from the purely cosmetics purchases (which, truth be told, costs far too much gold each), a hero can purchase a relic (which gives him/her an useful activated ability), a talisman (which holds a specific passive ability) or a new weapon (since different weapons carry different activated abilities).
The game has three modes. The story mode, which is somehow brief, is made of several mandatory dungeons plus some optional arena-like levels the players can run to gain more gold: the mode also spots unique but few boss characters who can be best described as puzzle bosses and are fairly challenging in their own right. The colosseum mode pits the players against waves after waves of enemies in a single arena map and is fairly challenging (to the point that even playing on normal difficulty will see your hero die in short order if you are not careful). The endless mode is instead, as the name implies, a mode where the heroes can navigate an endless stream of dungeons without any clear objective or end in sight: the challenge is about clearing as many dungeon's floors as possible. The dungeons and enemies you get to meet in this mode are basically entirely recycled from the story mode plain and simple.
Gauntlet: Slayer Edition is, by any means, a nice hack and slash game which is extremely enjoyable if played with friends, but it suffers somehow by a very brief story mode, a basically pointless and redundant endless mode and an incredibly hard and not that anjoyable arena mode

While there are some programs and games dedicated to polishing typing ability, only a handful of them can be described as both entertaining and good. Typing practice is not exactly associated with excitement; which is probably why the topic is mostly avoided.
However, Epistory creators managed to combine the core idea of typing with beauty and fun.
Everything in this game revolves around words, texts and typing. The menu can be navigated by typing commands, the abilities are switched by typing their names. The enemies are fended off with the power of typing as well. Every time the narrator reads out another bit of the enigmatic story, the text appears on the ground, where it stays at least until the end of the chapter. Also, the land is formed out of what looks like sheets of paper filled with writing. Every time the player unlocks a new patch of land, the world unfolds beautifully, like a cross between pop-up books and origami figurines. While the graphic style might seem simplistic, it goes very well with the aesthetic of a world of paper.
As for how typing works in battles, I personally find it very well implemented. One might complain that the set up looks hardly exciting - the main character typically stands in a stone circle during longer battles and the enemies approach her - but this is not the case. Once one of the beasts comes too close, the girl and her companion fox are killed and the entire fight sequence has to be repeated. Additionally, enemy types are varied not only in terms of size and speed but also the number of words assigned to them (think of them as their "health") and their difficulty.
The player collects four elemental abilities throughout the game, each one having a different debilitating effect on adversaries (fire burns additional word, ice freezes enemies in place, lightning jumps between them and wind gusts push them back), but once the player learns new skills... monsters immune to all skills but one corresponding to their colour start to appear. This makes the combat a bit nerve-wracking at times - the enemies approach slowly but steadily, getting closer and closer while the player tries to make no mistakes.
Personally I think that my experience with Epistory helped me improve the way I type. Although, I have never loathed and feared my mother tongue more than I did when I saw monsters adorned with words like "gżegżółka" and "pięćdziesięciogroszówka". Playing Epistory in Polish is not for the faint of heart.
Apart from fighting enemies and unearthing lost treasures, the player has to face some environmental puzzles as well. Sadly, this is probably the least satisfying element of the game. The puzzles are on the easy side to the point they can be considered a bit boring. There really isn't much to talk about - some ice physics, pressing switches here and there, finding a code and pressing some more switches in the right order.
TL;DR Epistory is a great experience, with beautiful visuals and a cool idea. Also, playing it can actually improve your typing skill. Beware the Polish language in this game.

The puzzles are references to psychosis in a certain way and are quite easy but not too underchallenging. That's okay but not really special or a reason to buy the game, and sometimes they feel like they're stretching the game since they appear quite often. So they're basically "nice" or "interesting" puzzles but nothing more.
Inbetween the walking and puzzling solving and cutscene watching, the game offers you some combat encounters.
And the issue with the combat is that the combat system isn't really... well... memorable?
The combat is just sooo simple, it requires no learning or training, you just simply learn the combat automatically.
The combat itself kinda looks like this most of the time: Your opponent strikes -> you parry his strike shortly before the impact with the blocking button, which is by default the ctrl-key for some reason -> the you go nuts on your enemy using the Left Mouse Button for light attacks and the Right Mouse Button for heavy attacks -> if you're fighting against multiple opponents and if one of them who isn't in the field of view of your camera attacks you then you'll get an audial warning from the voices in Senua's head saying something like "Watch out! Behind you!". In this case simply press the block button in order to parry the attack, Senua will parry and now focus the camera on this opponent so you can again go nuts  on him. This cycle of parrying and attacking will go on and on. There are only a few exceptions, one is the one type of enemy with a shield where you simply have to press f which results in a kick which then results into opening the defense of the enemy, after that simply go nuts on him. The other exception is a certain enemy which is a heavier enemy with a big axe or something like that. When you encounter this guy then you simply have to dodge more of since not every attack by him can be parried ( on the other hand if it's not parryable it will be blockable so you can still block instead of dodging if you want to). And that's it, a very simple combat system. In my opinion it's not memorable at all. It actually contains combos but i never ever bothered to learn them because you simply don't have to in order to beat the game, since the combat is easy enough already.
There are a few boss fights here and there but every attack of a boss can simply be either dodged, blocked or parried. The only thing that makes boss fights kinda difficult is the surprising aspect of an attack f.e. the boss does an attack you haven't seen before out of nowhere and it kind of surprises you, plus the boss fights last quite long because the bosses have a high HP pool so they pretty much endure a lot of attacks from you.
The ending of the game is quite weird, there's no boss fight, there are only 3 fights:
The first 2 are simple fights against normal enemies which you've already encountered before in the game.
The last fight is again a fight against all the normal enemies you've encountered before but this time they spawn infinitely, and you can only progress if you let them kill you, so basically the end cutscene triggers after you've died.
And in my opinion it's not really a challenge to let enemies kill you.
So in the end it's a linear story with a too simple combat system and a main character who always has to scream all the time.
I don't recommend this game, furthermore i managed to play through it in 6 hours in only one session, so it's not a very long game.

Finished the game, and oh I had a lot of fun.
It is not for everyone, like most games, has a few things in it that make no sense, kinda wish it was longer a bit, but overall, I loved every moment of it.
It had a few cons like, Why do we have to walk around for another minute instead of climbig up that knee-high rock, or why can't we just toss the torch through the fence right next to the gatethat has water falling down from above it.
Pros are plenty.
It is immersive, the voices are perfect, made me want to tell them to shut the hell up multiple times.
Soundtrack is brilliant as well, didn't much like them at the end, felt like it didn't really fit, but made the battles far more fun overall. And the environmental sounds were great too.
Loved how good Senua was overall, Melina did an amazing job with her. Loved the flashbacks, loved her story, hope to see some more Senua in the future. And more games that tackle mental health issues,
Combat was fun, several types of enemies, the berserker was annoying as hell,  bosses were all unique, with a bunch of of their own moves. And a little advice: don't block, like ever, unless it is just a 1v1. You can dodge sideways pretty much all the attacks.
So, tl;dr: Hella good game, bit short, a flaw or two here and there, but it was money well spent on such an immersive story.

Honestly I expected more from Ninja Theory, I loved their other games, because they actually were GAMES. Hellblade is barely a game, it's a linear interactive movie with voices telling you exactly what to do even if there is only one path anyway. And Oh boy are those voices annoying after only 2 minutes.
I don't like it when I don't know if I'm controlling the character/camera or if it's just a cinematic, most of the time I can't tell the difference.
I also think it was not a good idea to start the story when Senua is already insane. I thought there would be a descent into madness, you know, maybe like that old Gamecube game Eternal Darkness ? That would have been more interesting, to witness the character slowly loosing grip over reality. Instead they chose to start the story 7 years after Senua's journey began, so she's totally insane already.
Anyway, it's not worth 30 euros, it feels like an UE4 tech demo. I'm not saying it's bad, the story is probably really good ( unless there is a silly plot twist like "everything was in her head because she's crazy" ), graphics and atmosphere are nice, and Senua is really well done and well acted ( and realistic, she's not a supermodel like 99% of the females in games ).
But it was boring after 30 minutes, I checked other negatives reviews which confirmed that the game didn't become more interesting later, and I asked for a refund.
Next time either make a real game, or a movie.

The New Colossus (TNC) is the sequel to The New Order (TNO), which is a Wolfenstein series that depicts a world where the Nazis won WW2 and took over the world. Now... I really liked TNO for its gameplay, the surprisingly strong storytelling, and all taking place in a grim backdrop that is similar to the actual Nazi plans if they had won WW2. My only real gripe with it was that the crazy science and the whole "ancient Jewish order with sci-fi tech" business firmly put the game in fantasy-land when much of the rest was actually disturbingly plausible alternate history. So I was looking forward to the sequel when it was announced.
TNC ended up being about what I expected: TNO, but a bit more polished and set in a Nazi-occupied US. So that straight away tells you really all you need to know about this game. Namely, that it is pretty damn good. Brutal, disturbing, filled with crazy sci-fi stuff, and with lots of great characterization. I'm not sure whether or not I like TNC more than TNO, but they certainly are comparable in how much I liked them. The fact that I marathoned the entire game is both a testament to my complete lack of sanity as well as a game I deeply enjoyed. There are only a handful of other games, such as Bioshock Infinite, that can claim the same.
...Though that also has a downside. It took me roughly 10 hours to finish the game on the "medium" difficulty setting. While this isn't a surprise, it still bugs me since it's a $60 game (that I didn't actually buy, but more on that later). That is one of a handful of issues I have with this game. A second is that, as with TNO, the science gets really crazy in this. Especially when a certain plot event happens that requires some "replacements" to be acquired (you will know what I mean when you see it). Third, I was a bit turned off by when a certain historical figure shows up for a bit (
), and they are depicted as a completely unhinged psychopath who likes to just shoot people who annoy them. While it is true that this person most certainly was unhinged and a completely despicable human being, I've never heard anything about them outright shooting people that irritated them. They tended to leave the actual killing to suboordinates, of which they did... quite alot.
Lastly, there are some stability issues that need work. For me, the only actual problem I faced was that the Steam overlay didn't work, but I was still getting achievements and the like. Others have talked about freezes and crashes, but nothing of the sort happened with my PC. Still, it is an issue worth considering since those stability issues might affect you... at least until it is all patched up.
One other thing is that I actually didn't buy this game, but rather was gifted it by a good friend who was amused by the ridiculous amount of rage this game has generated on the so-called "alt-right" and wanted to support the devs who helped to annoy those people. I certainly found the spam on the Steam forums to be ridiculous and depressing since it's yet another example of how politics infests everything these days and how seemingly anything can cause a fight online. After having played TNC, I found that much of nutter rage over this game was, predictably, stupid and based only on suspicions rather than actual experience with the game. It reminds me of the "outrage" people had when the first Mass Effect game came out, and "moral guardians" were losing it over how there was going to be sex in the game and how games were turning into porn or whatever. And then it turned out that the sex actually in Mass Effect was so benign that the rage over it ended up being a big joke.
TNC has plenty of characters with varied political opinions, but isn't afraid to call out when someone is being stupid. Examples of this include a southern communist who goes off about "the evils of capitalist America" and refusing to fight for it even as it was losing to the far bigger menace of Nazism, or a collaborator who sold out his own family members to get rich, earn favor, and help make a "white man's world". The idea that you would be working with a black leftist revolution to kill white people is debunked when you actually meet Grace (the badass mom with an afro) and find that she is neither a homicidal maniac nor a racist. And even Grace isn't immune to being called out, which ends up happening to her late in the game over the one notable prejudice she puts on display.
Ultimately, people who raged over how this game was going to be "commie propaganda" or a "white genocide simulator" were complete morons. If this game does have a political message, it is that political extremism and discrimination of all types are bad. Some people apparently have forgotten that the Nazis have both extreme nationalism and murderous racism at the center of their ideology, and that opposing that doesn't make you a supporter of "white genocide" or whatever BS people come up with. It makes you someone opposed to one of the most evil ideologies this world has ever known.
Ok... i'll stop with that. Just felt like it needed to be said since the forums for this game were infested with garbage ever since the game got on Steam in the summer.
So, in summary, TNC is much like its predecessor: an excellent shooter with above-average storytelling that takes place in an alternate history dystopia that we should all be thankful never became a reality. And that it should ♥♥♥♥in stay that way. :o

Trine is a game about three typical fantasy hero archetypes (the mage, the thief, and the knight) on a typical quest through typical locales to get (as typically) three artifacts. Along the way, you'll use typical weapons and fight typical enemies while solving typical puzzles and looking for typical secrets.
Despite all this, Trine is fantastic. You play as one hero at a time, swapping on the fly, and they each play differently; the Thief has a grappling hook and a bow, the Knight is an excellent melee fighter and can lift and destroy heavy objects, and the Wizard can create and move platforms, crates, and the like.
The game itself is beautiful, mostly thanks to stunning art and level design, and the soundtrack is excellent, fitting the game thematically and doing its part to add an overall sense of exploration. The gameplay is top-notch, although the platforming can be a bit floaty at times.
The game is a decent length (6-8 hours or so) and never really overstayed its welcome, and finishes with a fantastic level that's much different from any previous one. Throughout the game, you'll level up your characters and find hidden items that you can equip to any of the three for stat and ability boosts.
I really enjoyed my time with Trine and recommend it at almost any price, but I did have one gripe with it: the heroes are vastly varied, but unfortunately that applies to how fun they are, too. The Wizard is by far the least fun to play, although he's probably the most useful; the Knight I had the least amount of fun with, until I got a late-game upgrade that made him feel, at least, powerful; but I almost exclusively used the Thief, whose grappling hook and ranged weapon made her incredibly fun to play and almost made the other characters obsolete for platforming and most combat scenarios.
That, however, is only a personal problem and completely subjective. Other people might find the Wizard to be the most fun, given his versatility, or the Knight, since he can throw rocks and smash skeletons to pieces in an instant.
I wholeheartedly recommend Trine to anyone who enjoys solid platformers with a tiny bit of puzzling, fantasy themes, or beautiful scenery.

I LOVE this game! It's so unique and is a great way of visually teaching the logical thought processes and patterns of programming without scaring people off too much with all the syntax. I strongly recommend staying away from this game.  The idea is good, but the execution is terrible.  About halfway through, the puzzles change from occasionally obscure to extremely obscure, convoluted, and tedious, a sudden leap in difficulty that can't be justified due to the game's short length.  In addition, the game softlocked on me multiple times and I'm not talking about the universe crashing mechanic.  The first time I played through, I inadvertently sequence broke by simply hacking my speed to the max to get past a certain obstacle and later ended up with an unsolvable puzzle because I skipped over the section that made the game's programming labels readable.
The puzzles themselves revolve around simplified computer language, a field that I have taken a couple classes in, but if the aim was to get players interested in programming, they went way off.  At least with compilers you could assign new variables, rewrite whole sections to bypass problems, and utilize a checking function to make you aware of crash-inducing problems without the universe ending and forcing you to start all over.
I do hope that someone is eventually able to give the idea behind this game the attention and devotion it deserves, especially since Hack 'n' Slash failed as a game at the most fundamental level: it's not fun.

So the short version of the game, is I love it. It isn't very long to finish, but it is extremely well crafted from the audio to the atmosphere, and they did an excellent job accurately portraying the possible ways to experience psychosis.
Here's the long version.  The most important thing to me is the obvious quality and attention to detail in every aspect of this game so far.  The environments are gorgeous, the character animation has real feeling, the audio is spot on, and the game play feels smooth and easy to understand.
The game is essentially played in two different states.  The first is something of an exploration state.  Senua wanders through the world, navigating her environment and experiencing sudden changes in atmosphere as her psychosis causes her to hear things, or see shapes, shadows, or even physcial changes in the landscape.  This also involves solving certain puzzles by looking for shapes that match a rune to open a door, or picking your way through certain arch shaped structures that seem to change the world as you pass through them.
The second state is a combat state that triggers when an enemy appears.  Combat took a little bit to figure out, but once I did I was able to string some combos together and dodge without too much difficulty.  It feels clean, and visceral.  If I make a mistake and get hit, I don't feel like it's because the game didn't respond, I feel like it is because I didn't do the right thing.   It is also immensely satisfying to charge in and interrupt your oppenent, cutting into them with a flurry of strikes.
The last major positive to this is that the game feels original.  The madness of the character makes this an experience unlike any other I've seen so far.  This is most evident in the audio as everywhere you go, Senua is plagued by voices.  Some of them are telling you to turn back, others give advice, and still others encourage you or even warn if you if an enemy is about to attack you.  All these voices together create a feeling of chaos that breathes real life into the struggles of navigating a land you know nothing about.
Now that I've completed it, I can't wait to play more of this game.  I want to see more of the environments, learn more about the story and why I'm in this scenario, and collect the remaining lorestones I don't have to learn more about the mythology.  It is a surprising breath of fresh air to play something so different in an industry that thrives on the latest craze of game genres, or new releases to an ongoing franchise.

4/5. Fanstastic, beautiful game, heartwrenching prologue. Astonishingly good puzzle-platforming, great controls, awesome sound.
My major complaint, which is significant enough to warrant a 1 star drop, is the lack of difficulty in the combat. There are very few challenging encounters in the game, and no boss fights. Most of the gameplay is more about puzzle-platforming than surviving in combat (even the most game-changing "combat" ability is used primarily for movement later in the game, and it's mechanics discourage using it for combat in many areas). There are a few challenging monsters, but they die in 1-2 hits through a pseudo-quicktime ability use or by running them into a wall.
Another minor complaint is that some of the areas become locked through the game progression, preventing 100% completion. There's no real reason they *need* to be locked, for instance there's a water area that becomes flooded and locked via the storyline, but the player can get a water-breathing perk through the skill-trees. There's no reason that area couldn't be re-accessed as an underwater level.
All in all though, this game was fantastic and I highly recommend it for ANYONE who enjoys Puzzle-Platformer games. If you're expecting a solid Metrovania, don't level up the combat skill-tree unless necessary or the combat will become too easy to be satisfying. If you're a completionist, treat any zone you have to "enter" as if it would become locked when you finish it.
Edit: (Note: I 99% completed this game in ~12 hours. It's pretty short, but still worth the buy imo.)

This is a game that's hard to review under Steam's binary system. I like the game well enough, but t has frustrating elements and the non-typing aspects, which is why I bought this game instead of playing Typing of the Dead, are minimal and don't carry the gameplay outside of keyboard-mashing. Epistory is a fun typing tutor, but that's pretty much all it is. I've seen it billed as a mashup of typing tutors and RPGs like Bastion, but it's not as deep as games in that genre can be. There are some puzzles along the way that are a bit tricky, and the art is well done and interesting, but those elements on its own are pretty weak. If you are looking for a typing game, this one does the trick, but don't expect it to be any deeper than that. Full disclosure, I am 30+ years old and lifelong gamer, so my expectations may be a bit high. It could be that if you are buying this game for a child, they will find it utterly delightful.
First, the typing. The game is pretty good there. It's easy to control the game and explore the world while keeping your hands on home row. You move around with either WASD or an alternative control that uses F and J, the "anchor keys" of home row and I and E, which is the key your middle fingers hit on the row above. It's quite comfortable to navigate the isometric game world that way. I do wish I could rebind the keys, though. I think shifting the WASD setup over to the right a bit would also work well for movement while keeping my hands on home row.
When an enemy or destructible barrier shows up, you shift into combat mode by pressing space, and start typing away. To reach the menu, you hit Tab. One of my favorite details is that you can navigate the menu by typing. You want to open the upgrade screen, you can type "upgrade." It's a nice touch that keeps the flow of the typing going.
Combat is okay. Again, at its core, it's a typing game and there's only so much you can do to spice that up. Enemies approach you from all directions, and you hurt them and knock them back by typing the words that appear above them. Most combat happens at fixed points, and you are frozen in place while the enemies come at you. If a single enemy gets close enough to touch you, it's game over. You will unlock elemental powers along the way that have different effects. Ice will freeze them, fire will damage them over time and burn the next word over time, etc. You switch powers by typing "Ice" or "fire." It works well and doesn't break flow, but sometimes I did accidentally switch to ice while typing something else.
Towards the end of the game (hopefully), the combat just becomes a slog. Since all you do is type at enemies, the only thing the game can do to make it challenging is to throw more enemies at you. These encounters can become tedious, especially since you have a single hit point, and battles can last for several minutes. One particular maddening fight, which prompted me to write ths review, had me struggling for a long time. I was in a dark cave, and I had to constantly attack crystals to keep the lights on. If the crystal went out, I couldn't see the words above the enemies and couldn't fight them. I died four times before I gave up and turned on the "adaptive difficulty." I couldn't manually go to a lower setting, I had to die a couple times before the game knocked me down to an easy enough fight that I could finish. As bad as that was, it was the next fight that really bothered me. It was a normal fight, enemies came at me and I could see them right away. The lowered difficulty manifested itself by slower and fewer enemies. I rarely had more than 2 enemies on the screen at a time, but the fight still dragged on forever, all the while my dog was whimpering to go outside because you can't pause the game mid-battle for some reason. I beat that fight without really feeling challenged, let my dog out, anf when I saw the next fight coming, I just had to quit. I couldn't stand the thought of another five-minute slog.
Outside combat, there's exploration, hard-to-find chests, backtracking as your new elemental powers open new areas, unlockable artwork which fills in some backstory, and some puzzles here and there. All of that is fairly bland and unchallenging. You have buttons you have to walk across in sequence, patches of ice where you can't change direction until you hit a wall, and other puzzles that I've seen in several other games. Nothing particularly stood out as being very fun or challenging, but again as an adult I may be expecting more variety than most people looking to play a typing game. Your reward for most of this is experience, which you can use to buy upgrades. There's nothing game-changing about the upgrades, nor is there much of a choice about what to upgrade. Right now, I have enough experience to have everything upgraded
The story is pretty vague, your character's identity is only "the Muse," and so far I haven't really found any answers. Each dungeon has 4 or 5 chests with a piece of a picture. Each one adds an element to that dungeon's picture. Collect them all and you will see a picture of (presumably) the main character's life on the planet earth. But there's still no mention of how or why she got to this book-themed world. It's probably going to end up as some sort of allegory, one dungeon had some definite colegiate overtones, but there's not enough there to relly entice me.
I don't know if I'm going to pick this game up again. If I do, it won't be for the story, the puzzles, or the art. It'll just be to sharpen my typing skills. Maybe it was foolish for me to expect more from a typing game. Just don't go in expecting the same, either.

My friend go used to the wizard play of using combinations to get spells, but it definitely was not my play style and I could not adapt to it.

I have only played this game for a few days now, but at this point I am not sure I would be playing this game after a few weeks. I bought Off Road Drive awhile back, and I can honestly say it's the closest to reality out of all other off roading games I've played. It's awesome, almost as fun as off roading for real. But, it's not without it's flaws. The first one I noticed is that despite it's description there is no snow courses in the entire game. Another is that for game modes you have a choice of career or.. career. While you can go back and replay courses, you can't choose the exact track you want to play on, rather you have to play an entire series of tracks. Oh and I should note that if you lose in the series while replaying it will override your previously clearing it and possibly make trucks you've unlocked unavailible. But the biggest flaw is that the game does not have a free roaming mode, and is abosultely humorless if you try and do anything other than drive on the course in the exact way it wants you to.
I wouldn't have bothered with writing a review if I hadn't noticed that 1c just released a French translation a short while ago, which must mean the developers still care about the game on some level, and perhaps they'll listen to me. Please add a mode where the game doesnt force you back on to the track. Possibly add inverted courses to change it up a bit. And maybe add some snow tracks if the first two things end up being easy fixes. Don't let this game's potential go to waste! :)
TL;DR Game is good if you get into real off roading, but don't expect to have as much freedom as you'd have in an older game like MotorM4x.

I think this game is everything a multiplayer fps fan is looking for. The developers really had the common shooter fan in mind, that's for sure. You have the usual rent a gear system, you can make your character look as cool as you want, or if it's goofiness you are looking for, it's in there too. You can buy weapons permanently, if you want to try them out first, you just have to get them from daily rewards, or capsules. Sadly you can't put attachments on your weapons, if you want guns with holo sights, you can to open capsules. There are a lot of game modes besides the usual TDM and bomb planting, like convoy, manhunt, seizure, escape, pve and a lot more. The biggest charm of the game for me is the lack of loading times, the action is almost constant. You get in a room, hit F5, and you are in the game. Also before joining a running game you actually get the scores the two teams are having, so you know, if a game is ending soon. The graphics are pretty, the reload animations are well done, ragdolls look so real. There is killcam, even showing the path of the grenade that killed you. While gun damage is pretty realistic (considering the players have armor on), you can play a less forgiving hardcore mode. if you want to. You can buy countless skins, boosts, premium membership (that gives other players xp, and money boost), equipment for real money, but i think the prices might be a bit high. I can only recommend this game. Reminds me a lot of Call of Duty 4, and that's one of my favorite shooters.

It's rare that a game can hit the mark in so many different and often conflicting areas. Fallout 3 offers freedom without sacrificing a focused story. It delivers fantastic combat without forgoing a deep role-playing system. The characters you meet are engaging and oftentimes hilarious without feeling out of place in this harsh world. The game has a few flaws -- most of them technical -- but it's a case where the whole is greater than the sum. It's a fantastic game with incredible atmosphere that offers fun in so many different ways that you're almost sure to get hooked.
The Game of the Year Edition adds five big expansions to the world. Some of the new additions are better than others, which means those with the game already might simply want to download a couple from Xbox Live and call it a day. If you haven't yet played Fallout 3, this is the disc to own. Stop dragging your feet and give it a shot.
10/10

I really love this game and recommend it any day. Period.
If you're turned away by the age (8 years old, as of this review...my god I feel old), realise that there are always mods to do anything you felt was missing, or that you thought the game needed to compete with newer roleplaying games. Although the modding community is absolutely incredible, I recommend completing one playthrough without mods. Just to get the intended experience at least once. Now, as for what the game offers...I'll do this in a simple way that I've seen pretty often on here, so you should know it.
PROS:
+ Atmosphere is perfect. There's something about the look and feel of the wasteland that just makes you feel really immersed
+ Soundtrack is very good, using classic songs from the 50s-60s era, which is a nice bit of irony. Cheery music, destroyed world
+ Character building and connections are done extremely well in this game, which a few exceptions. I personally cared about many of the characters throughout my travels of the Capital Wasteland
+ SO MUCH TO EXPLORE! There are just over a hundred (if my memory is correct) marked locations in the base game world, but so many more hidden in all of the nooks and crannies of DC. And often you'll find yourself learning more about what happened to people in those locations, which really helps establish the open world
+ The player has many choices to make, some make subtle changes, while others completely change everything. Choose wisely
+ Lots of variety and freedom. The quest design is done so that the player can take so many different paths to achieve something, which definitely adds to the roleplaying experience
+ Incredible amounts of replayability. Tying in with the last two points, this game has so many things to do, it is impossible to see everything in just one playthrough
+ Variety in weapons and armour. Want to deck yourself out in full power armour? Sure. Just want to chill out in pyjamas? You've got it. What about running around in a duster coat and a clown mask? I don't see why not. And as for weapons...there are dozens of weapons at your disposal, most of which have unique variants for you to collect
+ So much to do! There are hundreds of quests to be completed, dozens of unique weapons and armour to be found, hundreds of locations to explore and learn about, and so much more. This game is filled to the brim with content
+ If you want more, the Fallout 3 Nexus has thousands of mods for you to tweak your game with, allowing for even more replayability
CONS:
- Gunplay is horrible. You do get used to it after a while, but it still has a slight cringe factor
- Some of the voice acting is a little weak. Given the scale of the game, I do give it a bit of a pass on it
- Pretty annoying to actually start up. It took me a few hours of tinkering with files and downloading patches before it worked, but now it runs fantastic and I don't believe that it has crashed on me yet

Don't look at the amount of time I put in the game because steam doesn't count them past the launcher. Fallout 3 is a hell of a good game, I've put countless hours in it and still do. I posted a positive review after around 10 hours of playing the game, of which I completed the main story on hard difficulty, which turned out not to be too much of a challenge at all. I really really REALLY wanted to give this game a positive review but sadly I feel that I didn't get much content for how much I paid. I spent almost 30 hours playing The New Order and figured a Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus would be much longer and have more content but sadly the games story seemed to just rush into the next segment.
The reason I posted a positive review orignally was because I actually did enjoy what I played. But coming back and trying to do some of the forced in side missions made me realise how little there was in this game. I found the combat to be genuinely good, although I do miss the old double barrel shotgun.
10 hours for a full price game is not okay, I know pre-order people get some sort of extra mission soon but I can't imagine it will be any more than a couple of hours at most.
The story was kinda varied, some moments will have you floored and stunned and made make you laugh, but the rest is just kinda boring to tell you the truth, it seemed like they had some really great story ideas but in a rushed manner.
The choice of weapons were kinda sad really, for a shooter there wasn't anything really all that fun to use, as soon as I slapped the scope on that assult rifle you get straight away it was game over, enemies went down like nothing after that. That and a combo of the supressed pistol to one shot basic enemies every time.
Performace wise I can't say I had any issues really, only some strange audio issues like certain sounds like gunfire and such not working in the Metro levels but that was really it for me.
Game straight up crashes at random times after the new update, great.
Now this gets into the spoiler territory here so watch out.
Characters are great, some epic moments and some emotional.
Blaskowitz auditioning beside other actors to play himself in a movie about himself infront of Hitler was genius, they sure kept that one quiet in the trailers and I'm so glad they did, but the trailers ruined a lot of the game for me, seeing that Blaskowitz clearly gets a head transplant in the game just made the scene where Frau Engel cuts his head off just less of a shock, they should have just removed that ring around his neck in the trailers.  but honestly I still did enjoy the bad-assery of how Blaskowitz can even survive losing his head.
The ending was trash, it really was, going up to Frau Engel after hating her for 2 games and Blaskowitz just ending her, I felt absolutely nothing. It was too fast. I was hoping for some kind of epic boss battle with her but all we got were some 2 random robot dudes who were insanely easy to kill (I had no idea it was even the final boss (Or even a boss battle at all!) after I finished it.)
Yeah so It's not a bad game really but don't expect a long story, cost for me was a little too much but if you don't mind paying full price for a 10 hour story and some tacked on side missions (No new locations but re-used levels from single player.) then go ahead but I'd advise you just watch the story on Youtube or wait until you have get this for like £20 or lower.
