The game has potential, but has a serious lack of content and polish and is definitely not worth the asking price of £10.59 (at least not in its current state). If you badly want to play this game, I'd recommend waiting for it to go down in price or waiting for it to come out of early access.
If this game does look like your kind of thing, read this review before making your decision as the game is very flawed and just not really good. The following is my experience with Zero Gravity.
First of all, I couldn't get the game to run properly as the game kept defaulting to the highest settings. So if your rig isn't the best (or even your monitor as the game kept resetting the resolution) don't buy this game in its current state as it may not run properly. Thankfully, I got in contact with the dev and he gave me access to a developer's version of the game in which these issues are fixed. The developer was very helpful. However, I'm friends with the guy in real life so my experience with this might be bias. Also, not all of the issues were fixed.
I then went through the puzzle levels. They're very Portal-eque in the sense that everything takes place in a white testing space. I had no issues with these levels apart from the fact that these levels rely too much on dodging lazers. A feat that isn't easy in a first person game. There are also only 3 puzzle levels and they're all relatively short.
Next was the platformer levels. These are very unintuitive and very lazily designed. Every single level takes place in exactly the same environment with cubes in different places that act as platforms. The platformer levels just feel so lazily designed it's unbearable. Nothing in these levels are centred which is also very annoying. and very OCD testing. These levels just feel like they've been slapped together in a day or two. I ended up giving up on level 6 (of which there are 10) because the levels themselves are very unintuitive. All the platforms in these areas do different things but it isn't made clear what differentiates them. Yes, red ones explode but it's hard to tell what colour these things are from a distance. There are also spheres which act exactly the same as the cubes and, as far as I can tell, they serve no purpose but to maybe spice up the visuals and variety... which they don't.
Next was the EVA. This was probably the best mode out of all of them. Drifting through space and completing space walking missions feels so cool. I gave up on the first level though because I made it back to base but the game wouldn't actually acknowledge that I had. Very annoying.
I didn't even attempt to play the docking levels as I've played them before and they're too hard for any sane person to enjoy. I enjoy a challenge but that challenge has to be engaging and fun, which this isn't.
Overall, this game has massive potential but I urge anyone to not buy this game while it's in Alpha 0.1. It's just not worth the asking price of £10.59 at all. I may have received this game for free but if I hadn't I would've asked for a refund.

Gauntlet was always an attrition style game not and not an 'instant death on mistakes with no idea why'.  It was about pushing forward and falling back, pushing forward and falling back.
Death ate your health over time and was defeated by potions (not kill you instantly, and immue to everything), for good reasons.  The former is fun the latter just annoying.
Many of the characters dont even fit their traditional roles.  Merlin doesnt do huge magic damage, Questor isnt all that much faster than anyone else (and often the same speed or slower than many enemies), while Thor and Thyra have no ranged attacks at all.  Potions are super infrequent and mostly not all that effective for that limited supply.
Questor, Thor and Thyra all have a small (3) allotment of skills yet Merlin has a vast array (9 spells) of 2 element combos as if ripped straight out of magicka, making Merlin feel like he is made by a completly different team to the others.
I dont recomend getting this (even if its cheap), it just isnt gauntlet and felt more like a scrolling shooter (akin to Raiden or R-Type). I can only recomend if you want to play a real Gauntlet game, play one of the many previous ones, it will be much more fun experience overall.

A great game thus far.
The story is rather basic good rogue guys taking revenge on evil superior guys stuff being closest to the original AC and AC2 in this manner where Altaïr and Ezio had similarily "primal" reasons for acting.
But the settings are interesting and believable (well, as far as I can tell as a non-Chinese) and the gameplay is a lot of fun. You traverse lenghty, visually impressively and technically cleverly, diverse and constantly refreshingly designed levels in highly asymmetrical ways (directly or by climbing, covering the X, Y and Z axis and utilising various tools and dimensional movements like pressing yourself against pillars, hiding in specific spots or dashing between them). At their core the levels are linear but often offering multiple paths and approaches around obstacles and towards your goal. This is a 2.5D game that probably can't get closer to a 3D one. With this change it at first glance deviates greatly from the open world AC titles I've played previously, and yet it stays very faithful to some core recipes of the franchise and to the feelings that make them enjoyable.
The animations are fluid and great, as was to be expected. Even the stealth lovers should try to fight at one point or another to see Shao Jun's combat animations. Movement is fun, I think they projected the parcouring/freerunning very nicely into the 2.5D world (as best as I could imagine, at least). Stealth is rewarded, but not mandatory. Most levels can be "ghosted", being neither seen nor killing anyone (at least one level starts with permanent alert, rewarding you for getting through it as swiftly as possible instead). Primary and some secondary targets must be killed but they don't count into the rating you get after every small level portion and at the end of each map.
Combat is more difficult compared to the main AC installments. Could you block most attacks in them by simply holding down one button you now need to time your blocking with the attacks of your enemies instead. This isn't too difficult, it's a mechanic I know from other brawlers, you can get used to it and there are indicators that usually tell you about immediate incoming attacks. But when there are two or more enemies engaging you from both sides - meeleing and/or shooting at you from afar and some possibly placed on elevated spots you can't climb right away without exposing yourself - you can get overwhelmed. Your weapon arsenal is heavily limited: Basically just your sword. There are throwing knives but I don't think I've ever actually killed someone with them, their numbers are strongly limited, they don't kill (alerted) guards in one hit and thus they are more useful to interact with certain level elements with. You are given a good deal of moves like parrying and performing roll-over/side-changing manouvers and your blocking ability has no cooldown, and if you play smart you can get your enemies into less pressing spots, but your health is fairly limited and sometimes the enemies take a few swings that aren't indicated as well. This is why it's sometimes a bit harder to brawl your way through than to stealth, actually, but at the same time it makes every kill more rewarding than how they would feel in the main AC games.
Not just stealth but assassinations and direct combat is rated a bit too, giving you a "style bonus" if you stick to roughly the same course per level section it seems. Still, being a ghost who won't touch more than she has to appears to get you more bonuses.
What can be irritating is that the A.I. of the enemies usually won't see past their own dimensional plane and that they are utterly unable to climb even the smallest gaps (which is intended maybe, not to overcomplicate the gameplay). What can make (some) sense for guards who are in passive mode (maybe they are very tired and their helmets block their peripheral view?) looks a bit silly when those on high alert turning around and around to desperately find you are basically just one or two meters standing away from you in plain sight only on a different dimensional plane thinking you had miraculously vanished into thin air.
There are some collectibles which give some incentive to pay attention to your map and to roam the levels a bit more. Animus shards and high level-end ratings unlock health or gear upgrades (carry more tool ammo) or shorten the time needed for specific actions. I am not the most genuinely interested one when it comes to such unlockables, but roaming the levels is fun and thus I like trying to obtain them as well. From what I've seen some collectibles require you to kill non-mandatory targets however ruining your otherwise clean stealth rating. This can be circumvented by simply getting yourself killed shortly after to reload the checkpoint just before (it seems you retain the collectibles then). Treasure chests contain short texts that tell what happened before the game starts and what lead to the plot that plays out, which I find to be the more interesting collectibles because they give you some historical context and are fairly interesting to read even if the plot itself isn't too complicated. There are the usual "animus database" entries too, giving brief info on some historical outlines, people, enemy types and locations.
Some other reviewers complain a bit about the key voice actors having British accents apparently rather than to sound genuinely Chinese. I'm no expert there. The unnamed guards in the game speak Chinese. Shao Jun may not sound Chinese, but that doesn't make her voice acting bad per-se. It can break a bit of immersion for some players, but unless you are riding this badly or unless you are Chinese yourself you probably won't notice as much. I like to hear Shao Jun's voice actress even though she isn't giving massive amounts of lines.
Someone criticized the cutscenes are comic-like rather than being properly animated (as can be seen in the launch trailer). This is correct. But for a 10,00 EUR game I didn't expect groundbreaking CGI bombs. The comic-ishy scenes fit (they have the painting-ishy look/share the art style realized within the game engine) and they tell what needs to be told.
What bugs me a bit: Ezio is there as seen as an old man in AC: Embers mentoring Shao Jun. But they gave him a different voice, one I find rather odd and not as striking as the one he had in his own games. So, perhaps it's for the better he only appears in Animus training sequences.
Also, Ubisoft needs to be more creative with the Templar motives. The first one you kill gives you the same uninspiring kind of speech they've all been telling you since the first game.
Sadly the game apparently isn't the most stable one. Mine sometimes crashes when loading checkpoints or in the middle of the game, but since my graphics card has been troubling me in some ways lately I do not necessarily blame the game. Numerous people in the game hub however seem to get a crash right when they start it, possibly related to NVIDIA cards in particular. There appears to be a player-discovered solution to that, but still. Some complain about the keyboard controls and little to no graphical options, but I don't have issues there because the game per default runs like a charm on my rig performance-wise and because I've been playing this with an Xbox controller right away.
Just to be safe I recommend creating regular backups of your savegames, which can be found in the  Uplay folder, and to occassionally check if the files within are up-to-date with your latest ingame auto saving (not by alt-tabbing though because this may add to the instability some people have with this game). Maybe people should disconnect and reconnect with Uplay after each few hours or so too. I haven't had any save game losses thus far in this game but I was gravely branded by experiences of that kind in Child of Light and far more heavily in Black Flag.

For $10, it's a good enough port of the AC series to a lighter, simpler genre -- frustrations and all.
The game tells the story of Chinese Assassin Shao Jun, whose Brotherhood has been wiped out by a group of Chinese politicians controlled by the Templars. Before the game starts, Shao and her master had fled to Italy to study under Ezio Auditore, and return to China to try to overturn the Templar-controlled group and avenge and reestablish their Brotherhood. The game takes you through China as you hunt down and assassinate members of the enemy group one by one. All in all, an interesting story.
The art is beautiful, inspired by Chinese ink-wash painting techniques. There are no animated cutscenes, just art prints set to narration. Not a bad thing, personally. I'm looking forward to seeing how the other games they have planned for this series use their cultural art styles. My only gripe here is that the character models in gameplay are lacking...something. I can't quite put my finger on it though.
It's a "2.5D" game, so it's a sidescroller, but you can sometimes duck into the background or foreground for hiding spots, and you'll sometimes turn corners or move to another play area "behind" or "in front of" the area you're in via bridges and swings and stuff.
The main focus of the game is definitely the platforming/"parkour". In general, it all flows pretty well; every so often you'll hit a snag or a little glitch or whatever, and the game will kill you because even though Shao Jun started the grab animation, she was apparently one or two pixels outside the hitbox, so she falls and you lose ten minutes of progress. Like I said, it's a pretty good port of the frustrations AC series.
The assassinations and open combat are okay, but not quite as fun as in the main games. It's the same "block-counter-block-kill animation" flow you're used to, but the smaller, less detailed character models make it harder to see the signals of the enemy attacks. Or at least that's the case for me. Your mileage there may vary. There's no real difference here between the "high-profile" and "low-profile" attacks (e.g., in ACII you can kill with your sword in a flashy, slashy animation, or just slip by someone and shank them with the hidden blade). Regardless of whether you press X or Y, you'll get a randomly selected kill animation. In combat, your only weapon is a sword. No choice to try to fight with just the hidden blade -- which she hides in her boot for some really cool whip-kick, dancey, foot-to-the-throat kills. Which makes it all the more a shame that I can't select it.
It doesn't really matter anyways, because combat is definitely the lowest priority of the experience. The game is arranged in memories, which are individual levels. There is no free-roaming, just moving from one level to a cutscene and a loading screen, to the next level (as you'd expect for this style of game, I guess). Levels are scored and ranked based on your "Style" -- Shadow is no killing, no  being seen, Assassin is killing but no being seen, and Brawler is killing and being seen. Each Style is graded Gold, Silver and Bronze, but they may as well be called A, B, C for all the difference it makes. The game gives the most points for Shadow, medium for Assassin, and minimal for Brawler. And since you need to get a certain score to unlock the upgrades at the end of a level (health, gadget ammo, damage upgrades, etc), there's no real reason to start a fight instead of restarting the last checkpoint.
All in all, it's a good game, but it's just an okay Assassin's Creed game, if that makes any sense. But at $10 it's worth picking up. And if it's on sale for less, it's definitely worth it.
One thing I'd love to see in the future games (and in an update to this one) is an actual Style system. Like, go for the Shadow style and earn points towards upgrades that help with stealth, like a quicker Hide Dash and better distraction gadgets; go Assassin and earn things that help with stealth killing like hidden blade techniques, new ways to hide bodies, and deadlier gadgets; go Brawler and get armor, stronger swords, more weapon techniques, etc. This would literally triple the replayability without too much extra work.

I really love this game and recommend it any day. Period.
If you're turned away by the age (8 years old, as of this review...my god I feel old), realise that there are always mods to do anything you felt was missing, or that you thought the game needed to compete with newer roleplaying games. Although the modding community is absolutely incredible, I recommend completing one playthrough without mods. Just to get the intended experience at least once. Now, as for what the game offers...I'll do this in a simple way that I've seen pretty often on here, so you should know it.
PROS:
+ Atmosphere is perfect. There's something about the look and feel of the wasteland that just makes you feel really immersed
+ Soundtrack is very good, using classic songs from the 50s-60s era, which is a nice bit of irony. Cheery music, destroyed world
+ Character building and connections are done extremely well in this game, which a few exceptions. I personally cared about many of the characters throughout my travels of the Capital Wasteland
+ SO MUCH TO EXPLORE! There are just over a hundred (if my memory is correct) marked locations in the base game world, but so many more hidden in all of the nooks and crannies of DC. And often you'll find yourself learning more about what happened to people in those locations, which really helps establish the open world
+ The player has many choices to make, some make subtle changes, while others completely change everything. Choose wisely
+ Lots of variety and freedom. The quest design is done so that the player can take so many different paths to achieve something, which definitely adds to the roleplaying experience
+ Incredible amounts of replayability. Tying in with the last two points, this game has so many things to do, it is impossible to see everything in just one playthrough
+ Variety in weapons and armour. Want to deck yourself out in full power armour? Sure. Just want to chill out in pyjamas? You've got it. What about running around in a duster coat and a clown mask? I don't see why not. And as for weapons...there are dozens of weapons at your disposal, most of which have unique variants for you to collect
+ So much to do! There are hundreds of quests to be completed, dozens of unique weapons and armour to be found, hundreds of locations to explore and learn about, and so much more. This game is filled to the brim with content
+ If you want more, the Fallout 3 Nexus has thousands of mods for you to tweak your game with, allowing for even more replayability
CONS:
- Gunplay is horrible. You do get used to it after a while, but it still has a slight cringe factor
- Some of the voice acting is a little weak. Given the scale of the game, I do give it a bit of a pass on it
- Pretty annoying to actually start up. It took me a few hours of tinkering with files and downloading patches before it worked, but now it runs fantastic and I don't believe that it has crashed on me yet

I really wanted to like Hack 'n' Slash as one of Doublefine's games and as a programming tutorial but it falls short in a few important areas, making it neither particularly fun nor educational. This game's a near-miss that feels unfinished in some respects.
You take on the role of a girl who finds herself in a dungeon with a sword that can hack any object with a USB port, able to change the parameters of things around her. It starts out simply enough with a door that can simply be set to be unlocked, but rapidly begins to encompass more. Enemies have entire lists of parameters and even idle behaviors that can be changed to either make sense or give silly results, like making a turtle do nothing but 'turn left' with no delay, resulting in him spinning as rapidly as possible in place. You're encouraged to break the game in gentle fashion and given artifacts that can change the flow of time or that display the variable names of everything around you. This creates a very open-ended experience where there are several possible solutions to puzzles, like hacking a guard to be good instead of bad so he stops chasing you, or changing your own speed to be much higher than that of the guard so you can simply run around him.
Where the game runs into trouble is how it introduces programming concepts. The first couple of acts deals only with parameters and has simple puzzles. Later on, the player is given access to dive into functions and things suddenly start getting messy. Collision detection can be a little dicey which can lead to confusion about what is editable and what is not in a function. Additionally everything is written in Lua which is fine, but someone without programming experience will have difficulty deciphering anything beyond the first couple of function-based puzzles. By the final act, the player is given access to quite a lot of scripts with minimal hand-holding and the Lua scripts become multiple-page affairs that all link to each other (as expected from real code) but I found the code very difficult to read and parse due to the way the player navigates through all these scripts.
The graphics are cartoony and fun though it's not always clear what is a path out of a room and what isn't. The controls are a bit weak between the mediocre hit detection and the inventory system that only allows you to access four of your items at a time, sometimes requiring you to switch back and forth between items in your bags. Screens reset often when going back and forth between them, usually not a problem but occasionally resetting events that have to be done again and again to get by. As much as I like the concept and theory of it, the clever bits of this game are overshadowed by the clunkiness. If you're looking for a programming game, perhaps try Glitchspace or Human Resource Machine.

The game tells you the story of Senua, a female Warrior who suffers from psychosis. In a very linear way.
The game almost feels like a movie, there are no decisions you can make, and every savestate of every person who owns this game is pretty much the same.
Additionally to the story you have some battles and some puzzles.
The puzzles are references to psychosis in a certain way and are quite easy but not too underchallenging. That's okay but not really special or a reason to buy the game, and sometimes they feel like they're stretching the game since they appear quite often. So they're basically "nice" or "interesting" puzzles but nothing more.
Inbetween the walking and puzzling solving and cutscene watching, the game offers you some combat encounters.
And the issue with the combat is that the combat system isn't really... well... memorable?
The combat is just sooo simple, it requires no learning or training, you just simply learn the combat automatically.
The combat itself kinda looks like this most of the time: Your opponent strikes -> you parry his strike shortly before the impact with the blocking button, which is by default the ctrl-key for some reason -> the you go nuts on your enemy using the Left Mouse Button for light attacks and the Right Mouse Button for heavy attacks -> if you're fighting against multiple opponents and if one of them who isn't in the field of view of your camera attacks you then you'll get an audial warning from the voices in Senua's head saying something like "Watch out! Behind you!". In this case simply press the block button in order to parry the attack, Senua will parry and now focus the camera on this opponent so you can again go nuts  on him. This cycle of parrying and attacking will go on and on. There are only a few exceptions, one is the one type of enemy with a shield where you simply have to press f which results in a kick which then results into opening the defense of the enemy, after that simply go nuts on him. The other exception is a certain enemy which is a heavier enemy with a big axe or something like that. When you encounter this guy then you simply have to dodge more of since not every attack by him can be parried ( on the other hand if it's not parryable it will be blockable so you can still block instead of dodging if you want to). And that's it, a very simple combat system. In my opinion it's not memorable at all. It actually contains combos but i never ever bothered to learn them because you simply don't have to in order to beat the game, since the combat is easy enough already.
There are a few boss fights here and there but every attack of a boss can simply be either dodged, blocked or parried. The only thing that makes boss fights kinda difficult is the surprising aspect of an attack f.e. the boss does an attack you haven't seen before out of nowhere and it kind of surprises you, plus the boss fights last quite long because the bosses have a high HP pool so they pretty much endure a lot of attacks from you.
The ending of the game is quite weird, there's no boss fight, there are only 3 fights:
The first 2 are simple fights against normal enemies which you've already encountered before in the game.
The last fight is again a fight against all the normal enemies you've encountered before but this time they spawn infinitely, and you can only progress if you let them kill you, so basically the end cutscene triggers after you've died.
And in my opinion it's not really a challenge to let enemies kill you.
So in the end it's a linear story with a too simple combat system and a main character who always has to scream all the time.
I don't recommend this game, furthermore i managed to play through it in 6 hours in only one session, so it's not a very long game.

A slightly unusual, but very well-executed, combat-heavy platformer. Anyone who's seen screenshots will know that this game is extremely beautiful; every background is gorgeous, the characters are detailed and the effects are bright and colourful, all of which mixes seamlessly together to make an aesthetic masterpiece. The main focus of gameplay is platforming, accompanied with fast-paced combat and the ocassional puzzle. But while these usually tend to be the cornerstones of children's games all of these are in fact quite difficult, with an surprisingly (and satisfyingly) high learning curve and one of the most difficult final bosses I've ever fought.
While you can potentially complete the game in a day, I highly discourage you from doing so; I discovered to my chagrin that upon completing the game the save file then becomes unusable, so exploration after this point is impossible. With this in mind, I recommend as much exploration as possible upon completing each new objective; do not make the same mistake I did. Exploration is rewarding both in terms of finding yet more pretty areas, but also in unlocking powerups for Ori which, while not necessary, can make the game a lot easier if you choose to use them.
And now for the plot: while the story is by no means original or unique it is nonetheless heartwarming, considerably more so than I had originally anticipated. Of all the characters in the game only two are able to speak (the two least important to the progression of the story as a whole, at that) and yet the characters all have their own personalities, even hopes and fears, making the whole experience surprisingly charming and emotional. It has to be said that the ending does feel ever so slightly like a cop-out, but if you imagine this game as a children's game for adults it's easily forgiven - praiseworthy, even. Every detail of the game essentially amounts to this: nostalgiac but difficult gameplay with beautiful settings and a done-before-but-still-sweet storyline, it's the best children's game an adult could ever play. Highly recommended.

Very, very beautiful (both visuals and the soundtrack) and different platformer. Has a profound story and good game mechanics. I opted in for controller. You play Ori, an orphan creature searching for home. He can level up and gains new abilities in the course of the story. His basic resources are energy and life points, which he gathers and upgrades throughout the game. His objectives in the game are to restore different elements (water, wind, fire, ...) and, not suprisingly, has to deal with enemies and puzzles from all those categories. The difficulty level is proper, so that at times I found myself really frustrated by some sections, but the famous "one more try" got me finally through them. The game also has a nice save game mechanics, as you need energy to create a save game point, and there is a cooldown effect on this. So, especially in the early game where your energy reserves are low, you need to carefully think when to save your game. At the save game points, you can also check your ability tree for possible level ups.
Overall, there's around 8-9 hours of playtime, and it was all worth it :). I recommend this one for everyone who fancy nice story, beautiful graphics, good atmosphere, and tricky platform jumping.

This is a wonderful fighting game that I want to recommend to anyone even remotely interested in the genre. With an expansive (optional) tutorial mode that explains basic mechanics very well, a great roster/gameplay, and a wonderful dev team, it's a must-have in the fighting genre.
The art style and animations are done very well, and the backgrounds and stages are all very pretty to look at while you beat your opponent to a pulp. On top of that, some of the game mechanics are truly innovative; you can string 100+ hit combos if you practice hard enough because of the organic and fluid combo system that let's you string essentially any move with another, but if you reach any 'infinite' territory, repeated moves can be punished with a block breaker. The characters are also all unique and interesting, enough that you'll want to try to learn how to play much more than just one of them.
Overall, it's a fast-paced game and I can't help but hope that many more people buy it, since it is definitely worth much more than the 3$ asking price. Especially since all future DLC is free for the first 3 months after its release. Beowulf is free right now, and so will the next few characters.

Apparently a 3 frame "Tell" is all that you get. That's less than 1/10th of a second, which is not enough for a human being to respond to. You basically have to blindly guess what your opponent is going to do and hope you get lucky.  So basically this game amounts to nothing more than Rock-Paper-Scissors in the guise of a brawler (which makes you memorize hundreds of complex combos unlike fighting games where you can just quickly mash buttons). I'm not impressed. So what if there are moe anime lolis with big bussoms? Seriously, I could play any of hundreds of other more satisfying games or even turn on Crunchyroll for that. If you don't have a satisfying game beyond a themed Sansukumi-ken/Roshambeaux then it's really not worth the price of admission IMHO.

This game combines a unique art style, with a unique combat system. The art style is consistent throughout the game. The combat system sees you typing out words to attack creatures, and to interact with the environment around you.
The story is linear, in the regard that you have to go from one area to the next, gradually picking up experience and different elemental spells along the way.
A simple RPG-like system is implemented that allows you to speed your character up, increase the power of your spells, and reveal points of interest on the map.
In terms of difficulty, there are some encounters that will cause some frustration as you simply are not able to type fast enough or made poor choices with your spells.
If you are a "hunt and peck" typist, that is you look at your keyboard whilst typing, then you will battle in this game.
Overall, I would recommend this game. It is fun, and I thoroughly enjoyed it, despite one encounter which saw me attempt it anywhere between 8 and 16 times, because of the reasons I outlined above.
To the developer: please make more.

O atual sucesso de jogos mais simples - "old school" mesmo - é um campo perfeito para que a pequena desenvolvedora finlandesa Frozenbyte, conhecida pelo seu Shadogrounds, traga a luz uma aventura em plataforma que parece saída diretamente de um conto de fadas. Trine traz ambientes profusamente coloridos, diversos puzzles e uma enorme "biodiversidade" que vai de cogumelos (certamente diferentes dos que você conhece) a esqueletos.
Num ambiente essencialmente dinâmico, parte graças à utilização da PhysX, a idéia é confrontar vários desafios utilizando auxílio mágico. Onde poderas "invocar" uma caixa para ajudar a alcançar um local mais elevado, ou ainda uma rampa para um fim semelhante. Os desenvolvedores garantem que os desafios podem ter várias soluções possíveis.
Mas a magia em Trine não é apenas um utilitário. Todo o ambiente rescende um conceito totalmente surrealista, compondo cenários com plantas ornamentais, cogumelos, engrenagens e criaturas oníricas. Além de resolver puzzles de diversas maneiras, existem ainda níveis de dificuldade para a faceta mais "beat'm up" de Trine. Assim sendo, caso queira uma verdadeira "avalanche" de seres encantados, basta aumentar a dificuldade.

Trine is a sidescrolling platformer with 3D graphics and environments. There is combat, but also a plethora of physics and environmental puzzles and a healthy amount of hidden items and secret rooms. You can conjur up blocks and stack them to make ladders, manipulate platforms attached to vines to make them swing, and even crush enemies with conjured items. The voice acting is so-so but the dialogue is very silly and lighthearted.
If you enjoy games like Portal, and Mario, and like games with fantasy settings, then Trine is definitely worth playing.

Trine is absolutely one of the most appealing games I have ever played! From it's gorgeous visuals, fantastic soundtrack, excellent narration, and fluent mechanics, it's no wonder this game was such a success!
Trine focuses on the diversity of it's titular characters, and the level design of it's extremely well built maps. Each character has a unique role in the game, from the Knight, Wizard, and Thief - with each character being compatible with the other in terms of move sets, and combat. The games platforming works exceptionally well, and the puzzles (while not necessarily that difficult), provide enough thought and complexity to some of the maps level design thus creating entertainment and replayability in leaps and bounds!
Now, while the game is incredibly fun playing solo, it should definitely be tackled cooperatively. Amusing antics and crazy combinations will put a smile on your face, and keep you coming back repeatedly! However, Trine doesn't boast "online multiplayer", but "local co-op". That being said, it is still an excellent title and definitely deserves a playthrough! In the end, Trine is well worth the asking price in terms of content, replayability, and quality!
EDIT:
Trine: Enhanced Edition is on the horizon! This update brings much needed online multiplayer, graphical enhancements, and many bug fixes! Kudos to the developers for reviving an old game - and for free no less!

I bought this game for the sole purpose of Co-op with friends. And here's what we collectively thought about it. There are no pros, only cons.
1. Progression is slow and repetitive. The game is so grindy and so boring that you will eventually fall asleep trying to get past their long and unoriginal gameplay.
2. Slow reward system. The rewards of this game are not introduced quick enough for you to be constantly captivated by the game. You're stuck with the same two skills for an extended period of time, until you grind the money for other stuff.
3. Even if you manage to grind the gold required to unlock the final tiers of equipment, they're completely boring as well. I got so bored with the game that I used a CheatEngine to get infinite gold, and EVEN THEN the most expensive items weren't fun enough to keep me motivated.
4. This is nothing but Hack n Slash. There's no special puzzles to solve like Forced, no special OP loot like Diablo, no special boss fights that require skills to kill like Lara Croft.
5. Boring enemies, boring music, boring dialogue, boring combat. Boooooooooooooooooooooooooooooooring everything.
6. No skill trees, stats, mana system, etc. In short, this game doesn't have any complex systems in place to give it more depth.
7. You never feel powerful. Games like Diablo allow your characters to always feel powerful even at all stages of the game. But in this game, you always feel like your characters just don't do enough damage fast enough no matter what equipment you buy. You also don't actually get stronger as you progress, something that needs 2 hits to kill, will always need 2 hits to kill with the same skill no matter how long you play. YOU NEVER LEVEL UP OR GROW STRONGER.
8. Limited Options. There perhaps 3 main weapons per character, 3ish potion options, several relics. And that's it. Not much difference among them other than the skill you wanna use.
If you like spending hours doing repetitive♥♥♥♥♥♥to get money to get boring♥♥♥♥♥♥ get an office job. You'll at least feel like you accomplished something at the end of the day.
Score: 3/10 (Go play Diablo 3, Forced, Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light instead)

LEGO Worlds is an interesting contribution to Lego games in a few ways. Instead of having a narrative, it's totally open-world. Though there are a few objectives you can complete, the player is free to roam as they please. I think this really hits on something Lego hasn't really had in its repitoire since it shut down Lego Universe a few years ago. It's an important counterpoint to the more linear games that Lego has made through the years; those have their place, but they're only one part of the Lego experience. Roaming around and experimenting are a key part of Lego-ing, and Worlds gives the player the tools to do it.
It's still in development, but from the looks of it the devs are truly committed to making this a good game. I would say this is a good buy outside of a sale. Of all of the games I've seen in Early Access recently this one is a safe bet.

This kinetic visual novel with turn-based RPG Maker-based combat by Mia Blais-Côté features a group of two boys and two girls Alex, Aime, Lily and Nana who are part of a group of rift breakers abbreviated after each person's name A.L.A.N. and have the supernatural ability to see rifts from which monsters can enter from another dimension to cause havoc on the city of Xodias without anyone else knowing the existence of the rifts or monsters. The rift breakers are also able to wield magic in the form of Focus which confers healing, status buffs and debuffs or multiple attacks and Voices which deals a different elemental damage of the player's choice. Over 6 chapters, the members of A.L.A.N. will team up to fight groups of monsters and a final boss monster while attending school together as schoolmates and friends.
The story and plot is written like a horror comedy with a fair amount of humour in the dialogue. Having played through Mia Blais-Côté's earlier visual novel
, adding in the turn-based combat in this game which requires a bit of strategy and experimentation helped in making this game more interesting. By automatically restoring all characters' health to full at the end of every battle, the combat system is also not too difficult making the game more accessible to a larger audience. Recommended when at discount or bundle offer as it takes less than 10 hours to finish through all battles and read through the entire kinetic visual novel.

I'd much rather wait a bit before making my review, but seeing the absolute review-bombing that's occurred in the last few weeks I thought I would drop my two cents on the game.
I may be only an hour in, but so far DF's Hack n Slash has been nothing short of superb.  To be fair, I didn't follow this game's development, and received the game as compensation after Spacebase DF-9 fell apart (which still leaves me a bit upset considering what it could have been, though RimWorld has since healed these wounds).  I'm not quite sure why I never gave it a chance as long as I had it, but after Steam Big Picture reminded me of its existence and shamed me for having never touched it nor even looked at the store page, I decided to give it a chance.  With both the acclaimed Double Fine Productions, and of course the legendary
and
developers at
, this game certainly has a lot going for it!  Then again, Spacebase DF-9 did as well, so perhaps it's worth clarifying why.
The concept alone is worth a look; a mix of educational and entertaining puzzles entirely based around coding, and modifying the world around you to cheat your way through the game.  In practice, however, it seems that DF has nailed it.  Whether it's hacking an enemy raven to do negative damage (therefore healing you on hit) or hacking the Day/Night cycle to speed up time and make a 50-days-later chest spawn quickly, it has a reasonable difficulty curve that eventually throws you into the mess of code we all know and love, aside from the actual top-down RPG presentation.
Of course, this game is purely meant for those with coding knowledge.  It starts with a Magic Circle-esque basic exploration into code with modifying public vars, but by the final act you'll be diving into the game's Source Code in order to solve puzzles.  It takes a slow but sure leap from hacking-themed to actual hacking, and when it fully jumps to that latter category, it comes as a bit of a shock.
If you pick it up on sale, I do recommend it broadly if only for the first two hours of gameplay, where it mixes RPG elements in with "hacking" shenanigans; if you're looking for a challenging but rewarding experience with LUA and aren't one of the blinded DF haters, though, I can't recommend it enough.  Most importantly, it is NOT FOR EVERYONE, and a bit of prior knowledge is pretty much essential before you get into the main part of the game.

How best to enjoy Hellblade
1. Stop Reading reviews on this game.
2. Get a set of good headphones set up.
3. Don't read any guides
4. Go nuts.
But if you INSIST on reading a review I will try very hard to relay some fine points of the game in order to help you decide if you would like it without giving anything away. That by the way is a very difficult task.
1. The pace is very slow, you will have long periods in between combat.
2. The sound and graphics are the best I have played in years.
3. The combat is completely devoid of ornementation. No skill points to earn, no weapons or inventory to upgrade/manage, no quick time events (thank god), and only one special power. Essentially it's just your skills of observation and reflexes against some tough enemies that want you dead.
4. The puzzles are a large part of the game and rely on non isometric level design (think of a dumbed down antichamber).
None of that is why I consider this the best game I have played this year. It's the story, and the deep immersion in the way the devs manage to connect you with the character. It is one of those games that shows that a game can transend just being fun, and become meaningful art.
If you want a great hack n slash....skip it (the combat is good, but better can be had). If you want to enjoy masterful storytelling, this game is a must play.

They're not taking notes, I thought. All those man hours on the phone convincing potential consultant neuroscience professors and real psychotics that an issue-conscious game can be more than a game of pong wherein the paddles periodically can't move because of their major depressive disorder; to be shipped out of their way to watch their lives represented as a Viking ghoul getting duffed up in the chest cavity.. someone get these guys a PAD!
That's the rumbling worry just below the surface, isn't it? There's veritable Hel(l) to pay if you get this wrong. Gamification of mental funkiness (and fully embracing the anti-stigma message, I mean funky) needs to be baked into the goods as visceral affect, not some visual effects.
Thankfully, this is a HAUNTING game. The haunting house that haunting house employees have to go into to get their kicks. It's a tightly scripted cinematic tour de not forced. The shop window is the shop and this is a tightly scripted experience with mental illness all quarter winds and centre. Sound design pitch-perfect., performances incredible and the kind of shots and imagery that film will be calling the police there's been a break-in over.
Enough about the gentry, you say, for gameplay is king, queen, and country. Combat struck a power chord with me. It has no aspirations for mastery beyond usability, but by never breaking your over the shoulder front row seat, it's claustrophobic and personal. Three's a crowd and if it were less forgiving in your ability to recover like a downed boxer being counted down, it would be intensely challenging. Like most everything in the game, it's never treated with tutorial and is something you work out yourself. There's been a lot of media attention over permadeath. It's an interesting aside, but for numerous reasons, it's not as important as you'd hope. It does what it should -  succeeds in hanging over you at times, like a heavy chandelier in a condemned building.
The other side of the mechanical coin involves puzzles that may be thematically integral, but can grate by playing hide and seek with the player. They're not taxing and not offensive, but as a major part of the gameplay loop, they're the adverts before the show; like colouring in the sky whilst you work out what colours the house should be. Exploration remains cable car ride marvellous thanks to the home run in its environments and the constant colouring by the eerie choir of binaural voices in your head.
And at points you'll  be overwhelmed. Four voices will swarm you at once. Terrible sound mixing here, you think, until you realise that you're actually experiencing psychosis through interactive medium. Bloody hell, you say, they must have been writing notes on their hands.

This game undoubtedly a masterpiece work of game industry. Hats off to Ninja Theory, I hope your vision of future of the game industry will be shared by the other gamedevs.
As for me: gotta take some cigarettes and a calm music to get rid of the voices in my head.

TLDR: This is definitely primarily an atmospheric and character driven game. If you enjoy those you'll LOVE this game. If you need deep gameplay and challenging combat you will not. On to the review now.
So... I'm one of those who LOVE purely character driven games and WOW does this game deliver. Senua is the most instantly compelling character I've seen in a game in years, maybe ever. Despite the very small cast the story really draws you in and you feel what Senua feels and want what Senua wants.
This is the bulk of the game /\ /\ /\
If that right there isn't what you're looking for in a game then this is NOT for you. The combat is easy and shallow (though ridiculously fun. More on that later) and the puzzles are not all that challenging and very repetitive. Basically you spend 75% of the game  lining up shapes, 15% in combat and about 10% in interesting and unique puzzles. The story is deep but the gameplay is NOT.
Now just because the combat is easy doesn't mean it isn't also really fun. All your abilities are unlocked from the beginning but you're never told about any of them. While the combat will always essentially be dodge/counter or block//counter once the game starts throwing more enemies at you at once and you start to learn some of the hidden moves combat becomes extremely cinematic. Senua doesn't moan when swinging and taking hits like pretty much all other female heros but actually screams and grunts. The camera angles know exactly when you need full control and when a more dramatic angle is appropriate. And as easy as the game is you can only die a certain amount of times before it's game over and you have to start from the beginning. The end result is a visually spectacular exprience that manages to be intense and fun without the frustration.
The graphics are top notch. Senua's model is so detailed you can see individual hairs. Her eyes are the most expressive I've ever seen in a game and the facial animations somehow top even Oddessy to the West. The environment is beautifully rendered in UE4. While I've seen more detailed environments these ones frequently result in impressive set pieces.
The game took me 9 hours taking my time. Could be done in half if I rushed and knew all the puzzles.
At the end of the day I whole heartedly recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a character driven game.

This is a wonderful fighting game that I want to recommend to anyone even remotely interested in the genre. With an expansive (optional) tutorial mode that explains basic mechanics very well, a great roster/gameplay, and a wonderful dev team, it's a must-have in the fighting genre.
The art style and animations are done very well, and the backgrounds and stages are all very pretty to look at while you beat your opponent to a pulp. On top of that, some of the game mechanics are truly innovative; you can string 100+ hit combos if you practice hard enough because of the organic and fluid combo system that let's you string essentially any move with another, but if you reach any 'infinite' territory, repeated moves can be punished with a block breaker. The characters are also all unique and interesting, enough that you'll want to try to learn how to play much more than just one of them.
Overall, it's a fast-paced game and I can't help but hope that many more people buy it, since it is definitely worth much more than the 3$ asking price. Especially since all future DLC is free for the first 3 months after its release. Beowulf is free right now, and so will the next few characters.

I wanted to like this game, I really, really, really did. However, I cannot recommend it. I should have known when my GF who plays brawlers 24/7 with her arcade stick rage-quit this game after 15 min that it was going to be a futile attempt in frustration for an JRPGer like me to play it on a keyboard. Sure enough, the game did not disappoint in that department. After spending 10 minutes trying to figure out how to select a menu item ('A' key, really?) and after 30 tries finally got the keys remapped to something that made a modicum of sense (i.e., like every other game's standard keyboard layout) I then started the Tutorial. Should be easy right? Tutorials are always easy. Well, 45 minutes later I realize I made it through 5 of 50 Tutorials and couldn't progress past the Blocking Tutorial. Apparently a 3 frame "Tell" is all that you get. That's less than 1/10th of a second, which is not enough for a human being to respond to. You basically have to blindly guess what your opponent is going to do and hope you get lucky.  So basically this game amounts to nothing more than Rock-Paper-Scissors in the guise of a brawler (which makes you memorize hundreds of complex combos unlike fighting games where you can just quickly mash buttons). I'm not impressed. So what if there are moe anime lolis with big bussoms? Seriously, I could play any of hundreds of other more satisfying games or even turn on Crunchyroll for that. If you don't have a satisfying game beyond a themed Sansukumi-ken/Roshambeaux then it's really not worth the price of admission IMHO.

First attempt, well, there's almost no guidance on "normal" mode. I ran out of charge on my mining laser almost immediately, and the only way to charge it is with plutonium, which, well, I couldn't pick up now, because I was out of mining laser charge. Went to start a new game. . . .
. . . couldn't find a way to start a new game. Because there isn't one.
Alt-tabbing out to read up on the game on the internet caused a black screen crash, had to restart my computer, check my drive for errors, get back in, do some research. . . yeah. There's no way to start a new game. In fact, to restart, you have to delete your only available game requires going into the bowels of Steam and conducting file necromancy. (Yes, there's a 'go back to an old save' option buried in the options menu. I found that later. It's right next to 'exit to desktop' which is a story I'll get to in a minute.)
I sighed, and downloaded it to my son's machine, told him it was similar to Minecraft and Starbound, and he could try it once it was installed, via my Steam library. Except, yeah. Wouldn't even start on his brand-new laptop.
I sighed again, and figured I would kick it around a bit in creative mode.
I played for about 20 minutes. Tried to lift off into the sky to look for a space station. Promptly couldn't get my ship out of warp, and oh, look, no directions to on do so. Grabbed my phone, because I knew that alt-tabbing out to conduct a web search was a no-go. No directions online for *basic ship controls* that I was able to find--all kind of directions for upgrading ships, but basic controls that should have been covered in a tutorial? No.
Reloaded to an old save, built a save point, saved properly, and tried to exit the game using the actual exit to desktop command (which, as I noted before, is buried in the Options menus). . . and promptly got a black screen which dictated that I had to crash my machine again.
So. That's pretty much the end of that game for me. Glaring bugs that crash a pretty herky machine, horrible user interface (lack of basic game utilities, like saving and exiting that function?), and no tutorial or documentation. Strike three, you're out. Which makes me sad, as I wanted to give it a real chance.

Like many others, I watched this game before actually bothering to purchase. Gaming is now often done on a budget and we all want to get the most for our buck, so I'll make this quick:
Pros:
-Massive potential for exploration.
-Immersive gameplay and unique species with unique personalities. (Some even help you gather items if you feed them.)
-Dozens upon Dozens of vehicles, as well as ships in a variety of classes. Unlike most space exploration games such as Elite Dangerous, or EVE online, you can actually just find ships on planets and take them for your own, provided you gather the materials to get them fixed.
-Bases, Outposts, and Community areas, Oh my! (You can spend your entire time in this game on a single planet and still manage not to get bored, I keep finding myself wishing I could just stay on each world I visit indefinitely, but sadly, I yearn to see the stars more.)
-Easy controls (I have spent 3+ hours just trying to understand the basic keyboard and controller setups involved in a variety of space sims, never mind mastering the actual flight itself. In No Man's Sky, you don't have to have a yoke or joystick to be a flying ace.)
Cons:
-There is no jump system. By that I mean if you are to try and gain altitude, it is only based upon the thrust your jetpack generates. (Ironically, exovehicles have a jump.)
-Scaling issues with the RNGs will leave you with some creatures that are not  proportionate, to the point their existence in a world with the physics being portrayed could even support. That said, the fact there is variety somewhat makes up for this.
-Inventory is a crucial element in a space exploration game such as this, when you're going planet to planet, star to star, the fact you cannot have multiple ships with multiple inventories is a major let down, ideally I'd like to see some manner of orbital base one can craft to hold their potential ships in the future if possible, though the fact you can buy freighters somewhat makes up for this.
-Trade networking could be a bit more advanced, perhaps even offer the option to trade items for others instead of working simply off the premise of currency exchange. I feel some NPCs would require materials, much like I often find myself needing. Rather than trying to sell and buy off each other, I'd like to trade and increase my standing with other species in the process, though this would mean finding traders looking for the particular item you were hoping to sell.
-Fleet Dynamics can be a bit sluggish, or even dimwitted at times, you will rarely struggle to take on a ship provided you're willing to dive back into orbit for a few seconds to avoid sentinels. I would like to see the fleets break formation, actually maneuver and try to run / defend themselves rather than just sit in orbit like a space station.
Over all, I encourage you to try this game, but if you are hoping for a game where everything is exciting, you will be let down. There is a fair amount of monotony in this game, though like many games nowadays, grinding towards a goal is commonplace. There is fighting, but it is few and far between at times. You may find yourself provoking animals simply to get some manner of challenge out of the map, Just make sure you bring enough fuel for your life support, and you'll enjoy yourself rather thoroughly in this game.

Such a charming game! Beautiful papercraft visuals, good voiceover and a nice (though threadbare) story make this game a good way to spend a few hours. The typing mechanics are surprisingly fun - battling insects with words is a novel idea, and there are just enough RPG elements to ensure a sense of progression. There are four different types of typing magic you can use - Fire burns away the next word, Spark does a chain effect, etc. - which keep things interesting.

Fun in some ways, but there are enough flaws here that it's really not worth your time.
I was not able to pay any attention to the story during frantic typing sections, so I can't comment on the story much. It seems throwaway, though, trying to be thoughtful and provokative but really just lots of empty words to fill the space and show a specific kind of style.
The world map layout is confusing and it took me a lot of backtracking and random wandering around to be able to figure out where to go. I stumbled onto chapter 4 before chapter 3, because that's actually possible, but I couldn't progress because I hadn't unlocked the right type of magic.
When adaptive difficulty is on, the game actually gets to be too hard too fast. No amount of strategy is going to save you from the absolutely overwhelming swarm of words you have to type if you're a good typist to begin with. I had to turn adaptive difficulty off to stand a chance, at which point the game was still frantic enough to be fun...
...until I got to the wind dungeon. There's a section here where it zooms out (so everything is small), and there are both birds and wasps (the birds are harmless, the wasps aren't, and they're small enough that you can't really tell them apart), and the wasps only have 1 letter to type each (making them difficult to spot sometimes), and the background is really bright (making it hard to tell the letters apart from the background). What a completely awful encounter design. It's like it's hand-crafted to frustrate, and after quite a bit of interesting and thoughtful encounter design it was just a complete experience-killing 180.
Don't waste your time. If you're just in it for some fast typing practice, there are plenty of free websites out there.

[Updated Review]
^ Rewriting this review actually makes me want to replay the game again soon.
=== Pros ===
- Wow. It's a typing game!
I used to play old school typing games from the 90's as a kid, so I found this a nostalgic, yet very refreshing and engaging take on the genre.
- Lovely, soothing narration
- Great adaptation of a less mainstream genre, ie. typing games.
- Pretty unique artstyle and animation that stands out by itself.
- ^ Stands out, AND suits the game's concept amazingly well. (Paper, writing or typing, unfolding a story, uncovering ...areas)
- Satisfying to "level up"
- Achievements were satisfying
- Riding on the back of a fox vaguely reminds me of riding on the back of the wolf (sort of) in Okami, another nostalgic game
- It's great being able to freely explore a lovely world in a typing game for a change.
- I do like foxes :p
=== Little details I appreciate: ===
- When selecting an option at the main menu and such, you can type the letters of what you want to select rather than just clicking.
- There are several different ways to control the characters. You can use the recommended EF and IJ, or WASD, or another set of keys. I used the recommended EF/IJ setting.
=== Cons (?) ===
#1.
I'm really nitpicking here. Whether this point is a plus or minus for you would depend on your own personal typing skills in general, or how relaxing you want this experience to be.
At chapter 1, there was already a lot of frantic typing. I was worried it would eventually become so difficult that it would be unplayable later on, but I was wrong. The tough part for me was at the beginning when I needed to get used to the game, the different "elements" (you'll see what I mean when you unlock more areas), and just having to warm up my fingers.
In fact, towards the end of the last chapter I found it wasn't challenging or fresh enough for me. I was disappointed, but I think that was more of my own fault. I tend to get carried away playing and start anticipating crazy boss fights that I can win to feel smug about.
Still, I think this level of difficulty might be just right for others. It definitely doesn't make it unplayable for people who haven't grown up with stressful typing games like The Typing Of The Dead. Plus, there's always the difficulty settings to tweak.
...
#2.
Nitpicking again. I felt the ending was a teeeeny bit on the simple side.
Actually, I don't know if this can be considered a bad thing. The only reason I felt the ending was too simple was the fact that the narration and build up was so fantastic. It made me think and wonder about what was going on story-wise as I typed and typed frantically throughout the game.
It probably works for some people who want simple stories. Also, if I recall correctly (finished it a year earlier), the ending might have had a bit of an open-ended aspect so you could probably imagine your own backstory or interpretation in addition to the simple one. And I appreciate stuff like that. I like it when my thoughts linger on a game or story even when I'm not playing. :D
=== Glitches ===
- I don't recall anything specifically game-breaking?
- I might have had like...two (?) problematic instances, but it was easily solved by relaunching the game. I don't remember what the problems were exactly because they didn't happen enough for me to take note of.
=== Summary ===
- It's a well-made game.
- I really enjoyed this.
- I'd recommend this.

One of those games that popped out of my steam library under the "Typing" tag. That is curious, because there aren't so much typing games here on Steam. Fired up the game and something caught my attention: eveything is a piece of paper, from the protagonist to the world around her. A nice, soft touch that this game embraced completely, and helped to define its identity since the first minute of gameplay. You will be confused about the plot at the beginning, but it isn't the core of the experience. You are asked to travel places and fight monsters only using your keyboard. No mouse, no frenetic button smashing, there's only you accompanied with a narrator and the words printed directly on the level.
The core mechanic is to fight your foes standing on the ground and type the words above them as quickly as possible in order to defeat them. If you're typing faster enough the game will reward you with lots of experience points that you can use for upgrading your skills and abilities. You'll be getting more powers throughout the game as unlockables, and those are selectable just by typing them.
These simple mechanics united with a peculiar art style makes a perfect "break game" when you just need to sit and relax, enjoying the journey.
Yes, it's definitely a journey, and one of the best in my opinion.
The only thing that I did not like personally was the ending, but it's not important. The gameplay is perfectly refined to make it very enjoyable.
Sure, it isn't perfect, has its flaws (a bit repetitive maybe and a few minor bugs), but the price it's worth the ticket. And in these days there aren't so many games that can rely on that.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is gorgeous. Character models and landscapes can approach photorealism to the point you question whether you're looking at a video game model or full motion video with a few filters applied. In some cases I'm still not sure of the process Ninja Theory used to create such convincing visuals, but it's an impressive graphical showcase if nothing else. Thankfully, playing the game is an emotional journey worth experiencing as well.
 
  You control Senua, and in an immediate fourth wall breaking performance she is aware of that. Senua hears voices in her head, and you are one of them. Carrying her dead boyfriend's head in a sack, you must guide her to the land of the dead so he can properly be put to rest. She is cursed with the “dark rot”: mental illness that causes her to see runes and patterns everywhere, hallucinate, and her tribesmen claim it is responsible for a deadly plague. The dark rot is manifested in the game as supernatural beasts Senua must battle, geometric puzzles, and perspective warping mazes to navigate. Black corruption infects Senua every time you die, starting at her hand and creeping up her arm. If it reaches her head, she will have failed her journey.
 
  Much has been made about Hellblade tackling mental health issues seriously. Ninja Theory hired multiple psychological experts to help out, previews for the game made sure to mention this, and there are warnings front and center in-game to warn anyone who may be triggered by such depictions. How all of that expertise is delivered... eh, it's a little overblown. While the research most definitely helped Senua's actress get into character and the developers to get in that mindset, the final product isn't that far removed from your average fantasy or horror game. Hellblade just adds a meta-layer of the player being aware of the disconnect between Senua and her reality.
 
  Hellblade is artsy, bordering on pretentious but never quite crossing the line. Despite some extended cutscenes showcasing the expressive performance by Senua and the art team, the majority of the game is spent exploring large, fairly open areas and engaging in Dark Souls-lite sword battles. The environments range from beautiful, picturesque landscapes to nightmarish visions of Hell, dark claustrophobic crumbling castles and otherworldly, ghostly seas, all rooted in Norse mythology. One complaint here is that the levels can be a little too big, requiring excessive amounts of times jogging from one place to another and making it easy to get turned around on linear paths. So much jogging...
 
  When you're engaged in combat, the simple system should be instantly familiar to anyone who has played a modern third person melee action game. You have quick and heavy strikes with your sword, a block button which can parry enemies light attacks if timed properly, and a generous roll to avoid heavy attacks or position yourself at their flanks. Once shielded types are introduced you have to kick them to open up their defenses. You also have access to a buff that slows down time, increases damage and heals, so that is vital. While not exactly innovative, the combat is fluid, tense, and satisfying. If you're worried Hellblade is going to be another elitist non-game, just give it time. It's a slow burn, but the action ramps up and is actually helped by the connections forged from the narrative.
 
  At it's worst, Hellblade is a masturbatory exercise for Ninja Theory to show off it's mastery of technical artistry and for Senua's actress to perform a one woman play in front of facial capture cameras. While this may cause the occasional douchebump to tickle the back of your neck, if you stick it through the game pays off with exceptional set piece after set piece and a memorable, affecting, personal journey through hell.

There are a few things that need reworked in the game; Object boundaries are pretty shoddily done, the respawn system is pretty infuriating, vehicle handling, and the vehicles ability to turn their wheels.
First, object boundaries, its pretty obvious when you're in rocks that the boundaries of the vehicles and the rocks are pretty lax. By this, I mean the game will register that the object are colliding when on screen they aren't. This will make taking a particular line difficult, its pretty infuriating when you should be able to make it up a ledge but the game won't let you. I can tell that this was done to ease the work needed in programming and less processing to do client-side, it would be nice to see it refined, however. This also ties into #5, vehicles ability to turn their wheels, more when I get there, though.
Respawn system, the forced respawn is rather annoying, there have been countless times when I was forcibly respawned even though I wasn't in the situation it was telling me I was. I think forced respawn should be removed and a 'You appear to be stuck, would you like a penalty-free respawn?' should be in its place. There's just no excuses for the respawn, something like that should have been fixed long ago.
Vehicle handling is another spot that I can had corners cut to ease the work on the devs. When vehicle handling is lower, the vehicle isn't harder to handle, it simply won't respond to inputs as well. Yes, this is essentially the same thing, however its not. When handling is low, the vehicle simply refuses to do what you're telling it to do, IE. solid ground, full lock steering, and going 4 KPH the vehicle should turn very sharply, there is no reason for it not to, however it simply refuses to turn due to the handling mechanisms in the game.
Torque, this is kinda in with the traction mechanisms of the game, low gear isn't as powerful as it should be. In most 4-wheel drive vehicles 4-low is almost unstoppable, however in the game the vehicles get bogged down far too easily. The vehicle get far too much 'traction' this is tied in with the object boundaries being lax.
(Un)fortunately, this is the only game that I have found that fills this genre (Hardcore Offroad Racing), so I would have to say its the best one like it. I would recommend it because it isn't a horrible game, it just needs work to refine it.

The good:
Epistory was my first experience with typing games, and a lovely one at that. I type quickly, so I played the adaptive difficulty and had just enough challenge to keep me interested in the well-paced typing adventure. Eventually your character learns new magic types, making battles more dynamic. Your typing destroys enemies - woodland insects and arachnids - as well as terrain, opening up new areas to explore and chests to open. The typing mechanic never feels forced; the game is linguistic through and through. Each word typed feels organic and relevant to the unfolding story. There's much to explore (even more than is necessary for the storyline), and the quaint yet geometric art style encourages you to do so. The story itself is beautiful and unassuming; Epistory is unexpectedly touching. (And don't worry, you are still free to explore the world even after the story's final chapter.)
The bad:
As much as I treasure this indie gem, I had a few issues. Some of the ice puzzles were nothing but tedious and incredibly difficult to complete - not because they were difficult to solve, but because the design was antagonistic. The game has an arena option, where you can put your typing skills to the test and compete on the leaderboards. It's a fun game mode for nerds like me who enjoy typing, but it's buggy in fullscreen. Speaking of typing nerds - I type over 100 wpm, which is (at times) faster than the game could register - problematic during some battles.
The end:
Epistory is surprising. It's charming, it's unique, it's enjoyable. It's one of those games you play on a bit of a whim, and then you come to revel in your discovery of. Epistory is one of those lovely games none of your friends know about... until you tell them... and you will.

To the Moon is a sincere story told through 16-bit-style graphics and simplistic gameplay. You control the characters Dr. Wyatt and Dr. Rosaleane, scientists within a wolrd in which it is possible to recover an alter memories of their dying patients for a chance to live their final requests and dreams - even if it was not reality and only in their minds.
"Occasionally I'm fortunate enough to play a game that reminds me what's important. Not only what's important in making a great piece of interactive media, but also what's important in life." - Anthony Gallegos
This story centers around a dying man named Johnny who wished to visit the moon, hence the games title, To the Moon. Along the journey of recovering Johnny's memory a wonderful story of love, and loss unfolds before your eyes. As you progress through layers of memories Johnny will slowly go from being an unconscious old man you don't really care about, to a complex human being whose life you are certain to empathize with. By the end of the game I came to care about Johnny, despite never meeting his "real" self in the overworld.
The gameplay consists of simple puzzles in order to break through layers of memories and then comes to exploring the memory and watching the story unfold. In other words if you are someone who's interested in fancy graphics and gameplay this isn't for you.
My weak puzzle solving skills and exploration are not why I have 4 hours in this game, I rather rushed through these parts in order to reach the next scene or dialogue sequence allowing me sight into the minds and hearts of the characters presented. Some games are mindless and are carried through the repetitive actions, gameplay and graphics. To the Moon is reliant on the excellent plot of which will leave you broken.

4 Player Co-Op, there is no duplicate classing  (ex. no 2 people can be the wizard). 1 class per person, a full group consisting of 1 of each of the original 4, Wizard, Warrior, Elf, and Valkyrie.
Gameplay-wise, each class has its own unique style of play, somewhat reflecting their original counterparts. The Warrior boastst the highest health-pool in the game and plays aggressively with his powerful melee swings and Invulnerability-Framed abilities. Valkyrie plays like warrior, only much more defensive, having a literal invulnerability skill blocking everything she faces. Elf is ranged DPS, sporting a low healthbar and having many ranged options. Wizard is the most versatile, as he has a spell for any given situation, be it long range support, holding down a choke point, freezing enemies that get too close to him, and escaping enemies all together. However, he also sports the lowest health-pool in the game, and takes practice to get the muscle memory for the spells when you need them.
The environment is nothing to brag about. You go into a cave and go as deep as you can. There are basically 3 worlds to go through. Not very diverse, but they aren't boring atleast.
Endless mode is where you will spend most of your time after you beat the story. I find that it also gives plenty of gold as well.
Friends make this game infinitely more enjoyable, as with the Gauntlets before it. I had a blast going to level 50 on Endless with just one other friend. Clutching in this game can give it life.
Is this game worth $20? For the amount of content: No. Is it worth $10 or $15? Maybe. Is is worth $5? Hell yes!

If you took some of the worst aspects of a Diablo game (rogue-like levels which are composed of all-too-few room types), coupled it with level mechanics which constantly lock you into tiny rooms with overwhelming numbers of monsters, took away the player's ability to manuever or use any real level of tactics, added a rather useless RPG store mechanism which encourages you to die until you and buy enough to stop dying as often, totally ignored any concept of class balance or fair play, constantly spawned invulnerable enemies or one-hit-kill traps against the player, and then slapped a Gauntlet skin and audio track on the mess...  That's this game.
It's not a challenge...  It's just keep dying until you can buy enough so you don't.
And you won't really know enough about this game to decide whether you like it until you've played too much to get a refund.  It takes hours to figure out that the class balance is completely out of whack.  It takes hours to get upgrades.  It takes hours to figure out that all you really have to do is keep dying...
The Gauntlet of old was, at its best, a game of tactics and planning.  You were playing alone or with friends against hordes of enemies, setting up choke points, solving puzzles, sweeping a floor in a careful, methodical method, and pressing on.  It was a game about tactics, planning, and puzzle solving as much as action.  This isn't that game.  This game...  Just run for the gold, hope you can blast enough enemies to keep some of it.  Repeat.  Buy upgrades.  Repeat.
So, if you like mindless action and lots of dying, go for it.  But I can't even really call it Gauntlet.  It lacks Gauntlet's spirit.
