I found this game absurdly buggy.  The interface was controller-friendly, though.  I also like the concept behind the game.  The overall experience was just too buggy and frustrating to recommend buying the game at any price.
What the game has going for it is a vector art style similar to a typical Flash-powered game.  Whether or not this game leveraged Flash is beyond my knowledge, but it looks like all the art was drawn in Flash or a similar vector drawing tool.  it also has one of the coolest concepts ever seen in action RPGs: hack things using their USB ports.  It's not simply a gag, though!  It's utilized at the game's core design level, allowing for very interesting puzzles.  The time travel aspect is cool, too, but I found myself avoiding that aspect of the game as much as possible.
Where this game goes wrong is it does not hold your hand enough in the beginning and has a very unintuitive hacking interface.  There's a slab near the beginning that shows you code that you can't edit at all... though it spawns a chest right away... not sure if that was hinting that future puzzles would use these slabs to give you clues, but that's my assumption.  Anyway, a lot of the puzzles can be messed up and require you to really think about what you're doing.  You have to contend with the game's poor implementation of riding on moving platforms, like swimming turtles, only to finally get across a small body of water after countless times getting pushed into the water by invisible forces.  Mildly frustrating... becomes tedious... becomes too tedious to keep going.  During playing this game, I felt like it would be easier to code my own game from scratch than it would be to play this game about hacking a game's logic.  It's silly, because I could just as easily really hack the game and just beat it right away, ruining what little gameplay the game provides.

Simply amazing. I cannot believe this game was only $30. I played with a controller because I prefer playing these types of games that way.
Graphics: One of the most beautiful games I've ever played. Everything from the physics, partical effects, textures, weather, environment, and animations all scream AAA. The entire time, I was constantly shocked at how good this game looks. This might be the best looking game I've ever played. All of the environments are beautiful, some are awe-inspiring. The enemy design is truly incredible. Attack an enemy and you will see their wounds. This comes to full light later in the game when fighting a large enemy, and you see their skin(?) ripping off of them as you attack. Incredibly visceral and what I'm sure is a technical feat.
Sound: All voice actors are spot on. There is zero cheese. Sound effects are excellent and never distracting. There isn't much music, but it kicks in at the right moments with the right feel. Because of the nature of the story, you hear voices. They do not repeat. I repeat, they do not repeat. The voices give contextual qeues, but can't always be trusted. Amazing concept, absolutely loved this.
Gameplay: This is where some might take issue. There is a lot of talking, story, and drama. Especially in the early parts of the game, there isn't very much fighting. However, I would argue that a lot of fighting during the early parts of the game wouldn't make much sense in regards to the story and flow of this game. You'll be listening, exploring, and solving puzzles. However, combat definitely picks up later as Senua dives deeper into her quest. As for combat, I had a lot of fun. Parry, block, light and heavy attacks, guard breaking, and (my favorite) running towards the enemy and executing a heavy attack. You also have a focus ability that increases your perception and allows you to move faster than your enemies.
Story: This is where it's at. The story of Senua will forever stay with me. She is a character that I can relate to, even as a man, because she deeply suffers from a mental illness. She has suffered greatly. She is on a quest for her love, literally carrying his head with her as she goes. This game is dark. There are very few bright moments in it. The story flows, makes sense, and comes to a satisfying conclusion. I do not personally feel like there was a single misstep in the story.
Conclusion: Overall, I absolutely loved this game. If it was $60, I might not have purchased it, not knowing how incredibly good it was. After playing it, I happily would have paid $60. If Ninja Theory releases a $30 skin that changes Senua's shoes, I'll buy it. Part way through, I wasn't sure if I'd play it again. Not that I didn't like it, I just didn't know if I'd want to go through the puzzles because I thought that was kind of the focus of the gameplay. It's not. I will definitely be playing this again. 10/10.
As for the bad reviews, just look at how much time they put in. Yes, the game starts off slow and there isn't a ton of combat at the beginning. It's right for this game. This isn't God of War or Dark Souls, nor did anyone (including the devs) claim it was.
Perma-death: It never came up for me. I died twice. The game isn't incredibly difficult, but it's challenging enough that I almost died several times.

It is ground breaking for sure as a game that is tackling mental illness however it does so with such a disjointed story and mediocre gameplay that the journey was even more of a slog then the afforementioned Get Even which also lacked in the area of gameplay while it excelled in story.
I feel that the combat in Hellblade while fun once you got your head around it lacked depth for the length of the game. Instead of adding gameplay systems with each boss I felt they just stuck to the metaphor of the story religiously and this hurt the gameplay. The threat of perma death made no sense as well as it doesn't fit with the metaphor of mental illness at all and seems more as a way to artificially extend the games length for people that will breeze through it on the highest difficulty because the enemies lack depth, again this could be because they didn't want any encounter to be to hard as the perma death would then put people off. I feel as though that one mechanic in one fell swoop killed the potential for combat depth and as it was an unnecessary one I hope they patch it out.
I say this as someone that never experienced it and got through every enemy encounter and boss fight on hard difficulty bar one particullarly annoying area that had a puzzle that kept killing me so I cranked it down to easy so I wouldn't have to replay the game then back up to hard after I got through the stupid area where the beast was roaming....(pro tip ....if the beast is stalking you and you keep running down one path and crouching thinking the area is unreachable to light a torch it is go back to the other side of the room past the water to light it, you only need to lower the bridge then turn back)...
Bottom line the gameplay is not hard, the puzzles are not hard just annoying to find.. the only things that actually killed me were...
1. a small beam I had to walk across that was different from all the others in the game as the beam itself was near invisible and a beast was roaming under it so It threw off my depth perception and on top of this the controller was vibrating and the game started  artificially moving the character balance back and forth to throw you off the beam...I died once then took it really slow till I figured out you could just press focus to cheese it somewhat and light the area up...This was not a skillful thing just annoying lazy game design that again would risk ending peoples playtime with multiple deaths many hours in for no reason whatsoever...
2. the afore mentioned puzzle where you had to stay in the light and light torches or an unseen unattackable beast would insta kill you with no chance of recovery. You will know when you are in the bad area because you will have to light a torch then go through a gate that extinguishes it immediately after just remember to turn back after you drop the bridge the game makes you think you can keep going that way again which would probably lead to many people dying and having to replay 3/4 of the game but you don't you turn back there and go to the opposite side of the room back past the water to light the torch from the other side. Again this is poor game design as making a puzzle that insta kills you in a game that has perma death makes no goddamn sense as you feel like a death that is not in combat is arbitrary and meaningless.
I have zero reservations about spoiling these two areas because if you play with the auto or hard mode perma death rules apply so cheap deaths should not be a thing in this game which unfortuanately they are.
That said the game is a total breeze to get through in combat not a single enemy or boss killed me on hard and once I figured out the focus system and parry mechanic, guard break and charge attacks it was gg for anything the game threw at me basically you can parry by pressing block at the last minute on anything but a shield bash and a boss charge or kick from enemies or weapon throw attack.  You can charge attack with left  bumper or L1 and heavy or light attack you will either do a straight charge stab with light which is faster or a heafty spining vertical swing with heavy. You can also hold L1 or bumper and run at the enemy then press the combination when you are closer. the focus button basically puts you into bullet time and lets you tear enemies to pieces with combos even repositioning mid combo say uppercutting them then dodging to the side and charge stabbing their mid air boddy or focus into a side roll by double tapping the dodge button and you will go to the side of a shield enemy to get in and attack from the side. The melee button does guard break and on anything but the duel axe wielder bosses and shielded enemies can practically be used to do infinite combos on enemies. You can also cheap enemies off the sides of bridges by doing multilple melee attacks just make sure you don't do a stabbing charge attack at a shield enemy with his back to a pit as he will lift you and flip you over every time and this will likely lead to a death and one step closer to perma death....
While all these mechanics are sound and there is a point early on where they come together and to great effect they never get any additions. You find 2 weapon upgrades the whole game...the mirror that lets you do focus attacks and a glowing sword that lets you do more damage and thats it...This is a game that more than any other feels like it sacrificed gameplay to the narrative gods. I usually don't have an issue with this I love telltale games and Get Even is as earlier stated my game narrative of the year gameplay aside. However the fact that the battle mechanics were so sound and fun meant that there was potential there for a proper fun combat system they basically gave you a taste of how good it could have been and then decided to stop giving after that.
The narrative while meaty did not feel as deep as the work that went into it. I saw the making of and the professors and mental health recovery people they used to consult and really appreciated what they were trying to bring to life however all that work really didn't bring me anything that mind blowing. I felt like the main character would have been far more likeable if we had played through her backstory as opposed to having it revealed through flash backs and psycosis  seeing her lose her mind instead of it being a plot reveal that was spoiled by the opening scroll warning...in the end this is  a sevicable story 6/10 with servicable game mechanics 6/10 with an amazing interface 10/10 (no ingame hud done right for the first time)

Finished up my first playthrough about 90 minutes ago and since then I've spent the majority of my time racking my brain trying to think of a character in any game that I've ever been more invested in. Nothing is coming to mind.
Right off the bat you should know, this game deals with issues relating to, and contains a very effective performance of a person experiencing, deep psychological troubles. For myself it fostered a kind of empathy I've never felt for a player character before, but I can absolutely imagine and understand people being upset or uncomfortable while watching such a portrayal. It really is quite breathtakingly great/borderline painful to watch.
Hellblade is 2 parts puzzle/walking sim and 1 part Souls-lite combat and is held together by a plot chock full of Norse/Celtic mythology and which is so well written and performed that... Well, you read how I feel about the main character so that tells the story of the story.
Puzzles are moderately challenging with a lot of visual alignment and "find the weird shape in the ocean of weird shaped things" style conundrums. Thankfully they rarely outstay their welcome in part due to some subtle hints here and there from various sources.
Combat on surface level is very Souls like. You have a heavy, a light and "THE BOOT" for dealing with shield wielders as well as the obligatory dodge button. However in execution the combat feels satisfyingly refreshing and proves to be far more forgiving and emotive than it's sadistic ancestor. The dodge feels much more subtle varying, depending on circumstance, from a slight feint to a full on combat roll with variations in between. You can mash lights and heavies to your heart's content and probably get the job done no problem at all. But should you wish to play around with the button inputs you might be delighted with the things you can find. I certainly was and that was before I realised you could use the run button to do crazy badass flying knee attacks to those shield bearing bast*rds. Damn I enjoyed the combat in this game!
Overall I feel Hellblade is a tremendous achievement, blending two seemingly disparate genres together in a manner that beautifully conveys the strengths of both without falling prey to the follies of either. This genuinely may be one of the very best games I've ever played.

Oh boy oh boy oh boy.
From the time I first started up this game, I never thought I could be impacted that much by a game that cost about $10 and ran in a small square window.
Boy was I wrong.
This game is pretty much an interactive adventure story. The story is about how 2 doctors enter the memories of a dying patient to fulfill their last wishes, and with it, comes with ethical issues and such. This ultimatley leads to the two main characters in a small conflict. The way the story is told through the use of the different points of views of the different charcaters tells the story very mysteriously and efficiently.
The gameplay works out to be somewhat of a free roam. If I had to choose a game that this reminded me of, it'd be Pokemon Rangers. The game revloves around finding 5 memory links to progress to the next memory. Most of the time, you'll then need to solve a little puzzle to progress, which I find very interesting. There are also other aspects and minigames in the gameplay, like shooting down virtual zombies, avoiding traps, and playing whack-a-mole. I find the little addition of these minigames and the ability to access them only once a very cool addition. I did save at thsoe areas though, so I could go back once in a while to play again.
The art in this game is fantastic in my opinion. The use of pixel art throughout the game really gives the gamem the adventurous vibe, and in this sense, it reminded me of Pokemon Rangers as well. The soundtrack is also great, and the little sound effects and tracks do really well in setting the mood and tension in the story. I found myself having an exhilerating experience with these. The uses of small flashes of white, black, or red, to foreshadow / add effect to an upcoming scene is also very well done.
If I had to complain about one thing in this game though, it'd be the few opportunities to save, once you have started antoher piece of storytelling. Oh, and the fact that you can only have 3 save files.
I really really recommend this game. Don't look down or be put off buy the price or the game style. The feel-filled story itself is worth it alone imo.
Sorry if any of you felt I was not detailed enough talking about the story. I tried my best to avoid spoilers.

When I think of action typing games the most prominent game that comes to mind is Typing of the Dead. A classic and there's been nothing close to it since, until now. Epistory takes you on an adventure through a paper landscape riding on a large origami fox. This game has those feverish typing to kill enemies element but this one is more family friendly.
When you start off it's not clear how or why you're in this strange paper world or what your end game is but that's okay as the game leads you down many paths to uncover your story. The more you explore the more your world expands. As you fight and type your way through enemies you gain points for unlocking more areas. Pretty straightforward right? As you make your journey through the vast wilderness your chronicles are narrated by the girl in a way that seems more like a walk through memory lane.
There are various zones throughout the world that break up the monotony and a couple of magic powers to provide a little variety for your typing skills. While this game is way more family friendly than the aforementioned title that no way diminishes the  hardcore difficulty of this game. You will periodically face waves of enemies and the words to defeat foes gets progressively more complex. There are some words I didn't even know existed in the English language. But I should also mention that if English isn't your go to native language don't fear as you can play in several different languages.
So to sum it up:
+Great art style
+Several languages to choose from
+Innovative battle system
+Ability to make your own word lists

This 2014 edition of Gauntlet is a game I want to like, but that's simply impossible. It's a tedious, monotonous game with serious design problems. The game recently got polished into Gauntlet: Slayer Edition, but the problems remained.
Conclusion: looks good, but not worth of any money. Maybe, if you get it for free, or as a part of humble bundle. Otherwise, no.
Regrettably, this game is not fun to play at all.
After 4 to 5 first levels the game starts to repeat itself. First levels are fairly enjoyable, but after that: nothing new. Controlling game characters (4 different + 1 dlc) is not rewarding, because most of the time your character is very hard to spot from the screen. That's because of three of the worst design flaws: walls obstruct your view, the viewpoint (camera) is zoomed out way too far away from your character AND the levels have very few light sources.
Playing the game makes you wish you had binoculars and a flashlight pointed at the screen.
How about multiplayer mode? You need a friend for that, because there is never anyone playing multiplayer otherwise. Once you get online with your friend, you will experience even more design flaws. You think you cannot get motion sickness from a game? I dare you to try this one on multiplayer mode. Have a bucket next to you when you try. I mean, what were the devs thinking? On single-player you have to strain your eyes to be able see your tiny character on a dim screen, and on multiplayer mode the screen jumps and jolts around making sure you'll vomit, or at least get a headache.
Even if I pretend I can endure the flaws I mentioned, the boring map design and clearing a floor after a floor from the same enemies over and over again is just not worth the time. It is very sad to give this game thumbs down, because I really loved previous Gauntlet games, such as Gauntlet: Dark Legacy and the original Gauntlet and Gauntlet 2. Yes, even the original Gauntlet is less monotonous than this one. At least the original Gauntlet had proper level design and a feeling of progress in the game.

Simply amazing. I cannot believe this game was only $30. I played with a controller because I prefer playing these types of games that way.
Graphics: One of the most beautiful games I've ever played. Everything from the physics, partical effects, textures, weather, environment, and animations all scream AAA. The entire time, I was constantly shocked at how good this game looks. This might be the best looking game I've ever played. All of the environments are beautiful, some are awe-inspiring. The enemy design is truly incredible. Attack an enemy and you will see their wounds. This comes to full light later in the game when fighting a large enemy, and you see their skin(?) ripping off of them as you attack. Incredibly visceral and what I'm sure is a technical feat.
Sound: All voice actors are spot on. There is zero cheese. Sound effects are excellent and never distracting. There isn't much music, but it kicks in at the right moments with the right feel. Because of the nature of the story, you hear voices. They do not repeat. I repeat, they do not repeat. The voices give contextual qeues, but can't always be trusted. Amazing concept, absolutely loved this.
Gameplay: This is where some might take issue. There is a lot of talking, story, and drama. Especially in the early parts of the game, there isn't very much fighting. However, I would argue that a lot of fighting during the early parts of the game wouldn't make much sense in regards to the story and flow of this game. You'll be listening, exploring, and solving puzzles. However, combat definitely picks up later as Senua dives deeper into her quest. As for combat, I had a lot of fun. Parry, block, light and heavy attacks, guard breaking, and (my favorite) running towards the enemy and executing a heavy attack. You also have a focus ability that increases your perception and allows you to move faster than your enemies.
Story: This is where it's at. The story of Senua will forever stay with me. She is a character that I can relate to, even as a man, because she deeply suffers from a mental illness. She has suffered greatly. She is on a quest for her love, literally carrying his head with her as she goes. This game is dark. There are very few bright moments in it. The story flows, makes sense, and comes to a satisfying conclusion. I do not personally feel like there was a single misstep in the story.
Conclusion: Overall, I absolutely loved this game. If it was $60, I might not have purchased it, not knowing how incredibly good it was. After playing it, I happily would have paid $60. If Ninja Theory releases a $30 skin that changes Senua's shoes, I'll buy it. Part way through, I wasn't sure if I'd play it again. Not that I didn't like it, I just didn't know if I'd want to go through the puzzles because I thought that was kind of the focus of the gameplay. It's not. I will definitely be playing this again. 10/10.
As for the bad reviews, just look at how much time they put in. Yes, the game starts off slow and there isn't a ton of combat at the beginning. It's right for this game. This isn't God of War or Dark Souls, nor did anyone (including the devs) claim it was.
Perma-death: It never came up for me. I died twice. The game isn't incredibly difficult, but it's challenging enough that I almost died several times.

So I just finished Hellblade and I have mixed emotions to say the least. When I first started It felt like a pretentious walking simulator by the time I fought the boss nicknamed "The master of Illusion" I was feeling giddy and ready for the next battle as the nuance of the combat system were just coming to light for me but a few hours after that I was frustrated to all hell because of an area that was insta killing me with balancing on a beam and insta death from not staying in the light. All while on the highest difficulty with the threat of perma death and a game save wipe on the line....yeah that's a thing...
...after that I was thouroughly bored with the puzzle mechanics and the fun of the combat wore off as I could easily dispatch any foe with zero fear of death and the only fear was dying to a cheap insta kill death mechainic that was more an issue of poor game design then actual skill and I was slogging thorugh the last bit hoping I didn't die cause if I did I had no intention of replaying though 6-9 hours of gameplay...
I'm not sure of my exact time as I went to get lunch with the game paused and I also watched the making of the game video that is in game which artificially added to game time. I feel like this is going to be a critical darling but story wise it is not in the same plane as Get Even which is also a budget tripple A game and is still the best narrative in a game this year. It is ground breaking for sure as a game that is tackling mental illness however it does so with such a disjointed story and mediocre gameplay that the journey was even more of a slog then the afforementioned Get Even which also lacked in the area of gameplay while it excelled in story.
I feel that the combat in Hellblade while fun once you got your head around it lacked depth for the length of the game. Instead of adding gameplay systems with each boss I felt they just stuck to the metaphor of the story religiously and this hurt the gameplay. The threat of perma death made no sense as well as it doesn't fit with the metaphor of mental illness at all and seems more as a way to artificially extend the games length for people that will breeze through it on the highest difficulty because the enemies lack depth, again this could be because they didn't want any encounter to be to hard as the perma death would then put people off. I feel as though that one mechanic in one fell swoop killed the potential for combat depth and as it was an unnecessary one I hope they patch it out.
I say this as someone that never experienced it and got through every enemy encounter and boss fight on hard difficulty bar one particullarly annoying area that had a puzzle that kept killing me so I cranked it down to easy so I wouldn't have to replay the game then back up to hard after I got through the stupid area where the beast was roaming....(pro tip ....if the beast is stalking you and you keep running down one path and crouching thinking the area is unreachable to light a torch it is go back to the other side of the room past the water to light it, you only need to lower the bridge then turn back)...
Bottom line the gameplay is not hard, the puzzles are not hard just annoying to find.. the only things that actually killed me were...
1. a small beam I had to walk across that was different from all the others in the game as the beam itself was near invisible and a beast was roaming under it so It threw off my depth perception and on top of this the controller was vibrating and the game started  artificially moving the character balance back and forth to throw you off the beam...I died once then took it really slow till I figured out you could just press focus to cheese it somewhat and light the area up...This was not a skillful thing just annoying lazy game design that again would risk ending peoples playtime with multiple deaths many hours in for no reason whatsoever...
2. the afore mentioned puzzle where you had to stay in the light and light torches or an unseen unattackable beast would insta kill you with no chance of recovery. You will know when you are in the bad area because you will have to light a torch then go through a gate that extinguishes it immediately after just remember to turn back after you drop the bridge the game makes you think you can keep going that way again which would probably lead to many people dying and having to replay 3/4 of the game but you don't you turn back there and go to the opposite side of the room back past the water to light the torch from the other side. Again this is poor game design as making a puzzle that insta kills you in a game that has perma death makes no goddamn sense as you feel like a death that is not in combat is arbitrary and meaningless.
I have zero reservations about spoiling these two areas because if you play with the auto or hard mode perma death rules apply so cheap deaths should not be a thing in this game which unfortuanately they are.
That said the game is a total breeze to get through in combat not a single enemy or boss killed me on hard and once I figured out the focus system and parry mechanic, guard break and charge attacks it was gg for anything the game threw at me basically you can parry by pressing block at the last minute on anything but a shield bash and a boss charge or kick from enemies or weapon throw attack.  You can charge attack with left  bumper or L1 and heavy or light attack you will either do a straight charge stab with light which is faster or a heafty spining vertical swing with heavy. You can also hold L1 or bumper and run at the enemy then press the combination when you are closer. the focus button basically puts you into bullet time and lets you tear enemies to pieces with combos even repositioning mid combo say uppercutting them then dodging to the side and charge stabbing their mid air boddy or focus into a side roll by double tapping the dodge button and you will go to the side of a shield enemy to get in and attack from the side. The melee button does guard break and on anything but the duel axe wielder bosses and shielded enemies can practically be used to do infinite combos on enemies. You can also cheap enemies off the sides of bridges by doing multilple melee attacks just make sure you don't do a stabbing charge attack at a shield enemy with his back to a pit as he will lift you and flip you over every time and this will likely lead to a death and one step closer to perma death....
While all these mechanics are sound and there is a point early on where they come together and to great effect they never get any additions. You find 2 weapon upgrades the whole game...the mirror that lets you do focus attacks and a glowing sword that lets you do more damage and thats it...This is a game that more than any other feels like it sacrificed gameplay to the narrative gods. I usually don't have an issue with this I love telltale games and Get Even is as earlier stated my game narrative of the year gameplay aside. However the fact that the battle mechanics were so sound and fun meant that there was potential there for a proper fun combat system they basically gave you a taste of how good it could have been and then decided to stop giving after that.
The narrative while meaty did not feel as deep as the work that went into it. I saw the making of and the professors and mental health recovery people they used to consult and really appreciated what they were trying to bring to life however all that work really didn't bring me anything that mind blowing. I felt like the main character would have been far more likeable if we had played through her backstory as opposed to having it revealed through flash backs and psycosis  seeing her lose her mind instead of it being a plot reveal that was spoiled by the opening scroll warning...in the end this is  a sevicable story 6/10 with servicable game mechanics 6/10 with an amazing interface 10/10 (no ingame hud done right for the first time)

Finished up my first playthrough about 90 minutes ago and since then I've spent the majority of my time racking my brain trying to think of a character in any game that I've ever been more invested in. Nothing is coming to mind.
Right off the bat you should know, this game deals with issues relating to, and contains a very effective performance of a person experiencing, deep psychological troubles. For myself it fostered a kind of empathy I've never felt for a player character before, but I can absolutely imagine and understand people being upset or uncomfortable while watching such a portrayal. It really is quite breathtakingly great/borderline painful to watch.
Hellblade is 2 parts puzzle/walking sim and 1 part Souls-lite combat and is held together by a plot chock full of Norse/Celtic mythology and which is so well written and performed that... Well, you read how I feel about the main character so that tells the story of the story.
Puzzles are moderately challenging with a lot of visual alignment and "find the weird shape in the ocean of weird shaped things" style conundrums. Thankfully they rarely outstay their welcome in part due to some subtle hints here and there from various sources.
Combat on surface level is very Souls like. You have a heavy, a light and "THE BOOT" for dealing with shield wielders as well as the obligatory dodge button. However in execution the combat feels satisfyingly refreshing and proves to be far more forgiving and emotive than it's sadistic ancestor. The dodge feels much more subtle varying, depending on circumstance, from a slight feint to a full on combat roll with variations in between. You can mash lights and heavies to your heart's content and probably get the job done no problem at all. But should you wish to play around with the button inputs you might be delighted with the things you can find. I certainly was and that was before I realised you could use the run button to do crazy badass flying knee attacks to those shield bearing bast*rds. Damn I enjoyed the combat in this game!
Overall I feel Hellblade is a tremendous achievement, blending two seemingly disparate genres together in a manner that beautifully conveys the strengths of both without falling prey to the follies of either. This genuinely may be one of the very best games I've ever played.

Not many video games use spelling or typing as a game mechanic and Epistory: Typing Chronicles does it flawlessly. This genre is relatively small and the only other typing game that I've played is Mario Teaches Typing on DOS which taught me the very basics of keyboard usage. Epistory takes it to the next level in many ways and all of them good.
First, the words you'll type are relative to the game and it's story. This creates a pattern that eases you into typing some very long and challenging words. Second, gameplay is never stale. From the very beginning you'll see areas blocked off and you'll know to return to these areas later once you've acquired certain skills. Straight to the very end, you'll have to quickly switch between these skills to achieve your goals and, for many, this won't be an easy feat. Third, you can play this game entirely with your keyboard without ever taking your fingers off the home row. Menus can be traversed by simply typing the option you want to adjust which is slower than simply using your mouse, but I enjoyed being immersed in my typing experience. Lastly, the story and voice-acting are nice rewards for your progression. A narrator tells the story as you walk along and acts as a guide so you know when you're walking in the right direction. I shouldn't have to tell you that this game won't be remembered for its story; it's the gameplay that you're looking for here.
Overall, I had a great time playing Epistory. If you're looking for a unique game, different from your usual strategy, RPG, or action-adventure, look no further. You won't regret your purchase here.

When I watched trailers for this game for the first time, I got the impression that the writing would be very literary, very highbrow, and a central part of the game. The trailers certainly try to imply that. In actuality, the writing is not that great, and almost tumblry at times. Although I will concede, that, a lot of it being in the form of disjointed sentences makes it harder to appraise. And also, the writing coming out of the protagonist in such disjointed sentences, one at a time, makes sense in the context of the story. Speaking of which...
The plot twist at the end of the game has got to be the oldest cliché in the, ahem, book. So much so, that people are reluctant to use it nowadays, which is a good thing. So when I saw the ending of Epistory, I literally did a mental triple take:
Ultimately, it doesn't make the game less satisfying, but I found it disapointing. A bit. The way the initial chapters play out, I was imagining the story is about a young novelist struggling with writer's block, trying to regain her inspiration or maybe a more literal search for a missing muse. But no.
Luckily, the gameplay is solid. The adaptive difficulty does a good job of picking a difficulty level for you, or you can manually choose out of like... five, I think. The graphics are gorgeous; the origami world "unfolding before your eyes" gimmick doesn't really get old. The audio is okay. The puzzles are so simple that at first I found them insulting, but as time went on, I warmed up to this emanation of casualness. There aren't that many typing games out there, so a new entry into the genre and as well-polished as this always makes me pleased. In terms of content it doesn't match up to the likes of The Typing of The Dead, but I don't mind.

Picture this:  you're playing the original Legend of Zelda (yeah the one for NES).  You walk up to a bush and hit it with your sword.  In the Zelda game, nothing would happen, right?  Well in this game, you insert the sword into the USB port on the back of the bush and you have the option to either make it moveable so you can push it out of the way, set it on fire, or extinguish the flame if it is on fire.  And you can set how many health hearts it drops if you let it burn.
Picture this:  you're playing the original Legend of Zelda (yeah same game as before but a different reference this time I promise) and an enemy is charging at you.  You swing your sword to attack.  In the Zelda game, it would take two or three hits, then the enemy would curl up and die... possibly dropping a rupee or a heart.  Well, in this game you insert your sword in the USB port on the enemy's head and now you have several options:
1.  you can change an enemy to a friend so it will seek and destroy other enemies!!
2.  you can change the amount of HP the enemy has to make it easier (or harder) to kill.
3.  you can change whether the enemy is looking for a fight, or running away.
4.  you can change the enemy's movement patterns using an advanced programming menu.
5.  you can change the amount of health hearts the enemy drops when it dies.
Similar changes are possible in all sorts of situations in this game.  In fact, if you are unwilling to hack your way out of trouble (as in computer hack, not hack and slash and stab) then you will FAIL.  Yep, this is the original game that is designed to be played BY CHEATING YOUR WAY THROUGH IT.  There are multiple solutions to most of the problems you encounter, but all of them will require creative use of MATH, LOGIC, and BASIC PROGRAMMING.
Bottom line:
it's reminiscent of the old-school adventure RPG games like Legend of Zelda, except your main tool here is a super-hacker USB sword that you use to change the parameters of every item, spell, and character you encounter.  If you HATE hacking, programming, math/logic problems, and things of that nature then you will hate this game.  If you want to play a new take on an old genre, well then you might have a little fun with this.

This is a good game.  You should play this game.  It has nice artwork, animation and wonderful music.  The game plays out like a children's bedtime story and comes to a satisfying conclusion.  The gameplay is fluid and responsive; you can use a mouse + keyboard combination, a controller, or just the keyboard.  While you can unlock a number of different abilities, there is an achievement for not using any ability points so it must be possible - albeit difficult - to beat the game without them.  Certain areas of the game are not terribly intuitive; a sudden change in pace or a spike in difficulty will catch many new players by surprise.  I would be very surprised if a new player did not die at least once.  Part of the challenge and fun of platformers is precision.  Not going to lie; certain parts of the game can be quite challenging and it may feel like you are being punished due to instant death but it also makes the game rewarding to beat.  Overall the scenes - especially those involving the antagonist - are creative and well-executed, giving an authentic feeling of being vulnerable.  Overall, beautiful, fun game.  Highly recommended.

-- Update --
Since my review got a significant amount of views, I will add some helpful information.
There is no in-game facility to change the keyboard/mouse controls. To do this, you go to your AC Chronicles China install location, specifically the config. Mine is "I:\Steam\SteamApps\common\Assassins Creed Chronicles China\ACCGame\Config".
Once there you are looking for a file called "DefaultInput.ini". Please make sure to make a backup before making any changes to this file.
In here you should have options for PlayerInput (gamepad) controls or Keyboard and Mouse controls. I haven't tested everything but you should be able to change the key name for each action to another of your choice.
As an example I changed the following line:
+Bindings=(Name="C",Command="Button bBButton | Button bCounterButton | DetachRope")
to
+Bindings=(Name="LeftAlt",Command="Button bBButton | Button bCounterButton | DetachRope")
If you are not sure what your keys are named, visiting the official Unreal Engine wiki might help:

Simply amazing. I cannot believe this game was only $30. I played with a controller because I prefer playing these types of games that way.
Graphics: One of the most beautiful games I've ever played. Everything from the physics, partical effects, textures, weather, environment, and animations all scream AAA. The entire time, I was constantly shocked at how good this game looks. This might be the best looking game I've ever played. All of the environments are beautiful, some are awe-inspiring. The enemy design is truly incredible. Attack an enemy and you will see their wounds. This comes to full light later in the game when fighting a large enemy, and you see their skin(?) ripping off of them as you attack. Incredibly visceral and what I'm sure is a technical feat.
Sound: All voice actors are spot on. There is zero cheese. Sound effects are excellent and never distracting. There isn't much music, but it kicks in at the right moments with the right feel. Because of the nature of the story, you hear voices. They do not repeat. I repeat, they do not repeat. The voices give contextual qeues, but can't always be trusted. Amazing concept, absolutely loved this.
Gameplay: This is where some might take issue. There is a lot of talking, story, and drama. Especially in the early parts of the game, there isn't very much fighting. However, I would argue that a lot of fighting during the early parts of the game wouldn't make much sense in regards to the story and flow of this game. You'll be listening, exploring, and solving puzzles. However, combat definitely picks up later as Senua dives deeper into her quest. As for combat, I had a lot of fun. Parry, block, light and heavy attacks, guard breaking, and (my favorite) running towards the enemy and executing a heavy attack. You also have a focus ability that increases your perception and allows you to move faster than your enemies.
Story: This is where it's at. The story of Senua will forever stay with me. She is a character that I can relate to, even as a man, because she deeply suffers from a mental illness. She has suffered greatly. She is on a quest for her love, literally carrying his head with her as she goes. This game is dark. There are very few bright moments in it. The story flows, makes sense, and comes to a satisfying conclusion. I do not personally feel like there was a single misstep in the story.
Conclusion: Overall, I absolutely loved this game. If it was $60, I might not have purchased it, not knowing how incredibly good it was. After playing it, I happily would have paid $60. If Ninja Theory releases a $30 skin that changes Senua's shoes, I'll buy it. Part way through, I wasn't sure if I'd play it again. Not that I didn't like it, I just didn't know if I'd want to go through the puzzles because I thought that was kind of the focus of the gameplay. It's not. I will definitely be playing this again. 10/10.

So I just finished Hellblade and I have mixed emotions to say the least. When I first started It felt like a pretentious walking simulator by the time I fought the boss nicknamed "The master of Illusion" I was feeling giddy and ready for the next battle as the nuance of the combat system were just coming to light for me but a few hours after that I was frustrated to all hell because of an area that was insta killing me with balancing on a beam and insta death from not staying in the light. All while on the highest difficulty with the threat of perma death and a game save wipe on the line....yeah that's a thing...
...after that I was thouroughly bored with the puzzle mechanics and the fun of the combat wore off as I could easily dispatch any foe with zero fear of death and the only fear was dying to a cheap insta kill death mechainic that was more an issue of poor game design then actual skill and I was slogging thorugh the last bit hoping I didn't die cause if I did I had no intention of replaying though 6-9 hours of gameplay...
I'm not sure of my exact time as I went to get lunch with the game paused and I also watched the making of the game video that is in game which artificially added to game time. I feel like this is going to be a critical darling but story wise it is not in the same plane as Get Even which is also a budget tripple A game and is still the best narrative in a game this year. It is ground breaking for sure as a game that is tackling mental illness however it does so with such a disjointed story and mediocre gameplay that the journey was even more of a slog then the afforementioned Get Even which also lacked in the area of gameplay while it excelled in story.
I feel that the combat in Hellblade while fun once you got your head around it lacked depth for the length of the game. Instead of adding gameplay systems with each boss I felt they just stuck to the metaphor of the story religiously and this hurt the gameplay. The threat of perma death made no sense as well as it doesn't fit with the metaphor of mental illness at all and seems more as a way to artificially extend the games length for people that will breeze through it on the highest difficulty because the enemies lack depth, again this could be because they didn't want any encounter to be to hard as the perma death would then put people off. I feel as though that one mechanic in one fell swoop killed the potential for combat depth and as it was an unnecessary one I hope they patch it out.
I say this as someone that never experienced it and got through every enemy encounter and boss fight on hard difficulty bar one particullarly annoying area that had a puzzle that kept killing me so I cranked it down to easy so I wouldn't have to replay the game then back up to hard after I got through the stupid area where the beast was roaming....(pro tip ....if the beast is stalking you and you keep running down one path and crouching thinking the area is unreachable to light a torch it is go back to the other side of the room past the water to light it, you only need to lower the bridge then turn back)...
Bottom line the gameplay is not hard, the puzzles are not hard just annoying to find.. the only things that actually killed me were...
1. a small beam I had to walk across that was different from all the others in the game as the beam itself was near invisible and a beast was roaming under it so It threw off my depth perception and on top of this the controller was vibrating and the game started  artificially moving the character balance back and forth to throw you off the beam...I died once then took it really slow till I figured out you could just press focus to cheese it somewhat and light the area up...This was not a skillful thing just annoying lazy game design that again would risk ending peoples playtime with multiple deaths many hours in for no reason whatsoever...
2. the afore mentioned puzzle where you had to stay in the light and light torches or an unseen unattackable beast would insta kill you with no chance of recovery. You will know when you are in the bad area because you will have to light a torch then go through a gate that extinguishes it immediately after just remember to turn back after you drop the bridge the game makes you think you can keep going that way again which would probably lead to many people dying and having to replay 3/4 of the game but you don't you turn back there and go to the opposite side of the room back past the water to light the torch from the other side. Again this is poor game design as making a puzzle that insta kills you in a game that has perma death makes no goddamn sense as you feel like a death that is not in combat is arbitrary and meaningless.
I have zero reservations about spoiling these two areas because if you play with the auto or hard mode perma death rules apply so cheap deaths should not be a thing in this game which unfortuanately they are.
That said the game is a total breeze to get through in combat not a single enemy or boss killed me on hard and once I figured out the focus system and parry mechanic, guard break and charge attacks it was gg for anything the game threw at me basically you can parry by pressing block at the last minute on anything but a shield bash and a boss charge or kick from enemies or weapon throw attack.  You can charge attack with left  bumper or L1 and heavy or light attack you will either do a straight charge stab with light which is faster or a heafty spining vertical swing with heavy. You can also hold L1 or bumper and run at the enemy then press the combination when you are closer. the focus button basically puts you into bullet time and lets you tear enemies to pieces with combos even repositioning mid combo say uppercutting them then dodging to the side and charge stabbing their mid air boddy or focus into a side roll by double tapping the dodge button and you will go to the side of a shield enemy to get in and attack from the side. The melee button does guard break and on anything but the duel axe wielder bosses and shielded enemies can practically be used to do infinite combos on enemies. You can also cheap enemies off the sides of bridges by doing multilple melee attacks just make sure you don't do a stabbing charge attack at a shield enemy with his back to a pit as he will lift you and flip you over every time and this will likely lead to a death and one step closer to perma death....
While all these mechanics are sound and there is a point early on where they come together and to great effect they never get any additions. You find 2 weapon upgrades the whole game...the mirror that lets you do focus attacks and a glowing sword that lets you do more damage and thats it...This is a game that more than any other feels like it sacrificed gameplay to the narrative gods. I usually don't have an issue with this I love telltale games and Get Even is as earlier stated my game narrative of the year gameplay aside. However the fact that the battle mechanics were so sound and fun meant that there was potential there for a proper fun combat system they basically gave you a taste of how good it could have been and then decided to stop giving after that.
The narrative while meaty did not feel as deep as the work that went into it. I saw the making of and the professors and mental health recovery people they used to consult and really appreciated what they were trying to bring to life however all that work really didn't bring me anything that mind blowing. I felt like the main character would have been far more likeable if we had played through her backstory as opposed to having it revealed through flash backs and psycosis  seeing her lose her mind instead of it being a plot reveal that was spoiled by the opening scroll warning...in the end this is  a sevicable story 6/10 with servicable game mechanics 6/10 with an amazing interface 10/10 (no ingame hud done right for the first time)

Finished up my first playthrough about 90 minutes ago and since then I've spent the majority of my time racking my brain trying to think of a character in any game that I've ever been more invested in. Nothing is coming to mind.
Right off the bat you should know, this game deals with issues relating to, and contains a very effective performance of a person experiencing, deep psychological troubles. For myself it fostered a kind of empathy I've never felt for a player character before, but I can absolutely imagine and understand people being upset or uncomfortable while watching such a portrayal. It really is quite breathtakingly great/borderline painful to watch.
Hellblade is 2 parts puzzle/walking sim and 1 part Souls-lite combat and is held together by a plot chock full of Norse/Celtic mythology and which is so well written and performed that... Well, you read how I feel about the main character so that tells the story of the story.
Puzzles are moderately challenging with a lot of visual alignment and "find the weird shape in the ocean of weird shaped things" style conundrums. Thankfully they rarely outstay their welcome in part due to some subtle hints here and there from various sources.
Combat on surface level is very Souls like. You have a heavy, a light and "THE BOOT" for dealing with shield wielders as well as the obligatory dodge button. However in execution the combat feels satisfyingly refreshing and proves to be far more forgiving and emotive than it's sadistic ancestor. The dodge feels much more subtle varying, depending on circumstance, from a slight feint to a full on combat roll with variations in between. You can mash lights and heavies to your heart's content and probably get the job done no problem at all. But should you wish to play around with the button inputs you might be delighted with the things you can find. I certainly was and that was before I realised you could use the run button to do crazy badass flying knee attacks to those shield bearing bast*rds. Damn I enjoyed the combat in this game!
Overall I feel Hellblade is a tremendous achievement, blending two seemingly disparate genres together in a manner that beautifully conveys the strengths of both without falling prey to the follies of either. This genuinely may be one of the very best games I've ever played.

I really gave this game a try.  Not knowing all of the hype, but knowing at least that it was a bit of a disappointment to some on release, I tried to at least remain unbiased.
The game was fun at first.  Figuring out how things worked was a bit of a pain as there is no real formal tutorial as such.  But soon I was jumping around the planet collecting resources and avoiding sentinels and some of the hostile indigenous wildlife.  Soon after that, I was warping to other planets and doing the same on those.
And that's when I started noticing that it didn't matter what planet you went to, what conditions it had on its surface, whether it be unbearably hot, or had toxic rain, or if it was bombarded by lethal radiation, everything looked the same.  All of the resources like plutonium looked the same even in different solar systems, as did all of the other common resources.  Zinc was present in the exact same yellow plant on the first planet as it was on the next planet, or even a planet a few warps away.
That's also when I started noticing that every planet had life.  For a game that touts it can generate up to a kajillion bazillion different planets, presumably for realism purposes, there are too many planets that are just teeming with life.  Where are the lifeless balls of gas or stone?  Where is the realism in every planet having life?  Where is the realism in every planet even being habitable?  Ya, I know this sounds like a nitpick, and maybe it isn't an issue to everyone, but I can honestly say that EVERY planet looking very similar to the other one makes me lose interest real fast.  How far does one have to go in the universe before something starts to look even a bit different?
And then there was the freezing.  No, I don't mean the temperatures of some of the planets.  Every time I got into a big battle, the game would freeze.  It started after I got into a battle with a number of sentinels on one planet.  (Not sure which one... I got into battle with sentinels on EVERY planet, because they're on ALL of them... another peeve against the game.)  I would have been happy playing for at least a few more hours on planets that started to look the same, but the freezing just got to me and I'm going to have to put this one aside for now hoping these issues get fixed in the coming weeks/months.
So, that's where my recommendation stands.  I think this game needs a modicum of polish yet and a bit more content to boot.  I'll give this another try a few months down the road and see if anything is different.  If it's not, well, then I should have learned to trust the reviews (when the majority are "Mostly Negative" and only the latest few are "Mixed") before purchasing.
EDIT  4/3/17:  Well, things are looking up.  I gave the game another try after seeing another couple patches had been issued since I originally made this review.  It seems that the freezing problems have been fixed and I can actually complete a battle without having to restart the game.  While this is definitely a step in the right direction, I'm not sure it's enough to make me reverse my recommendation just yet.
EDIT  4/8/27:  Hmmm... So I've been playing the game without incident lately and had a bit of fun at it.  If I had to change my recommendation now, it would be to a sideways thumb.  Things just got boring real fast.  I'm not sure what needs to be done... there is no direction.  It just seems a lot like "Fly around to different planets in different solar systems, collecting tech and mining stuff.  Get rich.  The end."  Tried the mining thing for hours on end.  Flew around to a few different planets, but found it easier to just stick to one really mineral rich planet.  Got rich... or at least got rich enough to upgrade my ship a couple times.  I already found out that if you mine a vein of something and leave the area for awhile, it respawns even in some limited amount.... so that just cheapened the experience of finding mineral veins on planets (unless it's a bug).  But unless there's a point to the game that I'm missing, there's only a few hours of actual fun here... then it turns into tedium and eventually boredom.  I actually fell asleep a few times in the middle of mining or wandering around the planet.  I know it sounds harsh, but I guess I can sum this whole thing up in one statement... This game seems very much unlike a game with a purpose and more like a demonstration of the procedural generation algorithms developed by Hello Games.

The core mechanics are very similar to those in Wolfenstein: A New Order, which is a good thing. The weapons are satisfying to use and seem well-balanced. The controls are good apart from the weapon wheel, which is awkward to operate with a mouse - the lead to me selecting the wrong weapon by accident and getting killed a few times.
The visuals of the game are impressive, but they are too repetetive within levels. On a few occasions, I got stuck for a couple of minutes because the little passage that I needed to go through to proceed (there's a lot of crawling in vents in this game) looked the same as the rest of the scenery so I didn't see it.
The enemies are fun to fight. They're fairly predicatble but not so much that you can outsmart them without trying. I wish there were more varieties - you fight the same few types of Nazi soldier again and again. If you keep moving, they are not very good at hitting you, but if they do then they can do a lot of damage very quickly, leading to some cheap deaths.
The story is OK, if a little inconsistent in tone. The main cast of characters is good, apart from B.J., which is a shame because he's the one you are playing as. He is essentially a two-dimensional action hero and feels out of place among the more complete characters. The voice acting and motion capture in cutscenes is impressive.
The game generally looks good, with excellent image quality, but poor use of colour and light in the indoor sections of the game leads to most of the scenery looking plain. There are a few areas in the game which look great, but most of it is fairly generic military-industrial interiors. The sound effects and music do the job but are nothing to write home about.
Performance is generally very good. I ran the game on the High preset at 1080p on my system (i5 4570, GTX 970, 16GB RAM, Win 10) and it was a smooth 60 FPS the vast majority of the time. The game hardlocked once, which is the only technical problem I had.

If you're like me and have grown far more fond of these indie games that don't last for more than 12 hours than any AAA game, then know that Epistory is one of these little gems that you will love.
The gameplay is one of these ideas that has been seen before, but that's perfectionned here to make a very enjoyable experience : typing to get through the puzzles and fights, and even through the menus and upgrade system if you wish. The graphics are original, and very nice to look at although they lose some of their original impact as the game goes on.
But what will make you look back and smile after you finish the game is the story. The narration is perfect, delivered through both the voice-over and the gameplay, as even the words you'll need to type to destroy enemies will send a different vibe depending on what point in the story you are at. The rhythm too is great, I found myself making and scrapping theories all along, wondering where this lovely game was leading me throughout the whole experience. Every "dungeon" is memorable on its own, and its particular aspects make sense in the story as much as in the gameplay.
In short : Epistory is worth buying at full price despite is short length if you have the money for it, as supporting this kind of innovative devs is something you should do ;) If you're a little bit tight on money, wait for it to go on sale and jump at it.

I bought this game because I’m learning BÉPO and I wanted something to practice with. I thoroughly enjoyed playing it through to the end. By far the best thing about this game is the art style and the pleasing paper effects when a new area unravels. It seems the game is somewhat inspired by Zelda-style games with a large map and several dungeons to explore. However I think this comparison sets you up for disappointment because it is lacking several elements which the real Zelda games do much better. The story begins by building up a lot of intrigue but in the end it doesn’t really seem to go anywhere and the random snippets of narration don’t really connect together. Like a Zelda game there are a few puzzle elements but in practice the puzzles are relatively easy and there are only a few different ideas which are repeated. In the dungeons you can find new magic powers and they have done a good job of making these interesting. All of them are useful in different circumstances. It would have been nice if they could have made more use of these powers in the puzzles or made the boss battles require the magic in interesting ways like when you gain a new item in Zelda. Sadly there aren’t really any bosses in Epistory and there are only a handful of different enemy types which are repeated over and over in different combinations.
I found the game relatively easy despite my typing speed still being a pitiful 20WPM. I wonder if this could be because the automatic difficulty adjustment recognised my terrible typing speed but didn’t manage to adjust as I improved. The first few nests were extremely difficult but for most of the later ones I was able to beat them on my first attempt.
Regardless of the criticism in my review I still highly recommend the game mostly because the innovative typing mechanic is such a joy to play. I hope one day they will be able to work on the idea and make an even cooler sequel.

Wow. Okay, I've played my fair range of typing games, ranging from the mundane to *this*. You may think, "how original can you get with a typing game? Is it worth buying this?" This is how original you can get with a typing game.
A story told not by a heavy-fisted hand but by respecting your intelligence and giving you the pieces to put the story together in your head, in a sense leaving the player to *write* the story themselves. A typing system lenient enough as to not frustratingly punish the player for the endless typos you will make in the intense battle sections, but hard enough to make this an extremely rewarding challenge that does actually make you markedly better at typing. A world so beautiful and varied that I even enjoyed the endless backtracking, I seemingly unturned new stones with every step I walked. A narrator you will never get tired of hearing the voice of, and neither the words. A pacing so well done that even through the many play sessions it took to get through the game, it still felt like a cohesive journey to the very end.
If you are decent at typing and have the money to spare, buy this game. I don't think you'll regret it.

Gauntlet is well...a pretty simple experience. The eponymous gauntlet is full of hordes of monsters and you have to destroy them, along with the summoning stones that spawn them, in order to reach the heart of the maze while collecting gold and eating/destroying food along the way. The complications arise around how to complete that straightforward task. The choice between warrior, valkyrie, elf, or wizard consists of more than a set of strengths and weaknesses; each represents a unique playstyle, from hack and slash to twin-stick shooter. It's that variety of tools, not the diversity of problems to solve, that lends the experience its interest. Joyful hours are spent not just killing the small number of unique enemies spread over a miniscule three environment types and learning the rudimentary story which is implied more than actually told, but in finding new and inventive ways to do so. The heart of Gauntlet has little to do with anything other than answering the very arcade-like question of how to reach the exit with your limited number of (skull) coins.

To be completely honest, this was probably the most dissapointing game ive ever bought. Is it bad? No, just not that much fun. I get that the appeal of the gauntlet series lies in its multi-player performance rather than going through the game solo. It is true that the game is a lot more enjoyable with a buddy, or two, or even three. Additionally, i like what they did with the personality of the main characters; in that they either follow tropes (Thor and Wizard) or break them entirely (like Thief and Valkyrie). They're easily the best interpretations of the original 4 classes in gauntlet because this aspect has rarely been focused on in previous entries.
As for the gameplay itself.... It's pretty repetitive. If you enjoy taking on hoardes of enemies using a small yet well animated number of combo's then you might enjoy this. However, what you may not enjoy is the length of the game. The main story line is short, As in there were three main bosses since last I played this. The first is a pretty well done first boss, the second is an intense boss fight, while the third is.... pretty dissapointing as the game was building up to something a lot more intense.
Now I'll give credit where its due, and that goes to the dev team. Like many early access games, Gauntlet's day one build was pretty messy, with the multiplayer being accessed via hub. Unlike most early access games, the Dev team has actually been responding to complaints, glitch reports, balancing etc; and has been suprisingly dedicated to this game despite that its already hit its sales peak. They're admirable for what they're doing so I greatly appreciate that aspect of the game.
In conclusion this was a dissapointing game upon release, but it also makes me optimistic that this same team could make a much better sequel.

As a progammer and a lover of puzzle games, I figured that I'd brave the mixed reviews since I fall within the target demographic. Despite that, this game was a disappointment. The puzzles are either uninspired or obscure, the game is liable to crash often, and the dialogue is grating.
Some of the early problems were promising, but simple. "Hacking" objects to modify high-level object properties made for some novel challenges, but there are few enough hackable objects and few enough properties within each that most of these puzzles reduced to "hack problem object, adjust obvious property."
At some point in the game we are given the ability to actually examine and edit objects' code. Unfortunately this also leads to either frustrating or overly simple puzzles. Many times in the game we simply enter an object's code and change it's "isHackable" property to true, then hack the object and change some obvious property. A fine puzzle to solve once, but to use it at several critical points seems repetitive.
I'm not familiar with Lua (the langauge the player manipulates in-game) and figured this game would at least give me a sense of the language. This was not the case. The structure of the in-game code was such that its purpose was often impossible to decipher - loops and conditions were presumably present but all code was displayed in a perfectly linear manner and I emerged even more confused about Lua than when I began.
Most of the late-game programming puzzles offer up the bit of code to be modified pretty easily. Upon entering an object's code you can visit various subclasses and functions, most of which are long and clearly critical to the game's normal function. The game does allow you to visit these blocks of code (though this sometimes crashes the game with longer sections) and does allow you to modify them, but their size and codepenence generally means that no meaningful changes can be made without "crashing the game" (errors created by the player result in the "end of the universe" and you must reload), and puzzles are rarely solved by doing so.
In contrast, other blocks of code have a very different style - short and with clearly labeled variables that pertain to the puzzle at hand. Identifying which blocks the game invites you to modify is pretty easy based only on this clear difference in style, and once you've found the critical function you can often change a simple boolean or integer without really understanding what you're doing, and solving the puzzle.
This is not to say the game is a breeze - many puzzles are not obvious. The challenge comes not from the innovation of the puzzles but by their obscurity. No direction is given to the player in several key sections, and it's often unclear whether you simply don't have the object required to get past a challenge, or if you haven't dig deep enough in the code.
The final puzzle was especially unrewarding. A deep delve into the final boss's code was fun, and I finally mananged to convice the boss to destroy itself. Success! ...or, nope, I'm just stuck in the boss screen with no boss. I reloaded and tried a different tactic, but this one defeated the boss as well as destroyed the universe. Suspecting a bug, I turned to a guide which presented a third, equally viable code tweak which was arbitrarily selected as the "correct" one by the designers and moved the plot forward.
I also was able to accidentally skip a final puzzle by reloading at a particular spot (which I only realized by reading a guide after completing the game), which makes me unsure if this happened at other points in the game.
A final note is the humor: The writers try painfully hard to make witty dialogue but it comes across as juvenile and bizzare. I'm a fan of good humor, high- or low-brow, but this game delivers neither.
I DID finish the game in the hopes that such a novel concept would yield at least a few inspired puzzles or challenges, and admittely a few did come close. Riding the line between puzzle game and programming chalenge, ultimately the game fails as either. To programmers and puzzlers, I advise you to seek fun elsewhere.

This is a good game.  You should play this game.  It has nice artwork, animation and wonderful music.  The game plays out like a children's bedtime story and comes to a satisfying conclusion.  The gameplay is fluid and responsive; you can use a mouse + keyboard combination, a controller, or just the keyboard.  While you can unlock a number of different abilities, there is an achievement for not using any ability points so it must be possible - albeit difficult - to beat the game without them.  Certain areas of the game are not terribly intuitive; a sudden change in pace or a spike in difficulty will catch many new players by surprise.  I would be very surprised if a new player did not die at least once.  Part of the challenge and fun of platformers is precision.  Not going to lie; certain parts of the game can be quite challenging and it may feel like you are being punished due to instant death but it also makes the game rewarding to beat.  Overall the scenes - especially those involving the antagonist - are creative and well-executed, giving an authentic feeling of being vulnerable.  Overall, beautiful, fun game.  Highly recommended.

This game is pretty great in all aspects. It's very pretty and has great atmosphere, and the parts that are trying to be cinematic do a great job of it. Controls are good in most circumstances, and you gain a wide variety of powerful-feeling abilities that leave you feeling versatile and give you many options in combat. The world does a great job of being interconnected, with new paths opening in old areas once you accomplish the major story objectives. And there's plenty of secrets to find. (Though a fast-travel would have been nice when tracking them down).
The biggest flaw I'd say is that the difficulty fluctuates too much. The game lets you heal and create checkpoints on command, which is great fun. But it leads to situations where a trap kills you in one hit (frequent) and you hadn't saved in a while because you were still at full health. More importantly, it renders most of the game a bit too easy, except for the race sequences. Those already would have been the hardest parts (equivalent to boss battles), but they're also the only spots in the game where you can't heal and make checkpoints, are quite long, and often feel like trial and error--a bad combination.
Other downsides: There's no bosses, just the aforementioned race sequences. And the story goes from good to amusingly cliche near the 2/3 mark.

Received this as a gift, and went in with little knowledge or expectation.  Having now played through it, I must say, it was a pleasant surprise out of nowhere.
While the principle is simple: It's a typing-based game, where you type words to attack enemies that move toward you.  It plays out quite nicely and adds an elemental dynamic that keeps you on your toes, essentially shifting modes to attack specific enemies, and with each element having bonus effects that can make attacking "Neutral" enemies easier or quicker.
That aside, the game is also very beautifully presented with a pleasing art style very similar to a pop-up picture book with a little bit of papercraft mixed in.  As you play, the map slowly unfolds (Quite literally!) from words on a page to reveal new areas and unique puzzles to solve as you work your way to uncovering the fox-riding protagonist's hidden story.
I'd say it's about 5-6 hours long if you don't go TOO crazy about collectable hunting. Maybe a bit more if you're a completionist. Consider nabbing it in a sale or if you want something to suit your fancy over a weekend binge.  You're unlikely to regret it, if you're OK with the style of gameplay.

The typing battles really got my heart pumping, helped by the great music score. I liked the different powers, and how you had to go through a new world to get it, and that the world had the same theme as the power you were picking up. As in ice world for the ice power etc. I also liked the detail that the words to type for each power were words assosiated with it. For instance all the words to type using the ice power were words such as: snow, winter, glacier, cold, shivering etc. And for fire it was: hot, fireplace, stove, sun, blazing etc.
Highly recommended if you like a beautiful game based on story, writing, and books.
And of course, you have to like to type! It felt so satisfying killing that big monster that had echocardiogram, photosensitivity, multimillionairs, and cinematograpy as the "killing words". Of course, at the same time all those little f*ckers came at me with their short words, ilk, axe, woe, ill, die, hat, mad, bow, tax, fee, foe, cat....... I'm just relieved that I didn't have to write this review on a timer!

Epistory is a typing game, entirely controlled with the keyboard and an interesting internal dictionary.
Unlike a game like typing of the dead, you fully control a character on a 2D plane, moving through a storybook land as it's built around you.  When you come across barriers you must type out a word highlighted in the world, which will cast a spell and destroy whatever is blocking your path.  The same principal applies with enemies.  This constitutes the central mechanic through which the game is played, and despite my initial difficulties in reconciling the 4 way directions with the 45 degree camera view (you'll see what I mean if you check out a video) it didn't take long to get to grips with.
The quirky mechanics aside, the main attraction of this game is the story.  The fantastical art direction and simple narration give the entire world an endearing momentum that swept me along during my playtime.
In this game the story is the thing, and that story is punctuated by an immaculate style that suits it to a tee.
