This is an all around excellent game that takes keyboarding as a gameplay mechanic and rolls with it gracefully.
The graphics have a delightful paper stylization that unfolds and forms as you explore the world.  Gameplay remains fresh by integrating a leveling up system, implementing 4 elemental powers and puzzles.  The player switches between powers by typing the relevant word: fire, ice, wind or spark.  Some enemies can only be harmed by certain elements and each elemental attach has it's own perks such as fire burning the next word in a que and spark bouncing to hurt multiple enemies when it attachs an enemy with multiple words in the que.  Total I went through the game fairly quickly coming in around 6 hours (not finding and doing everything but completing the main story).

I got this game out of a humble bundle, and was pretty interested in the concept, as I've always been a fan of writing and typing games.
The graphics and overall artstyle were beautiful and felt unique.
The overall gameplay got a bit tedious at times, and movement outside of combat felt a bit like a drawn-out fetch-quest.
That said, the combat was very enjoyable and continued to be interesting and engaging up until the end.
In regards to the ending and overarching plot, I'll be honest - I loathed it. The narration right from the start sounded very pretentious, and tried too hard to be profound. It worked somewhat as an auditory aid to the gameplay, but then towards the end the game suddenly tried to make out that the narration meant something.
While I'd been a bit dettered by the "plot", I still enjoyed the game up until the end. I'm sure different people will view it in different ways, but I was pretty infuriated by the incredibly cliché closing cinematic - so much so that I felt compelled to share my thoughts on it.
If you're considering buying this game based on the gameplay and elegance, then by all means it really delivers.
However, if you're looking primarily for a good story, then I'd suggest finding something else.

+ Beautiful, varied scenery
+ Great typing/combat mechanics
+ Simple albeit satisfying puzzles
+ Good light RPG elements (upgrades)
+ Serviceable music and voice acting
+ Support for many languages
- The game gets tediously repetitive a few hours in (explore, loot chests, combat wave of enemies, rinse, repeat multiple times until the end)
- Very short (although this could be viewed as a positive, considering the repetitiveness)
All in all, I get the impression that this was made with a pretty limited budget and the devs were able to successfully mask that fact in most aspects of the game. I bought it at a discount and I don't regret the purchase.

So I didn't want to write a review until I finished the game so I could give a fair perspective. Now that I'm finished I can say that this was a fantastic game!
The story is very good, although it somewhat lacks in context most of the time. This is definitely a trippy experience but very interesting to see what may go on in the mind of people with psychosis and creates a unique perspective. Not much narrative as there was only one real person in the game. You do get some back story but it leaves you with wanting to know more. If they had a bigger team I imagine they could have expanded on this into something truely visionary. As it stands it was still pretty good.
I was a little concerned when I saw previews of the game a few years back when it was first announced. The graphics seemed pretty bad however, I am pleased to say they must have done some upgrading since then as the graphics are currently top notch and very well done.
This game is greatly optimized. I am running an i7 3770K with a gtx 980ti and 16 GB of RAM on Windows 7. The game ran at max settings with a consistant 60fps, no stuttering, no glitches, no crashes. Considering that other huge AAA teams have been coming out with very unstable games lately, and the fact this one was made with only 13 people, show that there is no excuse to release a game in such a poor state. Other developers need to take note as this is how you release a game. To say that I finished a game on day one with no glitches or crashes of any kind with a solid frame rate is very rare these days. Proof that other developers are lazy, so definitely kudos to you Ninja Theory.
The gameplay was pretty fun. Some unique visual puzzles that got a bit repetitive after awhile but was still interesting nonetheless. Decent scenery and a few other unique things here and there that may surprise you. Now to talk about the one thing every one is complaining about...the combat. Ok honestly the combat isn't bad at all. Yes it's not Dark Souls, get over it. It was never supposed to be like Dark Souls. Personally I think that is a good thing. I don't understand this new fad where every video game now needs to be balls to the wall challenging. I personally hate those games. I like to relax and enjoy my video games, not get so frustrated and ticked off to the point of throwing my controller. Just don't see how that's fun. I will take easy, stylized, fun combat over super challenging combat any day, where all you do is dodge, one hit, dodge, one hit, dodge, one hit and repeat until dead. Just don't see how that entertains people. This game does a good job with the combat. It starts out easy but does get more difficult as the game goes on. I had the combat set to auto and it seemd to place me somewhere between normal and hard, however I had to turn it down to easy to beat a beast boss near the end, so there is some challenge to it. There is variety as well. There is light attack, heavy attack, and melee. There is also run, parry/block, and dodge and you can mix a combo of all these together to get a decent variety of different moves, you just need to experiment with it. You can even charge up your heavy attack by holding down the button. They don't explain a lot about the combat so you kinda have to figure it out but the variety is there. One last thing that a lot of people seem to be ticked off about and that is the permadeath system so if you want I can explain that which is this
Overall this is a great game. Considering the fact that this was a high quality, unique, fun experience delivered to you by only 13 people for only $30 is well worth the praise it gets. These guys must be supported. This may be the new thing that knocks the greed right out of these other developers. Some are $150 for the special editions for crap sakes. It is getting out of hand and this is a perfect example of getting back to video game's roots. Fun, unique, creative art for a good price. This is definitely worth your time.

Early, perhaps, but I like what Ninja Theory is doing enough to want to signal boost for it.
Despite the terrible advertising, what Hellblade actually is a Psychological Horror game melded with a simple but pointed sword fighter and coated with a helping of Norse Mythology (less high fantasy, more human sacrifice for flaming gods) and offered at a budget price to try and break free of the "$59.99 with Loot Boxes because you ♥♥♥♥ing cows will pay for it / Indie Pixel Art with Cheivos and Trading" mobius band that video games have been stuck in for the last half decade.
What's most striking about Hellblade is how different it feels. Few games would have a protagonist with an actual, documented psychological disorder (Senua is schizophrenic, and you feel it), fewer would have the balls to weave an FMV actor into story to act as greek chorus and lore advisor, and I can't think of any currently that opt to borrow horror devices from the Silent Hill series (the shadows on the ground twist into dark pulsing veins through rotting flesh, uncommented on and waiting for you, like the best monsters are) back when it was at it's prime, rather than the jumpscare knockoffs that have spawned from PT.
In a world where everything needs to be full retail price and still gets RMT shoved in to try and kick a few more dollars out of the consumer, Hellblade deserves a purchase if for no other reason than it shows Ninja Theory that this model can work. That we WILL buy quality games as a lowered price if they're made with artistic direction and interest, and the devs don't try to make every last possible dollar off of us. Vote with your wallets people.

Hello Games were put in a position where they were forced to push out their labor of love far before it was ready for public consumption, and as such received a lot of negativity upon launch. However, I believe that things will only get better. Hello Games has had numerous opportunities to vanish with the vast profit NMS brought them, but instead they are continuing to work on it, slowly and steadily crafting the experience we initially expected. Hello Games intends to make a good game, not money, and that is why I give NMS a thumbs up. In its current state, it may not be everything we hoped for, but I have faith that the No Man's Sky we all wanted will surface.

Summary: Hell of a game.  Great Story.  Great visuals.  Incredible immersion.  Play with a good headset.
This game definitely seems like one of those gaming experiences that will stick in your mind when you think back on your gaming history.
It's not overly long and that's not a bad thing, I beat it in about 6 and half hours, could be a bit longer to get all of the story collectables.  All in all it gets the story across without becoming stale, or adding unnecessary filler.
The graphics look great.  The voice acting, and facial recognition are top notch.  It all really kept me in the moment.
Combat is fine, not hard, not overly easy.  Enough variation to play with to keep things interesting for the duration.  Don't count on this being the selling point.
I think the point where this game shines, and the developers really tried their best, was to put you in a position where you can feel empathy for Senua.  The symptoms of psychosis really start to make you feel uncomfortable (in a good/interesting way?), especially if you play it completely through in one go.  Really made me come out the other side with a lingering sense of being on edge, almost expecting to hear the familiar voices calling out after taking the headset off.
The game takes more than a few liberties with your sanity.  One that particularly worried me was the stated "perma-death" system, which erases all of your progress if you die too many times and allow the "rot" to reach your head.  That was a stroke of genius on the part of the developer, because while it may alienate some players it really puts you in that desperate, paranoid mindset.  And for those that want to know if I failed too many times during my playthrough, the answer is yes... but, and only read if this would make or break the game for you...
So, if you like story and immersion, and can stand be a little frightened, uncomfortable, and paranoid, definitely try this one out!

Hack n slash is an interesting concept of a game: You need to hack it in order to win it. It excels in this in that, unlike some other "hacking" games, you're not simulating trying to get into some generic linux server, you're given a world and as you play you learn how it works. As you progress you are slowly given more and more control over it, until by the end where you are given access to the entire "library" of scripts, which in this case is an actual library.
As a meta-game it does very well. It acts as a fairly good RPG in its own right [i.e. it has good art, a fairly good story, good music], as well as being a hacking game. But it is worth mentioning that if you don't get programming, then you shouldn't even go near this. The hacking is simple to begin with [almost boring], but it starts become more involved as you get a few levels in. But when you get to seeing and editing actual code, unless you have a grasp of the underlying concepts, you won't be able to do much.
Definitely worth playing if you like to tinker with code.

NOTE: This review is for the Slayer Edition.
+++ Polished, consistent experience
+++ Great gameplay difference between the four characters
--- Uninspired art direction
--- Repetitive slog with little variance between the proposed challenges
--- Short and forgettable campaign, coupled with an overly drawn-out Endless Mode

Gauntlet attempts the impossible task of recapturing the allure of a long bygone era when coin-op arcades were king.  For the exercise, although it did produce a fairly solid foundation, fact remains that the project is doomed to failure: the classic Gauntlet game just cannot exist in today's world without profound changes.  In keeping its design philosophy close to the now thirty year-old original, Gauntlet by its own definition offers but little replay value.  A paper-thin story is laid on top of enough artifices to make it all seem like a modern game, but the facade quickly shatters away, and the game's true nature is revealed within minutes: room after room of same-y monsters and spawners, lost in a maze with little personality of its own.
Gauntlet feels a lot like a proof of concept, more than a genuine full-fledged game, and though Slayer Edition vastly improved on the first version, there is still a lot of work to be done for this to consider itself in any fashion a modern game adapted to today's world.  Right now, for the price, there are much more engrossing games in the same genre out there, with a lot more content and replay value.

You control a girl who rides a giant fox and has the power to fight off villainous baddies and reshape nature itself through words.  As you explore the mysterious world around you, you are both guided and followed by the melodious narration of your own story, which lures you ever deeper into the unknown.
Epistory's gameplay is wonderfully unique - you wander around on your giant fox, solving simple puzzles and magically eliminating any obstacles and enemies in your path by typing words that float above them.   You earn experience points by completing these typing challenges, and can earn many more points by rapidly completing multiple typing tasks in a combo.  Once you level up, you can develop various abilities that will help you better explore the world or chain longer word-combos.
The gameplay might end up feeling a bit repetitive (explore, solve simple puzzles, type floating words), but the added skill progression through leveling up, along with developing new magical spells as you continue through the game definitely helps alleviate that.  Meanwhile, the world itself is a joy to explore.  The colorful visuals are gorgeously lush, with a unique paper-art style that meshes perfectly with the story and gameplay.  The audio is also well done, with quality voice acting and pleasant background music that changes to fit your current situation.

Epistory is simply brilliant.  It is one of those games that does something so weird and new and does it so well that you'll remember it fondly years down the road.  Do yourself a favor, and give this remarkable game a try.

The gameplay itself is an interesting take on the dungeon crawler genre, but instead of swords or magic, you type words on your keyboard that correspond to a certain enemy. I was on the fence about purchasing this video game due to its $10 price tag for a short game, but I was lucky enough to grab this for $2 during the holiday sale and I have to say I am so glad I took the time to play this game.  You probably already know that this was made with RPG maker and that it is essentially a story-driven experience so there isn't much gameplay involved, however I would argue that it has just as much "gameplay" as (if not more than) some of the newer story indie games out now like "Everybody's Gone to the Rapture."  What makes this game so special are 2 things: heart, and charm.  The simple sprite-based graphics evoke a sense of nostalgia of playing great classic RPGs like FF6 (3 in the US) or chrono trigger, while the story makes you laugh, cry, wonder and care for all of the characters.  The writing is so clever that when things start to get a bit sappy, a character will throw in a joke and make you realize that this game is having fun with itself while telling a very serious story.  I will not give away too much of the plot but it reminds me a bit of Memento mixed with Inception.  The music is another area where this game shines.  Melancholy for the most part, but cheery at times and even a bit creepy which really helps set the mood.  There is this sense of wonderment you get from every line of dialogue and there are even sections that are eerie and creep you out.  I see a lot of negative reviews mostly because of the $10 price tag. While I can't say fairly whether or not this game is worth the price (I will reiterate that I was unsure myself and grabbed it while on sale) I do think it is funny what we choose to spend our money on.  At the time of this review, movie tickets are more than $13 for a 1.5-3 hour movie that you see once.  For the same price as 2 cups of coffee, you get about a 4 hour interactive experience that has more heart and mix of emotions than you will find in your average Hollywood Blockbuster.  If you are curious at all on this one, it is well worth it.

Epistory is a beautiful handcrafted game for which you explore an isometric landscape, exploring dungeons and of course type to destroy the infestation. How well does this work in motion? Surprisingly very well. The controls for moving your character may be a tad awkward initially -- it offers WASD but I found it to be inferior to using the game's recommended controls of ijfe which seem to be tighter. However once you get over that, you will find the game is very expertly crafted. Menu items, etc are all typable meaning that your hands will never need to leave your keyboard.
The game is challenging mostly in your speed of typing and lack of errors. If you make too many errors, your progress on a word will be reset. Towards the end of the game you are often sent a lot of enemies at once. There are powers which can help alleviate some stress however typing quickly and reading the screen quickly are very necessary.
The art style of the game is beautiful. Very reminiscent of orgami/paper mache. The animations are all very well done. Especially when revealing parts of the map.
Cons:
- Controls are initially awkward at first / WASD is less tight
- Map can be useless at times. I found it really hard to read in dungeons especially.
- Is a tad short (~4 hours for me to beat the story skipping two dungeon areas, with the rest of my hours doing achievements/completion)

Trine tells the tale of three heroes who's souls are tied together by the Trine and they must find a way to break apart. While the story is simple and shallow the game play is where it's at. You can play as a warrior knight who has a sword and shield and is your combat guy, the thief has a grappling hook for getting across long distances and a bow for long distance kills, and the wizard can create objects to climb on and levitate objects but it a no-go during combat.
The wizard is the most interesting character since he can create blocks to climb on and bridges to cross gaps. You can find things to add to your characters to give them new abililities as well as enhance them. The combat is pretty shallow as well with just a hack and slash everything that comes after you type play. It actually tends to get in the way of the tricky platforming and can get annoying after awhile. The game is based on physics so some physics puzzles are involved, but don't seem implimented very well.
The game looks great with a beautiful fantasy art style, good voice acting, and smooth controls. There are a few glitches in the game, but these are all wonky physics issues. The game is pretty much just get from left to right without dying, but you can respawn characters at checkpoints so dying seems kind of pointless since you aren't severly punished. In fact if you do die you can't use that character if the puzzle requires them so this just seems irritating. Over all the game is pretty good and worth a purchase thanks to its nice length, pleasing visuals, and good platforming segments.
~Score: 8/10

text: Have to say, after the two big content patches Hello have put out, this game is starting to turn around. I felt super burned by my purchase upon initial release. People do not seem to understand this, so I will clarify things.
Hello Games were put in a position where they were forced to push out their labor of love far before it was ready for public consumption, and as such received a lot of negativity upon launch. However, I believe that things will only get better. Hello Games has had numerous opportunities to vanish with the vast profit NMS brought them, but instead they are continuing to work on it, slowly and steadily crafting the experience we initially expected. Hello Games intends to make a good game, not money, and that is why I give NMS a thumbs up. In its current state, it may not be everything we hoped for, but I have faith that the No Man's Sky we all wanted will surface.

The new slayer edition of this game pretty much made things worse overall.
first off it reset my progress, doesnt matter so much if youre planning on buying but i was on the last level of the game...
The game still isnt very well optimized in fact i'd say it's worse, according to the system requirements i should be able to run this game on mid-high, unfortuntely i'm chugging 15 frames on the lowest settings possible.
I have an Intel i5 3rd generation proccessor, with 6gbs of ram, and a 2gb 740M  dedicated nvidia card.
The respawn system previously worked very nicely in co-op, skull coins (earmed by killing enemies) would grant you a 5 second respawn time, this is still the case. however if you didnt have skull coins you could respawn, you'd just have to wait for 20 seconds and hope your friends dont die. the new respawn system makes it so that after youre out of skull coins you cant respawn anymore. This could potentially mean that in some levels (where enemies are scarce) that you could die, and not respawn to help your team mate for almost the whole level.
The difficulty isnt all that difficult outside of the bosses either, the AI monsters will either swarm you or try to take you from range, with a more nimble class such as the elf or valkyrie dodging is easy unless swarmed, even at 15 FPS.
they did bring some improvements into the game, namely they changed the leveling system, equipment is unlocked through coins instead of beating a game on a certain difficulty, and the health difference between a low armor class (half of the classes) to a heavy armor class (the warrior) is more apparent, however it should be said that more health really doesnt make a difference since the warrior is melee only so he will be getting beat up quite a bit. They also added some more enemies (that teleport! or maybe they just introduced old enemies sooner) but again it's pretty much attack at range or a numbers sort of thing.
Overall, unless you have friends to play with and a mid-high range gaming pc this isnt worth your time. the game will take you at most 6-7 hours to beat, there's also a horde mode which is basically survive as long as possible, gets pretty boring after an hour or so since it's very repetitive.
While i welcome some changes made to the game in the new slayer edition, i can't recommend this game for it's overall horrible optimization and lack of interesting game play. it's fun with friends but it wont last you very long.

We were looking for a co-op game to play with out of town family, and when we found Gauntlet it was the perfect fit.  This was a casual game that we could play once a week for an evening, and something that even my (non-gamer) wife could, and did, enjoy with us. When we saw that the game had been given some love, we looked forward to a little polishing and even hoped for additional levels.  Unfortunately, what we got was some graphics polishing that added odd stutter and erratic movements to the display, deterioration of the camera control, and the removal of the RPG element of character advancement through the abilities improved through masteries.  Worse of all for our players was the elimination of “endless lives” when in a group (easy and normal difficulty prior to the patch), which had allowed the most casual to enjoy the game; those players are no longer interested in playing.  So, please bring this back in some form, maybe just to the easy difficulty level, or as an option in the game setup for the host (these scores do not need to be included in the leaderboards – some of us just want to allow more people to enjoy the game and not just try to game the high score).

Hack 'n' Slash is disappointing.
Great art, humor, and concept--just like any other Double Fine game, but the main "hacking" mechanic that is satisfying the first half of the game becomes an annoying impediment down the line. If you don't understand some computer programming, the game becomes awkwardly difficult very suddenly, and if you do, then hacking in the game becomes very frustrating because it disallows multiple and creative solutions to puzzles. On top of all of this, the game will force repetitive dialogue and gameplay if you make a small mistake and have to reset a puzzle. This is the first Double Fine game I don't like very much, but had a lot of hope for. It really just needed to be fleshed out or otherwise consider a steadier curve of gameplay.

This is an adventure/puzzle/programming game, NOT an action game of any sort. The puzzles revolve around you manipulating the programming of various objects and npcs. That sounds good, but what you can edit is very limited, at least in the beginning. Other reviews say it opens up a lot later, but is still more limited than you probably desire. Anyway, the game has a lot of quirks and frustrating design choices that typical adventure games have, and those turned me off completely. Examples include:
* Some objects or paths from one map to another are easy to miss. Not getting them means you eventually can't proceed but you won't know why because...
* No objective display to let you know or even hint at what you should be doing
* No map
* Solutions to puzzles are sometimes very obtuse
So as you might guess from the above, I got lost for over an hour, with no idea what to do next. I ended up turning to a guide, and quit soon after.
This is the kind of game where you need to be prepared to walk around every inch of the world looking for what changed since your last world-changing action. And you need to be ready to bash your head against the wall, trying everything you can think of, until you finally solve a puzzle. Lots of people find that fun. I don't. At all.

A unique concept which grows tiresome almost immediately. If you don't have an active interest in programming or a ton of patience for bad design, it's not worth getting.
As a game, Hack 'n' Slash is simply unfun for the average player looking to immerse themselves in a cohesive narrative. The characters have some potential, but the world feels incomplete and the main mechanic becomes a chore surprisingly quickly. Even something as simple as remembering properties assigned to objects would have helped ease some of the burden. Instead, the player is forced to reprogram each object (aka hit it with a sword to bring up a selection menu of user-alterable variables within a preset range) every time they come across it. In effect, you're basically reminding a block that it needs to move a tile over so you can pass. Dodging flying enemies was especially infuriating as they're pretty much guaranteed to strip you of at least a heart each time upon being encountered - even with pre-emptive maneuvers. Add to that, exploration is obtuse, with multiple paths but nowhere to go.
I'm likely not the target demographic here. I can imagine somebody out there will appreciate it as an example of game code being exposed in an interactive and novel way, but for the rest of us, it's just boring. I'd strongly discourage people from buying this game as anything but a curio.
Anyone looking for fun, interactive programming edutainment will have to keep looking.

I still remember meeting my first Deathclaw in Fallout 3 after having aimlessly wandered around after the tutorial with zero regard to the storyline and where I was supposed to go. I also remember overwriting my only saveslot after having pulled aggro (unknowingly). If also remember dying 30 times in a row in the attempt to finally manage to get away from the Deathclaw with four maimed limbs, 14 hitpoints and all my gear damaged massively. Oh the memories.
Fallout 3 was / is a milestone of the entire gaming history which didn't lose any of its charm and won't, for that matter, even 20 years laters and will forever be remembered along the likes of Morrowind and Skyrim, which are brilliant other Bethesda titles.

Tons of spoilers below, be warned.
Wolfenstein II presents our beloved BJ in a very strange and almost off series settings, the 60s, American, Nazis won WWII. Cool! We’re going to play a ton of awesomeness in varied settings around the globe. Nope, New York, nuked, looks like something from the Metro series, New Orleans, negative, feels like rehashed art from the last two games in the reboot with a ton of water. Texas was a breath of fresh desert air, however, still very lame IMO.
What happened to the use of the nazi dagger to take down sleeping Fritzs, the dog, etc. Now I'm carrying around 15 kilos of fire axes?!
The biggest killer for me is the over the top award for most arrogant black rights leader in any game, ever. Not all of us want to be associated with loud, in charge, get back at the man be it White, Nazi, Black, whatever. Coupled with bringing your pregnant girlfriend along on several deadly missions, Jesus, Wolfenstein II feels more like a linear COD clone than anything I’ve played in years.
Go back to your roots Machine Games and ID/Bethesda. Put BJ back in 1942, the OSS, not sure I’ll have a thumbs up for Wolfenstein III, 1981: The Nazi Coke Trade Epic, Featuring South America and Miami.

Pre-TL;DR: Epistory is such a rarity in that it handles a unique gameplay style so intuitively that in no moment does the game feel overly gimmicky. Responsive controls, cathartic gameplay, rewarding world, inventive powerups, and an interesting story. When Typing of the Dead is the main competition, I highly recommend you pick up Epistory.
PROS:
- Satisfying gameplay. I have gotten the most use out of my Corsair K70 keyboard playing this game than I have doing anything else on my PC. Even if you don't have a mechanical keyboard, killing waves of bugs with efficient typing attacks feels so amazing.
- Clever controls. The game recommends using E,F, J, and I to control your character through the overworld so you can seamlessly switch between moving and typing, which feels very natural. Also, fun little typing interactions like spamming R and U over and over again to simulate forcing a lock on a chest, and ASDF for turning a crank were some of my favorite moments of the game.
- Beautiful, diverse world full of secrets. The world is made of paper and origami, with the story literally being written on the stage. It's extremely rewarding to explore and unlock new areas to see everything the game has to offer. Great game for completionists (good luck with those "Diamond in the Rough" achievements though).
- Fun powerups. Throughout the game you gain 4 powerups that not only help you progress but aid with all types of battle. Often times you'll have to switch back and forth between powerups, so no power is ever made obsolete.
CONS:
- Can get repetitive during longer playtimes. The main objectives of this game are to 1.) Destroy waves of bugs and 2.) Solve puzzles to continue through the world. I only played this game for 1 to 2 hour sessions at a time, so I really didn't mind this and found every instance to be engaging. But if you like to binge your games, this might be a drawback.
- Kind of short. As of writing this I have 7 hours of gameplay, with about 1 hour being only the arena mode (which is so fun). Again, if you like to binge your games, you might beat this in one sitting. However, an indie game with 7 hours of gameplay is generally okay in my book regardless.
- Not terribly challenging. Maybe I'm just amazing at typing, but I didn't find the game to be all that challenging. I also wish the level cap was a bit higher. I was able to unlock all of the upgrades before the last dungeon.

Simple, elegant and more entertaining than you would come to expect from a typing/puzzle game.

Where to start with this game...
A lot of great AAA single player games these days are rare and few. Most of us want great gameplay and mechanics, voice acting, and a wonderful story to boot to keep us engaged.
This game however is special in a perculiar way.
No its not the best single player game that ever was and frankly the combat and puzzle solving (while some sections can be quite challenging at first before you figure out the mechanics pretty quickly) are rather basic and nothing to boast about. This game's core strength is in the character Senua and narrative of her journey through Hel (no not the christian hell the Norse one) on a quest to find her lost love's soul (you learn pretty quickly why she's there so not really a spoiler). The guardians or rather "demons" of Hel are the northmen (basically norse worshipers who pray to the gods associated with Hel and are bigger than you and wear masks b/c why not?) serve as the physical and combat experience of the game while the puzzles are environmental linve em up perspective pieces that can be challenging at times but the game trys its best to offer you vague clues when your close to the solution.
What draws you into the game is Senua, her coping with her "curse" in regards to reality (what we call psychosis today) and of course the lore of norse mythology told by a spectre. The narrative of this game IMO is really well done and one of the best of 2017 by far.
A lot of people are mixed on this game and for good reason. If you want to go through a rather intriguing, disturbing and engaging story without paying too much mind to game mechanics PICK THIS UP. It's worth it.
If you want a game that has more action, fantastic gameplay mechanics and progression go somewhere else. This game is not for you. This is for those looking for a good storybased game to play without having to worry too much if they are ready and prepped for the next boss encounter. This is journey you were meant to follow along with a tortured soul and help her get through her quest.
PC could use a bit more optimatization. I'm getting quite a few framedrops in certain sections of the game which kinda ruins the immersion for me but its not a complete turn off.

To those looking for an experience reminiscent of the old-school Gauntlet: Legends, reconsider your purchase. Legends is one of the first quarter-feed games I ever devoted myself to, so when I saw Gauntlet: Slayer Edition, I bought the game without hesitation. Not the best $20 I ever spent. Bearing in mind I wasn't expecting an exact replica of GL, other than the four base characters and the famous "don't shoot the food" rule (though it is incessently drilled into your head every time it happens), I did not find much connection to the classic.
The game mechanics are simple and easy, which makes for great playability, and the multiplayer factor is has not been lost in this edition; the more, the merrier. Single player is actually quite difficult on its hardest setting due to limited control input and the room to room top-down action (which reminded me more of SmashTV rather than Gauntlet) makes thinning the horde a bit more difficult without the ability to efficiently bottle-neck as you could in GL. Character upgrades are limited only to item purchases (NO LEVEL UP?? IS THIS GAUNTLET??) and is rather unexciting.
An okay dungeon crawler. Finding a better one to enjoy with friends is not difficult.
Devoted Gauntlet: Legends fans; walk away.

I'm pretty sure my dad gave me this game as a gift. On the one hand, I feel like I'm a bit too old for it, and on the other hand, there are certain parts that I think children and younger teens might not have the vocabulary and/or knowledge to solve. That said, it's a good game overall.
Pros:
+ It's fun seeing what sorts of things you can create and change.
+ Hours of gameplay, even after you save Maxwell's sister Lily. There are far more Starites you can earn in the game than are necessary to save her - lots more puzzles to solve - and, for a while at least, it can be fun to create and modify things just to see the weirdest things you can manage to make.
+ Gameplay is simple, and if you misspell things the game offers suggestions of words you might have meant instead.
+ Although many of the puzzles were very simple (I tried to make things harder for myself by thinking up more creative ways to solve them than by using words that seemed obvious), there were still quite a few that were very hard. It took me several tries to get through the prison break Starite puzzle, for example, even with the game's built-in hints.
Cons:
- Although Maxwell is supposed to be helping people, there are quite a few instances where his "help" is actually harmful.
- Speaking of Maxwell's help being harmful, I raised an eyebrow at the game developers setting things up so that there were some words you couldn't use and things you couldn't create, and yet still allowing players to kill things.
- Although there is no such thing as permanent death in this game, you
be killed. Considering how fluffy and cheerful the game looks, it was a bit of a shock the first time I accidentally got myself killed. (For those who are worried, it's not in the least bit graphic. You have several hearts representing how much "life" you have left, and when you get to zero you "die" and have to start the level over, although you don't have to re-earn all the Shards and Starites you already managed to get.)
- It got a bit boring after a while, so I had to go play other things and then get back to it later. That said, I'm an adult and this game feels, for the most part, like it's aimed at children.

The replay value of this game is much better than games like Portal simply because you can play through it again and again with the mindset of "let's see if I can solve this in some other way..." I think this sums it up nicely: Play time in Trine: 109 hours. Play time in Portal: 18 hours.

My experience with Hellblade has me a bit torn. On the one hand I like what they are trying to accomplish here, but on the other it just seems a bit outside of my gaming sweet spot for me to really enjoy. To be clear I picked up this game before knowing anything about it other then simply the devs that made Enslaved made this. This means I had zero notions on what the games was about.
I'll list what I liked and what I didn't like below:
Likes:
+ Graphics: This has to be one of the nicest looking games I have played. Really. Kudos to Team Ninja for making the game look absolutely stunning (whenever I was on a beach I was especially blown away).
+ Sound/Ambience: With headphones on, Hellblade sounds amazing. The dialougue and sounds are all top notch and really make the experience feel tense and unique (The Soot's victims screams were bone chilling).
+ Motion Capture: The actress who plays Senua did an amazing job in the motion capture department. Her movement feels good and looks even better.
+ Subject Matter: Addressing the subject matter they do in Hellblade is no small task. Good on Team Ninja for actually jumping into something most studios shy away from.
+ Stability: Game is stable and runs well.
+ Combat: Combat makes my likes and dislikes. I like how the combat feels, but think the shallowness of it kind of hurts the experience.
Dislike
- Levels + Game feel long: I don't know what it is, but everything about Hellblade just feels unneccesarily long. Each 'level' feels like it could have 10 minutes shaved off without anyone noticing.
- Combat: Combat is simplistic and plays like a watered down For Honor. The combat you get at the begining is the same  combat at the game's end. This makes fights feel like a chore as every encounter devolves into button mashing and dodging.
- Sword Sponge Enemies: I'm cool with having enemies with health, but some of the enemies you fight take minutes of wailing on to kill. This hurts the combat and adds to the chore like feeling.
- Story: While I respect the subject matter, I didn't really like how it was presented. It never really resonated with me (I respect your opinion if it did for you). The voices mechanic I found especially off as it becomes somewhat of a 'backseat' gaming like experience (may annoy some).
Overall Hellblade was a mixed bag for me. As I played I couldn't help but imagine the same game but with more RPG like trappings. With that being said, I think this is one game you should experience for yourself and make your own decision on. The storyline may deeply resonate with you in ways it doesn't for others. I also think the graphic/sound + ambience really make a strong case for picking this game up (just to experience expert level production).
6.5/10

This game mixes a rather unique thing (the typing) with a familiar thing. The result is interesting, though I'm not sure if there is any synergie between the two.
The main mechanic is the unique thing: you attack by typing words. Once you come near chests, objects or enemies, words appear above it. By correctly typing that word (and usually a couple following words) on your keyboard, you wipe it out. It's strange and at times pretty bizarre, but it works. I'm not sure how this mechanic works if you barely know how to type - there's a difficulty-adjusting mechanic, but I don't know how well-tailored it'll be for others - but it certainly hit a sweet difficulty spot on my end.
The familiar thing is the story and narration. You're a girl on a fox for some reason who is on a quest to...erm...to restore...erm...okay, it doesn't make much sense when I tell it, but it's captivating, well told and the papier mache aesthetics are absolutely gorgeous. The world is Zelda-ish with treasures, enemies and ways to expand things. The latter is usually by reaching a certain experience-index or a newly gained power found in a dungeon-of-sort. The narration is great as well.
So...these are two things I like. Do I like the combination? Erm...mostly. It's a fun (and even educational!) mechanic, but I honestly don't see it match with the storytelling part. Why do I open a gate by typing "AZER" four times? (for those wondering: it has support for other keyboard layouts). How does killing something by typing a word work? Why does that huge bug fly around with a "incendiary"-word above it? I won't lie: it's a gamy mechanic that distracts. On the other hand, it's important to stress that both parts in themselves are absolutely good enough - perhaps even better than they should be - to carry the game. As such, it deserves my thumbs up.

Writing this to try and combat some of the negative reviews.
Specs: i5 6600k OC  |  GTX 1080  |  16GB RAM  |  NVME Solid state
Negative Reviews:
Most of the negative reviews seem to come from bugs, performance and missing "features" such as the steam overlay. These definitely ARE problems, no doubt. But they dont warrant the binary "Not recommended" reviews. Not by a long shot, there is a gem of a game under those problems, one that will be remembered for a long time to come.
When I first installed and started trying to play the game, it would crash every 10 or so minutes. Frustrated I also wrote a short negative review stating the crashes as the reason. However, updating to latest Nvidia drivers and disabling "Async Computing" in the advance graphics menu completely sorted it for me.
As for bugs, I can't say I've encountered any. Certainly no game breaking bugs. One thing to note though is that I just cannot Alt-Tab out of the game, it will crash.
PC Performance/Graphics:
The first game wasnt perfect and needed third party tools to uncap the framerate to go over 60. This game however, wow. Machine Games knocked it completely out of the park. I never drop below 120FPS on ultra/"Uber" and the game looks F***ING GORGEOUS. It has this Fallout 4/dishonored vibe going on and I love it.
Gameplay:
Improved upon the first in every way, new guns, new abilities, movement has been really tightened up. Lots of difficulty settings with the higher ones being really punishing but fair.
Story:
Havent finished the game yet, but so far its better than the first, and the first was great.
Even though I havent beat it yet, this is looking like my game of the year so far unless it really takes a turn for the worse which I highly doubt.
Buy it, update your graphics drivers and turn off Async compute to fix the crashing. If you dont love it within 2 hours, refund it.. simples. HIGHLY HIGHLY RECOMMENDED

Good gravy, nearly an hour and a half in (as of 8/8) and I can tell I'm going to love the hell out of this game.
Hellbalde follows Senua, a Celtic hunter seeking to avenge the death of her lover at the hands of Vikings (Called "Northmen" in game), and hearing that you'd think, typical hack and slash, God of War Norse, right?
Nope. It's clear, from the second you start the game, whatever horrors Senua has experienced have caused her to have a psychotic break. Her lover's skull whispers to her, the voices (just at the edge of hearing) argue over urging her on or accepting defeat and taunting her impending doom - In fact, You (The player) are not-so-subtly implied to be one of those voices, further reinforced during a scene early in the game where Senua seems to address the camera directly.
Make no mistake, this is a story heavy game. Anyone coming in to expect an action heavy game is going to be *sorely* disappointed, Hellblade serves up combat as something akin to punctuation in telling it's story - a bit of a break to give a physical form to the things that torment Senua so.
In short, if you love story heavy games with gorgeous scenery and mind ♥♥♥♥-ery combined with light action elements, grab it. If you're looking for something with Action *and* story, I'd highly recommend Nier Automata. Either way, this game is in my books as a solid contender for Indie GOTY.

This game is well worth the price. It combines adventuring and puzzle-solving elements of modern Tomb Raider games, with combat that is reminicent of the Dark Souls series. It also accomplishes this without any kind of information stuck to your screen (no health bar, button prompts, etc), which greatly enhances the immersion.
I had my difficulty set to Auto, so I can't quite say how difficult the game would be for someone else, but it was certainly challenging for me. The game has a feature where if you die enough, you game just ends, making the situation feel dire towards the end,and always pushing you to do better. You can sprint, light attack, heavy attack, kick, dodge, and few more cool tricks later. These attacks will also combo together for things like stabs and shoulder charges, but without any kind of combo guide, it can be tricky to do the same thing again. I had been worried from the gameplay previews that it might be too "slashy" like Devil May Cry or Bayonetta (which I'm not fond of), but I was happy to see that enemies didn't require too much overkill to take care of, and that they even get scarred up as you slice them.
The world and atmosphere are beautifully crafted, and the features can change completely in seconds, due to her Senua's Psychosis. One moment you might be in a serene field, the next surrounded by hanging bodies, amidst a wildfire, or even in complete darkness. There is always a unique theme to the environment as well, so each place feels fresh and new. Senua's face, expressions, and acting are also incredibly complex and convincing. She displays a wide range of emotions throughout the game, and even had me starting to tear up in a couple scenes. There are also little tidbits of Norse mythology that you can find and listen to as you traverse the world. While I didn't find all of them, they were quite interesting to listen to, as well as nicely slowing the pace of the intense adventure.
The story itself is incredible. It's Senua's quest to the underworld, in order to save the soul of her lost boyfriend. I spent a good chunk of the game trying to figure out what she might be seeing without the psychosis, but by the end, you don't really care. And I think that's part of what the developers were trying to convey about psychosis: it's real for them, and that's what matters. The voices in her head even develop as characters, since you interact with them so much. Senua herself also has quite a few flashback moments, revealing a very deep backstory. These flashbacks show not only the events that led to where she is, but also her early life, and how her life was growing up in Celtec society with her mental illness. The detail is astonishing.
I feel like the representation of mental illness needs a mention on its own too. One might remember as a kid, running away from monsters, never being able to run fast enough. That sense of urgency is replicated perfectly in some of the chase scenes. Most also have spent some time fumbling around in complete darkness, trying to find a lightswitch. That's here too. These are maybe among the more relatable features seen, and while I can't comment on them from personal experience, the more advanced mental states are quite fascinating. These include seeing faces or objects hidden in the world, or the aforementioned parts where the entire scenery changes in an instant. Senua herself is constantly reacting to these things as well, be it a little comment to the voices, a shriek at a hanging body, or losing herself when the world explodes before her.
I did encounter a few bugs, but nothing gamebreaking. A couple were short lines of desynced audio, not too bad. The worst bug was when my sword didn't render for the final fight, so I had to reload the checkpoint. I wasn't too frustrated about it though.
I absolutely recommend this. Game of the Year material, for half the price. Well done, Ninja Theory.

The five characters (one character is in purchaseable DLC) have just enough different moves, which are fun in their executions to keep the game from feeling mundane.  Each character that you play with does make you feel like the hero!  You get the chance to demolish large hordes of monsters, which either clear the way or save your team mates from taking hits (or dying!).
The co-op is fantastic.  As is mostly the case, the more the merrier.  Currently finding online players is no problem, there seems to be a healthy playerbase at the moment.  Let's hope it holds for the future.
The graphics artists have done a good job on the in game graphics.  The characters on the select screen look a bit blocky, but doesn't effect anything important!
You can alter the abilities of your character by collecting gold in the game, speed ups, different special moves, magic, etc.
The devs implemented quite a big update recently which frustrated some of the community, this is the reason for such a large number of unwarranted negative reviews.  Sadly with patches that change many things in a game, some will see it as progress and some will feel alienated.  My advice if you like dungeon crawlers, don't be deterred by these opinions, you will be missing out!

Now that we have that out of the way, Skullgirls is a fantastic fighting game that plays similar to Marvel Vs Capcom that even has a similar jazzy soundtrack. It features solo to triple tag team gameplay through a randomly generated arcade mode, head-to-head online play, and a story mode. All characters have special moves, combos, and "Blockbusters" that can only be used if your super meter is charged enough. All characters are styled around one major style point that separates them from everyone else on the roster. Zero Labs Games' efforts to make sure this style is seen and felt in every attack is exceptionally well done. Some of these styled characters include a circus performer with a hat that grows giant arms, a girl with a demon for hair, a shape-shifting nun/horrible blob monstrosity, a cat-burglar that is loosely stitched together at the limbs after being hacked to pieces by the mob, a living cartoon character, and a big-time wrestler version of the epic poem character Beowulf. If hand drawn, triple tag team with a roster that insane sounds awesome then I would highly advise buying this.

Simply great fun! I have had so much fun in this game; generating worlds then exploring them. The game is a bit similar to Minecraft --- a world is generated then your character can visit that world, or generate another world to visit. As your character moves through the world their are lego items to discover, and NPCs walking around. There are also animals.
Unlike Minecraft however, the standard building blocks are avaliable to use pretty much anytime. Built whatever you want. The main points of this game are: exploring, finding new sets/items/characters and building. As you spend tim,e playing the game you find more items/characters/vehicles, etc.  This is very much an open world "game"; there is not a story, no quests, etc -- simply wonder about, do what you want and find stuff. The landscape can be edited (by adding or removing legos) as mostly everything is a lego piece.
Why is this fun?
Because its a lego open world!! Do what you want!
Want to destory everything and build your own world, piece by piece ? you can do that. Perhaps its best for me to share what I did in game.
I started the game, generated a world, chose a lego figure and arrived there. I walked around, saw some lego people and punched them. After taking away all their health, a few of them game me their clothes (i.e. lego body, hat, etc). I continued to wonder around and eventually discovered a sports car. The thing is fast and drives over just about anything.
I saved my progress.
The next time I started, I loaded the same world, explored a bit, and discovered a sheep. When your character gets near certain items (plants, vehicles, animals etc) your character discovers that item. The item can then be purchased later (with studs) although some items can be built for free after they are discovered.
After finding the sheep, I bought it. Anything bought then appears near your character. The sheep appeared near me and started running. I chased the sheep down and was able to ride it. I laughed out loud as I rode my superfast sheep over hills and all around the generated island!
From time to time you enmcounter animals and people who want something. For example, a horse I found generated a though bubble with a picture of an apple in it. The horse never let me ride it. A few weeks later, in a different world, I discoivered some horses near an apple tree. Punching things can destory them so I punched the tree. A few apples appears on the ground after the tree was destroyed. I gave an apple to a horse that wanted it, and now I can ride that horse! Any items you get in any world can be used in any other world --  just be sure to save your game after you get items.
Over time I found a front loader, airplane, helicopter, etc.  The front loader is a lot of fun because the front sholver can be lowered. Upon driving forward the front shovel cuts into the ground. Upon driving into a mountain, the shovel will cut a tunnel in the mountain ---  I spent lots of time driving aroung cutting out various tunnels.
This game is a lot of fun! Explore, build, use your imagination!!  A++

Still, having collected 60+ Starites in Scribblenauts Unlimited I have to say that that puzzle was far more entertaining and creative than any of the new puzzles I've encountered so far.
Part of the marvel of Scribblenauts is that you can use any of the fully programmed objects to accomplish your goal: create an axe to cut the tree down, ride a pegasus to the top or suck in into a black hole. 5th Cell seem to have either forgotten or ignored this crucial aspect. Whilst the creation features are a phenomenal improvement on the original, the freeform nature of the puzzles has been lost and replaced by a disappointingly formulaic template. A typical puzzle consists of walking up to an NPC, reading their problem and creating the type of object which they've hinted at (warm, weapon, ugly, etc). Each level will also have one or two longer form puzzles, which consist of 3-5 puzzles of the previous type.
This was quite upsetting to me. Common amongst almost all of these puzzles was that they were solved as soon as you spawn the item, with the NPC taking it from you and running off to engage in a prepared skit which half of the time wouldn't even use the object you choose. The developers went to all of the trouble of creating these gorgeous, fully working objects and you barely even get to use them - the game could easily be rewritten as a text adventure and none of the puzzles would suffer. I played through to the end in the hope that the puzzles would increase in difficulty, but I only managed to find one puzzle which tried to offer the same scope as the original (in the final space-themed zone, where you have to help an astronaut escape an alien base).
I can see the appeal of this as an edutainment game for young (5-8 years) children, as lots of puzzles require a knowledge of antonyms, as well as basic science and a working vocabulary. Disappointingly however, due to the breadth of items available the game is rated for ages 10+.
Very disappointing. The story and visuals are cute and cheery, but the puzzles are designed in a way which prevents you from really getting to play with the toys they sold you.

TL;DR: Depth is an astonishing game. Imagine Evolve except with two of the monsters, five or six (I forgot) shark types, different skill sets for the sharks, and different weapons and equipment for the survivors. That's Depth.
While there are multiple gamemodes, I'm going to be focusing on 'Blood and gold,' my favorite gamemode.
The Divers:
In this gamemode four divers submerge themselves underwater in the search of treasure with their trusty companion S.T.E.V.E. Though at first you may think: "Kill a bunch of sharks? Seems easy!" You're in for a surprise. Both teams have extreme strengths and weaknesses. Humans have more numbers, but are weak. Depending on the class of shark you choose you might have less health but go faster, or you might have more health but go slower. By collecting gold scattered around the map you can toss it to S.T.E.V.E, but if a shark manages to thrash you, then you lose the bag you had when they attack you. You also earn gold from killing sharks. If you get enough gold the next time you die you'll be able to buy new weapons and equipment to fight off the sharks better. Equipment such as sentry turrets, scanners, mines, harpoon guns, tracking device upgrades to your guns and more. After S.T.E.V.E visits a few different locations collecting treasure they will lead you back to your diving cage and you win. The problem is you don't have an unlimited number of respawns. If you die too many times you can't respawn, and you're out of the match permanently. Though you can still spectate, you can't really do anything gameplay related.
The Sharks:
Playing as a shark can be pretty challenging at first, as you don't have many skills built up at all. Slowly though as you progress through the match you'll be able to unlock more and more abilites until you become so powerful that the enemy team might freak out when they sense you coming by. When you bite onto a player you'll have to thrash your mouse around quickly to lower their health. They can stab you while you're doing this and other players can attack you as well so be careful. Obviously your goal is to eat the survivors and make sure they don't secure the treasure and win the match. You only have one ally in this gamemode. Also the same rule applies to sharks: If you lose too many lives you can't respawn for the rest of the match. Personally my favorite shark to play as is the Hammerhead shark.
Overall: It's probably not a game for everybody, especially not a game for people who don't like competition games. But if that is your cup of tea then I highly recommend this game. It's one of my favorite games on Steam actually. It feels fun to play as both divers and sharks.
(Also did I mention the sharks can break bits of the diver cage as well?)
10/10 would cry like a baby in the corner waiting for S.T.E.V.E to get the loot again.

Good gravy, nearly an hour and a half in (as of 8/8) and I can tell I'm going to love the hell out of this game.
Hellbalde follows Senua, a Celtic hunter seeking to avenge the death of her lover at the hands of Vikings (Called "Northmen" in game), and hearing that you'd think, typical hack and slash, God of War Norse, right?
Nope. It's clear, from the second you start the game, whatever horrors Senua has experienced have caused her to have a psychotic break. Her lover's skull whispers to her, the voices (just at the edge of hearing) argue over urging her on or accepting defeat and taunting her impending doom - In fact, You (The player) are not-so-subtly implied to be one of those voices, further reinforced during a scene early in the game where Senua seems to address the camera directly.
Make no mistake, this is a story heavy game. Anyone coming in to expect an action heavy game is going to be *sorely* disappointed, Hellblade serves up combat as something akin to punctuation in telling it's story - a bit of a break to give a physical form to the things that torment Senua so.
In short, if you love story heavy games with gorgeous scenery and mind ♥♥♥♥-ery combined with light action elements, grab it. If you're looking for something with Action *and* story, I'd highly recommend Nier Automata. Either way, this game is in my books as a solid contender for Indie GOTY.

This game is well worth the price. It combines adventuring and puzzle-solving elements of modern Tomb Raider games, with combat that is reminicent of the Dark Souls series. It also accomplishes this without any kind of information stuck to your screen (no health bar, button prompts, etc), which greatly enhances the immersion.
I had my difficulty set to Auto, so I can't quite say how difficult the game would be for someone else, but it was certainly challenging for me. The game has a feature where if you die enough, you game just ends, making the situation feel dire towards the end,and always pushing you to do better. You can sprint, light attack, heavy attack, kick, dodge, and few more cool tricks later. These attacks will also combo together for things like stabs and shoulder charges, but without any kind of combo guide, it can be tricky to do the same thing again. I had been worried from the gameplay previews that it might be too "slashy" like Devil May Cry or Bayonetta (which I'm not fond of), but I was happy to see that enemies didn't require too much overkill to take care of, and that they even get scarred up as you slice them.
The world and atmosphere are beautifully crafted, and the features can change completely in seconds, due to her Senua's Psychosis. One moment you might be in a serene field, the next surrounded by hanging bodies, amidst a wildfire, or even in complete darkness. There is always a unique theme to the environment as well, so each place feels fresh and new. Senua's face, expressions, and acting are also incredibly complex and convincing. She displays a wide range of emotions throughout the game, and even had me starting to tear up in a couple scenes. There are also little tidbits of Norse mythology that you can find and listen to as you traverse the world. While I didn't find all of them, they were quite interesting to listen to, as well as nicely slowing the pace of the intense adventure.
The story itself is incredible. It's Senua's quest to the underworld, in order to save the soul of her lost boyfriend. I spent a good chunk of the game trying to figure out what she might be seeing without the psychosis, but by the end, you don't really care. And I think that's part of what the developers were trying to convey about psychosis: it's real for them, and that's what matters. The voices in her head even develop as characters, since you interact with them so much. Senua herself also has quite a few flashback moments, revealing a very deep backstory. These flashbacks show not only the events that led to where she is, but also her early life, and how her life was growing up in Celtec society with her mental illness. The detail is astonishing.
I feel like the representation of mental illness needs a mention on its own too. One might remember as a kid, running away from monsters, never being able to run fast enough. That sense of urgency is replicated perfectly in some of the chase scenes. Most also have spent some time fumbling around in complete darkness, trying to find a lightswitch. That's here too. These are maybe among the more relatable features seen, and while I can't comment on them from personal experience, the more advanced mental states are quite fascinating. These include seeing faces or objects hidden in the world, or the aforementioned parts where the entire scenery changes in an instant. Senua herself is constantly reacting to these things as well, be it a little comment to the voices, a shriek at a hanging body, or losing herself when the world explodes before her.
I did encounter a few bugs, but nothing gamebreaking. A couple were short lines of desynced audio, not too bad. The worst bug was when my sword didn't render for the final fight, so I had to reload the checkpoint. I wasn't too frustrated about it though.
I absolutely recommend this. Game of the Year material, for half the price. Well done, Ninja Theory.

Recommended for programmers/tinkerers. Others will probably be confused and disappointed. This review itself will likely not make that much sense to the latter group.
It's in the current Humble Bundle Weekly at the $1 tier (ends 2015-11-5). Worth it at that price for sure.
This is not a "programming" game (like TIS-100, SpaceChem, Human Resource Machine, etc). It is a "hacking" game.
It is definitely not a "Hack and Slash" game as it may seem to be at first glance. There is very little of anything resembling a normal game here, although it has a vaguely Zelda-esque facade.
As a minor connoisseur of sorts when it comes to programming/hacking games, I'm not aware of any other game that has done what HnS has (Edit: The more recently released Else Heart.Break() seems to do something similar, but I haven't played it yet).
The title is more of a proof of concept than a fully featured game. Not really a surprise at this point coming from Double Fine. But the proof of concept alone should be worth the price of admission and the time for those interested in this sort of thing.
Most of the game is written in Lua (a very common game scripting language). The game (gradually) exposes the ability to modify itself, but only to a limited extent. You start off being able to only modify some instance variables of certain entities (and later
). Eventually you gain the ability to examine the code of just about everything, but you can only modify constants (including the names of called functions in some cases). You can also swap a few operators.
Although that sounds like a lot of power, there is actually fairly little you can do that is interesting or useful. The majority of the "puzzles" reduce to finding the right variable or operator to alter in typically fairly mundane ways (e.g. flip a bool, comparison operator, make a number very large or very small). That's not all that surprising considering how difficult it is to accomplish something more meaningful from a gameplay perspective in this kind of system. But what
there is reasonably fun/amusing. And thankfully it doesn't grow old because the game is quite short.
Typically hackable entities can be "hacked" (have their state/instance vars altered) by attacking them with a weapon. Later in the game, you gain the ability to hack into a larger variety of entities by actually modifying the code (again, only specific parts of the code). This is done in an unusual, noteworthy fashion:
Instead of simply editing the code text/values directly, a visual/spatial representation of the code is created in which you can walk around and modify particular constants and operators.
Strangely, when the game shows you the Lua code, it doesn't actually show you the raw code. Instead, it displays it in a rather strange, awkward syntax that actually makes it more obfuscated than it is in the original Lua (for a typical programmer, at least). I guess it could be said that this better immerses already experienced programmers, forcing them to "learn" the system even if they already know Lua.
Near the end of the game, you also gain the ability to
. Again, despite how much power this seemingly conveys, the actual usefulness of this is quite limited. But it's a cool experiment.

I got it for $1 and it was definitely worth that. It's fairly short, but I'd recommend it for $5-10 depending on how interested you are. This game is almost entirely programming/logic puzzles, and if that's what you're after, you'll have fun with this.
Initially I was quite disappointed that the early puzzles were as simple as changing an enemy's damage to 0 or similar, but as the game progresses your toolkit expands quite drastically. It gets to the point where, for many puzzles, the "solution" you'll find is just to completely break it in a way that happens to work out for you.
For example, I had a room which spawned several quite annoying enemies, and shut the doors until they were destroyed. My "solution", rather than try to destroy the enemies, was to replace the part of the level script that closes the doors with another instance of the part that spawns the enemies, so there were now twice as many enemies, but I could just run past them and out the door. The later levels are really very fun, and you'll find yourself doing this sort of thing a lot. It's a pity there aren't more of them, but by the time I got to the final levels I was completely unsure whether I was "supposed" to be there or not, so I guess that would've only gotten worse.
Anyway, if these scenarios sound like fun, give this a shot. It could do to be longer, but I think the Workshop might add levels (I haven't checked). This game is great for programmers or anyone who thinks messing with how the game world works while you're playing sounds like it could be interesting.

Plays more like a series of logic puzzles than a RPG. The puzzles are solid but may require a few runs to a walkthrough. Manipulating the game "variables" such as enemy behaviour and game speed is the core mechanic rather than Zelda-esque action battles (on a side note: variables values CAN be negative, this is important in many places). The humour is good but often you may feel a bit "lost" as to where to go. It's worth while exploring all the corners, there are optional artifacts that makes the game much more pleasurable to play (e.g. time speed up/slow down). Where it does suffer is that the graphics aren't consistently good (feels like a flash game in places with pixel art thrown in) and the movement model can feel glitchy at times especially around edges of cliffs and lakes where you sometimes (but not always) "slide" in.
Similar meta-gaming asthetic to games like Unepic and Evoland and although it is less tedious than the former and lacks the graphical and tight gameplay of the latter. It's worth it on a good special, but wouldn't play it for more than a weekend or two.

I'd like to see them take another crack at this concept, with a few things in mind:
1) no filler!  this game is mostly filler.  if something's not great, leave it out!  good games can be short
2) never make the player repeat complex, tedious actions just to pass through an area they previously beat
2a) don't make the player spend time just walking unless the music and atmosphere are amazing (Zelda had this, you don't)
3) straightforward, responsive interface which keeps clumsy blunders rare even for people who've never played
4) separate action from puzzles -- don't open something clunkier than a text editor during combat
4a) in fact, nothing in a game should ever be clunkier than a text editor

Zelda teaches typing is the easiest way I can explain this one. If that sounds interesting and you can touch type, this is well worth a look even at full price. If you can't already touch type, it's not going to make any effort to teach you, and certain areas are almost definitely going to be impossbile unless you're *very* fast at hunting and pecking.
Gameplay consists of wondering around the world and typing words to kill or activate stuff. There are four main dungeons that add elemental powers to your typing and four sub-dungeons that offer more challenging and creative uses of the powers. Both dungeon types have fully optional image fragments to collect, which is usually fun enough to be worthwhile. There are also something like 24 Nests between the overworld and dungeons that offer a progressively more difficult rush of enemies coming from all directions. These are the hardest and most enjoyable parts of the game.
Even as someone who loves abstract stories, I found this one too abstract to be enjoyable. I think it got lost in a lot of its own metaphors and made a huge mistake in not revealing the frame until the end. It doesn't detract from the game, but I don't think it added anything.
The soundtrack is basic, but decent enough. Ambient noises are very well done. I had some seemingly arbitrary frame rate dips early on, but otherwise it performs and looks acceptable.
I've only got two real complaints: The electric chaining on the Spark power is unpredictable to the point of being useless, particularly if you want to get the no mistakes for X characters achievements. Second, the game does not check if one enemy's active word is a substring of another active word. This doesn't break the game, but it's very annoying when you start typing, for example, "barren" only for the game to instead attack the less dangerous enemy with "bar." I believe the intended behavior in this instance is to shoot the shorter enemy while maintaining your progress against the other, but I had numerous cases where only the shorter enemy got shot and I had to start typing the longer word from the beginning again.

I got this game through the Humble Monthly and, having never heard of it before and not having seen the trailer, I didn't know what to expect when I clicked the play button. What I got was better than I could have possibly hoped for. Skip to the bottom for a TL;DR. WARNING: Possible SPOILERS ahead.
Right off the bat, this game is incredibly atomspheric and lovely. The narration is great, the art style is absolutely fabulous, and having never played a typing game like this before, I thought the idea was really neat as well. The game has some really great sound effects when the world unfolds--it makes the sound of pages being flipped and turned and it's a really incredibly experience on its own. I need to play this game with headphones more bc it could seriously work as as really nice ASMR thing.
The gameplay itself is really interesting bc you can use EFJI to move or WASD or the arrow keys. (EFJI makes it easier to move around certain terrains, like ice, bc of the angle of the world compared to the camera, but WASD works just as well. Both control sets don't interfer and actually work really well together to get unique key bindings for eight different directions.) You type various words to unlock new pathways and the more things you unlock, the more points you get to unlock new areas and new upgrades for your fox friend. You get these cool elemental powers (so far I only have two, but the Steam achievements say that there's four of them) that serve different functions and have different effects on the enemies you fight--that you also defeat by typing out words or letters. Sometimes the words are three or four letters but I've also had the word "counteroffenses" and another really long word I can't remember.
The music in this game is really nice as well. It only play sometimes and in some cases, it works as a sort of plot point. Sometimes you'll come across these puzzle situations and it plays different/more music as you complete the puzzle. Sometimes there's no music at all and all you hear is the quiet thud of the fox's feet as it runs. It's really nice and the music totally adds to the charm--whether it's playing or not. The sound design is an absolute joy and helps add to the relaxing atmosphere--or adds to the tension when you're wiping out an enemy nest.
The story is really neat as well. It's a little cryptic, a whole lot emotional, and the way it's told is really neat. There's a narration and subtitles but done in a way that's really neat. You're free to explore on your own, wherever you wanna go, and the narrative follows. Early in the game you get to a fork in the path and it says something like "Is the story leading her?" and if you go on the side that the text isn't on, it says "Or is she leading it?" and I thought it was super cool. The subtitles show up on the ground that you walk on or as features of the world expansion mini cutscenes. It's really artistic and a lot of the words stay even after completing new areas. You can come back to see really important story pieces whenever you want.
The upgrades it gives you are neat too bc they make your elemental powers work better or make combos last longer and there's even upgrades to make you faster. There's also a power to lead you to the closest point of interest (usually a reveal spot or a new dungeon type area) and the ability to teleport to dungeons you've beaten. It's a subtle little thin it does but it's nice. The world is constantly getting bigger and bigger with the more muse points you get--points that you get for typing out the words in areas to bring back plants and cut logs and the points you get from killing enemies.
TL;DR: This is a cool, colorful, atmospheric game with cool mechanics and an emotional story that keeps getting better as I play it. There's exploration, a lovely narration, and a superb soundtrack. I highly recommend this game and if I hadn't gotten this game from Humble Monthly, I would have gladly paid $15 for it. If you're thinking about buying this game, then do it. It's definitely worth it.
