TL;DR: Ori and the Blind Forest is brillant and pretty much flawless. If you are after a platformer with metroidvania elements that is (in my opinion) the perfect length, scroll up and hit that Add to Cart button.
What I've Played: Begining to End, about 90% map completion. Took about 6 hours.
Graphics
You might have gone and looked at the screenshots and maybe thought 'oh, they're just picked the best spots to screenshot'. Put that fear to bed; Ori is gorgeous pretty much all the time, and even more so in motion at whatever framerate you feel like running it at. Dead set, this probably has the best animation I've seen in a platformer, or anything else for that matter. Shout outs to the animator(s); I really can't praise the work you've done hard enough.
Gameplay/Technical
A platformer needs to have simple, but fluid and tight contols to be successful, and Ori nails that. I felt that every death was definitely my fault, and not due to slight movement or any 'give' in how Ori moves around. It behaves very similarly to how Rayman Legends does. Also amazing is the lack of an fps lock - I mean it SHOULD be the norm now, but this shows off how it should be done.
I did mention this is a platformer/metroidvania game; while the platforming is certainly the main attraction, along with puzzle elements, you will be gaining new ablities throughout, and some backtracking will be involved to explore the new areas you can now visit, and to hunt out those juicy hidden secrets - however the backtracking is actually quite minimal, and at no point was I lost of where to go next.
Now, this is a 2.5D platformer, which traditionally have had issues distguishing the backgrond (the scenery) from the foreground (what you actually play on). Thankfully Ori pretty much avoids that issue entirely; the background is obviously set much further back the foreground. with only a few places where it may not be obvious what you can and cannot stand on.
Audio
Ori has hands down some of the best original game soundtrack to come out this year. Effects are well done, make sense,  and sell the experience. It is said the best music and audio effects are the ones that don't stand out and add to the experience - Ori does that very well.
Story
Honestly, I'm going to let the other reviews talk this point for me - the Opening is truly an amazing and emotional one - told in what I'd like to call an interactive way, where you never really put down the controller to read exposition and dialog, and to great effect.
Conculsion
If this genre in any way appeals to you, buy Ori and the Blind Forest. Heck, even if you've never played a platformer before, you owe it to yourself to at least try it.

While at first I thought to compare this game to classics like Carmaggedon and other race/kill/destro type games this was not the case at all.  This game requires a good bit of skill and finesse to accomplish the tasks required to complete the levels.
Pros: Very challenging with no abilities, interesting difficulty adjustments, and reasonable replayability
Cons: it's really, really easy to get stuck, no tutorial/learning mode to teach you what you're doing, and it has no learning curve that I could tell.
If I had to suggest anything it would perhaps be to have the difficulty range over the different Mall properties as they all feel about the same with limited 'progression'.  Also it would be nice to have a tutorial of some sort to hone driving skills more than for learning how to play.  It's not a complex game per se but it would be nice to be able to practice in a more open environment with fewer obstacles to get a better feel for it early on.  Also, vehicle upgrades and/or the ability to buy other vehicles would be awesome.  *hint* bigger tires so as not to high side on every pebble *hint*  One little nitpick I have is the view map does not seem to have the option to rotate to keep a camera view, I'd surely enjoy this over the manual camera controls.
In summary, I've enjoyed the game but I find I get stuck a bit more quickly than I think I should sometimes.  This game wears the banner of 'easy to learn, difficult to master' quite well.  I'd recommend it due to the low price and high entertainment value I've had with it but if it were much more expensive I'd have to perhaps reconsider.  I'd like to see some tweaks and improvements as time passes for sure.

Achievements: There's a lot to say about the achievements in Bloons TD 5... While they are all possible, they are terrible to earn.
Firstly, there are some achievements that require levels to be completed in multiplayer, essentially requiring you to have a loyal friend who owns this game.
The grindiness of the achievements is also horrible.  85 achievements(including the multiplayer ones) require levels to be beaten in easy, medium, and hard in order to earn each of the 3 medals.  Beating a level on hard does NOT earn the medals for easy and medium.  This means one has to(at the minimum) beat 85 maps three times equating to 17,000 waves! In a game with little to no map-to-map enemy variation and no fast forward greater than x2, this is a very tedious, time-consuming task.
There is an achievement called "Centurion" for completing 100 daily challenges.  Though (I think) 4 can be completed per day, this still means one must consistently play this game for 25 days! Not to mention some of the daily challenges are in the impoppable difficulty which I very often skipped because they were too hard to reliably win.  Also(since daily missions give you randomized towers to use) they may turn out impossible(or at least really, really difficult) because you cannot pop certain bloons.  This achievement will likely take a month or more to achieve.
+Addicting
+Easy to learn
+Great time killer
+Interesting towers
+Lots of maps
+Fun upgrade/unlock system
+Some nice game modes
-No enemy variation across maps
-Still manages to feel like a mobile port by having two separate currencies(cash/gold)
-Horrible achievements

Honestly, playing this game for so long to earn the achievements has really opened my eyes to its negative features.  When playing the normal game (not in a random mission or anything), each wave will be exactly the same.  While this may not be jarring to some not versed in tower defense games, this is actually a really horrible thing.  One does not have to switch up strategies because there is not enough variance in the enemy types.  You are not rushed with enough pink bloons to warrant a glue tower or enough camo to warrant a bunch of ninjas.  There's simply no reason to place down some of the available towers when you've figured out a winning strategy.  This makes the game pretty tedious.
Some might say a game like this is meant to be tedious and is not meant to be rushed for achievements or anything.  It's meant to be played a little bit at a time.  I suppose they would be right.  That's why this game works so well on a mobile platform.  On PC, there's an abundancy of other, better tower defense games to play.
While some of the game modes help to randomize the fun, I still can't bring myself to recommend it.  If you only want something to kill time and you don't care about achievements, give it a shot.

Whether or not this game will appeal to you can pretty much be answered by one simple question: "Could you ever see yourself playing a text based management sim?" If your answer is pretty much any variant of yes or maybe, you will probably enjoy this game. It isn't strictly text based, but it's close. If the answer is no, hell no, or "that's a thing?" then stay FAR, FAR away. This game is not for you.
Pros:
-Non-standard maze building...Having a stacked 3x3 grid pushes you to be a bit more creative with your space.
-On the fly difficulty adjustment. There are two aspects to the difficulty of the game, fame and threat (the latter isn't called such, but shush). Fame determines how frequently you get visitors to your dungeon (and is based on a combination of the MacGuffin you choose for your dungeon and how much satisfaction the npcs had before returning to whence they came (Assuming you let them go). The latter gradually accumulates (and cannot be modified by the player) Fame determines how frequently adventurers stop by on their way to your dungeon.Threat on the other hand is based off of who you mark as your final boss as well as accumulating based on your monsters levels; this generates the enemies' level.
Cons
-No snarky dialog. Every game about being evil needs snarky dialog.
-Cheap kills. There are equips that have a % chance to insta-kill whatever the hero is fighting per attack, often at a pretty good chance too. One (at least) of these equips doubles the attack speed of the hero. Said heroes will probably be attacking 5 or more times for every monster attack you can make. Hah, nothing gets past my super powerful, aaaaand it's dead. I lost a level 20 V-Golem this way (perhaps not a top tier monster, but close), at the time one of if not my most powerful monster. The only reason my dungeon survived the invasion of a swordmaster with said attack speed buffing insta-kill bot artifact is because he got himself stuck in a side hall that I'd created and slowly whittled himself to death on my traps (my zombies sure as hell couldn't do anything to him)
-Unless you know in advance what all of the equips do, there's really no way for you to know ahead of time that said hero will be one-shotting all your dudes, because it'll tell you the name of the equip, but not what it does. So you won't know that putting your L20 V-Golem a room ahead of his L8 self with half a dozen zombies in a floor that boosts earth creatures (such as a V-Golem) is a quick recipe to lose that V-Golem. I'm not bitter.
I enjoy the genre: if I were asked how much I would buy this game for, knowing what I know but not otherwise owning it, I'd probably pay 4-5 bucks for it. So, if you're interested, wishlist it and pick it up on sale.
And seriously Valve, can we get a better rating system already?

I really, really tried to like this game because I like Double Fine with their quirky ideas. Unfortunately, this game which has the very original idea of breaking the barrier between the developer and the player by letting the latter change actual variables in order to progress, has a few flaws that turn it into a boring, repetitive chore. Just imagine having to cross different screens or rooms in a Zelda-like world, trying to find some clue to let you progress and having to fight the same ennemies and move the same blocks every time you pass by. Now imagine having to do this by a rather cumbersome system of reprogramming those ennemies and blocks every single time. Imagine there is no reward for this: no gold, souls or XP. You just run around aimlessly, hoping to find some clue somewhere that will finally allow you to progress. Imagine finding artifacts with functions so puzzling that you can't shake off the feeling that they might allow you to progress somehow, somewhere, but you don't have any clue about how and where because the game loves to troll you with garbled messages or nonsensical gibberish. That's my experience in Hack 'n' Slash.
The game could have been something if the developers had shown a little more concern about the players: give him a clue now and then, leave cleared stages cleared. I hate it when I have to use Google to progress in a game. No game in the world should ever need you to use a walkthrough or a forum in order to progress. This game makes it essential.
Pros:
- Nice, retroish Zelda-like game world and graphics
- Open world
- Very original concept
Cons:
- Repetitive, repetitive, repetitive, repetitive, repetitive, ...
- Puzzles are often too abstract to figure out; no clues
- I heard you could make the game crash by fiddling with some variables
Tl;dr: This game has a very original concept. Get it if you're curious or if you're comfortable with the idea of playing a game that will make you feel completely lost in a world that makes you overcome the same obstacles over and over.

I want to like this game, so much.
It plays like this, though:
1)
2) Neat idea! A Zelda-like game where you actively manipulate the game's internal structure to progress! Cool! Fun art style, buildup to a story, alright!
3) Expands on 2. The puzzles ramp up, but in a mostly expected way. Wait, why did THAT crash everything? No worry. It still looks pretty fun.
4) Um, ok, this is a huge step up from the past. Like, a completely different type of hacking. I did enjoy this part, as a legit challenge, since I do like learning about coding/scripting and and it seems like this is building up to a few hours of neat, coding inspired gameplay. ... Story here is basically nonexistent, though.
5) ...What. Just, what. If you're going to throw THAT at me, why did you chose the very last couple of puzzles to do so?
Basically, this is a game with a massive difficulty cliff at the very end of it for those not initially familiar with scripting. It is a game that can probably be beaten in 3 hours or less if you are, and if you are, you're wondering why you have to go through the game's UI of chapter 5 to do what you already know you need to do. Really, who on earth is the intended audience for the last chapter?! I'm pretty sure almost everyone is either nowhere near experienced enough in scripting to even know what to do, at all, or is experienced enough, and the ending is more an exercise in coping with a weird UI instead of just doing what you have to do yourself.
And this is why I cannot recommend it. The first parts of the game as a great draw to people who like to think about changing variables, with an engaging gameplay style. The middle will do what's essentially a bait-and-switch from fun puzzle-action-adventure game to really tricky introduction to coding stuff. I had a hard time getting through Chapter 5 even WITH a walkthrough. I beat Chapter 4 without a guide or prior scripting experience in LUA.
That game really, REALLY feels like it ran out of budget in the end, and had to be really awkwardly compressed. The story's compression seems to second this.
I beat that which I could be reasonably expected to complete, given my past coding/scripting knowledge, in about 2 and a half hours, and the last chapter felt completely inaccessible to me. For a game that costs over $10, it gives either 3-6 hours of gameplay before you hit a wall (be it the later parts of Chapter 3, Chapter 4 or Chapter 5)l or 3 or so hours of gameplay which is really not challenging because you KNOW what you're doing. Which isn't worth it.
Maybe if you can get it on a pretty big discount, or in a bundle, it's worth experiencing. You're probably going to have fun for a little while, then wonder what the hell happened. I'd have loved a few hours of the first three or so chapters, instead of what I got.

Fantastic fun!  This game looks great, sounds great, tells an engaging story, and has a phenomenal typing mechanic.  

As you walk around, you interact with the environment and attack enemy insects by typing words.  You'll also learn special abilities that will imbue your words with special power.  Fire will burn the next word for multiple-word enemies or light torches and bushes on fire if used on the environment.  Ice will freeze an enemy in place or freeze water.  Spark will zap multiple enemies at once or activate electric devices.  Wind will push enemies back or activate wind turbines.  These abilities can greatly sway combat in your favor, allowing for interesting strategies to tackle the larger enemies or hordes of smaller insects.  I found spark to be the most effective as attacking several enemies simultaneously is a huge help when facing a large swarm of insects.  Later battles require you to use specific powers on specific enemies, so you'll need to constantly shift between your abilities while holding back the swarm of insects.

The map is broken up into several areas that you can unlock as you explore, as well as metroidvania aspects that reward you for revisiting areas you've explored previously.  There are also several simple puzzles to the game, so you're not merely walking around and just typing words.  The one thing I didn't like about the environment is it let's you access Chapters out of order.  This doesn't affect the game at all, but I'd rather unlock the story linearly.

The game features an adaptive difficulty, so you should enjoy it regardless of whether or not you're a dual finger-wielding keyboard♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥or a proficient typist.  I type at 90+ words per minute, and I felt challenged playing this game.  Part of the challenge here is that the words will overlap or blend into the environment, making it difficult to see what you're supposed to type.  Also, the Wind-specific font color is very similar to the generic font color, so it's often difficult to tell when an insect needs to be attacked with wind.  This leaves you typing a word repeatedly wondering why the insect won't die.

TLDR

Pros:
- Great storytelling
- Great voice acting
- Adaptive difficulty
- Beautiful environment and art style
- Interesting, fun, and challenging typing mechanic
- Great merging of words into the environment
- Supports large selection of keyboard layouts, including QWERTY, AZERTY,  and DVORAK

Cons:
- Words can be difficult to read during combat (stack on top of each other, blend in with background, move quickly, etc)
- Able to progress story non-linearly
- Difficult to tell which enemies must be attacked with Wind
- Inaccurate typing statistics
 -- words per minute is recorded anytime words are on the screen, regardless of whether or not you're typing them
 -- game records an error if you switch to a new word before finishing the first one (sometimes you need to do this to attack a fast-approaching enemy)
- Difficult to switch between abilities during heavy combat
- Uses several esoteric words for big enemies, making you have to try and read the word letter-by-letter to see what you're supposed to type (refer to Con #1 to see why this is bad)

Trine is a great game for fans of old school side scrolling adventure games.  There are also some minor puzzle elements thrown in, which goes nicely with that old school nostalgia.  Despites its links to the past, Trine is a new spin on old concepts.  Basically the game centers around the 3 characters who touch some magic item blah blah blah they all become one person, which means throughout the game you switch between the characters to get past different areas.  The wizard is essentially your puzzle solver, able to move objects and create boxes/planks out of mid air to access new areas.  The theif is the "get to places" character with a grappling hook and a bow, so she can swing around the map.  And of course the warrior dude is, well a warrior dude who just kills everything and has a shield which allows him to get past certain areas as well.  You gather items and experience to level up certain abilities throughout the game as well.  Overall, a satisfying game especially for the price

Looks wonderful and is a delight to play in short segments.  It's possible to play almost entirely with only one of the three characters, however, and would have suited more segments that focused more on using one of the particular characters to proceed.

Trine is ridiculously fun in both co-op and single-player.  There are multiple ways of solving the various puzzles, many of which are crude and feel like cheating, which only makes things even more fun.  Flinging skeletons around and strategically knocking down towers never gets old!

You're going to be a magical squirrel-thing jumping, climbing, and exploring an equally magical forest, and by god, you're going to like it.  Ori and the Blind Forest is one of my favorite games this year, and if you like sidescrolling platformers and/or metroidvanias even a little bit, you owe it to yourself to pick up this game.
Ori is actually one of the best metroidvanias I've played.  It's got great gamefeel, first foremost.  It's a ton of fun running, climbing, jumping, and blasting all over the place.  The game is highly focused on its platforming elements, which can be very difficult and are highly varied.  The combat is pretty basic and mostly involves buttonmashing.  The puzzles are simple but enjoyable seasoning for a delicious platformer stew.  The exploration is cool--lots of secrets to find, gorgeous environments, and the stuff you acquire is rewarding to pick up.  The save system works well by allowing you to save anywhere but forcing you to do some resource management and put some thought into when you do it.
The story seems like it's going to be amazing at the beginning, but suffers a bit from '09 Trek / Pixar's UP syndrome where it has a ton of feels to offer in the prologue but the emotions mostly fade to the background for the rest of the game.  It works, but at least for me, wasn't a driving reason to keep playing.
The art and music may be the strongest point of the whole game.  They're both gorgeous and inspired.
While Ori probably isn't an all-time classic that I'm going to come back to every couple years, it's a great game, and I got a lot of enjoyment out of it.

TLDR: One of the best TD games out there, with a crazy amount of replayability, but could use some balancing and reworking to remain fun.
What I think:
If you've played any of the Bloons games in flash or on mobile, then you know what to expect... This is like the super version of any of those. If you haven't, google it and try one. Bloons TD 5 contains a great variety of maps and towers, and some interesting challenges. If it's on sale, I highly recommend buying it, but at full price it feels steep compared to the mobile version.
Ultimately the game is a lot of fun. I find myself coming back to it like a crack addict for bursts of play. I do have some minor ♥♥♥♥♥ing to express, which I've seen mentioned by others. I feel I should state my opinions so that if you're considering buying this game for long-term play, you will know about the end-game.
There are two main issues with Bloons TD 5, which are the repetitiveness of the experience, and the ease of gaining god-like overpoweredness without consequence. In my opinion, the biggest offender is double money, which either shouldn't be a thing, or should be treated as a "cheat" and have achievements disabled while it's active. It's just way too overpowered. After I bought it with the in-game currency (which only takes a few hours of gameplay at first to earn), I eventually turned it off to make the game a fair challenge. I saw this game compared to the football manager games, but it really does not work all that well.  I also noticed a large number of reviews saying that there is just not enough content for the game.
There are some interesting concepts availible here, but there is also a lack of variety in the basic dungeon design and populating scheme.
The game is built around a 3 X 3 matrix for each floor, where each room automatically connects to any neighboring room.  The 'heroes' flow into the dungeon in semi-random directions working their way down to the bottom or until they take enough damage that they want to go back out and try to work their way back to escape.
There are 16 possible floors where each room starting at level 1 can have 2+(1 X floor level) at a max of 9 of zombie defenders as well as a single trap that also has a level based on floor level max 9.  So on level 3 you can have 5 zombies per room as well as a single L3 trap.  Additionally you can place hero items into rooms as well as a single monster defender.  You have to make certain that your monster defenders do not die otherwise you loose them permanately, this causes a bunch of active micro-management where I pull out the near death monster and replace it with a monster that is healthy.  The real goal here is to level up the monsters as high as possible and then mix the different monsters using a few different monster recipies.
All this actually sounds pretty decent except that your room monster is your main damage dealer and your zombies are expensive blockers to protect your monsters.  With the limited resource maximum a wave of powerful heroes can easily wipe out your resources while you are desperately trying to keep your high leveled, demon type units from getting wiped out.  Early on with low levels of fame it is fairly manageable, but when your fame rises your monsters that you have leveled up to preprare to make stronger evoved monsters that can actually tank late game heroes, this really is all about micromangement.  The lack of variety in the auto spawn meaning just weak zombies means that as you progress you are going to get overwhelmed.
My most recent game I kept pulling back deeper and eliminating all the zombies and monsters that cost a significant amount to respawn each time they are killed and I have 3 populated rooms at this time.  1 is an evolved golom, while the other two are dragons.  All three can tank and still do some damage to passing heroes.  And I kill enough of them to make more than the zombies and traps cost me as well as the resurection.  Anything else I put in just drains my resources for no real gain while being very hectic.

Casual "spreadsheet sim" with solid strategy. Good resource management mechanics in the beginning and some interesting variance in the monsters you can summon. There's also a Hard difficulty I haven't tried, and I'm interested in seeing how fun it can be.
I would enjoy greater complexity and customization within the dungeon. I only used ten of the sixteen available floors, and the sole reason I went down so far was because one monster type must be placed deep underground. Speaking of monsters, you'll have to keep track of which monster combinations make what; the game doesn't do that for you. It is a minor inconvenience, as there are only a handful of possibilities, but a tab showing you all your unlocked fusion recipes would be useful.
I recommend
with one caveat: This ain't an intricate game. You're not getting
levels of nuance here - you'd be lucky to get one-fifth. If you're a genre fan and/or like relaxing with text-based strategy, then go for it. Otherwise, don't bother.

Scribblenauts as a game and an IP did not start life on the PC platform. Nevertheless, no other input method serves it better than the mouse and keyboard, which I experienced as
was among the crop of titles bought on the cheap in my first summer sale, a gentle entry into the world of Steam games.
You’d be surprised at the depth and breadth the game has in conjuring up your words. Insert a noun, chain together as many adjectives humanly possible and, hey presto! You’ll be having oodles of fun concocting convoluted pieces to fit into the puzzles, which like any good puzzle affords the player some leeway in solving them, but don’t be surprised when your giant, speedy, levitating bathtub is not recognised as a wholly viable alternative to cars.
There might be some argument as to whether the game is totally educational. Its value as a serious language teaching tool is questionable (in my opinion not quite useable in that capacity) but considering it that way is losing sight of what the game really is: a fun, light-hearted entertainment experience that satisfyingly stirs your little grey cells just enough.
There’s a decent amount of length and challenge in the game if you take the time to complete side objectives and progress is easily saved, ideal for pick-up-and-play sessions with kids anytime. I’ve also never tried it, but apparently playing it in a group setting turns it into a hilarious word salad jumblefest . No idea about how the sequels play out, but Scribblenauts unlimited is a fun “snack” of a puzzle game.

To the Moon is the simplest, shortest, most emotional game that I've ever played. The only other game close to meeting that description is Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons, but that game requires more effort than To the Moon, and therefore does not get "simplest." Nothing else that I've played has really gotten near these attributes.
I went into this game expecting it to be highly overrated. My main reasoning for that is because I have played many RPG Maker games before, years and years back, and never found any to be really great. Therefore, I was extremely surprised to hear this RPG Maker game getting so much praise almost universally, for so long.
And surprise hit me again when I realized how much I agreed with everybody else. To the Moon has very great artistic style for something made in RPG Maker. The maps are simple but very well-made, with lots of thought in organization and layout. The characters actually have nice movements to fit their actions. The animations and designs work with the premise of the story - all are done well.
The story itself, so unexpectedly emotional. Learning about the old man in reverse time is, theoretically, a simple idea in such a sci-fi / futuristic type of story, but it was so efficiently planned. There are so much questions that pop up along the way, and as you slowly get your answers, they just make you feel more attached to the story, to the characters, despite only being invested in them for a few hours. Every little 16-bit person seems like they are real. They seem more natural than many people I've ever seen in such a simple video game.
The music and sound fit in so well with all of their scenes, and only serve to help the emotions you get as you play. It all made me smile, laugh, get angry, want to cry - you name it. The ending of the game and the song played there... I think many people have gone to listen to the soundtrack long after playing this game, and I understand why.
As I said, the game is the "simplest" - and really, it is a story. You have control of the characters; you explore to learn; you solve puzzles to continue. But the game does not require much effort to keep moving, and in many ways, it makes sense that this choice was made. The story would not be so touching if you had to spend a lot of time trying to get past difficult puzzles, as you would only get more angry at the game itself.
I definitely wish that I could experience this game again, without knowing anything about it. But of course that is not possible... unless Neil and Eva were to help me out.

DISCLAIMER: This game is still in Early Access. All thoughts and opinions therein are related to the game during its development state. Features/content are subject to change and not a final representation of the game.
Monster and Monocles(hence forth M&M) is a very ambitious game. Look at the laundry list of features; we have procedurally generated environments, a variety of weapons, enemies, abilities, unique random events, traps, and unlockable characters. Also included is something I personally haven't seen in this genre, full Steam workshop support. Allowing you to create unique assets for the game itself.
When you look at the genre of this type of game, its going up against giants such as Binding of Isaac, Nuclear Throne, and Enter the Gungeon. No small feat to be sure. If we were solely looking at this game right now from an art standpoint, M&M is on par with its brethren and surpasses them. The sprite design is extremely eye catching and the overall design is unique. The animations, explosions, and level designs are all well done. In this case it blends cheeky steampunk Victorian style with almost a Halloween aesthetic. It's weird, but I dig it. Now in other aspects, there is still some catching up to do.
From a gameplay standpoint, it leans more towards that arcade style of a thumbstick shooter. Especially when you start adding people into the mix, up to four players can play locally and online. The game worked better in my opinion with a controller but it doesn't have too many buttons, you can dash, shoot and switch weapons.(I am sure it works fine with a key/mouse) It definitely feels geared to a fast paced chaotic type of game. You can certainly take your sweet time with it and if you are playing alone, you are more then likely going to have to.
The starting gun for characters is the revolver and it kinda blows. Enemies attack in very large groups with all sorts of different attack methods, exploding, dashing, splitting into tiny enemies. Combat can become very hectic, especially if you don't know what you are expecting, leading to a quick death.
There are shops, secrets, and there are currently three areas/bosses in the game. The flow as of right now, is you progress through two levels with random objectives, collecting guns, power ups along the way and then fight the boss. Rinse and repeat.
One gripe I did have is that because the levels are procedural, that sometimes their design can be rather silly. Sometimes it is littered with junk everywhere and has confusing pathing. It's a minor gripe and something I imagine that can be fine tuned as development continues.
The level of work that has been put into the game is very promising and well done. A good example of this, is the weapons, where you might find the crumpet launcher and teapot machine gun. There are buffs that you can find and bring back to your base to upgrade and use in future playthroughs for your guns and other passive abilities. This gives the game somewhat of a progression, and I would like to see the same idea that maybe allows for some modifications. You have a huge base area that could be used for all sorts of stuff.
Speaking from a personal perspective, I have been keeping my eyes on M&M for quite a while. For the aforementioned reasons, I am excited to see what the game has to offer once it is done. One thing to keep in mind about this title though is that it is far from finished.
If you buy into the Early Access of the game, it is currently to support the developer and give feedback. Some of the features are in the game but need polish, with more features to come. The game itself is rather short on replay and variety, and just replaying combat can become repetitive.
Keep in mind this is in no way derisive, comparing a game in Early Access to completed titles is silly. The only reason I mention it is to keep you aware of what is currently in the game. Once this bun is done in the oven, I am sure it will be a classic game and people will be loving this title.
Keep Monster and Monocles on your radar. The game looks spectacular and the developer seems to be consistent with the updates. Let those developers do their amazing work and in the mean time you go prep the table for tea and crumpets.

I am deeply sorry for whoever bought this game for more than $15 just to finish it in less than 2 hours. Unless changes occur, I stand by the fact that this game was one of the worst purchases I have made on steam.

Monsters & Monocles is a top-down shooter from developer Retro Dreamer. In M&M you fight your way through hordes of evil monsters that have been unleashed upon the world by yourself or with friends in online or local co-op. M&M currently features three different zones to fight your way through.
One of my biggest issues with M&M is the fact that I’ve seen all the game has to offer in less than an hour and a half and as it stands it has zero replay value. I’ve been through the entirety of each zone and without any kinds of unlocks or achievements there’s no reason for me to go back. I get that it’s an Early Access game and there will be another three zones but in its current state there’s simply not enough content to warrant a $15 price tag.
The main defense I’ve seen of the game’s lack of content is its procedural level generation, i.e. the fact that level 1 & 3 are always different. Yes, the layout of the level is different each time. Yes, you sometimes have objectives other than simply reaching the stairs that lead down to the next level. However, ‘procedurally generated levels’, or in M&M’s case randomized presets, is not enough to give a game replay value. Take The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth for example, it has randomized levels but the randomized levels by themselves do not make it a highly replayable game, it’s all the different items, enemies, bosses etc. that make it highly replayable. These things are all missing in M&M so far and that, combined with only having three zones in the game currently, is why this game is not worth $15.
The three different zones each have their own monsters (around five or six unique to each zone with a couple of monsters which may be found in more than one zone) and each zone features its own boss as well. The zones are split into four different levels; the first & third level are filled with hordes of enemies, the second level is a shop and the fourth floor is the boss fight. I found it a tad pointless to have the shop as the second floor since you don’t usually get enough coins in the first floor to buy much. You can backtrack but the levels are quite long so it’s not really worth doing. It would be nice to see another shop before the boss fight. I found the levels to be too long for their own good and filled with far too many enemies. I felt as though fighting off enemies (the only thing you do in the game) quickly descended into tedium. This was probably made worse by the fact that I played single-player. I did, however, quite like the boss fights. The bosses provide a good level of challenge (though that’s mainly due to how much health they have) and they have different stages dependent on their health which helped make things a bit more interesting.
As I mentioned earlier, there aren’t a whole lot of weapons in the game. This is a problem. Each character (identical except in appearance, another thing I wasn’t a fan of) starts with a revolver and then throughout the levels there’s a chance that weapons will be dropped by enemies, you can also find weapons in chests and of course you can buy them from the store level. From what I’ve seen there are around ten weapons in the game, around five of which are likely to be dropped by enemies. The lack of weapon variety made the combat fairly repetitive for me. Also worth mentioning, you can only carry two guns at once. This restriction isn’t too awful but due to the cooldown/overheating mechanics I feel like at least three weapons would be nice.
So about that cooldown/overheating mechanic for guns, it’s not great. This isn’t a problem for basic weapons such as the revolver or hand cannon but ‘better’ weapons overheat as you use them and when they overheat they have to cooldown. I felt like some of the weapons weren’t balanced in this area, for example the burst rifle overheats quite quickly and doesn’t cooldown at all between bursts of fire. My main problem with this mechanic ties into an issue I have with the overall combat in the game (I’ll circle back to overheating stuff in a second). M&M loves to throw large groups of enemies at you. This is a problem whether you have good weapons or not because if you’re presented with what I would consider a large group of enemies (six or more enemies) you’re not going to be able to fight them off before they reach you. At that point you become a pinball, bouncing between them as you’re smacked around with huge amounts of knockback and contact damage. You may be wondering what this has to do with weapon cooldowns. Well you see, if you have (for argument’s sake) a heavy machinegun and the default revolver, you may decide to use the machine gun to try and thin out the enemies getting close to you. Sucks to be you because your gun will overheat before you can get rid of all the enemies and your revolver won’t clear them out fast enough. I’ve lost my entire health bar in one go several times simply because my decent gun overheats before I get swamped by enemies and the other weapon I’m carrying doesn’t pack enough of a punch or has a really low fire rate. It gets pretty annoying.
There are a couple of other things I’ll touch on: dodging, weapon levels & items. Dodging is fairly self-explanatory, you have a recharging bar that is used when dodging, it recharges in a few seconds and the dodge does not negate damage so don’t try and dodge through enemies/projectiles. Your weapon level increases as you kill enemies, the higher the level of your weapon the more damage it does. You lose your level very quickly once you stop firing at enemies. And lastly those items I mentioned. Just like weapons, these have a chance to drop when you kill an enemy or open a chest. Most of the items have a positive and negative effect, such as a Donation Box item that gives you more health drops but less coin drops. The items are cool but I do have one problem with them, there’s no way to know what they do before you pick them up and there’s no way of dropping them. A simple description next to the name would be a nice addition.
The last thing I’ll mention is that there’s currently no way to rebind controls and in-game control prompts are always for an Xbox controller which is annoying if you’re using M&KB. I wasn’t completely satisfied by the game’s default M&KB bindings so I hope to see key rebinding in the near future.
Between its lack of content and gameplay that leaves a lot to be desired, Monster and Monocles simply isn’t worth the $15 price tag right now. M&M is an Early Access game so hopefully things will get better soon, this review will be updated/re-written if/when that happens, until then I cannot recommend this game for full price or on sale.

It might be difficult for Monsters & Monocles to stand out from the crowd in a suddenly very busy top-down shooter market, but the game is definitely fun and should be worth the value when all the content is released.
I'm not a huge Steampunk fan but I am a fan of M&M's horror-movie rogue's gallery, which brings back memories of Zombies Ate My Neighbors (hey, devs, how about a mission objective to rescue hostages?). It is true that when you find the weapons you like, you will probably stick with them, but there are plenty of effective weapons in the game. I was a big fan of the heavy machine gun and slime cannon, but the crumpet cannon, spreadshot, and blunderbuss are also effective in various scenarios.
Right now the difficulty feels about right for the three-zone loop, although I wonder if it will need to be balance-checked when they eventually get to six zones (three lives is not a lot to last on a two hour run!). The relics are alright but the temporary items are a lot more fun and when you get a bunch of them in one life, you become an unstoppable nightmare.
I don't know where to fit this in the review but I also like the amount of destruction, all sorts of props can be destroyed from pots to tables and chairs to streetlights. I wish that shooting props would maintain your combo meter (it's a lot easier to get to MAX in the mansion than in the tomb or the city) but I still mindlessly empty every room with bullets regardless.
It's hard to screw up a top-down shooter and the important thing is that Monsters & Monocles doesn't. I'm not sure that it brings anything particularly new to the table, but it's a fun flavor and a good ride while it lasts. There's going to be a content update soon that adds a 4th zone, it took me about 2 hours and a couple of runs to achieve a "loop" of the first three zones, so I would expect that the finished game will take you maybe 5-6 hours to see everything and a 90 minute perfect run to achieve a loop.

If you're a fan of this genre, don't hesitate for as long as I did...just get it. You will not regret this purchase. To think, there's more coming, as this is an early access game. Great stuff and a really solid title.

In a nutshell, SF2 can be described as 'eh'. I played in closed beta a year or so back, maybe somewhere around 10 hours. I can't seem to link my account to Steam and it's forcing me to make a new character which I do not care to do, so I'm sure as hell not going to be using Steam to play it.
Special Force 2 is the EU name for Soldier Front 2, the sequel to a Korean FPS made back in 2005, surprisingly named Soldier Front. SF1 had graphics from 2002 and game mechanics from 1995. Seriously. Creating a movement engine that doesn't allow you to go faster running diagonally was one of the first things I learnt as a hobbyist developer (Don't let anyone tell you Pythagoras' theory and trigonometry isn't useful), yet Soldier Front 1 still has this 'feature' well into 2015. I believe SF1 is on Greenlight in some form, but enough about that.
The graphics are fine. Not spectacular, but not an eye-sore. The game tries very hard to be Call of Duty, and you can see it in the aesthetics of the HUD (In places they're not even trying to look different), and the gunplay (run and gun, ADS, all of that, you can't really complain about it, unless it's about how cookie-cutter it is).
Game modes are your standard affair. 'Single' is deathmatch. Team Deathmatch is, well, team deathmatch. 'Blasting' is your standard Counterstrike bomb defusal mode. In 'Seizure', one team has to capture an item and bring it back to base, the other defends it. Simple enough. I haven't seen the 'Party' mode before, noted as the 'Glass' gamemode ingame, but it just seems to be a♥♥♥♥♥♥around mode probably taken from CS custom map. The real sore thumb is the 'Hero' mode, an FPS MOBA on some 3-laned alien landscape where you try to advance your load of aliens to the enemy base. Use gold earned from killing blows to buy stats and new guns. Cliche FPS mechanics fitted with cookie-cutter MOBA mechanics. Whatever.
Soldier Front 1's store returns here in Special Force 2, where you have to repair guns after each use, stat-boosting armor and equipment are timed items, and the coolest stuff is behind luck-based capsules and other paywalls. Unlike the first game however, it seems (I may be wrong) paywall guns aren't utterly broken. The VIP guns are just gold/chrome reskins, perhaps with a sight or something. If you want to pay for that, enjoy,I guess.I haven't given it the greatest look, but without level up rewards and EXP/SP boosters, I think people would run at a loss trying to maintain all of their guns and other equipment. Admittedly I could make a better effort to save money, but already a few hours in they're not just throwing it out anymore.
Maybe I will play it on occassion. Even I like a bit of Call of Duty sometimes. And I guess if you want to play Call of Duty without purchasing the latest games over and over again, this would be it.

I'm on the fence about this game.
The idea and basic premise is that instead of playing a regular Zelda-like game (which it looks like) you accidentally break your sword, expose a USB port in it and learn to hack the game itself.
Which would be cool... if it wasn't so annoyingly done in terms of plot, pacing, and what you can do. Initially you uncover the usual stuff - like get one heart more health etc. This seems important until basically two or three scenes later you discover how to raise your hearts to basically any amount you want. Yes, this teaches the basics of the game but is pretty disappointing, having such nonsensical interim achievements.
So, most of the first half of the game you interact with the game world by changing values in enemies and objects. This is generally fun and makes for some awesome puzzles, some of them so obscure they are true headscratchers. You also get to look at the first game scripts, but you cannot manipulate them directly, only the world.
In this way you keep collecting items that help you alter the game world and overcome scene by scene. Initially it seems like it is an open game world where you run around and do stuff in your own order. The walking around takes too long and adds no fun to the game itself or makes it more immersive. In reality it obscures that you can access maybe half a dozen initial areas, only half of which you can solve. The game is pretty linear in what order you must tackle things, it only makes solving the puzzles harder by not letting you know what fits where and what needs to be done next. Often frustratingly so! I missed up on the first boss because I didn't know where it would show up.
In general, the puzzles are between clever and entertaining to downright obscure in the first half of the game. Progress is good and you feel like accomplishing something. Just don't expect much of a plot or ability to divert from the order in which puzzles must be solved. The puzzles often involve manipulating the environment in new ways, sometimes you even miss out on the fact that you can affect the environment - like your little friend. Kudos to everyone who can beat this part without any sneak peeking, some stuff was really obscure.
Just to make sure you know how the puzzles in this game are (mild spoiler follows):
In the second half of the game you get to manipulate "game code" directly. So, you get access to the little scripts that steer things - doors, triggers, ports, etc. These scripts are written in some colorful Lua it seems. Expect no tutorial. People not knowing how to program need not apply. Don't know what a "continue" statement does? Now you will be in trouble. There is no help, no real tutorial, nothing. You just get presented with code and that's it. You then cannot freely modify it but only parts of it through a fairly obscure "walk around in the code" mini game. Most of the time the structure of the code is or seems fixed and you can only change values or operators to affect things.
To make matters worse and challening, the code is hacked and cobbled together. The more you progress, the more obscure the code becomes, and I still haven't found out how certain things work - especially since there seems to be some colored diamonds acting as variables and you never get to see all the code, nor modify all of it. As I understand it so far, you don't get to manipulate input parameters to the scripts - or to see them - and this makes the hacking all the more - well, hacky.
I write code for a living and I find as I progress the game becomes more and more obscure. Lua is easy to pick up, but only the more logic-minded individuals with some previous programming knowledge will have a chance at succeeding. Plus, the code is deliberately obscure, so you will spend most of your time towards the end trying to outwit whoever wrote those scripts to solve puzzles. The game then becomes rather slow and tedious.
I would say this game has a good and novel premise. It does not execute it well, nor does it a good job with teaching how to play itself, how to code, or how to understand code. There are sudden jumps in how challenging stuff is. Even trying to get a minor chest that was empty early on to spawn an item requires going through dozens of lines of obscure code, apparently even mixed up even with how the animations work. I gave up on that one.
Most people who aren't into coding probably won't enjoy the game at all. Not everyone who does know how to write code might enjoy it either. The fun and charm of the characters from the beginning is practically absent in the second half where puzzles completely replace plot and all other elements of the game. Prepare to code yourself to victory. I didn't finish yet. Sooo tedious...

Okay, I'll start off by saying that Ninjakiwi is clearly greedy as hell, since the 20 or so towers they came up with is all they use in the same game in a different form, for instance, BTD5, BTD Battles, Earlier BTD Games are very similar as well, so in other words, the idea is not original.
The game was pretty fun for the first 60 hours, getting Extreme Track mastery was quite boring to grind for, however, after that is completed, there is much more repetitive grinding! Wooo!
Let me point out that I don't consider a game "beaten" until either all achievements or a strong majority of achievements are done.
So to "beat" this nightmarish game, you must do 100 daily challenges, do 250 random missions, most of which take place in the same 6 maps or so despite being over 50 throughout the game, and not only do you have to grind for the extreme track mastery, but you must also grind many, many co-op maps.
This is utterly ridiculous, taking a simple idea, adding more to it, making several games out of it, and making each game a huge, unnecessary grind is absolute-
Sorry got carried away.
Anyhow, this game is very boring, and I wish I never bought it in the first place to waste 100+ hours of my life. Unless you want to make my mistake, don't buy this game.

I'll start with the positive stuff:

The game is easy and fun to learn. It's great for kids and anyone wishing to kill some time while in school or at work. The artstyle is pretty, and watching the bloons get popped is really satisfying and addictive. Most Tower Defense games doesn't achieve this, and I guess that's why Bloons TD is so popular.

The bad stuff:

The towers and their upgrades are quite cool, but 80% of them are bad. The "best" strategy is spamming the same towers over and over again regardless of the map, and this is something you'll realize after just a few hours of playtime. And even worse, there is one tower that amplifies the power of all nearby towers, so placing all your firepower in one tiny area is always your best option, even though a tower would have better map synergy if placed elsewhere. This makes the game extremely repetitive, and sadly, most of this game is about grinding.

To unlock the hardest difficulty, you must win 17 of the 19 easiest maps on ALL other difficulties. Yes, you must also complete these beginner tracks on "easy" and "normal" even though you have already beaten them on "hard". This is the level of grinding you can expect if you decide to purchase this game.

And finally, you can get passive upgrades that just makes the game way too easy. You can easily boost the firepower of your towers by 20-40% by using tokens that you unlock by - yes, you guessed it - grinding for several hours. You can even unlock "cheats" such as double cash which breaks the game, and even while using said cheats you can complete tracks and earn medals as though you didn't use them. So the medal you get for winning a difficult map is pretty much irrelevant, because they can be earnen very easy by activaring various game-breaking bonuses. Comparing your progress with your friends' is therefore irrelevant.

Overall, the game is a satisfying-to-play time-killer. But the gameplay is repetitive and grindly, and would be much better as a Free-to-Play. I don't belive it's worth $10.

Skullgirls, let's talk about this game. Skullgirls is probably hands down my favorite fighting game. While more technical fighters certainly exist, this game nails exactly what it's going for. If you're looking for a fighting game that can ease you into the genre, I'd suggest this hands down, the tutorial teaches you everything basic you need to know from walking to more technical play, to a character by character breakdown! With a diverse cast of different afflicted women (and now a few men) with strange powers, there's certainly no lack of variety. The game has an amalgation of mechanics from several fighting games such as Marvel Vs. Capcom 2, Jojo's Bizarre Adventure: Heritage for the Future, Guilty Gear and so on, not to mention a range of subtle to not so subtle references to comics, anime and media in general. It's easy to spread the basics you learn here to other fighters and pick those up as well!

TL, DR: This is a mix of SimTower and Unholy Heights. Breeding, building and the slow accumulation of power and resources. If you enjoyed one or both of the above games, you should give this a try.
This game plays like SimTower, you gradually accumulate more resources and build to expand your domain. In exchange for a simpler building system, this game adds complexity in the form of monsters that you need to nurture and cross breed to evolve ever stronger monsters. The gameplay is surprisingly addictive; I'm writing this at 2am in the morning after a "short" session became 2 hours. Although there are no graphics, the user interface is functional and the status of your dungeon is clearly presented. I think this game is worth its asking price if you're looking for a game that has the intensity of an RTS, the atmosphere of Dungeon Keeper, and easily-understood game mechanics.

is a first-person open world post-apocalyptic RPG. After escaping from Vault 101, a subterranean nuclear fallout shelter you lived in all your life, you explore the post-nuclear war-torn wastelands of Washington DC while on the trace of your father's footsteps.
1st person perspective is a huge departure from the original
games that add to the immersiveness. The game offers a very large world to explore, filled with bandits, super mutants, ghouls and radioactive creatures. I love the bottle caps as currency, although you're likely to mostly barter for ammos and equipment in exchange for the incredible amount of scraps and junk you can scavenge. There's a nice amount of guns to get your hands on, drugs (or chems) to give you boosts, and an assortment of food and medicine to keep your health up, most of which is irradiated which forces you to carefully manage your radiation poisoning. Quests are plentiful, and everywhere you go you'll have people asking for help in these hard times. The RPG elements consists of your basic attributes and trained skills, while leveling up allows you to train those skills and assign perk points to an increasing list of perk options, so that you may make your character just the way you want it. The VATS system allows you do precision targeting in fights, with VATS points just limited enough to avoid over use.
The world design is not on par with modern post-apocalyptic setting: wastelands feel barren and empty, buildings look and feel repetitive, and the urban DC area is nothing but impassable walls of concrete rubble with only the occasional building you can actually get in. Graphics and character designs feel repetitive and didn't age well. Gameplay does include a third-person option, but it's basically the same as the first-person option except that you see your character's back. Getting started can discourage newcomers as the early game is much harder and players spend most of their time going back and forth carrying junk with their limited carrying capacity to barter for barely as much ammos as they spent getting their loot, assuming the few vendors even have any stock of ammos compatible with the guns you have.

. Otherwise, this game and its DLCs will give you dozens upon dozens of hours of gameplay, so of course I recommend it!

Cosmophony starts out as a rhythm game and ends as a hardcore memorization game. It also starts very simple and ends brutally difficult.
I wish there were more levels that you could play without having to memorize them (I wish there were more levels at all, there's only 5). The music is amazing and the mechanics can be fun, but by the final level you have a certain specific path that you can't deviate from at all, and it becomes entirely about remembering what comes next and what specific moves to make when that happens, with the music giving you cues. The previous level is similar, but with a little more room for variety, and the first three are more like other rhythm games. Those I played though on the first try for 1 & 2, and a restart or two on 3.
Overall I did have a good time with the game, and I'd recommend it to people who don't get frustrated easily, like D&B (or uptempo electronic music in general), and can handle a challenge. Just remember that it's going to be your memorization skills being challenged much more than your twitch gaming reflexes or sense of rhythm.

Honestly, the biggest gripe I have with this game is the marketing and expectations set by Hello Games as compared with reality. This game will be forever rememered in many gamer's minds as a lesson about the dangers of hype, pre-orders, and advertising in general.
I do not and probably will never regain trust for Hello Games, Hello Labs or even Sean Murray, as these entities have blantantly lied and falsified information about No Man's Sky to the point I would consider criminal.
This game would be considered fantastic, innovative and exciting had the game been sold as a $10-30 (even 30 is feeling very generous) early access title. The flora, fauna and planet random generation combined with the ability to catalog and "discover" these new forms brought a breath of fresh air into the "survival" genre. I felt like an early renaissance explorer going from planet to planet claiming these new forms with my name along with the name I chose to give it. I put a good amount of effort in the nomenclature of my new creatures, bringing in latin roots and clever puns, imagining someday someone coming to my planet and appreciating the effort I went into classifying the bizarre alien world. The smooth transitions from planet to space were amazing and was one of the trademark looks from the very first peaks at the game.
Once a few hours were put in and the novelty wore off, the true shaky framework of the game become readily apparent. Ignoring the graphical and performance problems that seem to pervade AAA games nontheless, the 'features' that Sean Murray had gamers ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ their pants in excitement for turned into mere tricks to give the illusion they existed. What do I mean? I will give some examples.
Lets take multiplayer for the easiest example. Hello Games was very clear that you could run into people while exploring, but it was 'very unlikely' due to the sheer vastness of the universe. Shortly after the game was released, there is a video of two streamers meeting at the exact spot, yet they could not see each other. Sean Murray and Hello Games change the goal post of what they mean as "multiplayer", but now its readily clear there is no ♥♥♥♥ing multiplayer.
Beyond that, the controls flying around the planet feel like they were coded in an hour tops. The algorithm for generation started to show as features became familar and repeated. The "end" of the game was
.( I put a spoiler there just in case, but just a hint it isn't that great). Fighting is elementary and the core game is just a big grindfest. I could go on, but there are many good videos out there that show all of the promises they made versus what it really is.
Oh, and that feature I loved where it recorded who found and named the flora/fauna/planets? Didn't even ♥♥♥♥ing save when I came back a few days later.

Recently No Man's Sky has become more complex, interesting, and overall more fun. Its good to see they still haven't given up on this.

Bought this primarily for my son but I have also found it quite addictive actually. It is one of those games where you have to get this to make that to make something else to get somewhere ie the same game as 'Pyjamarama' that I used to play on my Spectrum thirty years ago just with better graphics lol. So I am going to recommend this game with the caveat that its only suitable for one player profile or playing the same game together, if you have two people wanting to play differnet games on the same Steam computer they have to play differnet game styles - ie one plays normal and one plays surivival. I am sure it would have been very easy for the devs to make two save slots available for the normal game or as they should really have, made four slots available for any type of game.
Overall its a fun game and worth a try if its reduced in price but the repetition and limitations on profiles mean its not worth the full price at the moment.

Trine is a fairly short but beautiful game.  It isn't really challenging and the story lacks any big luster.  However, I think it's worth buying.  You get to control 3 heroes, each with unique abilities.  While linear, you have the option of getting to the end of each level with the help of each hero, in whatever way works for you.

Monsters and Monocles is a roguelite twin-stick shooter that can be played either solo or with up to four players in local or online co-op.
Your goal is to shoot and kill hordes of monsters, to make your way through the levels, and then kill the end boss in each zone. You’ll have to do this while dodging projectiles and kiting enemies to avoid dying. You have limited lives, and once you lose them, it’s game over and you have to restart.
It took me about 3.5 hours to successfully complete all 3 zones while solo without running out of lives. Once you finish all the levels, the enemies gain additional health and damage, and you can continue with your lives and items and play the levels again. I tried playing online co-op, but I had some issues connecting to a few lobbies, and didn’t bother to continue trying. I expect it would be even more enjoyable while playing as co-op, where you can revive your allies.
I’m looking forward to playing Monsters and Monocles again once all of the content is released. Even though the game is currently lacking on content, it’s still fun, and it’s not too difficult either. There are some pathing and balance issues that need to be addressed, but other that, I didn’t experience any bugs. Overall, I still prefer Enter the Gungeon, but I think Monsters and Monocles is off to a good start, and it’s worth keeping an eye on.

Retro Dreamer
Retro Dreamer
is a 4-player coop twin-stick shooter developed and published by Retro Dreamer.
The game doesn't have a story, but the basic premise is that a mad scientist has unwillingly unleashed a giant purple cloud that spawns monsters all over the world, and it's the job of four aristocrats (a man, a woman, a robot, and a dog) to save the world.
Even though the levels are randomly generated, each area looks great: the pixelated assets and enemies each fit perfectly in their area, be it a gothic town or the Egyptian desert. The animations are very smooth, and the performance surpasses 90FPS most of the time.
The game is a 4-player twin-stick shooter. Each level has a different objective: kill X amounts of enemies, find a key to open the exit door, find Y objects... They are pretty standard objectives, but the best thing of all is how consistently engaging the combat is, thanks to a huge variety of enemies and weapons. At the end of each area you also visit a small shop where you can buy health, weapons, or even perks that improve your character. And after having finished two levels, you have to fight a big bad boss that usually requires you to strafe and keep on shooting him.
The game is very, very hard. Your health goes down quickly, and after you have lost your two hearts you have to restart the game from scratch! The boss fights are really challenging, and playing with other players is paramount if you want to finish the game in a reasonable amount of time.
The soundtrack is great, fitting each area perfectly. The sound design is also pretty great, with monster sounds and gunshots that are never annoying.
Even though it is randomly generated, the game is so hard and frustrating that after you finally finish it you don't want to revisit it at all.
Overall, fans of twin-stick shooters are going to love this one, and I think it is one of the better entries of the genre for this year. It also reminded me of LucasArts' classic
, so if you like that you are going to love this.

G:'14 = Gauntlet 2014
G:SE = Slayer Edition
AH = Arrowhead
AH was undoubtedly thrilled to apply their mantra to their childhood franchise by quickening the series with a more tactical reboot. They indeed elaborated on the action, but did they make a winning formula and is this truly Gauntlet? I'll add that this Gauntlet is as much an arcade game as the first and the hack n' slash gameplay is the best you'll find in the genre.
If your perspective on nostalgia consists of 4 buddies coming together as Warrior, Valkyrie, Wizard, and Elf and challenging the Gauntlet, you're in for a real treat. AH's expansion to them is very worthy and each possesses nostalgic nods to their original concept. Merlin's spells are an absolute joy to wield, and though the others have less to work with, there is elegance in their designs. All are solid and all depend on player skill and improvisation. Suffice it to say, there are no predetermined roles in Gauntlet.
Thor became a confident, unyielding brute, and aside from one weapon set, has nothing but all-rounded, close-range attacks. This deceptively makes him appear straight-forward, however, he cannot be played casually. This is due, in part, to the clumsy demeanor of his attacks. Fortunately, he has the greatest vitality, possessing the highest health pool and the most invincibility states.
Thyra became a stoic, battle-hardened shieldmaiden of death. Like Thor, Thyra cannot be played casually, however, she possesses keener attacks—owed to her valkyrian discipline—that allow her to hastily fell the machinations of the Gauntlet. Her shield can ward any attack and it allows her to take defensive postures or guard allies. She, most of all, requires precision. Anything less will leave her open to counter-attack.
Merlin became a wise yet patronizing, mythical grandmaster of magic and is unabashedly the reason I bought Gauntlet, being fit with a miniaturized version of the wizardry from Magicka. He has nine spells in total. Together, they give him immense power through versatility. This factor easily and expressly makes Merlin the greatest of the four. Although he is undoubtedly the greatest, presence of mind is required to unleash his phenominal, pseudo-cosmic power.
Questor became an absurd yet graceful arcane bowman. He is straightforward, stylish, and by far the easiest class to play due to his ranged capabilities, subtle magic, and manueverability. Fans of fantasy archer archetypes will definitely appreciate what he brings to the table, and he plays how an elven, veritable, twin-stick archer should.
Forget everything you knew about G:'14 because the gameplay and monsters have been heavily revised. Most importantly, the heroes were expanded upon, particularly the melee classes.
Relics—magic items which cast an offensive, defensive, or supportive spell—are now tagged with a relevant cooldown and only one may be equipped. My favorite is the Tempest Locket. It unleashes a slow-paced tornado that breaks up even the most densely packed hordes. Talismans are the new equippables, taking the role of effectual potion magic. Tailored to each class, they allow for a totally awesome, welcome expansion to the heroes' personalities. What's more is each class has a small selection. For instance, Elf's Ultimate Arrow fires a powerful, pervading missile, the Enchanted Willow Branch summons three spirits which orbit him, and Dryad's Song plays a magic melody that placates enemies.
Unfortunately, these items are hit or miss. Inquire about them in the community and choose wisely.
Weapon sets now grant each class unique abilities, such as Merlin's Eldritch Sphere which replaces a school with extended lightning magic, or Elf's Shadowstrike which replaces Magic Bomb with Smoke Bomb—a wicked cloak power. Some aren't as obvious in their use, while some are in dire need of AH lovin' to make them more viable. Overall, this change is mind-blowing and I guarantee you'll find some combination of Talisman, Relic, and weapon that thrills you.
If you're familiar with the original games, you'll recognize at least a few of the throwbacks. G:SE's iteration of the monster roster has bestowed very welcome refinements, particularly to the tougher variety. You may find yourself under constant threat from Orc Berserkers once they lose their temper, being charged by a Skeleton Defender once you demolish their shield, or dodgeing projectile barrages from Grunt Shamans. There are also some new enemies, such as the enchanted skeleton archer, tougher spiders, and a Temple miniboss.
AH has lain a much tastier variety of monsters to slay, but quite a few of the enemies were gutted and a few of the revisions are simply unpalatable (see:
). Almost the entire roster lacks appropriate aggressiveness and movement speed on Hard difficulty. This is somewhat counter-acted by their excessive reach and a very frustrating oversight that allows for stupid fast melee attacks. Temple enemies are the prime abusers of this. Basically, when you're in Temple levels, all the game's 'fair play' is demized in the fire of a thousand exploding suns.
G:SE sports a tethered camera and UGH, is it hideous. One grievance is how adjustments throw off your aim, but that's just the beginning! Previously, it was full overhead. Now, it's half isometric, and you'll find yourself fighting it as fiercely as your enemies. The camera subjects players to all kinds of nonsense, including death, 'stucktitude', wobbling, and many more! This call to nostalgia enforces cooperative play, but the cost is incredibly steep.
The delightful hub from G:'14 was removed in favor of an artsy but practical map screen. I'm going to miss the ol' hub, but having control over the exact level you play is very convenient, and the unwanted interruption to the flow, known as 'run' levels, can be skipped (thank Gaia).
Campaign offers a good experience for newbies and as a side venture, however—by virtue of its difficulty alone—you'll find it unsatisfying if you're an expert. While many encounters (arenas included) were greatly improved, the rest lost some of the magic from G:'14, also, only one boss recieved an upgrade, with the others being castrated. Speaking of arenas, the Colosseum made a return and is on a rotating schedule. One Colosseum map is chosen at random, per day, with a random Summoning Stone affix. Defeating the challenge earns you that day's bonus.
The heart of G:SE. AH has smartly answered the thunderous cries for a worthy procedural mode! Not worthy of the classic games, mind you, because there is a distinct lack of elegant labyrinths in which to wander. Nonetheless, Endless is a welcome addition. Floors consist of the highly linear run levels from G:'14, reconstructed. Sadly, Endless is plagued by some major issues, the greatest of which is the curves that are thrown at you. Sometimes you'll mosey through a pointless, barren level, while other times you'll be treated to the Mini-Battle of Endor. Still, Endless provides a good experience despite its wild difficulty, limited variety, and hacked-together presentation.
The lack of retro, procedural labyrinths is highly disappointing, but this is definitely Gauntlet, and it boasts superb co-op and gameplay. While it has a semi-solid foundation, there is a mind-numbing amount of frustrating bugs and balance issues, and the game is still considerably content starved. It's a bummer G:SE couldn't be supported further.
Ultimately, the action is the juice. Don't bother with G:SE if you can't appreciate that. Otherwise, take up the Gauntlet and
!

Epistory is a typing action game. You control a young lady who rides a fox around the world. In order to progress, you must hit the space bar, then type words which pop up over various items of scenery – or various enemies.
At its heart, this is a very simple game – you spend most of your time either running around on your fox solving simple 2D overhead puzzles, or you are fighting enemies. Many enemies simply appear around levels, but there are 24 pitched battles throughout the game where you stand stationary while waves of enemies come at you. It is here that the game is at its most intense, and where strategy is most meaningful.
But even still, there isn’t much.
Over the course of the game, you unlock four special magical powers – a fire power (which burns away the next word over the head of a multi-hit enemy), an ice power (which freezes multi-hit enemies in place), a lightning power (which jumps from enemy to enemy if you hit an enemy with at least two words left, allowing you to greatly diminish what is coming at you), and a wind power (which allows you to blow back enemies, which is pretty much the weakest power in the game as the spark power is almost always more useful).
You also gain experience points which allow you to upgrade your powers. If you are reasonably decent at stringing together kills, you can probably cap out your experience before the last three dungeons, at which point it is largely pointless. This experience allows you to upgrade your powers, your fox’s speed, and give you some convenient abilities, such as the ability to see things on your overworld map, and the ability to teleport to the entrance of the dungeon of your choice.
There are various collectables in the game, hidden in treasure chests, and the game mixes up the combat a little bit by facing you off against some enemies who can only be harmed by a specific magical power (which you switch between by typing Fire, Ice, Spark, and Wind). The enemies themselves are pretty samey, with the main difference being number of hit points and the complexity of the words which pop up over their head. As you progress deeper into the game, you’ll face off with enemies which have extremely long words over their heads, and if you play the arena mode, you can even face off against enemies with words from medical dictionaries which are several dozen words long.
Sadly, while the base mechanic is kind of a cute idea, in the end the game never really does anything very impressive. The story is not very involving, and while the voice-over work is good, the lack of anything really interesting coming out of the story renders it somewhat moot – more like background noise than anything. The game is reasonably visually attractive as well, with everything having a construction paper, cut paper, or origami aesthetic, but in the end, all of that is window dressing for the core action – and the core action, while okay, simply isn’t anything special.
This game isn’t bad. It is just kind of mediocre, and I don’t think there’s much reason to go out of your way to play it.
