Disclaimer: This is a review of this game upon its release into early access.  The game may change as it is being developed.
Monsters and Monocles is a local and online multiplayer top-down shooter with a pixellated steampunk aesthetic.  You play as one of four characters as you gather new weapons and upgrades in six different worlds.  There is always a gamble when you purchase an Early Access title. You could be given a broken or flawed product that is barely playable with the promise of a better working game later. The developer could abandon the game later and leave you with a bad purchase. However, in this case you get a fully working game that seems well optimized, several characters and weapons to choose from, and six areas to explore. The gameplay, animations, and aesthetic so far have been solid and I have enjoyed my time with the game so far.
Even though the game plays very well and is very bright and colorful, it is not without it's problems. My first gripe is that the dodge mechanic is a bit jarring and not as fluid as the dodge roll animation in Enter the Gungeon (for example). Instead, your character jaggedly teleports in the direction you are moving.  My second reservation about this game is that you don't really feel like you are progressing. In similar games like Enter the Gungeon or Nuclear Throne you upgrade your characters and/or weapons and see an immediate change. These changes directly influence the way that you approach the game and the decisions that you make going forward.  the upgrade system in Monsters and Monocles consists of a choice of up to 3 stat upgrades from the main area and a few stat upgrade badges collected throughout the levels.  The different weapons you acquire have a bigger effect, but I find myself holding on to the same 3-4 different weapons and discarding anything new.
So far I have enjoyed playing Monsters and Monocles. I sincerely hope that the developer continues to work on the title and adds more areas, weapons, and better upgrades.  The current state of the game is definitely playable and fun, although it is not as well fleshed out as other twin-stick shooter games.  i will be keeping an eye on this title and look forward the the finished game.

Excellent Tower Defense Game. Beautiful artwork and controls are easy to drag and drop your favorite characters to choose the best strategy of the enemies: balloons. The replayability and maps are what keep me playing this game-you can never get bored. Easily worth the money, as I have Bloons TD5 also on my iPad. My only gripe is the functionality of co-op, but playing against a friend is fun just as much as solo play.

There are some things I like a lot about this game... but some aspects of it make me hate it far more. Because of these latter characteristics, I have decided I shall stop torturing myself with this game.
Basically, I like brinkmanship and getting perfect scores. Unfortunately, Bloons TD *really* punishes you for these.
First off, levels are very long - close to 100 waves at the higher difficulty settings, with each wave possibly lasting minutes.
Second: if you fail a level, you have to replay it from the beginning unless you're willing to shell out a goodly amount of hard-earned (in-game) cash; there is no cheaper rewind function.
Third: the waves progress in difficulty in very uneven fashion - not only is the difficulty increase not linear, some levels can only be cleared if your towers have specific properties.
Fourth: there is no indicator of what you will face in upcoming waves. Either you memorize the wave patterns or you build blindly and hope for the best.
Fifth: if you fail a level, you gain absolutely nothing.
Together, these facts mean that you can't easily experiment to find a near-perfect solution. If you do not relish having to continually replay the same tedious parts of the same tedious levels over and over, you have to go for stop-gap imperfect solutions (which may still result in you still losing the level several tens of waves later). And because you don't get a single coin or dollar or whatever from failed experiments, a perfectionist can spend hours testing a map and have nothing tangible to show for them.
A second thing I hate about this game is the pixel-hunting required for truly optimal tower placement. Again, perfectionists will end up tearing their hair out. Sure, you could just plop down towers unthinkingly. But if you're trying to maximally use the map space available to you, pixel-hunting is your only choice. I really much prefer systems in which you have clearly defined spaces to build on.
Finally, I really hate the music in this game. It's frankly annoying as hell. I very rarely play a game with the sound/music muted, but this is one of those.
Edit: why have I clocked 25 hours in this game if I hate it so much? Actually, most of those hours were logged after I had fallen asleep from boredom while playing. Not even kidding.

An emotional, personal experience from start to finish, especially to someone that has personal experience with voice-hearing.
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is a chilling, terrifying yet thrilling game that expresses almost a fantasy-like world held within the mind of a girl with severe psychotic illness, experiecings voice hearing, delusions and hallucinations, many scenes within this game are horrific, terrifying and disturbed; holding to the realism of the true horrors of real world psychosis.
The game is incredibly imersive and beautiful, featuring some of the best graphics and textures I have ever seen in a game, especially with the facial animations alone. What makes Hellblade stand out by far is it's sound design, HEADPHONES ARE A MUST, when it comes to this game, whispering voices float around your head, sounding both internal and external, comenting on Senua's actions, her objectivces and subconcious thoughts; as someone that has experienced psychosis personally and voice hearing, I can certainly say that the way in which it is portrayed is incredibly accurate and true to life.
The combat in the game is brutal and fluid, you can truly hear and turmoil and anger within Senua's voice and breath as she fights against her own mind. During combat the voices also become incredibly important, expressing when Senua is in danger or an enermy is coming up behind her. The entire narative of the game is told by several destinct character voices besides the 'furies' which are the multitude of female voices.
There are however a couple flaws that I've came across yet I'm sure one of them will be fixed.
Firstly the combat can become repetitive, however there is a few bosses that mix things up from time to time.
Secondly within my playthrough I cam across two instances where Senua became glitched outside a boss arena and stuck and another where she got stuck within some rocks; but I'm sure these will be patched eventually.
I personally want to say thank you to Ninja Theory for this game, it gives people suffering from psychotic mental illness like myself a voice and a way to give people an insight into our world, sheding some light on a subject held within controvercy and stigma.
I'd happily give this game a 9/10 and recomend it to anybody.

The game is mediocre at best.  I never played any of the previous Gauntlets so I never felt any nostalgia people wrote in their reviews.  I felt the game had a lot of potential but it fell flat.  The graphics were decent and made the game looked very interesting in the screenshots.  However, the game was extremely repetitive. I played D3 when it first launched and I thought it was fast.  Well, this game is even faster.  However, there is incentive to grind in D3 for better gear.  Here, you grind to level up your skill but really you just get a longer duration or deal more damage with your skill most of the time.
A lot of people said this is a coop game and I imagine this might be the reason.  I played single player and felt the game was really boring the whole time.  The only real replay incentive is if you want to beat at the highest level of difficulty (there are easy, normal, hard and unfair). Playing as one of the two man-eating sharks that stalk the four human divers in each match is definitely the star of the show. Navigating swiftly and silently in third-person perspective, I quickly developed a sense that these oceans were mine to lord over. The sluggish, clumsy humans huddled in groups as they inched their way from treasure stash to to treasure stash, knowing I was out there somewhere, but never sure from what direction I’d attack, or when. Regular sonar pulses showed me outlines of my prey, allowing me to keep tabs on them at great distances.
Match to match, both sharks and divers can unlock new weapons and upgrades. These must still be purchased within each match (with gold for divers, and kills for sharks), but it gives at least some sense of persistent progression. The extra hardware and predatory adaptations I earned opened up some interesting, new gameplay styles, but each match still ultimately felt like it came down to the same sets of tactics. Each shark and each diver filled, essentially, the same role. What it comes down to is one hell of a fun time with friends and other players.
You get out of this one what you put in. I highly suggest playing with a friend as the voice chat is half the fun. 7/10 would get my legs ripped off diving for buried treasure again!

Chime# is a musical puzzler borrowing its mechanics more from Tetris than Stepmania. Technicallly, Chime# is a marked improvement over its predecessor, fixing the issues of mouse input lag and stutter. Unfortunately, it trades them in for a new problems of its own, particulary in its muddy visual language. It's more difficult now to accurately place quads due to the move away from a 2D perspective, and inconsistent color schemes makes it more difficult to tell what's left to fill in.
The soundtrack works well and samples from talented musicians. Unforunately, the promise of a dynamic soundtrack affected by the quads feels significantly less fulfilled with some levels not giving you much of an impression that you're making an impact through anything other than level completion.
Perhaps the largest complaint of its predecessor was that the song selection was limited, and not only was there any support for user-generated content, but also no expansions. Unfortunately, that's still the case.
If you're looking for a relaxing music game to unwind after work, Chime# will scratch the itch even but falls flat as a true improvement to the original XBLA/Steam darling.

Do I select In to Opt In for the Opt Out or Out to reconfirm the Opt Out? Wahhh??? Language ambiguity. I’m not native English, but I’m pretty sure I’m not the only one left confused.
Overall not enjoyable. I could only take halve an hour of it. I might reconsider buying it after some major updates, but until then I unfortunately can’t recommend it.

Scribblenauts unlimited is a 2d puzzle-adventure game developed by 5th Cell Media (who are renowned for other titles such as lock's quest and the dran to life series). You play as Maxwell a young boy who needs rescue his sister, Lilly, from turning to stone. To do this you need to travel around the globe helping people to collect starites, through creating objects by typing words into your notebook.
Positives
- Colourful artstyle
- Nice calming soundtrack
- You can create almost anything through typing words in your notebook, hence promoting creativity when solving puzzles
- Workshop integration to download new characters
- Funny interactions with characters and objects
- Replayability
- Plenty of levels and puzzles to solve
Negatives
- May get repetitive solving similar puzzles over and over
- Limited vocabulary in the game means that you can't make certain objects.
- Will need walkthrough to collect all starites

To review Fallout 3 or New Vegas is a difficult challenge. Not because their content is too hard but their expectations of what players want to enjoy are different. While seemingly similar in their mechanics, both games diverge in what players expect to enjoy in a "Fallout" game.

I cannot say I regret my  30+ hours of F3 because it led me to appreciate NV. This game was my introduction to Fallout. However, I cannot say it's a good "role-playing" game for what it offers, and I'll hopefully explain why.
This preface information is to ask that you should take any review of F3 with information regarding the player's history of Fallout. More often fans of either game will fall back on arguments of Bethesda messing with the lore or how old fogies don't like innovation. If I reference NV it's because those similar mechanics were changed for the better, and reasons given as to why F3's mechanics are horrid.
I aim to explain why Fallout 3 is a bad "role-playing" game by the only objective aspects of a game: The Mechanics. You be the judge of whether the game is redeemable for what it does and does not offer.
Although I want to avoid the plot, I do want to bring up F3's means of storytelling and of motivation because it differs from NV.
F3's benefit/vice is its more personal approach of the Player and the father, James. The intro sequence, while repetitive for later playthroughs, goes to show how great F3 can be when it develops smaller, personal areas. You can read conversations about the Overseer's dictatorship's effects through a poem or medical notes, or you can overhear dialogue that explains things further. It also contextualizes S.P.E.C.I.A.L. and Perks in-game, and provides an easy means for players unfamiliar with FPS/RPG hybrids plenty of time to ease in.
That last statement is important because the hour-long intro does its job of hooking the player for the long run, especially in an open-world environment. Even if you don't like James, searching for someone familiar in a hostile wasteland is a good motivaton to explore.
Unfortunately, that attention to detail is not reflected for the rest of the game.  There are areas like the simulation of Vault 112 and a few notable set pieces and landmarks that are memorable, but the majority of places to explore are one-stop fairs for quests and loot. The world of Fallout 3 feels very dead, and not for the atmosphere.
If the game is played as a one-time commitment, then why do people replay the game? The simple answer is that hidden caches, the ability to go anywhere from the beginning of the game. and the level-design of D.C. are all more interesting than the Mojave.  Being set at the start in the center with no overall scalling of enemies allows the player the freedom to find caches and bonuses.

I wouldn't say the game is designed for speedrunning, but it's how the player feels like the roads they travel are their own that leaves these players satisfied of the memories they make. That is Fallout 3's strongest-suit.


On the flipside, F3's mechanics for role-playing are either shallow of your decisions or absolutely broken. The main problem is that for whatever character build you want to make your characters they will end all the same.
The first major offender are the S.PE.C.I.A.L. stats themselves. You are given far too many to be a jack-of-all-trades with no issues. And if you want more points as you play you can invest into them with a Level Up or by finding Bobbleheads,.
Worse, some stats are arguably superior to others. Investing into Intelligence is always superior because you will earn more skill-points with each level (15 - 20), which in turn can be used to level up your stats faster. And when you level up, you can also choose perks that mainly increase two stats by five points each, or you can choose perks that may offer something slightly interesting. By level 10, I had accumulated enough points to max out two or three stats to 100.

The problem with this system is that the game expects you to max out specific skills because some content can only be accessed by improving the stat. Because there are no skill magazines (like in New Vegas) or various tools to supplement skills like Lockpicking, Explosives or Science you will invest your skill points into all of them so you don't feel like you're gated out of content.
Unlike NV, however, leveling up takes more time to achieve but you'll make about as perfect of a character well before you reach max level. This issue mainly comes from F3's uninteresting perk-systems where as NV focused on character-building perks.
A few starter examples of  NV's perks include Wild Wasteland's wacky antics, the skilled but not experienced perk, or something as simple as Four Eyes that gives a character with glasses +1 Perception. Perks in F3 will give you ten points for two skills, others may give you a few wacky effects, and even one will give you fifteen points per each level. They don't shape or define your character—they just make your stats better.
I could delve further about weapon stats affecting damage and spread, but each game handles it similarly. I personally find it stupid for a stat to affect gun-damage. (Swordsmanship in TES can be rationalized by physical capabilities; bullets should not be affected by player stats.) However, I think my point had been made and it can be simply said that the leveling up system of F3 feels more like I'm playing a game rather than making meaningful character choices.
Some may not consider builds or the "role-playing" of "role-playing games" that important when it comes to the decisions you can make. After all, shouldn't your actions matter more than whatever you define yourself as? F3, however, restricts your choices in such an arbitrary manner in what should be a morally gray world.
The extent of your choices are often in a good, neutral or evil response. It would be unfair to criticize F3 for lacking the factions' system of NV. Bethesda was focused on building the game from the ground up, and NV had the time to flesh out its systems. This morality doesn't excuse how blatant the choices you make are for goody two shoes or for heartless a-holes.
Groups such as the Brotherhood or Enclave are portrayed in such a manner. Quest-outcomes, usually, result in a good or bad result. And because the storyline is a linear set of objectives that have no bearing on your actions, the extent of your decisions feels pointless except for when you reminisce for what you have done. None of these aspects are as bad as the Karma system.
The Karma system in both F3 and NV is either a hypocritical or broken mess that should enforce player's actions as consequences. Instead, the whole system feels more like a joke. If you kill a certain type of "bad guy", you will receive good karma. Kill a whole town by blowing up an atom bomb? Don't worry, you can pay off your Karma dues by giving purified water to a homeless guy.
This system lacks any bite or long-lasting effects to enforce any lessons to learn except not to be a d0uche to others. If there were more risk-rewards associated with the good or bad options, such as the Giant Ant quest where if you don't harm the queen you get a bonus to strength or perception, then the binary outcomes could mean something more so than a bland morality in place.

If you want a Fallout experience that revolves around exploration, discovery and light RPG elements, then F3 is okay at best. However, if you are looking for something with more "role-playing" elements, then F3 will disappoint you as its mechanics are not thought-out.
If you did not find F3 interesting or NV as engaging, I am hoping that this review will spark curiosity to visit the Mojave.

"To The Moon" is an indie story-telling game.  It wants you to experience the events through
+ Deep Story-telling experience using 2d RPG-style gameplay with cute nostalgic pixel art
+ Soundtracks
+ Characters were fun and sometimes can be relatable.
The game really has no major problems since it is focused on story. So the following are probably minor issues that I think could've been improved for perfect game design.
- The controls are not customizables and are configured weirdly. For one thing, you can move the character using the ARROW keys on keyboard. That feels awkward when you want to use the mouse as well (since the mouse can be used to highlight the items you can interact with).
- Character movement on the level is stiff. When you press once on an ARROW key to move, the character will move precisely one tile for example. You can't stop in mid movement so sometimes it feels hard to take turns.
- Gamepad uses analog only. Would have been a lot better with D-PAD option.
I highly recommend this game if you are interested in story. It is not a long game and might take you 4-6 hours at most. So you could probably think of this game as an interactive pixel art movie. If you are looking for gameplay only, then I do not recommend you to get this game.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is an unique experience for me. The developing team, Ninja Theory, did create a tense atmosphere for this game. They managed to use various objects in the world to tell a story. I highly recommend using headphone or a full set 5.1 speakers for a better immersion. The music is almost inaudible, but goes along with the atmosphere pretty well. Plus, the voices in Senua's head are recorded via a 3d microphone, which is really cool. The character feels real, with all the details and great acting performed by Milena Juergens. Other characters shown are actual people on camera, but blended in with the game world.
Personally speaking, I found the combat system way too easy. Part of the reason is the quick button response. You can do a decent combo with brainless button smashes. Even if you are beaten down, as long as you keep smashing the buttons, you can still get back up. As other action games, there is a rewarding mechanics for blocking at the correct timing, which is super easy to master. There are something that you have to figure out on your own in order to beat certain types of enemies, and there are not many of them in the game. The only difficulty is paying attention to enemies behind you, or by your side. You have to position yourself properly to gain advantage over multiple enemies. However, it still fails to post a challenge for me. You are welcome to change the difficulty in game.
The environmental puzzles are well constructed in the world. Usually, you have to wander around to find the solution to a certain puzzle. There are plenty ingenious ideas about them. My favorite one is the "gates", some parts of the environment would shift once you go through them. Unfortunately, there are some serious issues with them as well. For some of the puzzles, you have to find a certain shape of object in an environment, there are hints for them, but it still can be a pain sometimes.
Since there is only one type of collectibles in the game, I think it is better to discuss it along with the puzzles, because they are both environment based. You can find about twenty "plates" with symbols on them in the game. Once you *focused* on those plates, you will hear a short background story narration. Some of them are well hidden, inside a cave or behind a secret path, etc. It is not really enjoyable for me, as it forces me to pause in a linear progression of gameplay.
For full immersion and the atmosphere, the game does not have any HUD in game. The subtitles are also turned off by default. You have to check all the controls manually, and it is vital to do so. Go to settings and check everything out before you start a new game. Other than that, the interactive objects in the game are relatively obvious, you do not really need an UI for that. If you are new to action games, or video games in general, there's not much guidance in the game, and you are going to have a hard time playing it.
In conclusion, I would recommend it for the experience, despite many things are not satisfactory. Consider the price, this game is extraodinary.

CHIME SHARP (v.2.5)
PUBLISHER – Chilled Mouse
DEVELOPER – Ste Curran, Twistplay
GENRE – Puzzle/Music
THE BASICS:
Picture Tetris. Now, instead of the pieces falling down and you making lines – Imagine, if you would, that you have full control over where the pieces go on a flat grid. While you're at it, add a few new pieces and a much more varied soundtrack. Also, instead of making lines, you're making squares and rectangles in an attempt to fill up that grid, and you're on a timer. That's Chime. The original by Zoë Mode was innovative and well-received, and this is the even more challenging follow-up.
THE FLOW:
The game has a fairly large assortment of pieces to place, though you only get a specific subset for each level/song (the game shows them to you before you begin the level). More and more parts of each song get revealed as you cover more of the area in valid blocks. Get high enough coverage, and you'll unlock additional modes and songs within the game – the songlist stands at fifteen as of this writing, and another is planned for the next patch.
CONTROLS:
Supports mouse, XBONE controllers, and “standard”/generic Windows controllers. Pad/mouse to move, one button to rotate, the other to place. That's it, and that's all you need.
GRAPHICS:
Colored grids and blocks over unobtrusive backgrounds. In some levels, the blocks you have placed will fade in and out, or even change colors – which is a neat trick, but they sometimes fade a bit too much, adding artificial difficulty to the game. Placing the blocks becomes a bit tricky when you can't easily distinguish them from the backdrop. Hopefully, an option to alter this behavior will show up in a future patch.
SOUND:
An eclectic array of electronica/EDM tunes. Successfully gaining coverage in a level brings in more instruments and tracks, allowing you to hear more of the song as you go.
OVERALL:
Did you like the original Chime? Then you'll like this. More of the same, but tougher, with new music and new gameplay types. And it's glorious. In their words, “the rusty edges [have been] filed off.” Never tried it, but you like puzzle games or the musical choices? Give it a shot.
SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS:
On the low end. Not terribly demanding, so just about any system that can handle Windows 7 can run this game.
OS: Windows 7+ / Mac OS 2010 or later / Linux & SteamOS Ubuntu 12.04LTS+
Processor: Dual Core, Intel Core i5 (3rd generation Ivy Bridge)+
Memory: 4 GB RAM
Graphics: GeForce 200 series+
Storage: 2 GB available space
STORY:  n/a

FUN FACTOR: 85

Nice game! It's best summed up as "Tetris in zero gravity". It's a bit of an oversimplification, but it's workable. Not going to lie, though, in comparison to Chime Superdeluxe, the track lineup is sort of weak. While SD had big-name electronica producers (Fred Deakin of Lemon Jelly, one half of Orbital, Sabrepulse, Moby) bringing some fantastic tracks in, Sharp is mostly made out of indie composers. The most notable names here are Chipzel and Chvrches, and I'll be honest I'm not even sure about Chvrches. None of the tracks here are bad in any way, but they're often kind of mediocre and fail to match Superdeluxes' fantastic lineup. In additon the gameplay has changed up a bit: Now, there's only 3-minute Standard mode, and 3 new gamemodes. Sharp is the most notable gamemode, as it sticks with this game's theme of trimming edges and minimalizing. There's no time limit in Sharp, but every Fragment you leave counts down your lifemeter. It sounds easier than Standard, but Sharp has every ability to kick your puzzle-lovin' behind. There's also Strike mode, which has a non-extending minute-and-a-half timer, and a quicker timeline. It's kind of weak compared to Sharp, honestly, but a welcome addition. The third mode is Challenge, which I haven't gotten to yet because 3-minute Standard is HAAAAARD, so i'll leave that up to somebody with actual skill to look at. Overall it's got a lot of fun additions, although it's sometimes a bit weak in parts.

To review Fallout 3 or New Vegas is a difficult challenge. Not because their content is too hard but their expectations of what players want to enjoy are different. While seemingly similar in their mechanics, both games diverge in what players expect to enjoy in a "Fallout" game.

I cannot say I regret my  30+ hours of F3 because it led me to appreciate NV. This game was my introduction to Fallout. However, I cannot say it's a good "role-playing" game for what it offers, and I'll hopefully explain why.
This preface information is to ask that you should take any review of F3 with information regarding the player's history of Fallout. More often fans of either game will fall back on arguments of Bethesda messing with the lore or how old fogies don't like innovation. If I reference NV it's because those similar mechanics were changed for the better, and reasons given as to why F3's mechanics are horrid.
I aim to explain why Fallout 3 is a bad "role-playing" game by the only objective aspects of a game: The Mechanics. You be the judge of whether the game is redeemable for what it does and does not offer.
Although I want to avoid the plot, I do want to bring up F3's means of storytelling and of motivation because it differs from NV.
F3's benefit/vice is its more personal approach of the Player and the father, James. The intro sequence, while repetitive for later playthroughs, goes to show how great F3 can be when it develops smaller, personal areas. You can read conversations about the Overseer's dictatorship's effects through a poem or medical notes, or you can overhear dialogue that explains things further. It also contextualizes S.P.E.C.I.A.L. and Perks in-game, and provides an easy means for players unfamiliar with FPS/RPG hybrids plenty of time to ease in.
That last statement is important because the hour-long intro does its job of hooking the player for the long run, especially in an open-world environment. Even if you don't like James, searching for someone familiar in a hostile wasteland is a good motivaton to explore.
Unfortunately, that attention to detail is not reflected for the rest of the game.  There are areas like the simulation of Vault 112 and a few notable set pieces and landmarks that are memorable, but the majority of places to explore are one-stop fairs for quests and loot. The world of Fallout 3 feels very dead, and not for the atmosphere.
If the game is played as a one-time commitment, then why do people replay the game? The simple answer is that hidden caches, the ability to go anywhere from the beginning of the game. and the level-design of D.C. are all more interesting than the Mojave.  Being set at the start in the center with no overall scalling of enemies allows the player the freedom to find caches and bonuses.

I wouldn't say the game is designed for speedrunning, but it's how the player feels like the roads they travel are their own that leaves these players satisfied of the memories they make. That is Fallout 3's strongest-suit.


On the flipside, F3's mechanics for role-playing are either shallow of your decisions or absolutely broken. The main problem is that for whatever character build you want to make your characters they will end all the same.
The first major offender are the S.PE.C.I.A.L. stats themselves. You are given far too many to be a jack-of-all-trades with no issues. And if you want more points as you play you can invest into them with a Level Up or by finding Bobbleheads,.
Worse, some stats are arguably superior to others. Investing into Intelligence is always superior because you will earn more skill-points with each level (15 - 20), which in turn can be used to level up your stats faster. And when you level up, you can also choose perks that mainly increase two stats by five points each, or you can choose perks that may offer something slightly interesting. By level 10, I had accumulated enough points to max out two or three stats to 100.

The problem with this system is that the game expects you to max out specific skills because some content can only be accessed by improving the stat. Because there are no skill magazines (like in New Vegas) or various tools to supplement skills like Lockpicking, Explosives or Science you will invest your skill points into all of them so you don't feel like you're gated out of content.
Unlike NV, however, leveling up takes more time to achieve but you'll make about as perfect of a character well before you reach max level. This issue mainly comes from F3's uninteresting perk-systems where as NV focused on character-building perks.
A few starter examples of  NV's perks include Wild Wasteland's wacky antics, the skilled but not experienced perk, or something as simple as Four Eyes that gives a character with glasses +1 Perception. Perks in F3 will give you ten points for two skills, others may give you a few wacky effects, and even one will give you fifteen points per each level. They don't shape or define your character—they just make your stats better.
I could delve further about weapon stats affecting damage and spread, but each game handles it similarly. I personally find it stupid for a stat to affect gun-damage. (Swordsmanship in TES can be rationalized by physical capabilities; bullets should not be affected by player stats.) However, I think my point had been made and it can be simply said that the leveling up system of F3 feels more like I'm playing a game rather than making meaningful character choices.
Some may not consider builds or the "role-playing" of "role-playing games" that important when it comes to the decisions you can make. After all, shouldn't your actions matter more than whatever you define yourself as? F3, however, restricts your choices in such an arbitrary manner in what should be a morally gray world.
The extent of your choices are often in a good, neutral or evil response. It would be unfair to criticize F3 for lacking the factions' system of NV. Bethesda was focused on building the game from the ground up, and NV had the time to flesh out its systems. This morality doesn't excuse how blatant the choices you make are for goody two shoes or for heartless a-holes.
Groups such as the Brotherhood or Enclave are portrayed in such a manner. Quest-outcomes, usually, result in a good or bad result. And because the storyline is a linear set of objectives that have no bearing on your actions, the extent of your decisions feels pointless except for when you reminisce for what you have done. None of these aspects are as bad as the Karma system.
The Karma system in both F3 and NV is either a hypocritical or broken mess that should enforce player's actions as consequences. Instead, the whole system feels more like a joke. If you kill a certain type of "bad guy", you will receive good karma. Kill a whole town by blowing up an atom bomb? Don't worry, you can pay off your Karma dues by giving purified water to a homeless guy.
This system lacks any bite or long-lasting effects to enforce any lessons to learn except not to be a d0uche to others. If there were more risk-rewards associated with the good or bad options, such as the Giant Ant quest where if you don't harm the queen you get a bonus to strength or perception, then the binary outcomes could mean something more so than a bland morality in place.

If you want a Fallout experience that revolves around exploration, discovery and light RPG elements, then F3 is okay at best. However, if you are looking for something with more "role-playing" elements, then F3 will disappoint you as its mechanics are not thought-out.
If you did not find F3 interesting or NV as engaging, I am hoping that this review will spark curiosity to visit the Mojave.

The game lets you manipulate code somewhat, but not nearly as much as it makes you believe.
On each object that you can hack, you can see all the 'relevant' functions and their code, which you kind of have power over.  Except that all you can actually change in the code is the value of a few of the assigned variables.
As a result, most battles can be won by turning a true to false or vice versa, or incrementing /decrementing a number.
This isn't TOO bad by itself.  But the game also gives you access to some strings and function calls that you can change which makes you think you could do a lot more more.  Except that the moment you change a single character in the string, the entire game crashes.  Sometimes the crash is contained by the game, and you just have to reload a save.  Other times (and quite often) the crash isn't contained and the entire game will actually freeze, forcing you to give exit the game and close the game with task manager.
Overall, the game actually is somewhat enjoyable, but it's hard to say that it would really appeal to anyone.  Having more versatility for injecting your own code into creatures would have made the challenges more thought provoking, I think.
Oh, before I forget.  There's also entire segments of the game, such as challenges that reset after a certain point in the game, and revisiting any of them and attempting to redefeat the challenge/boss will also cause the game to either crash or glitch out.

Version: 2.1.2.1
My playtime: 11.8 h (last boss killed, normal difficulty, map size 70, dungeon level 10) (based on steam)
Your Quest is a semi idle-open world rpg themed game where you can build a village and slay monsters. The game will end after you slain the last boss.
The graphics in this game looks like RPG maker graphics, and it looks worse than that because it's zoomed out. The UI is also quite simple and only shows what's important.
The music is decent. It sounds like music from old RPG games where everything is on bass.
When you are starting a new game, you'll be provided with several options based on what world that you want to create. Will it be a big or a small map? Will it have lots of few caves? Will it have easy or difficult enemies? You can also modify your stats and character looks.
At first, there will be a tutorial to help you understand the game. The game might start slow because of the delay between actions (chopping a tree and pickaxing a stone might take like one minute) but you can make it faster after you upgrade the tools. Although there will still be some delay between actions after upgrading it to the "ultimate gear", it's still bearable compared to the initial gear. Note that the character clothes will change based on the armor you are using. In the first few hours, you'll mostly looking for resources in order to be able to build anything you need to slay the monsters.
You are supposed to build a village in this game, which means, you will build houses. Houses will grant you housing for people which will come to your village whenever there is a food. The villagers can be assigned to a job which will be unlocked after you build a certain buildings. The villagers can look for food themselves or even help you to look for materials. This is what makes the game to be semi-idle. You can just wait for the villagers to collect the material for you and leave the game running while you are doing something else.
Besides the collecting resources, crafting, and building, there is a minimum of one cave in each game which can be explored. There are several floors in the cave (a minimum of 10 floors), and the last floor will contain a monster which is supposed to be the last boss. You'll need to be prepared to beat it because it's very strong.
The game will end after you slain the boss, and you'll have to start a new game when it happens.
The game itself is heavily moddable. You can add new equipments, buildings, everything! You can also even edit the save file in order to change whatever you want. In my case, i change the movement speed to 32 to make my character (and monsters) run faster.
Pros:
- Heavily moddable game content
- You can start the game in your preferable setting
Cons:
- Starts very slow
This is a game which will require you to be patient. You'll need to wait a lot and i advise you to play it idle. Although this game mostly will be played idle, you actually can make it non idle by changing the save file. The game's fun can be ruined by changing the save file though.

As someone who's sunk 90+ hours into the original Chime (that's a LOT of reps of "For Silence"...), it was a no-brainer when I saw the Kickstarter for Chime Sharp pop up.  So, now that it's out and the rough edges have been smoothed, was it worth the wait and the money?
For me, absolutely.  I've plunged right into Chime Sharp and enjoyed it.  This game is a welcome return for fans of the original Chime.  For fans of puzzle and music games, I think both aspects of the game are engaging and simple enough for there to be plenty of replay.
First, a larger music selection is hard to go wrong with.  I do like most of the fifteen songs, but it does lean heavily into the electronic/ambient genres; while they're solid pieces, a little more variety would have been nice, particularly towards pop or a fun easter egg song, like "Still Alive" from the original Chime.  Still, a fair few of them have earwormed their way into my head.  There is talk of DLC to add music if the game is successful enough, and I would love to see this happen to expand the music out by genre.
Modes are an interesting shuffle this time around.  Classic is the old timed mode and improved slightly by the fact you no longer need 100% to finish a level. although there is a sense of accomplishment if you can get it now, especially since the boards have gotten more complicated compared to the original game.  Sharp Mode, which encourages players to arrange pieces in a way to leave the fewest fragments sitting around, is a nice addition, and I've enjoyed it more than I thought I would since fragment management has always been a weakness for me in the game.  Strike Mode is tricky and I haven't done as much with it yet, but I'm sure it will also come to me.
One nice thing in addition is that the devs have been very good at listening to input for the game; they've included options to make old fans like me happy.  For example, despite my best efforts, I just can't quite get the hang of the 3D styled boards; there is thankfully an option to apply the classic 2D view instead.
I also had an incident where a big bug basically made one level unplayable for me and a few others in the game's final release; the dev team got straight on it when I brought it up and had it fixed within the week.  Other fixes and features have been added in a similar fashion.  Chilled Mouse and Ste Curran have been very engaged with the community, and I think that bodes well for the game's future.

So let me tell you why I think so.
This is a new experience. It's unlike anything ever seen in games. Sure it has similarities from other games in terms of gameplay and they kept that very simple and not confusing but I'm talking about the way this game tells it's story and how it presents certain elements of Norse mythology.
The creators pushed the boundaries and explored a new setting with the core focus on psychosis.
It's about mental illness that breaks reality. The person suffering from it creates a fantasy and turns it into reality not knowing what is real anymore. They hear voices in their head mocking them and telling them to do inhuman things. They lose control and go crazy at times. They see things that are not real. They also suffer severe depression even to the brink of insanity and ultimately leading to suicidal thoughts. And keep in mind this is just a very basic explanation because psychosis has unlimited types of mental illnesses.
The game dives far deeper into what it feels like to suffer from psychosis and this is what got me interested so I bought the game and I have no regrets.
This is a wild adventure with very basic and simple mechanics. Basic but unique puzzle solving and very fun and satisfying combat.

So yes I 100% love and recommend this game.

I only played a litte bit, and then wanted to make sure what I thought was right, so I watched other youtubers playing this, where they played for many more hours, and as I skimmed through the middle of the gameplays, it confirmed my thoughts and I believe it's ok to post this review.
Graphics: 11/10
The graphics just don't get any better than this. Using the Unreal 4 engine, this game's graphics is incredible. It's probably safe to say that it has the best graphics of 2017, or near it. It's incredibly atmospheric and realistic.
Atmosphere: 9.5/10
The 3D sound, incredible graphics, realistic movement(?), lighting, etc. make this a pretty immersive experience. But...
Combat: 5/10
It does look like the company put some work into the melee combat but it's just too rudimentary and consequently boring and non-challenging. The enemy will usually make a huge grunt or telegraph the swing, you side-step, then mash buttons. Or break his guard with a kick, then hit repeatedly. It really wasn't the complex melee system I believe they marketed it as. The combat is pretty non-challenging, repetitive, and the combat gets boring fast. Also, all the enemies look pretty much the same.
Let's just say, it's no dark souls.
Gameplay: 4/10
REAALLLLLYYYY slow! 70% of the time you're walking, 20% you're looking at amazing cinematographic graphics and cutscenes, etc. and 10% you're doing repetive, boring combat.
This game is more of a walking simulator, atmospheric game with some light, simple combat.
That is why I just can't recommend it. It has amazing graphics, but at the end of the day, It's really boring.
EDIT:
I understand this game is supposed to show what psychosis is like, but at the end of the day, we don't really need 6~9 hours of this. "Ok, I get it, voices in my head, hallucinations, etc." In the end, what kind of game is this?
Is this a walking simulator?
Is this an action game?
Is this an immersive, educational experience about psychosis?
The game doesn't do any of the above well. It just mashes those elements together and hopes to create value out of it, but the end result is just boring...

"DAMN YOU, I CAN'T TYPE 'CREDITWORTHINESSES' ANY FASTER!"
And it's not even the worst this game threw at me, but I somehow managed to pull through. The adaptive difficulty setting seems to be doing its job well, as throughout the game I was always kept on my toes and progressively had to get more serious about my typing, without having to retry any boss encounter more than twice (and up to 5-6 times for a couple of the end-game optional nests). The visuals are fantastic and set a great mood, along with the audio and narration. The story takes a backseat and ends with a variant of "it was just a dream!" that I loathe but seems fairly common in indie games that take a self-reflection approach. Anyway the focus is really more on the action and gameplay, so I never really cared about where the narration was going and I could see the "reveal" coming after a few of the dungeons.
Overall, a very solid game that I would recommend to anyone looking for a challenging action game (with some simple puzzles in the dungeons) that feels very rewarding, as long as you don't mind relying entirely on a keyboard. Took me close to 8 hours to complete, and there's an arena mode if you want to push yourself further.
A note for Linux users: I'm playing this under Linux Mint and had occasional crashes when leaving/entering areas, a few of which made me lose progress. Others have reported the same issue.

Unique and addicting game. The controls are intuitive and simple. As an extra, after you've finished the world play, "Arenas" let you test your skill against the leaderboards, which lends a new competitive (and humbling) aspect to Epistory.
I will say that regardless of the title's name, the story itself is the weakest part of the package, so if you're looking for an RPG-style game I would think twice before buying this. Otherwise, though, I can recommend this to almost anyone.

I want to start by saying this game is probably one of the most beautiful ones I have ever played. Not only is it beautiful to look at, the story behind it drives you to keep playing to find out what happened that caused it. After the opening, you get hit with a huge twist that you can both see coming cause every good game is sad but not see because it's pretty left field. This game is sad. Absolutely heartbreaking all the way through. I cried from start to finish.
But don't be fooled!
Yes this game is pretty. And yes, it's super sad. But make no mistake. This game is really HARD. The longest part of this game is probably getting to each of the places to go through the tasks of getting items back for the tree and besides that, it isn't a super long game. However, you would never know because you spend so much time going back through areas that you knew you should have saved at because you died and got reset back at your last save point.
The main things I'd like to point out:
You will die. A lot. If you hate dying in games and it absolutely eats you alive when you die, this game isn't for you. In the course of this game, I died roughly 1000 times. And I'm actually proud of that since I should and could have easily died a lot more.
This game is hard. You will get fustrated, you will get angry. Take breaks from it and go cry about the sad things you've learned about the plot already. But don't sit there and scream at Ori for not double jumping when you could swear you told him to. It doesn't help.
Save often. There will be a small handful of places that will give you a save point automatically. However, most of the time you have to make something called a "Soul Link" and it acts as a save point. If you think you just did something you never want to have to do again, save it. Otherwise, you will do it countless times more. The only thing about saving is you have to keep what is essentially Mana in order to save the game but you also use it on other moves throughout the game.
At a certain part of the game, the controls will start getting weird. I was totally unprepaired to start walking up walls and so the controls when you do that get a little funny. The important part is to ignore which way Ori is walking and hold the joystick in the position it was in before you began up the wall.
Lastly, you need a controller for this game. I really suggest it. This game was hard with a controller and I couldn't imagine doing it with a mouse and keyboard.

'Hack 'n' Slash' resembles 'The Legend of Zelda', but with hacking puzzles. It sounds like a good combination in theory, but not so so in execution. What I love about 'The Legend of Zelda' games is the sense of adventure they convey and the freedom they give you to explore. 'Hack 'n' Slash' lacks both early in the game, and by the time the so-called "adventure" has begun, I had grown disinterested.
The early hacking puzzles were amusing at first. The game doesn't seem to give the player much of a tutorial on what to do with each weapon or artifact and how to "hack". Worse, many, if not all, puzzles reset after you returned from the next area. This made the puzzles repetitive and annoying quickly. Furthermore, it feels that your actions in the game have little consequence on your suroundings. It also doesn't help that objectives of some puzzles are not clearly explained.
Prior to playing 'Hack 'n' Slash', I had less-than-exciting first impressions of 'The Witcher' and 'LEGO: Batman'. I was really hoping third time's the charm, but that is not so. I can't recommend 'Hack 'n' Slash'; it is a great collection of ideas, but quite unpolished. If only someone could hack it and make it better.

Its an interesting take on a sandbox game for sure.  It has a very long way to go though.  I bought this when it was very first released on steam and waited a few months to review it.
Graphics:
The graphics are ok, but for some reason show up a little bit blurry.  Your eyes need to adjust to the game a bit which is really not a good thing.   Seems this is due to the ground you walk upon,  Understanding that  there are tons of legos beneath your characters feet but lets not make those graphics lesser quality than the characters, items, and shrubbery.
Music:
The music is alright but nothing amazing.  After quite a bit of long drawn out silences the game endures between music rotation and when a song finally comes on your left with a very watered down what usually is deemed to be "epic adventure traveling soundtrack" that eventually and quickly becomes boring.
Gameplay:
You are lego; you choose whether or not you want to start off as a female or male adventurer in the game, with a pretty sad layout screen.  The options you switch between are rather confusing when you first install the game,  there is a top left button on the main screen that for the first time you play the game has hard to view under and over buttons to know that you can even switch the options/character/etc (This is also where you would Quit the game, if you can find it).   Even selecting your chosen world at first is confusing, usually you just select the only one you can see, the Selection screen layout really needs to be fixed, especially since I watched a few little kids struggle with figuring this out and also adults.
When your character starts in his or her chosen world they fall high from the sky descending upon an unknown world you can guide them as they fall as to where you might want them closer to something.  Now your on a world, now what?  you walk around a bit punch trees, bushes,  might find a house thats usually empty, meet some random other npc characters that just wave at you.  But now all those things you beat up you now have lego money and can buy items that the characters where wearing in a selection screen.  The worlds are basically dead though, you barely see anything worth while to do, not many enemies still except for random skeletons that are no threat at all (and you barely can find anyhow).  Your character can't really die or anything.  There are no real enemies in the game as of yet.  You can find automobiles, planes, digging equipment, but it all gets pretty boring fast.
You can build!  Sounds great right?  Unfortunately the game has a slight issue.. We all played with lego's pretty much growing up.  We know the size of the legos compared to the lego people.  Unfortunately in the game the lego pieces seem a bit smaller than the characters.  You can make an automatic house/barn/building they supply you with or you can sit there for hours making your own home out of blocks, which will take forever.  Placing the blocks doesnt feel that great either as it can be a pain to set them up just right sometimes.
Annoyances:
Whenever you come to a new area in the game, instead of just having an overhead subtitle saying "Green Forest" or something it makes your character completely stop in his/her tracks just so a camera and go all around them, above them, pull out the camera just to say ...your here.. It happens very Very often!  Same occurs when you find an animal, person, pretty much anything in the damn game.
The Camera angles itself while you walk, if you just want an overhead view - sorry can't do that, as soon as you angle the camera above your head and start walking the camera angle always slopes back down more towards the ground, there is no option to change this.
Tutorial:
There isn't really one
As much as I liked lego's as a kid and thought "Wow this is a great idea!" It really has a very long way to go and I probably most likely wont check up on this for quite a while.

To be honest, I'm not really into this RPG Maker wave of games.
Not that I don't like old school JRPGs ; I was a big fan of Chrono Trigger and Bahamut Lagoon, back in the days ; but they lost their appeal to me, and I don't play much with this type of games anymore.
But today, I was given away this one, YOUR QUEST, and was like "Seems nice! Let's try it out!".
So, this is a kind of RPG where you play a character lost in a forest and with a quest. Which one, you ask? Creating a village and protecting it from monsters.
Simple pitch for a simple game.
At the beginning, you'll be starting with minimal equipment and a guy named "mentor" who gives you small missions and advices. Soon enough, you'll be cutting trees, building a house, hunting squirrels and plowing fields...
Nothing very original, neither specially bad, you might say!
So why the bad grade and recommendation?
The first thing that hit me was the music.
Not being a big fan of MIDI tunes doesn't help, but the score of this game is kind of dull and uninspired. A few tracks are  better than the others, but it gets boring and repetitive real quick.
So I went into the menu and cut it out after thirty-five minutes of gameplay.
The second thing was the lack of animations.
Note that in this game, they are not really of importance. But, well, it's all very stiff. And slow. Yes. Your character must be the son of a turtle and an snail, cause taking a few steps from its house to the next tree takes him almost one hour of its time. And it can't run.
Talking about time, I hope you got loads to lose, cause when you go to your house to rest your character, it just idle in front of the house, doing nothing, and the time passes as if you were still playing.
After I had a few villagers and some bread, I never rested again.
What hit me next was the save system.
6 slots, no control over them. So, when you save the game, better remember what was the previous spot, cause you'll be reloading a few times to find the good savestate. It lacks a log showing you which save is which.
And so I was hit again (my nose started to bleed). This time by the ressource management system.
Why on earth do the same house needs 350 logs when the previous, which was its exact copy, needed only 300 of them, and so on? Are they playing JENGA with the logs? Making mountains of toothpicks?
I rapidly found out the answer. It virtually adds some lifespan to the game, which would be quite short if not for this kind of subterfuges.
So? It's a mobile game concept. It's like playing a fartphone app like "TRIBEZ AND CASTLEZ", minus the "pay-to-win" part.
And I don't like this kind of games.
Too repetitive.
Boring.
And pointless.

The original Chime is a relaxing puzzler with an interactive music experience.  Each song provides a different experience, and the variety that the music provides is a big reason why Chime is so enjoyable.
Chime Sharp provides the same type of gameplay with 15 new songs to play, but for no good reason at all the developer has decided to lock 10 of the songs behind a challenge wall.  Rather than let you experience all of the songs while you practice and learn to get better at the puzzles, you are stuck repeating the same 5 songs over and over again while you  try to prove to the game that you are worthy of moving on to a new song.  If you are not particularly great at puzzle games, you could be locked out of 2/3 of the songs indefinitely.
I am writing this review after the developer has patched the game to make it easier, but the unnecessary blockade still exists and it still may be an impassable wall for some people.  Even if you are reasonably good at puzzle games, you might simply not feel inclined to push for that magic unlock number on every song.  You will undoubtedly find some songs more enjoyable than others, but the game does not give you a choice and requires you play every song thoroughly before you can advance to new ones.  It's not even clear to me what the requirement is to unlock songs; they say 60% coverage in "standard mode" but I have done this and I still only have access to the first 5 songs, so it's either bugged or it's something harder than that.
So on top of this unnecessary skill wall there may be some bugs.  And in my opinion the music in Chime Sharp is not as good as the music in the original Chime (at least the music that I could access).
I believe fans of Chime will find this sequel disappointing.

I seriously can not, and probably won't be able to undestand why is this game so praised pretty much everywhere.
It was the first Fallout game I ever played, and that was about 8 years ago, barely after the game's release.
Even though I was never a fan of post-apocalyptics atmosphere, I thought it's an overall decent game, just not for me.
Then, after about 5 years, I finally tried out the first two Fallout games, and even though it was really hard to get into them at first, I have come to love them both. It was then that I realized how awful Fallout 3 seems to me. It completely lacked the depth and atmosphere that were so strong in FO1 and FO2.
The NPCS were bland and boring, contrary to many loveable NPCs in the first two games, the quests were repetitive and focused either on fetching stuff, or killing stuff.
What suffered the most in my opinion was the character development.
In the first two games, you could roleplay as a typical, tough guy, an edgy, sarcastic anti-hero who tells bad puns, or even an ordinary idiot who's barely able to speak (and still somehow manages to save the world, doh...). Bethesda's writing has always been far from good, and their attempts at character development in FO3 are embarassing at times.
The Karma system introduced in FO2 was rather rushed and made little sense and it hasn't gotten much better. While even petty actions such as stealing and lying lower your Karma (which is a good thing), there are still some absurd mechanics surrounding it. Stealing from a Raider will drop your Karma, but then killing him will raise it
...
Whatever.
The gameplay is terribly unbalanced. The weapons deal very little damage (and I've seen it keeps getting worse later on, where both the play and enemies become real bullet sponges) and building your character is pointless, as you will end up with maxed out SPECIAL and Skills anyway. My latest character, with maxed out INT and CHA, not a single combat skill tagged and at level 2,managed to single-handedly eliminate the whole population of Megaton on Very Hard difficulty. Not to mention the groups of raiders, which were nothing more than walking target practice. Even if you somehow found an enemy that may overpower you, running away is extremely easy. It completely kills the feeling of danger everywhere around you while travelling you could feel in the previous games, especially in Fallout 2, where a Raider encounter was pretty much a game-over in the first hours of gameplay.
Children and essential NPCs are immortal, which also ruins the feeling that the harsh wasteland does not forgive anyone, even the weak and defenseless, and no one is really safe.
There are also many smaller issues: such as:
-being limited to only one companion
-the artificial intelligence that doesn't have much in common with term "intelligence"
-repetitive voice acting
but they aren't too important.
I'd give it 3/10, but hey, you can still plant explosives in people's pockets and there's a weapon that shoots mini=nukes, so I guess it's something. I give it 4,5/10

I want to start by saying this game is probably one of the most beautiful ones I have ever played. Not only is it beautiful to look at, the story behind it drives you to keep playing to find out what happened that caused it. After the opening, you get hit with a huge twist that you can both see coming cause every good game is sad but not see because it's pretty left field. This game is sad. Absolutely heartbreaking all the way through. I cried from start to finish.
But don't be fooled!
Yes this game is pretty. And yes, it's super sad. But make no mistake. This game is really HARD. The longest part of this game is probably getting to each of the places to go through the tasks of getting items back for the tree and besides that, it isn't a super long game. However, you would never know because you spend so much time going back through areas that you knew you should have saved at because you died and got reset back at your last save point.
The main things I'd like to point out:
You will die. A lot. If you hate dying in games and it absolutely eats you alive when you die, this game isn't for you. In the course of this game, I died roughly 1000 times. And I'm actually proud of that since I should and could have easily died a lot more.
This game is hard. You will get fustrated, you will get angry. Take breaks from it and go cry about the sad things you've learned about the plot already. But don't sit there and scream at Ori for not double jumping when you could swear you told him to. It doesn't help.
Save often. There will be a small handful of places that will give you a save point automatically. However, most of the time you have to make something called a "Soul Link" and it acts as a save point. If you think you just did something you never want to have to do again, save it. Otherwise, you will do it countless times more. The only thing about saving is you have to keep what is essentially Mana in order to save the game but you also use it on other moves throughout the game.
At a certain part of the game, the controls will start getting weird. I was totally unprepaired to start walking up walls and so the controls when you do that get a little funny. The important part is to ignore which way Ori is walking and hold the joystick in the position it was in before you began up the wall.
Lastly, you need a controller for this game. I really suggest it. This game was hard with a controller and I couldn't imagine doing it with a mouse and keyboard.
I love this game. It's beautiful, it's a challange, makes me think. I would absoolutely buy it again and I completely suggest it to anyone even a little interested in it.

I’m gonna be imagining four letter words whenever I see an insect now.  You’ll understand what I mean once you check out some gameplay.  I’d played the current Typing of the Dead game on steam, which is an on rails type-em-up horrorfest that I enjoyed well enough.   Epistory looked intriguing with the origami pop-up atmosphere and the infestation of bugs that looks like the world’s scariest spelling bee.  A typing challenge was something very different from my usual gaming, so I thought it would be a great change of pace.

Upon firing up the game, you’ll find the controls are all on the keyboard with the mouse only functioning on the menu screen.  Movement can be done with WASD, arrow keys, or EFJI.  The origami world unfolds into newspaper and trees as you level up from insect exterminations.  It’s quite a magical thing, really.  You never get tired of unlocking new parts of the map with origami animations.  It’s akin to having a little bird hatch in front of your eyes.
At first, I found the movement around the map a bit difficult with the keys.  It just felt a little stiff to me.  Often, I’d bonk into trees or shrubs without meaning to. This may be due to the fact that I rarely play WASD games that maneuver around objects.  The KB&M ones I play are generally platformers that jump, adventure games, or shooters where I don’t really have to worry about being stopped dead in my tracks by walking too close to an object.  I came up with a solution to speed things up – my steam controller.  Now I could use a controller for WASD and then stop and type whenever an insect came by.
Within minutes you are typing up trees from the ground and unlocking hidden treasure chests.  The narration appears on the ground as well as the voiceover while you are playing –a nice point for those with hearing impairments.  You’ll come across portals that unlock once you’ve got the required points at several locations in the map.  Inside these areas you will unlock the game levels as you find the entrances.  Each level corresponds to an elemental power that you use to attack the insects and solve some basic puzzles.  There are a variety of backgrounds such as fire, ice, and even portaled multi-level tiered platform levels.  Exploring the map to find those levels is not without it’s pitfalls, as there are bugs hidden here and there that can kill you if you don’t keep an eye out.  So, there is an exploratory aspect to the map.  However, sometimes it’s not extremely revealing – mostly just more of the same region with a treasure chest or two.  You’ll also find challenge areas to help level up XP points.  Only when you come to a portal with enough XP will you unlock a completely new area.  The ones including levels are the best unlocks.  I would not say it’s ground breaking or new, but that does give you something to look forward to when you know you need to attack more insects in order to move the game along.

After a good while, it does get a bit repetitive.  You look around, kill insects, solve a puzzle or two, and get to a final round.  No bosses to look forward to and no sudden fast paced typing rounds.  Perhaps it’s because it’s a one hit death, but the gameplay itself doesn’t have the kind of depth I was expecting. There are upgrades available, and that is helpful.  I upgraded my attack skills to the max and upgraded extra time to type as soon as I could. It really does help, especially in the later levels where there are some mini swarms once in awhile, switching between elements, and longer words to deal with.
There was no typing instruction or helpful skill lessons that I could see.  Don’t go in thinking your typing will improve.  If you speed up your typing speed, it’s entirely your own determination making that change.  Often, I’d still look down at the keyboard when typing - all the way down to the last levels.  I’m just not that good a typist.  Better than those who single letter type one finger at a time, perhaps, but my score wasn’t high.
I used the map a bit to get around, but it was so tiny and pixleated I had to stare at it in order to see what was around me.  The map could really be improved, sometimes I had no idea what it showed compared to my location.
Typing is supposed to have an adaptive difficulty.  I’m not sure if that is true or not.  It may be hard to tell from the player’s perspective.  I had the most trouble on the last two levels when I had to switch elements back and forth.  That part slowed me down more than the actual typing itself.
Visually, you can’t complain one bit.  It has a wonderful origami style and look that usually leaves people with a smile after each new area unfolds.  You feel as if you’ve walked into a pop up book of paper sculpture.  The art direction in Epistory is very organic and I get the feeling that the artists put a lot heart into each scene.  The sound is well done as well with a great compositional score, quite ethereal and ambient without being overbearing.  Sound effects are to the point and nothing too annoying.
It’s entirely a narrative, there is no character interaction between the fox and the girl.  The story that unfolds is a cross of two stories really.  One is from a narrator who tells the story of the world you are unfolding and of the woman writer trapped inside. You’ll get lines like “Sensing a terrible wrongness, she looked up.  Had a star died?  Had the moon fallen?”.  You’ll also get lines directly from the woman herself late in the game.
If you feel like a typing game, Epistory is probably right up your alley.  This game is a good challenge even if you have great typing skills.  Those who are single finger typists might not be able to get past the midway point, but with adaptive typing you might be able to get through to the end.  Even though it’s not a story-movie like Typing of the Dead, nor an RPG adventure with characters, it does a good job of providing a fun challenge of typing with a gorgeous game environment and a nice narrative story.
The game is weakened mostly by its lack of bosses or surprise levels – those would have been welcome.  With the only enemies being insects, it got a little repetitive even as the difficulty cranked up a bit at the end.  The game length is also adequate, even if it’s not very long.  I finished in about 8-9 hrs factoring in time while I was AFK.
All in all, Epistory is a good typing game, some leveling up involved, amazing art direction, and charm.  You may find it relaxing to play something like this compared to heart pounding action games or nerve wracking platformers.  Who knows, you may even self-teach yourself to stop looking at the keyboard when you type.

Epistory: Typing Chronicles is a stunning action-adventure game - although "stunning" does not do the visuals of this game any justice. Based on storybooks and origami, the richness in colour, texture, depth and
that this game manages to create is just mindblowing. Honestly some of the most breathtaking graphics I believe I have ever, ever seen from an indie title.
In terms of gameplay, the premise is simple - you are a girl riding atop a fox with magical powers, seeking to rid a forgotten kingdom of a mysterious darkness that has befallen it. To use your powers, you type; each correctly typed word sends a powerful bolt of magic straight at whatever you were aiming for, be it monsters, chests, gates or switches.
The main challenge comes in the enemy nests dotted around Epistory's various worlds, with waves of progressively harder enemies throwing longer and longer words at you
. These arenas are by far the most challenging part of the game, although Epistory comes with its fair share of puzzles, too; and with the experience-based upgrade system and the game's generous rewarding of exploration, it's actually all very typical action-adventure fare. Yet the way everything is done coupled with the unique typing mechanic (and the
gorgeous visuals) makes the whole formula feel new, exciting, and original.
Epistory has become one of my favourite titles in my Steam library very, very quickly, and I cannot recommend this enough; I'd genuinely pay more than the asking price for it. If you haven't picked it up yet, I sincerely hope you do!

I have played Epistory - Typing Chronicles quite a bit and even seen the credits rolled. So I shall share my experience playing this game and perhaps a tip or two for those interested.
I love this game. I never expected to fall in love with a second game but I did.
VISUALS
The visuals were beautiful. I loved the origami idea, and as you unlocked each new region they unfold like an origami present which was very lovely to watch. If you look closer, as I did towards the end, each tile that makes up the land is actually a stack of paper, which is a really neat idea reminding me on how an author's words alone create all the fantastical landscapes I see in my head as I read.
STORY
I also loved playing as the muse riding on her three-tailed fox. At first as the words appear on the land narrating a story, I thought that the unfolding story was about the muse on the fox, but as I kept progressing through the different landcsapes and unlocked more of The Bridge, I realised that the unfolding story was also about this unnamed girl. As I collect the fragments of each landscape and unlocked more regions, I learned more of her. It is never explicitly said what exactly happened to her in the end, but I believe that the fragments and the words on the land do give enough information that I can fill in the rest and construct my own interpretation of her story. This is the best part of Epistory -Typing Chronicles, discovering the story as you go along and feeling invested in it throughout the game.
KEYBOARD SKILLS
Now it may be a typing game. In fact you can operate everything using the keyboard alone. But there is also the element of puzzles which features quite a lot in this game, as well as a few cleverly-hidden spots. I won't spoil it for you, but if you do want to progress, a decent mastery of your keyboard will go a long way, not just for navigation and running away when you need to and killing insects by typing. That's another highlight. Ah, how I wish I could kill insects with my now-improved typing skills in real life :P
ICE NAVIGATION
In terms of navigation, I have previously read how some users struggled with navigating on ice. I did too at first, but once I figured it out I found ice to be very helpful at certain points in the game. Two things I learned
1) For me, I like to see my navigation keys of WASD like a compass. Going up is the W key, then it is my North, and so on for the other keys. Now in a compass there are also four more directions of northeast, northwest, southeast and southwest, which are combinations of the north south east west directions. I just treat my keyboard the same, and the eight directions afford more than enough precision to navigate smoothly across the land.
2)Also, the law of inertia applies on ice. A moving object continues to move unless being stopped by a wall or by a piece of land. Always remember this when on ice and you should be able to go wherever you need to go.
ORDER YOUR UPGRADE
Another thing I would like to point out is that despite reaching the end of the story, i.e. the credits, I did not unfold the story in its intended order which was a bummer for me. After unlocking the first few landscapes in the right order, I unlocked the rest in a haphazard order and completely missed one! I think that this was because that at certain parts of the game I had enough points to unlock more than one region at a time so I cluelessly went wherever I did. My advice would be to use your upgrade points on the Instinct upgrade as soon as you can, lest you go down the wrong path like me. I discovered too late that the Instinct upgrade is actually VERY USEFUL as it leads you to the next point in your journey. Besides that, I would also highly recommend the Velocity upgrade, but of course it will depend on your gameplay to choose which upgrade you need more urgently than the others.
EXPLORATION IS KEY
Also, before I forget, exploration is a key part of Epistory - Typing Chronicles. You will be rewarded if you have a penchant for exploring every nook and corner like me. I have stumbled upon chests placed off the main path as well as solutions to some puzzles by insisting on exploring my surroundings. I would not have found many of the chests and solved many puzzles in the relatively short time that I did if I did not constantly stray off the main path to explore the land, because boy oh boy there are so many goodies hidden off the main path.
So yes, in short, Thank You to Fishing Cactus and Co. for the epic Epistory - Typing Chronicles <3

1). Difference
So, what’s Different, you might ask. Instead of like other tycoon games, where you get to see your theme park, whatever it is grow visually, Game Dev Tycoon gives you growing numbers. If you ever made or make youtube videos, you would know how satisfying seeing it is to see that view count going up, and Game Dev Tycoon offers exactly that. This makes the game simpler, and more realistic, since as a game developer, there’s nothing more you can do than expect a review, and watch that sweet sweet revenue grow.
2). Gameplay
Man, what to say. Game Dev Tycoon’s mechanic simplifies game development so much, that not only does it simplify a complicated experience, but it also adds fun. In the game, oh wait, that’s spoilers. But anyway, the game gives the realistic feeling on how to manage your time during a game development process, and what to include during it. I’m pretty sure that’s what the developers felt before they developed this game. You can also replay the game as much as you want. The game’s randomness and the ability to replay which exists in the tycoon game genre makes every run-through different from each other. Plus, this game fuels through the development of the gaming industry in modern life. It’s possible that the game would have further updates that extend the experience to nowadays. Overall, this game is a great success. And for its potential for further updates, i’d recommend it.
