This is one of the most emotional games I have ever played. My wife happened to be sitting next to me during my play session last night and we both were in tears at the end of this game. The story of “To the Moon” is so incredibly sweet and has such great writing it’s incredible. The reason I love video games as we know them today is not only are they fun, but I love getting told REALLY good stories that are interactive. A good story will transcend any graphical style or not having millions of dollars behind you. This gets the label of an “indie” game which initially puts a bad taste in some people’s mouths but I don’t why  - It just means these are games not made by a giant conglomerate or corporation. This year I’ve found myself trying more Indie games out as I’ve been thoroughly impressed- For example - I have always loved the Call of Duty games for their camapaign modes - I thought they were interesting, put you in an action movie, and had some good writing - particularly Black Ops 1- But I just played Black ops III and this story was so terrible - This is supposedly a AAA game but you know what I had WAY more enjoyment with To the Moon and the writing in TO THE MOON BLOWS this out of the water. Seriously.
This game was designed on the RPG Maker XP engine - and really holds that 16-bit RPG feeling intact that I’m in love with - Just the other day I was talking to my wife and I was telling her how We will never see another AAA RPG title in the 16-bit style of old Final Fantasy Games, Chrono Trigger, or Dragon Quest games - and that I really prefer that art style when there is a really good story. There is something to reading dialogue apposed to voice actors. I love where voice acting has reached in video games, but a story like this is just really potent when you’re reading it and internalizing it.
In this world there exists a technology that allows doctors to implant artificial memories. This is sort of like a mix of the films Eternal Sunshine of a Spotless Mind and Inception - The idea is that a patient will ask for these memories to be created and when they wake up they will have memories of things that didn’t actually happen to them. The catch is that this process interferes with the the patients real memories and the result of receiving this new set of memories means your mind and body will shut down as a result; ultimately the patient will die. This procedure has been legalized for patients on their deathbeds to help fulfill their wishes they never accomplished in life and so they can die without any regrets.
The Story begins with you taking control of two doctors. Dr. Eva Rosalene & Dr. Neil Watts as they arrive at a house on a wooded cliffside of the dying Johnny Wyles to fulfill his wish which is To Go to the moon. Although he does not know why he wants to. The machine they bring with them allows the doctors to enter into the mind of Johnny and traverse backwards through his memories with the goal to plant the seed of desire that would alter his life into becoming an astronaut and ultimately getting him to the moon. During each memory sequence you control the doctors and you collect memory links which will allow you to unlock a mementos that tie back to an earlier part of the Johnny’s life which will allow you to jump further back into his memories. Unlocking a memento also includes a mini game where you have to reconstruct the image of the item before making the jump. Although the doctors are meant to remain professional and not get emotionally involved - Both Dr. Watts & Dr. Rosalene get emotionally invested in their own ways as Johnny’s past is revealed.
Throughout the game as much emotion as there is Dr. Watts is always there for comic relief and there is a lot of tongue and cheek humor that will keep things light. But the subject matter is wrapped in a mix of nostalgia, sorrow, love, and desire that it still overwhelms you and this is reinforced by the INCREDIBLE Music in this game. Just like I talked about old RPGs having power in you reading the dialogue there is power in the music and the MUSIC really propels and drives this story and will tug on your heart strings. Kan Gao & Laura Shigihara did an unbelievale amazing Job on the music. Seriously guys - it’s incredible.
A complete side note I wanted to say is there is one line that really struck me in this game and it’s said in passing, but it really struck a cord with me. As you travel through the memories strangers and other people will be representing as ghostly figures as Johnny doesn’t remember what they looked like and Dr. Rosalene says “The World would be a lot more beautiful if people just remembered faces more.” That’s really such a great line.
This game is drenched in love and you can complete the story in about 4 hours. It’s an incredible story and I am definitely going to be shouting this from the mountain tops and telling everyone I know to play it.
All I can say is Kan - Thank you for creating this beautiful work of art. I will definitely be checking out your other game A Bird Story next. - If 16 bit graphics can move you emotionally - that’s a stamp of approval that it is a great story. Of all the games I talk about this is my HIGHEST recommendation. Go Grab it on Steam - It works Windows, Mac, or Linux - and get ready to Go TO THE MOON -

Parts of this game are good - the combat is fast-paced and flashy, the core of the story is interesting, and the environments are pretty and evocative... but it's the little things that make the difference between a good game and one that is just OK.
...things like decent soundwork - a high quality microphone for the voice actors, and maybe just a bit more work on their performance. Footsteps to accompany your movements.
...things like multi-target tracking cameras, for those battles when you're surrounded and need to dodge attacks coming from many directions.
...things like good cutscene animation, as opposed to unmoving images of posed characters with voiceovers, or worse - black and white animation stills played like a flipbook.
...things like consistent character writing. The Bearer randomly switches between being a self-righteous jerk and a naive child. Ergo Mundus, in the meantime, sometimes changes his speaking style and makes meta jokes at unpredictable intervals.
...things like graceful,  slightly slower movement when jumping and platforming.
...things like good telegraphy for enemy melee attacks, which are not lost in the flurry of special effects coming from your own attacks.
...things like differing textures or colors to mark what parts of the terrain you can jump on and which parts are just for show.

As a fan of the Anima tabletop miniatures game, with its fantastic graphics and unique world, I kickstarted this game - then waited years for its much-delayed launch - and played only a few hours of the thing. It wasn't terrible - until the first boss fight. The constantly shifting shifting viewpoints change the movement controls back and forth in ways I could never adjust to. I've never been a fan of boss fights in games and would prefer developers to make them optional in some way, but usually I slog through and and am even usually capable of winning them at any difficulty level, despite my dislike of them. Not this time. I can deal with tough boss fights, even if I dont like them. Ones that change the process of play, on the other hand, break my interest in the game. A boss fight should be a part of the game, utilising the skills you've developed through play in interesting and challenging new ways - they shouldn't suddenly shift you into a whole different viewpoint or control scheme. at least, not for me.

Hello everybody, Shaun Meyers here from Universal Gaming Reviews to bring you our latest review summary for Epistory: Typing Chronicles by Fishing Cactus and Plug In Digital.
I'm going to say this right off the bat, this game is easily the best typing game that I've ever had the pleasure of playing.
Epistory is a narrative based tale that feels like Bastion crossed with a word game. It features some excellent narration that really adds to the overall experience. It also features an absolutely gorgeous paper art style, excelent voice work and very fun typing based gameplay.
It's an excellent tool for those looking to improve their typing skills but it also makes for a great game as well.  I managed to beat the game in 5 hours myself so don't mind that I only have 6 hours play time as of writing this review. (I'm used to typing everyday so I breezed through the entire game without much of a probllem)
Definitey a game worthy of checking out though, even if you aren't a fan of word/typing games, the game is worth playing just for the narration, art style and gameplay.
Thanks for taking the time to read our summary and full review folks, happy gaming!

A typing game unlike most.  This game is a gorgeous work of art - the isometric-view world looks like hand-crafted origami, and you guide a dreaming girl through it on her quick, brown fox.  (Yes.  That old gag.)
The narrative is a heavy-handed metaphor for a woman trying to convey how much inner strength is required to simply navigate the real world.  Each distinct and vibrant area you navigate your fox-riding author-avatar through represents the (traumatic) memory of phases of her life, whose mercifully-vague resolutions bring empowerment and... Whatever. You can easily ignore the breathless gushing of bad poetry and author catharsis to focus on the mechanics of typing to solve puzzles and kill insects.
The story might be one developer's alternative to expensive therapy, but we got a fantastic game out of it.  Different types of obstacle require different types of unlocked 'powers', allowing for that metroid style back-tracking fun.  Chaining together quick combos increases your exp generation, which affords you more upgrades to your typing power abilities and provides incentive to push forward swiftly, thoroughly typing at anything that moves.
I strongly recommend this game for typing fans.  It's novel, gorgeous, and has an incredibly solid variety of tricks to spice up the otherwise simple experience of typing as fast as you can.

"Please note that it is not yet another 'five nights at freddy's' clone."
Hmmm...now, let's see..."spoopy" atmosphere and jump-scares...check.  Time-management based mechanics taught to you by some guy who repeatedly contacts you via telephone...check.  A "survive 'til 6am for a number of consecutive nights" style of game structure...check.  A variety of different enemies and nights which all "behave" differently, and need to be strategized individually...check.  And last, but certainly not least of all: BEARS.  Checkity, check-check-check.

Aaaaah yes, I'm quite, quite sure this game would have existed in this particular space and time IRRESPECTIVE of the spectacularly-successful FNAF franchise preceding it by not much more than a year.  But you know what?  Let's let bygones be bygones, and ignore any questionable statements made on the - let's face it, ultimately inconsequential - marketing tool which we call a "Steam Store page".  Let's just ask the most important of questions, namely:  How does Bear Haven Nights stack up as a GAME, in and of its own right?

The answer, I'm relieved to say, is that it's actually pretty good.  Not entirely "logical"...but good.  Not as good as the first Five Nights at Freddy's...but good.  Certainly above and beyond the bounds of "competence", and let's face it, for a horror game recently released onto Steam, that's a pretty amazing start.

So what does Bear Haven Nights do right?  Well, it has an excellent tutorial and slowly incrementing difficulty curve, for starters.  It's not too hard to understand what you're supposed to do in this game.  More challenging to actually pull it off, of course...but it's all easy enough to get your head around.  It's also very aesthetically pleasing, both visually and aurally, and that's certainly never something to complain about.  And the gameplay, on the whole, is very smooth and mechanically sound, and doesn't seem to "cheat" quite as much as a lot of FNAF-style games do, at least for as far as I've played it.  None of my deaths to date have seemed excessively "cheap", in other words...in truth, I probably fully deserved them.  Well, ahem...certainly within the bounds of the game's thoroughly loopy "plot", that is.  Which brings us to some negatives...

While I'm undoubtedly a lover of almost all things child-like and creepy, I'm not really sure why you've been hired to work in a motel haunted by TEDDY BEARS.  The owners of this motel don't need a night-shift electrician...they need an EXORCIST!  The first Freddy's game pushed its luck a little with the scenario of a security guard working in a restaurant fully known to be plagued by homicidal animatronics, but on the whole, it seemed a feasible enough scenario if you lived in the same neighbourhood as David Lynch or Stephen King.
I mean, at least the animatronics were an actual ATTRACTION of the restaurant, so there was no reason the business owners would choose the welfare of some work-a-day slob over their true bread-and-butter earners.  The owners of the motel in Bear Haven Nights, on the other hand, appear to have no good financial reason to keep psychotic bears hanging about.  Surely they could just find this "Room X" that they have a security camera pointed at 24/7, and torch the little ♥♥♥♥ers back to the Hell from which they came?

I'm also not quite sure about the logic of why the bears apparently can't find you in the dark - despite the fact that they come right up in your face and stare at you with menacing red eyes - but if the telephone or TV turns on, WATCH OUT!  Jump-scare time!!  I guess the teddies hate the TV even more than I do, and sincerely believe that we live in a morally vacuous, culturally bankrupt era where telephones and televisions are killing what little remains of genuine human-to-human - er, bear-to-bear - contact.  I certainly wouldn't be one to completely disagree with them.

Finally, my last criticism would be that - quite UN-like the FNAF games - the jump-scares in this game JUST AREN'T SCARY.  They're perfectly cute and pleasing on a basic aesthetic level, but they sure as♥♥♥♥♥♥don't make you♥♥♥♥♥♥yo'self the way that those Scott Cawthon games do.  Everything else in the game is suitably spooky, though - the spinning fans, the ticking clocks, the red-eyed  bears looking through the windows trying to spot you, the fantastically spooky "Halloween"-esque music - so it at least delivers rather nicely on the suspense front.  But the jump-scares...a bit lame, unfortunately.

On the whole, though, this is by far one of the better FNAF "homages" currently available in the Steam marketplace.  And I know I said at the start of this review that I'd try to overlook such comparisons, but let's face it...it's nigh-on impossible!  This IS a Five Nights "clone", and possibly the closest in tone to the first Freddy game that I've yet encountered...which is mostly a good thing, even if it doesn't exactly qualify this as "original".  It is, in any case, really quite likeable in its own right, and if this is SunRay Games' first release, they may very well be a company to look out for in the near future.  Nice...a little TOO "nice" at times, if you get my gist...but definitely nice.  Do you dare the bear?  C'mon, you know you want to...
Verdict: 7.5/10.

Bear Haven Nights claims to be a horror game that's not simply another FNAF clone. The truth is, however, that it isvery similar to FNAF in many ways. Now this is not necessarily a bad thing and will depend on whether or not you liked the FNAF games to begin with. Interestingly, I personally was not a fan of FNAF, however I am finding BHN quite enjoyable.
BHN does a lot of the same things that similar games of the genre do, but it also has enough minor unique differences (at least in my opinion) that give it its own unique feel and style. Obviously, the first thing that is going to stand out is the ability to move around from location to location, which was not a feature of the FNAF series. It could be argued however that this in  essence is no different than jumping from camera to camera, and there would be little I could say to refute that, though I'm perfectly ok with that.
The art style is where the game really shines for me. It's a very simple art style indeed, but it gives the game this immense feeling of surrealism as though you may be in the Twilight Zone or inside of a dream. The game is not "frightening" and the jumpscares are not particularly scary, in comparison to other games that have come out recently (particularly Emily Wants to Play) but what the game lacks in pure fright factor, it makes up in its eerie and very well executed atmosphere. The motel setting no doubt adds to the atmophere as we've all come to associate desolate motels in the middle of nowhere with sinister occurences and crazy characters (Psycho, anyone?).
At the time of writing this, I've played the game for approximately 1.5 hours and am very satisfied with the amount of content and the way it was all put together and executed, and for less than $5, I can't help but recommend that anyone with a taste for these kinds of games give this one a try.
I popped up my first impressions and funny moments videos on YouTube and have linked them here for anyone that's interested in seeing more of the game played in English, as almost all of the videos on YouTube are in Russian, it seems.

During the first 10 hours of playing I loved this game. And I still wouldn't refund it if possible. However I can't really recommend it. Here's why:
The camera. You'll notice as soon as you start playing, it takes hours to get used to. If a tree gets in the way the camera moves, meaning that your vehicle starts steering. You can use an alternative camera mode, but that should just be fixed.
Building is nearly impossible. Using vehicles works horribly and you can't undo, using the Tools works slightly better as long as the undo key doesn't bug out and you can see what you're doing despite the sun always being in the wrong position to see everything clearly. And 3rd person building just isn't optimal. Manual saving isn't a real option either, so if you mess something up start all over again.
So if building is not a viable option, is exploration then at least fun? Well yes and now. It's great to find other biomes, characters and weapons, but if you put viewing distance on very far you can see for what's about 50 meters while driving at normal speed and if you're in a plane at top speed you can only see 1 meter in front of you even if you're in an area you've already seen. And you're not going to use your slowest mode of transportation.
Performance wise... It's okay, but you do need a GTX750 or better to get decent graphics. This will surely change though.
All in all fun to play around for 10 hours and I'm assuming the price will rise, so I'm happy I already have the game, but I can't honestly say it's good value for the money yet. I do have faith that it will become great though, but it just needs a lot of time.

Hack 'n' Slash is a love letter to both gamers and computer programmers. The game's many references to old-school games like the original Legend Of Zelda make it an enjoyable homage, and the game's rather innovative hacking mechanic challenged me in a way that I've never really experienced before. By hitting certain objects with your sword/USB drive, you can hack them, changing attributes to open locked doors, instantly defeat enemies, and give yourself extra health. With the ability to hack yourself to ludicrous levels of health, and the ability to hack enemies out of existence, you'd think that the game would get boring quickly, but that's not the case. The game barely pretends to be combat-oriented, and rather focuses on puzzles. Early in the game, the puzzles tend to be rather easy, such as hacking a movable block to increase the number of spaces it moves, but by the game's second chapter, the puzzles begin to become more complex. Around the game's third chapter, however, there is an abrupt gameplay shift.
At some point, you gain an item known as the "loupe", which allows you to, quite literally, look at and change the coding for in-game objects. At this point, the game shifts from relatively simple block-pushing puzzles to fiendishly difficult challenges that basically boil down to the problems you might find in a programming textbook. As a matter of fact, the second half of the game feels almost like an interactive tutorial to coding, and honestly, that's not neccesarily a bad thing. The puzzles may be difficult, but the game always provides you with more than enough information to solve them.  No programming knowledge is required to start this game, but once you get to the midpoint, you'll find that you may very well leave with some.
Overall, I think this is a creative game that uses its innovative mechanic to the fullest extent. If you're looking for a relaxing game to zone out playing, I'd advise you to look elsewhere, but if you're looking for a fun and interesting challenge, then I would heartily reccomend Hack 'n' Slash.

Probably the most famous GameDevSim.
TL:DR - Simple, fun and addictive, but sometimes frustrating a bit.
PROS:
+Gameplay
Pretty simple yet interesting and super-addictive - it's very easy to start from "i'm just gonna create one game" to end with "whoops, i have biggest game company ever now".
+Simplicity
As i mentioned, game is very simple. It's not "hardcore sim", so, if you're new in sim genre - GDT gonna be a very good choice for you to start.
+Possibilities
You can make pretty much every kind of game you want. Maybe sometimes you can feel the lack of genres and topics, but this is not too often.
+ Useful for learning the basics of gamedev
This game can help you to understand some important things in actual game development - every genre have it own priorities (action games, for example, really need focus on gameplay and engine), every console have it own audience, and all things like that. Of course, you're not gonna become new John Romero after 50+ hours in this game, but you're gonna understand at least some important things in gamedev.
+ Bug free
I play this game a lot, and didn't noticed any serious bugs. Maybe there is a couple minor ones, but, you know, they are minor.
+ Mods
Mods make any game better! Lack of topics? Get 200+ with mods! Want competition with other developers? Mods have that! Man, they even have multiplayer, if i got it right.
NEUTRAL MOMENTS:
~ Sound design and music
Not bad, but nothing really memorable and interesting
~ Graphic and animation
Same as previous
~ Score System
Score system is very simple - if you want high scores, you need to make your game a bit better than previous. Sounds perfect, but personally for me there is a problem - game suggest not to "make game as good as you possibly can right now", but "make new game a bit better than previous one or your next game gonna get 4/10 because lack of innovations", what really frustrate me. I'm a big perfectionist, and i just can't force myself to make my creative progress slower. But others is okay with that, so, this is why that paragraph in Neutral Moments, not Cons.
CONS:
- Head scratches
Yeah, seriously. Sometimes characters just randomly stop doing what they're doing, and start scratching their heads - while time is ticking and you're failing all deadlines. Is this suppose to make game more interesting??? All, what it does - frustrate and force me to use save-scumming.
- Topics on start
Game randomly give you 4 topics on start, and most of the time this is not the most interesting topics for you, if you're as picky as me. I wish we could just choose some  topics (not from all of them, but from simple ones, like Fantasy or Sci-Fi) before start of the game.
- Save System
For some reason you simply cannot delete save files from the games - if you want it, you need to do some work with SteamCloud. Ridiculous UI.
To be honest, i made this review only for a badge... I'm gonna delete it soon, or, maybe, just edit a lot, to make it better (After all, i chosed second, all thanks to RYBA).

This is my first review so please bare with me on this
Pros,

*super fun even when you're losing(just opinion like this entire review)
*2d bewbs....... what I'm just into that stuff.
Cons
*Difficult to get very good at even if you can do the tutorial mode
*Very difficult to be competitively succesful with just one character, so you have to learn at least 2
*In terms of player skill level, there's no middle ground, either you know what you're doing or you don't
*Although the game isn't execution heavy, its still kind of difficult to do specific combos if you don't practice
*Wait Fillia's not 18......... oh well at least we still have Parasoul.
Quick overview
Personally I love this game to death, it's one of the first fighting games I decided to competitively play(or at least try to). The gameplay is pretty fast, especially to the untrained eye. To people who are watching videos to find out whether or not they should buy this game, you might have noticed this, you might feel a bit like gohan when he's watching that one fight in dbz. The game by nature of air combos, IPS, and the "undizzy" system, is very reset heavy. To non fighting game players, what this means is that, this game is centered around getting a hit comboing, then perhaps setting up a situation where you can get another hit and continue comboing. Please note that there are no touch of death combos in this game. Learning to combo is probably more important in this game than in Street Fighter or BlazBlue. So for newer players this might be a bit of a turn off. But trust me, its pretty easy to learn combos. Thanks to the chain system, (basically, you can press lets say, light punch, medium punch, then hard punch and the attacks will "auto combo" or the more used term, "chain") the place where most newer fighting game players will probably be confused is when it comes to launching your opponent, but if you do the tutorial it shouldn't be a problem. Plus there are tons of basic combos online, just make sure that the version of the game in the video is up to date. Any way, onto some other stuff, so lets go over characters, this game is pretty diverse when it comes to characters, in terms of design and actual gameplay. To a newer player you might think that every character is rushdown and offensive based, with the exception of Peacock and maybe Parasoul. But actually its not really true. Every character can be played in many different ways, but there are optimal ways to play the character. The way you know what kind of character(rush down, grappler, etc.) you're playing, is how your character is supposed to play the neutral. For example, Peacock wants to play the neutral on the opposite side of the screen and chucking stuff at you at a distance, but for Fillia, she desperately wants to get into your face and just destory you, to do that she does a lot of dashing on the ground and lots of jumping HP because it has a huge hitbox. Or you have a character like Parasoul, she has good normals(a move that doesn't require a joystick motion), a projectile to use full screen, command normals for a threatening low high mixup, and a huge hitbox on Jumping HP, she's capable of playing a full screen neutral game, but also she can get in and rush people down. In terms of artstyle, stages, and aesthetic stuff, its really different, the artstyle is reminiscent of the batman the brave and the bold series, but still looks very unique. The backrounds are filled with funny references to other game series and FGC stuff too. Also the backrounds are animated as well, if you don't think your computer can handl it that's ok there's an option to turn that off in the options menu.
Conclusion
For about 15 dollars, you get one of the smoothest, craziest and most of all funnest fighting games on the PC. It's practically a steal. But to be honest it's not really for casual players although the visuals are something to be impressed about, you shouldn't buy the game just for that. If you are looking for a place to start getting good a fighting games, I would recommend this game only if you're willing to put in time and effort. Otherwise Street Fighter is a very good place to start, but does not contain as indepth of a tutorial as Skullgirls does. For Hardcore Fighting game players, you might notice that this game is very similar to the Marvel Vs. Capcom series, which was the creator's intention. I would highly recommend this to competitive fighting game players, it relieves some execution issues(such as instant air dashing), and very technical stuff(such as frame data) that the Marvel series has issues with. I love this game to death, its freaking awesome, and now that they've announced cross play between PS3 and PS4 I think it's only a matter of time before we can get cross play onto PC.

You can make a group of two police officers (Again, similar feature from old Police simulator games) and you can click the group and assign them to a patrol car then assign them on patrol or outright respond to crime call. If a suspect is too strong on a crime call (Measured the strength number), then the officer will not involve and stop him but wait for backup. If no backup is sent, then the luck is depended on officer's strength, he may be injured or seriously injured or even arrest him. Shootout is not uncommon in the game either and that's what gives me good feeling seeing multiple officers involving in a gunfight against four armed suspects. Let's not forget you can send riot police, swat! Investigation is another major gameplay aspect. Sometimes cops may not arrive on time to stop a crime so you will have to employ investigators to investigate where the suspect was gone from the scene and then arrest them. There are a lot more gameplay aspects and all of them require time management and patience.
Content speaking. Police tactics Imperio has a lot contents, really. SWAT, Riot police, Speed camera, van, military, helicopter, what the hell else you want? A lot!
Modes speaking. Currently it got ONLY Singleplay/Campaign and no free-roam UNTIL you finish the game where you then can do anything you want. A second mode as free-roam is in development I heard but no promises.
Bug/Issues speaking. Well. CyberphobX's previous Police Simulator games were completely bug mess with a lot issues and even crashes (Which were very uncommon) but this time, Police Tactics Imperio no longer has a lot bugs or even game-breaking bugs. There are a few minor bugs which are being ironed out by the development team.
Development team/developers behavior. I am speaking with a developer a lot times, he addresses my concerns and issues about the game and so on. They are very friendly and will not hesitate to help you on any issue and will listen to any feedback! But hey, it's still too early so give them time.
Overall, this game is very good despite having some bugs and it requires ton of PATIENCE time with good knowledge on how this game works. I vote it..

Anima gate of memories is an interesting hack'n Slash/RPG.
Anima have a pretty classic gameplay where you have to move forward and kill everything that come to you, it can feel repetitive but it's compensated by the fact that it's an open world (it's not linear, you can which "wing" to do first and so on). You also have an good variety of opponent so you wont get bored of combat. Talking of combat, this game have a "character switch" fonction : you can switch between The Bearer and Ergo (The two main characters) while doing a combo to enhance the possibility after that, and even if they have similar skills, you can specialise one for magic and the other for martial art in the skill tree. It's good to notice that they don't share the same health bar but if one of them die it's game over so it's important to switch often (since the character regain health when he's in standby). So, mostly Anima have a strong gameplay but there is one thing that annoyed me a lot : plateforms.... It's painful, when you jump from plateform to plateform, somehow, my camera is always reset so I can't see where I have to land and I end up falling... Thankfully most of the plateforms things are optional.
It's beautiful, not that the graphics or that light effect are very impressive but the design of every room is well done, and the fact that each wings give you a very different vibe is refreshing.
The musics are pretty good, it fit well with the vibe of each wings. Also, the game have a pretty good voice acting (Ergo wouldn't have been so funny without his voice).
It's a medieval/fantasy universe, pretty classic for a RPG but it's well executed, I really liked the universe even if I don't really like medieval fantasy. So basically, you are the Bearer of the calamities, you were in mission and somehow you ended up trapped in the Arcane and so you started to destroy the boss (The messengers) of each wings of the Arcane, won't say more so you won't get spoiled. I think that the story is not exeptional but interesting, it's worth paying attention to it and it's interesting to read the memories of the messengers (that you have to collect). You have 5 endings, the first run took me 16 hours (but I unlocked everything) and after that I took me 4 more hours to do the other endings (two of them are based on a choice in the end of the game so I just had to reload my save and redo the choice. The other two ending are very fast to do but the boss battle is nearly impossible if you are not in New game +) So if you want to do everything you will take more or less 20 hour.
Pros :
- Solid gameplay
- Beautiful design
- Well balanced difficulty
Con :
- Plateforms....

Anima is a mostly tabletop franchise that includes a wargame, a boardgame and a pen-and-paper RPG. My friend is a big fan of the series, and her recommendation is the only reason I’ve bought this game. I have zero emotional investment in it, I didn’t kickstart it, and now, 7 hours in, I’m dropping it. It’s not awful, but I’m simply not enjoying it and there are much better games in my backlog to waste my time playing another generic action RPG.
Generic is the word that describe most of the game’s features (as well as the setting it’s based on). It has some pretty, but not too memorable visuals in several levels: ruins of a burning town, lush green hills, a spooky mansion, an ancient castle — everything you would expect to encounter in a fantasy ARPG. Same goes for the enemies: most of them are magical or mechanical humanoids, but there are also some magitech metal spiders, some flying fishlike things and an actually pretty cool hydra. They are diverse enough not to be too boring, but otherwise not memorable.
One of the features the game brags about is the ability to switch between two characters mid combat. You have a moody paladin girl and an obnoxious ancient evil guy who’s constantly hitting on her and otherwise drives her mad, so she tells him to shut up — an “unlikely alliance” that has been done many times. The difference between them is almost nonexistent: most of their attacks are the same, the playstyle is the same, so the only thing this feature is good for is making the game harder (enjoyable so) by introducing enemies who are invincible to one of your characters — much like switching between red and blue magic attacks in Castlevania: Lords of Shadows. Most time dual characters stay a useless gimmick.
The writing is decent, but much too wordy. Don’t get me wrong, I love games with good stories, but size does not equal substance. NieR is one of my favorite ARPGs ever, mostly for its story, but it somehow manages to tell it without screens upon screens of text. We don’t need five pages of backstory on your generic mad artist or half-fairy kid boss! And if you do invest into storytelling, make it something one would care about!
The final nail in the joy's coffin came when I got to the 3d-platforming part. It’s incredibly hard to make right, enjoyable rather than frustrating, and here it’s frustrating as hell. I’m not sure if it’s a bug or a feature, but the game’s camera doesn’t follow your character’s back, you always need to rotate it manually. Good luck doing it while jumping on rapidly disappearing platforms.
All in all, the game is not really bad, it’s just even if you are a fan of the genre it's not good enough to choose it over the vast array of similar games, from oldies like Soul Reaver to modern ones like Darksiders.

I just finished playing "Hack 'n' Slash". And by "finished", I don't mean "completed the game"…
I got all the way to Act 4, or the "Tutorial", at which point the game expected me to modify increasingly complex graphical abstractions of Lua script. I am not a programer (not because I haven't ever tried), so this is the point where the game stopped being at all fun. I'm not saying that I couldn't possibly have figured it out and continued progressing, but…
I enjoyed what I played of this game, and don't regret purchasing it. However, I'm a bit disappointed that the game puts up such a brick wall, after what had been a fairly easy learning curve. I very quickly went from an "I am smart" feeling to a "this is the point where I fail to 'measure up'" feeling.

Hack 'n' Slash is a fun hacking based puzzle game. It has a good sense of humour and rolls out new mechanics and abilities at a nice pace; unfortunately the puzzle difficulty can be pretty spiky and I am not sure it really provides enough support for someone unfamiliar with programming to have a great time.
As the game progresses the level of abstraction increases and so there is a growing disconnect between your actions and the puzzles themselves. The end result is a puzzle solving process that is both more complicated and confusing, which means you really need to enjoy the process of experimenting in those machine states to continue to have fun.
If you enjoy programming and puzzle games I definitely recommend it otherwise I suspect there are better uses for your money.

I'm quite tired of completing a puzzle, only to have the game freeze or return me to the same screen, only to try and progress - putting in the same answer, and freezing the game in an infinite loop. Unrelated to the constant crashes and terrible UI, I think the game is cute with a great idea behind it. But it lacks any depth, is incredibly short, unpolished, and nowhere near worth the money.  For example - I thought there was a massive bug as the game starts you off in act 2, only to do some research online and find that it doesn't have an act 1. Did anyone test this game beforehand?

I'm finally starting to get stuck into act 5 of this game now 1.0 is out. It's probably one of my favourite Double Fine games ever so far. It really delivers on that concept of delving into the game code in a really clever way. I feel smart solving stuff, and don't feel like I'm being guided toward the solution in a really heavy-handed way.
It's a difficult game to get into if you're not willing to get your hands a little dirty. It rewards experimentation and isn't going to necessarily teach you all the steps so much as give you a bunch of tools and let you play. That's not to say there's no gradual introducing of concepts. There is, but it's not afraid to introduce quite a few new concepts at a time and expect you to wrap your head around that. It's a bit like SpaceChem in that you feel a little less like you're finding 'the' solution and more like you're given the tools, and with them you craft a solution. I find that very refreshing, but your mileage may vary!
One issue I've had is that the build doesn't seem entirely stable on my machine, I get a few crashes to desktop here and there. But they're pretty rare. Actually, when you mess with in-game code in such a way that would usually cause a crash, the game catches the error and lets you reload from a previous save state.

So, I highly recommend checking it out due to being so much fun and an interesting concept, but I do caution that the game is SHORT, and even more so once you get the coolest tools.  Maybe wait for a sale.

For a $30 game, I have to say it's well worth the money.
Intriguing storyline, beautiful graphics, and very well optimised, this deserves a lot of attention.
To keep it short, the combat is fairly basic with light, heavy and melee attack. Not to say that it makes the game less challenging, but it keeps gameplay very fun, thanks to the extremely fluid movement animation.
There are puzzles, and I have to say it's probably the only thing I dislike personally. Backtracking is evident to probably lengthen the game a bit, but they're also not hard so completing them won't be too much of a challenge.
The story is very engaging with use of psychosis to tell a story of a woman decending into madness - distancing herself from what is considered reality as her own mind is against her. It also helps with some game mechanics that involve such context, allowing them to fit them into the world.
Graphically, this game is astonishing. The facial animation is simply amazing, and the world created feels so immersive, however an option to remove the film grain would be nice, but it's a personal preference.
The sound design is also top notch. As some reviews have mentioned, as the game also recommends, USE HEADPHONES! It enchances the environment so well with the voices assisting you during combat and puzzles, as well as progressing the story.
Overall, I didn't expect this game to be as good as it is, considering my expectations for it were pretty high to begin with. The $30 price tag may seem like this game isn't 'full-length' or 'AAA material', however it definitely portrays itself as one, and I can't express enough how well this game turned out to be.

Quite simply if you're looking for engaging puzzles and challenging combat, you probably won't enjoy this game. This isn't Dark Souls. If you're the kind of player who loves a cinematic story and has a "stop and smell the roses" approach to exploration, you'll probably love this game.
You play as Senua, a Celtic girl who suffers from schizophrenia. Her partner was killed and his soul stolen, she travels to the viking version of hell to fight her way through and rescue his soul. You must face different gods and solve puzzles as you work your way deeper in to hell.
The story is brilliant from what I have played so far, and it's presented in a gorgeous world - the graphics are really well done. However, the main focus in this game is Senua's mental illness. There is no tutorial in this game and no arrows leading you where to go or text popups telling you what to do. Your guiding force is the voices in your head, of which there are many. They will taunt you, warn you of danger, try to fill you with doubt and argue over the top of each other - but they will generally always give you a hint of what is to come or what you need to do.
It's a unique concept and well executed, it can be interesting walking a long a high ledge and having voices mutter "look down" "no don't look down!" "you're going to die" "she won't die!".
This mental illness also plays in to a core feature of the game, the Rot. Hela, the God who rules over viking hell inflicts Senua with a rot on your hand, every time you die the rot extends - if it reaches Senua's head, it takes over and the game ends. Your progress is cleared at this point and you must start again.
Permadeath might not be for everyone, but the game isn't difficult and you would have to die a considerable amount of times before it becomes a threat.
There are a few cons to this game, the combat - while it is fluid and stylish, is very basic and not challenging. Also the puzzles are extremely repetitive and simple. This game is all about the story rather than gameplay.
The story and mental illness elements make this game a must play, just go in to it with the right expectations.

Epistory is, at it's heart, a cute game with an unravelling story. The core mechanic relies on typing: obstacles, puzzles and enemies are overcome by typing. But the game is so much deeper than that.
The level design is just brilliant. Even the seemingly random words you type hold part of the story. Lots of play on words and fun puzzles reinforce the entire world, perfecting the core mechanic.
Enemies are fun to type away, and there are four elements you can use (once you've mastered them) each with different results, giving you a varied gameplay experience and your own personal choice for combat (most of the time, anyway).
The story itself is nice. I can't really say much more without any spoilers, but I found it very enjoyable. Add the fact that world itself is telling part of it, a great voice actress, and a well-thought presentation, and you've got yourself a very fun and interesting joruney.
The game is very well paced, and it's neither too short nor too long. The progression system is neat, and unravelling the world (and the plot) feels very gratifying.
Then there's challenges for those who like to explore the game, and those who want to improve their typing skills. Hidden treasures and parts of the map, plus very cleverly thought out mechanics, and this game is a gem among a lot of mud.
As a final touch, you have the option (on by default) to use adaptive difficulty, which is a great way of not interrupting the flow of the game if you're distracted / having a bad day.
I heartily recommend this game for anyone who's looking for a fun, different game, that doesn't hold your hand through every step or insults your intelligence by making everything too easy / obvious.

WARNING: I'm a salty old man who drinks too much and hates idealistic youngsters.
I'm not quite sure who this game is for. The narrative seems like it was written by a special snowflake reflecting on her life and trying to tell the tale of growing up and the stresses of childhood vs those of adulthood through not subtle enough metaphor. The subject matter seems kid friendly at first, which makes me think this might be a good tool for teaching a daughter how to type, but by the time I'd want a child to start tackling topics like heart break and social pressure, I'd hope I'd have already taught her qwerty typing. As cautionary advice from someone who's been there, it falls flat again. The story reads like it was written by a young woman (mid to late 20s) fresh out of a tumultous time in her life (college and a couple relationships) with words of wisdom and reassurance for the younger people behind her. When the author gets a little older, she'll look back on the age she is now and realize she didn't know anything yet.
As an adult who can type, It's not terribly useful as a keyboarding instructional tool. There doesn't seem to be any way to up the difficulty to a set number of wpm and I'm not sure how well that'd work anyway. The game is entertaining enough, but the challenge portions get frustrating when 1 letter enemies come flying in and break up your flow. If I'm spelling vexation for instance, and a little thing attacks that requires me to type an x, often the game will think I misspelt vexation or it won't count it towards the word I was typing (making the correct solution to type vexxation). In any event, it is rather vexing.
I am intrigued by the language option. Will there be updates to allow me type in Spanish? That could be interesting. Hearing the dialogue in a language I don't speak would be nice too, only way it'd be new or original.
Visually, the game is appealing, if simplistic. The puzzles are clearly influenced by and seem like a simpler version of Legend of Zelda puzzles. The camera style is reminiscent of Bastion (a good thing). The music (where present) is well suited to the gameplay, though a bit more on the overworld map wouldn't have gone amiss.
Overall, it gets a recommendation, but only just, and only because the technical aspects of the game are pulled off mostly with some style and competently enough even in the rough spots. It's games like this that make me long for a third, neutral rating option. Sort of a wavy hand icon, as if to say "meh."
If you're looking for top down zelda esque game with strong narration and real life overtones, play Bastion. If you want a keyboarding program disguised as a game, Typing of the Dead is still a better buy for sheer customization options.
If you're trying to teach a youngster to type with a game, slap yourself. Then see if you can find an MSDOS copy of Reader Rabbit. Sure it's old, but you should be teaching a child to type at an age where they can't appreciate the difference between a 7 core souped up PC or a floppy disk IBM anyway, and besides, it's a better teaching tool.
If you want a more laid back, zombie-less keyboarding game with modern, but indie touched graphics and overtones of "childhood flowing into adult problems" vibe going for it, I guess this is your game.
All 8 of you young ladies in the feminist / early education / computer club at your local community college will love it.

Game play is basically:
1 - Explore the world and unlock new sections
2 - Solve puzzles (They are quite simple)
3 - Destroy obstacles and loot chests

All of this is done with your keyboard, there's no mouse input.  Even switching from Fire to Ice spell for example is done by typing "Ice" or "Fire".  Killing enemies is done by typing words.

I think the B side of this may be my favorite of the four CDs. It concludes the entirety of the series - main game, manga, and the CDs - so well that it kind of leaves a hole in my heart, especially considering how I have a total of over a hundred hours (at the time of this writing) in the lives and adventures of Yuna and co. I'd also like to consider the B side to be canon in a way, despite the obvious fourth-wall breaking, because it provides some closure for certain events that happen in the main game.
Somewhere I made a bold statement in comparing this series to Avatar, particuarly how it dealt with issues both real-world and in-universe in multifaceted ways. In both cases, this provided interesting and beautifully crafted characters that you really want to care for. In
case, the CDs reflect the sort of growth that occurs within each person. You watch (well, listen) as all of the characters from the game grow up, graduate, and leave Shirojo. Seeing Yuna in college with Miki in
was a little jarring, and hearing the broadcasting trio talk about graduating from high school shook me a bit as I realized these precious characters were growing up. It made me recall my own final years of high school and all the regrets I released and retained as that chapter in my life closed.
, after all, is about change, particularly change in oneself. If a work of fiction can make me feel a rollercoaster of emotions, well...it can't be bad, right?

: 3 updates so far and they broke a save, the game crashes when I alt-tab and audio breaks sometimes. I've reported audio and stability problems but they haven't fixed it yet. So far not going great... But don't be too alarmed, they do seem competent. Rest of review (written end of September) still below:
During the first 10 hours of playing I loved this game. And I still wouldn't refund it if possible. However I can't really recommend it. Here's why:
The camera. You'll notice as soon as you start playing, it takes hours to get used to. If a tree gets in the way the camera moves, meaning that your vehicle starts steering. You can use an alternative camera mode, but that should just be fixed.
Building is nearly impossible. Using vehicles works horribly and you can't undo, using the Tools works slightly better as long as the undo key doesn't bug out and you can see what you're doing despite the sun always being in the wrong position to see everything clearly. And 3rd person building just isn't optimal. Manual saving isn't a real option either, so if you mess something up start all over again.
So if building is not a viable option, is exploration then at least fun? Well yes and now. It's great to find other biomes, characters and weapons, but if you put viewing distance on very far you can see for what's about 50 meters while driving at normal speed and if you're in a plane at top speed you can only see 1 meter in front of you even if you're in an area you've already seen. And you're not going to use your slowest mode of transportation.
Performance wise... It's okay, but you do need a GTX750 or better to get decent graphics. This will surely change though.
All in all fun to play around for 10 hours and I'm assuming the price will rise, so I'm happy I already have the game, but I can't honestly say it's good value for the money yet. I do have faith that it will become great though, but it just needs a lot of time.

With my old GC II box-set I used to play monster custom maps that took as many hours to finish as I spent playing with other games overall. GC II feels like playing a board game that has the size of a football pitch. I kind of like its game mechanics and balance. It includes all the elements of a wide-range strategy gameplay but it does it without going too deep into them. During gameplay it means that you don't get drowned into micro management that is not a bad thing.
Ages ago there was a game called Imperium Galactica II that bests this one for me, despite the fact that is more than a decade older, because it included direct control over your planetary and space combat where your decisions could win or lose the battles (with immeasurably smaller maps I must add). With good tactics and right choices you could win against much bigger forces. I miss this "outsmarting" option from GC II where you have automated battles where the outcome has already been fixed before the encounter itself.
Anyway, it doesn't make the game any lesser. If you support the idea of LEGOing together your own spaceships and roast the hell out of your opponents with them, it would be hard to find a more capable and fun tool. Damn, you can even build your own death star.

Look, this game is amazing. I probably had 300 hours played before even getting it on Steam. It's the only worthy successor to Master of Orion 2. It's not insanely overcomplicated like MoO3 or dumbed down like Endless Space. A few caveats:
- The economy/production mechanics are significantly different than other 4x games, it takes some getting used to. Personally I like it.
- The automatic governors are pretty limited.
- The AI is extremely hostile; they'll only be your friend if your military is more powerful.
- The initial rush to colonize planets plays a huge factor because it's not until much later that you have the tech to invade and take over a planet.
Other reviews mention all the great things about GalCiv II so I don't need to go into it. Oh, and there's mods!

you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I've played for about 3 hours straight and feel that I've experienced suffiicient of the game to give a review. I'm at the bit with the shards, so I've played a good chunk so far.
TL:DR - overall I'm giving the game 8/10.
---------------------------------------------------
Pro's:
* Very well optimized. I've got the game maxed out and am running max fps constantly. Only very very few frame drops mostly when loading a new area.
* Absolutely gorgeous, I think Hellblade - Senua's Sacrifice must be one of the most beautiful games I have ever played in my life. I am playing everything maxed out on a 1080 Ti , on an Acer Predator X34a curved 3440x1440 Monitor.
* The story is intense and great so far, although not for everyone I think. Having worked with mentally ill people in the past myself (schizophrenia mostly) , I can relate to how the main character is feeling and the voices in the game. The story has not bored me and makes me want to continue playing.
* Combat is simplistic but intense. People have reported it being too easy, but this game would become very frustraing if you'd go game over all the time. I found the combat enjoyable and challenging enough to make me want to experience more. The difference in enemies could be a little more, but the boss fights have been great!
---------------------------------------------------
Cons:
* The character runs a bit slow. Some puzzles require quite a bit of running up and down which starts feeling like a drag.
* Puzzles are simple in the beginning but become more challenging throughout the game. What disappointed me was that the puzzles quickly become repetitive.
* Not really a con, but the story is a bit weird, definitely not for everyone!
---------------------------------------------------
Overall I am very happy with my purchase. It's definitely not for everyone, but it's a nice game changer. Lately I've been very bored and can't decide what to play, this game is nothing I have experienced before and is quite original. I feel there's a happy and good balance between challenging, storyline, combat, and narration.
I'm giving this game an 8/10 so far, with the main downside that the puzzles become a little bit repetitive.
I most definitely recommend buying this game, if you are into adventure games with simple but enjoyable combat, and if you don't shy away from an original, but weird storyline.

I can honestly say I couldn't be happier with this game. I saw it come across steam while searching for new games to play and jumped right in not knowing what to expect. I get a sick pleasure out of typing games and this certainly scratched that itch. What I didn't expect what such a rich and engaging storyline to go along with it. It tells the story and shapes the world around you very similarly to how Bastion did and I think it really works in it's favor. Watching the world unfold around you as you unlock it bit by bit is very rewarding as it unfolds through paper crafting it around you. The environments were unique and felt very well fleshed out with their own personalities and dynamic. The levels weren't difficult to navigate and generally made sense to get around. I found the game just challenging enough without getting overly frustrated. As you progress through the storyline you gain abilities that have various effects on the enemies you are fighting. Each has their own unique playstyle that feels like it gives you the freedom to choose how you want to play. There didn't appear to be one power that was more effective than the others, but just promoted different strategies. There were definitely times where the game forced you to use a specific power to fight the enemies, but instead of feeling bound the game choosing for me, I felt challenged as it would force you to think on your feet quickly to prioritize which enemies you went for as there would often be more than one type of element at a time. There were numerous scenarios where you were fighting enemies in wave like fashion where the game never forced you to use any one element. In terms of story, I felt like I maybe wanted a little bit more out of the ending, however there does appear to be a decent amount of replayability with upping the difficulty and the arena challenges.
Now while I enjoyed this game immensely and would recommend in a heartbeat, but there are things that I experienced that I feel should be talked about. The controls can be rather clunky at times making it difficult to navigate through some of the world. It isn't always clear what is part of the environment you can move through and what isn't. I found a couple instances where I would be working through a timed puzzle and would get stuck on an area that didn't look like it had anything hanging me up which was very frustrating. In terms of the game responding to the words I was typing felt very responsive for the most part, however I did find a couple weird issues on that front as well. There would be times that no matter what I did the words to kill an enemy would never pop up. Also, due to the perspective you are sitting in during fights it can be next to impossible to read the words from enemies very far away. It's not that they aren't popping up, but there is a distinct blur that doesn't get clear until they are basically right infront of you. The pop in of the longer words have presented problems for me as well. I understand that the longer words are supposed to be a challenge, however if a word that is like most of the alphabet long is coming from the right hand side of the screen, I won't be able to begin attempting to type it until the enemy is 5 seconds away from one-shotting me. In those instances I think it would help to zoom out from the arena a bit to give the ability to have a decent attempt at the word. There was a moment I had 3 huge monsters slithering towards me and when the words finally popped in there was a difficulty spike of damn near impossible. In issues with the enemies as well, there are moments where there are tiny flying enemies that only have one letter you have to press to kill them. This is fine through most of the game, however there are environments where you are in the sky or another light colored environment where you can't see the letter due to it blending with the background. The smaller enemies look like general non-threatening flies that add to the environment, so a combination of not seeing the letters pop up and the enemies looking like something that is always buzzing around anyway, led to some frustrating failures 5 minutes into a wave-fight that you have to start all over. My last and final gripe was the map....it never seemed to load correctly. There is no way to scroll through the level on the map and oftentimes it would just show black star-looking field of nothingness. I am sure this is something that can come through on a patch, I just hope it does.
I am excited to see how the arena aspect gets fleshed out. I don't know if the dev's are still working on it, but I think this aspect of the game will give longevity and replayability to it as you can compete against others on a world leaderboard. My only complaint there was that the first playthrough I had on arena was fairly easy and I acheived a high score on the leaderboard. However, the subsquent next times I attempted to play the same arena, the words were IMMENSELY harder and this seems to be due to the adaptive difficulty feature. I think that this feature is helpful in keeping the game at the player's pace, however I don't know the scoreboards are able to distinguish based on difficulty and score. It seems to me you could turn adaptive difficulty off and set it to the easiest difficulty and play the arena just to amass a huge score. This could use a bit of balance if that is the case.
All in all, despite it's flaws, this game was engaging enough for me to keep playing all the way through to the end and then some. I think the flaws are little tweaks that can be made to improve the game that is already fairly well-polished. The quirks aren't enough to make the game unplayable in any respect. I would like to see more games like this one and maybe even another one in the future by the dev's!

Epistory - Typing Chronicles is a typing game by heart, but a fantastic game with a beautiful world and great level design is found when you look at its layers.
The graphics of this game look fantastic. Everything from the paper mache/origami feel of the characters to the newspaper look of when the world expands; this game really utilises the Unity engine and gives something that is very unique to this game. Luckily, the graphics aren’t the only thing that makes this game unique.
The gameplay is much more than typing. You will explore the overworld; or as it’s called: “The Bridge”. Here there will be basic monsters to fight which you kill by typing, areas that can only be unlocked through abilities that you acquire as you progress through the game or other areas that has to be unlocked through ‘inspiration points’ which is the RPG element of this game. These points are given through fighting enemies and clearing dungeons.
The dungeons is where the gameplay absolutely shines. The level design is absolutely top notch with them looking simple at start but as you unlock the special ability of that dungeon lots of areas start to open up and it becomes really grand and lively. It feels amazing when you accomplish it.
Other than using Inspiration Points to unlock new areas you can use them to upgrade your character and get perks such as getting more points at a combo or making a special ability stronger so it is more effective. There is also another part of the gameplay that really focuses on fighting the monsters and this is called ‘Arena’.
You will find these arenas in dungeons and on the bridge and here you can not move as monsters come at you while you fight back and not let them get to you. While this feature is welcomed and is nice at the start; later on in the game these go on for way too long as instead of raising the intensity of the amount of monsters they just make it longer and it just drags on and becomes a bore.
I found the sound to be a hit and miss. The music is good at times and really works and emphasises on the emotional scenes but at other times it doesn’t really fit with what is happening on screen as there may a really intense moment but laid back light music is playing instead of something intense.
The narration however, is incredible with a really nice narrator telling the story of what is going on. And that leads us to the story, which is about a girl on a fox exploring the world around her but anything that was happening in the story I didn’t pick up as the narrator mainly talked about the environment and describing what the girl was feeling. So the main plot, until the end  was kind of was non-existent, but it doesn’t matter much either as a big story isn’t really needed in an overall relaxing game like this. It’s about the environments and gameplay, and that’s what this game does well.
By the I finished Epistory, I was in love with the game, even if the execution of this game was a little rough around the edges, all the elements add up to make a memorable and amazing game that shouldn’t be frowned upon just because it’s a typing game. Its unique and I recommend it to anyone willing to experience something different.
I give this game a 4.5/5

Cons:

-Arena sections go on for too long

An absolutely gorgeous Metroidvania-style game. Gorgeous sells it short - the game is a constant visual feast, with a seamless interweaving of 2d and 3d assets into a consistent hand-painted aesthetic.
The controls are responsive and feel great, and moving arond is an absolute charm, particularly after unlocking all of the powerups. Some areas can get difficult with what they expect you to execute later on, though, and dying is often quite easy. To make up for this, it uses a very interesting system where you can drop a save point almost anywhere in the game, and it will instantly respawn you at your last save point. This means that when faced with a difficult piece of platforming, you can save right beforehand and try again and again. The downside to this is there is not a sense of urgency when you attempt a puzzle, knowing how just quickly you will respawn if you fail, leading to a tendency to zerg-rush problems and become impatient.
Unlike most other Metroidvania games, the game has no true boss fights. Instead, there are intense platforming challenges that operate like boss fights. The player must quickly navigate through a challenging obstacle course, usually using whichever tools they just unlocked, and with minimal mistakes. Any mistake will generally lead to death and send the player back to the beginning of the sequence. While this is interesting on paper, I feel these are the weakest sections of the game. The player doesn't know what to expect going into it, but must execute perfectly, often taking an arbitrary path in order to survive. As a result, the first time through the game, a player must learn these sequences through trial and death, repeatedly redoing them until they finally make it through. Instead of being satisfying, by the end they can leave a feeling of frustrated impatience, like "it's about time."
The story is nothing to write home about. The setting is pretty nonsensical, but takes itself very seriously. The themes and motifs are pretty heavy-handed and awkwardly executed. Why is there a theme of compassion and kindness in a game where I must go around destroying monsters in order to progress? Where's the compassion for those creatures? Why did the world fall into chaos so easily? How are my actions able to repair everything so easily? When faced with even the smallest introspection the entire thing falls apart, and doesn't really add to the experience.
Setting those surface-level contradictions aside, the plot doesn't really matter to the fun of the game. The intro sequence  feels needlessly drawn out and it takes too long before the player has control of their character. Once the game gets going, though, the most the story intrudes is in the form of narration that plays as you navigate a new area, or through speech from the game's version of the annoying sprite. Hey! Listen! The dialogue is short enough that it doesn't get in the way, and usually pertains to where you need to go next or the power you just unlocked.
In summary, this game is fun. More than maybe any platformer I've ever played, the act of running around and jumping from platform to platform feels great. The ability to bounce off of enemies and projectiles is transformative. Honestly, they could have made a game that didn't have attacking at all and it would have been great, and perhaps even more in line with the themes of the story.

This game has zero indie hipster artsy garbage in it. Instead it's just truly amazing, well made, and awesome. Those are the sole reasons I recommend it.
What are other reasons? The graphics are amazing, although I think Trine 2 wins the best looking 2D (even though Trine isn't totally 2D) platformer contest of today. The controls are well done, smart, and never falter, and even though I usually never play these types of games on a keyboard and mouse I had no problems controlling Ori on them during the day I left my Xbox One controller at home. I still suggest using a controller.
The music is great, but the same song gets reused with different sounds surrounding it throughout the game so you'll probably have it running through your head by the end of the 8-9 hour story, which makes it even more important that the theme doesn't suck, and it does not. The story is thoughtful and a little sad but isn't tear-inducing like some other reviews I read said it was, and ends meaningfully leaving you saying "THIS GAME" when it's all over. And I'm really sad it's over.
There isn't a lot of replayability, and I can't even imagine rushing through this game to beat it in 3 hours like one of the achievements wants you to do, but if you're into that then there's a reason to keep playing along with the No Death achievement, something I'll never accomplish. While not too difficult this game does have it's WTF moments, but with one of the most inventive save systems I've ever seen (allowing you to save almost anywhere as long as you have energy) you're never short of a checkpoint and never feel angry when dying to a certain part. The game knows you have to get better to beat it, and getting better doesn't take very long at all. If I had one complaint it would be that Ori becomes blazingly overpowered about 60% through the game if you finish the combat tree first, but I still believe it has one of the best "power progressions of a main character" I've experienced recently.
If you haven't bought this game, buy it, play it, you get more game time out of it than you will in a Call of Duty single player and it costs so much less. Amazing game. It's also not Gone Home, and all of that would make me give this a 10/10 if I could.

In the little six hours I have played No Man's Sky, I can very safely say this has become of my favorite games. (hear me out) I never really followed this game or the hype that was built around it until the bad reviews started rolling in. At which point I decided to take a closer look at the reviews and what they had to say (lying, lack luster, and just overall a terrible game) blah blah so on.  It wasn't until yesterday, however, I decided to take the time and draw my own conclusions on "The worst game of 2016" or even to go as worst game ever!  I made sure to play a good while before writing this review to get a good understanding of how you do things, and what things there are to do.
Before going any further I will just say right now: If you're looking for an action packed space shoot 'em up, you will be let down!
I was aware of this before buying this game and I personally love games with a heavy emphasis on exploration which you sadly do not see more of. (Jurassic Park: Trespasser)
Off to the review now. When first I entered NMS I was very impressed with the landscape and overall scenery. It felt like I was really on another planet!  Noticing my first goal is to repair my heavily damaged ship, I head off to gather resources where I encountered many creatures both harmless, and hostile. Every creature I faced was unique and this greatly varies from planet to planet, where one may be thriving, while another can be completely baron. HOWEVER! This is not exactly a good thing, as it is so varied that some planets have laughable beasts that cannot be taken seriously and breaks the immersion. Almost like spore creatures made by a young child.. the algorithm for this is a little messy, but most times it makes some very interesting animals!  Which makes venturing out to other worlds very very fun for me.  But the interaction with player and the animals is almost non existent. This being said, this greatly hinders what NMS could be, seeing as interaction is one of the main keys to gameplay.
Moving on to resource gathering and base exploring.
Gathering resources for you or your ship is pretty average I must agree and I could see how this could get reptitive. But it is the way of getting to the materials you need that makes it fun. going in caves, climbing atop a vantage point to get a better view of your surroundings, exploring different parts of the worlds, and sometimes facing a dangerous run in with the beings that inhabit the world you are alien to or shooting down drones.
Base and ruin exploring is generally the same as resource gathering but you get the satisfying feeling of learning a new word, or obtaining a rare item!
Overall No Man's Sky is a very fun game for what it is and not what it was hyped up to be. If you have the time to explore distant lands and get the enjoyment out of doing so with tidbits of action, this is definately the game for you.
No Man's Sky has given me a very good memorable gaming experiance that no other game has given me. And for that I can't really complain.
I look forward to future updates on this flawed, yet amazing game

It's a game known for its humour, (see the Republic of Dave section for example), yet it can take itself fairly seriously at times. The RPG elements of the game work well, thought not as many customisation options as you might be expecting if you're comming straight from Fallout 4.
In fact, every moment you spend reading this review is a moment wasted, a moment you could've spent downloading Fallout 3 already. Seriously, get it!
