So far, from what I've played from the game, I am not insanely impressed and I will probably be asking for a refund.
I got it because I had a craving for a third person action RPG and it looked similar to NiER which I greatly enjoyed. There is a ton of potential here - the art design is outstanding, the game has nice music and it has an interesting character dynamic.
But ultimately what determines how good a game is is the gameplay and it feels too unpolished. Even a B-level game like NiER had more fluid feeling combat. I really wanted to like it, but it is basically up to the level of a PS2 era hack and slash and it's hard to get past that when you KNOW you could be playing a better hack and slash RPG. It sucks because I really do want to see more 3D games from indie developers, 2D is overdone and boring. But then I am reminded of exactly why few indies make 3D games, there is a high bar to overcome and it takes a skilled game designer to make sure that the game doesn't feel amateurish, which this game feels like.
That leaves the story to make up for the failings of the battle system so it better be damn good. And well... the story is JRPG-esque, which is good, but the dialogue is a little too awkward. It's not bad, but it's not incredible either, and the lack of any animation during cutscenes certainly doesn't bolster the impact of the story. The personality of Ergo never really rises to that of, say, a Grimoire Weiss from NiER or Gig from Soul Nomad. And switching to him in battle is... literally the same as the other "Bearer" character. There is not much "light and dark" dynamic going on when both types of attacks are the same thing.
Ultimately I think with some more money invested in the game polishing the gameplay and the cutscenes it would be a good game, and I commend them for trying to make a third person action RPG with a JRPG bent, but in its current state it's too unpolished to make me want to keep playing, at least for the current price.

Does this game have a brilliant concept?
Yes.
Is this game enjoyable for the general public?
Eh.
It's quite special for a developer to get an idea that rubs down to: Hey, isn't it fun to let players alter the game the way they like and hack almost anything?
But, somewhere down the line of production, I guess they forgot to realize how user-unfriendly this game can get beyond Act 4. It's not puzzle, oh no, not your every day 'explore-and-find-clues' puzzle, it's a confusing, excrusiatingly painful coding experience.
Worst of all, this game -crashes-, and by that I mean ALL the time. Any event where you mess up on either hacking things, digging into Algorithm, you have the potential to slam into different kind of bugs that the developer didn't iron out. If you hit too many bugs, it wouldn't even allow you to go back to your previous setting (An item in game that basically rewind what you do), forcing you to shut down the game and restart.
Option menu is totally devoided of any options other than choosing fullscreen/window mode, as well as sound. Where is the graphic options?
All around, it's a game with potential, but is underdeveloped. It's baffling that this game can even win an indie game award with the state it currently is in.

This game does not do a good job of explaining its mechanics, let alone its higher-level concepts. What begins as a generally fun and interesting educational puzzle game quickly devolves into a frustrating mess. The conveyance and presentation of important concepts, most notably the algorithm puzzles, is opaque. The paper-thin storyline, flat dialogue, and cardboard-cutout characters do nothing to make the puzzle headache worthwhile.
There are definitely a couple of good ideas that went into this game, but they're not developed adequately in the short playtime. The scarcity of interactive elements in the world makes the whole experience feel perfunctory and lifeless. With the sole exception of the clever and engaging boss fight with the corrupted turtle king early in the game, none of this really felt very fun. I managed to inadvertently skip about half of the prison level by rushing past the boss with the movement speed hack, which screwed me a bit later in the game as I was unable to decipher the runes made visible with the Third Eye Hat. The feeling the experience most left me with overall is confusion and frustration.
It took me about 3 hours in total to complete Hack N Slash, but I gave up and consulted a walkthrough upon being trapped in the algorithm puzzle caves of act IV. Had I not, I would likely never have been able to finish the game. Perhaps everything would have made more sense to a programmer, but it didn't to me and Double Fine made little effort to ameliorate that. Overall, this game is not worth $20. Pick it up for $5 if you can, but you're not missing much if you give it a miss entirely.

This series used to be good, and it still is in a way.  But after the adjective system was added, the challenge, and the value of most of the game, was lost.  What used to be a game that tested your ability in word association has now turned into a game about making up nonsensical items.  The ways you can solve puzzles now are so easy; you could complete a majority of the game using nothing but sticks.  Here are a few examples:
"Make an item that will put out this fire." CRYING STICK
"Prepare a steak for this customer" COOKING STICK
"Make something for this art museum" BEAUTIFUL MODERN STICK
"Give Santa something he likes, but doesn't already have" MERRY STICK
"Scare away the Vampire" HOLY STICK
"Make this date more romantic" ROMANTIC STI- actually, don't use that one.
Point is, the game has been simplified by this mechanic, and it doesn't reward you in any way for being logical or creative.  Kinda sad, because if they did, you would have a clear, straight upgrade of a game from the first Scribblenauts.  The workshop is flooded with poor remakes of copyrighted characters; something that was purposely left out in the original games.  Its a shame I can't recommend this, because the amount of work put into the engine and content would definitely be worth the $20 price tag if the single player wasn't so absurdly easy.  The most enjoyable part of this game is derping around like its a sandbox game.  If that sounds like something you would get a kick out of, by all means buy this.  Just know that the single player ain't worth♥♥♥♥♥♥
PS: This game has a sequel with DC Comic characters in it.  Same kind of game play, and the addition of DC characters doesn't do much for the game itself.  About the only thing that it does is add visual assets to the workshop mods.  So... you're not really missing much in that one either :v  I guess go for it if you are a fan of derping and comic book hero's?

I really didn't want to give this a negative review, but cannot justify recommending this without some clearly defined caveats. It seems many steam reviews have at most 2 hours clocked, and if you were to ask me during that period if I recommend the game it would be an unqualified yes. Things change by mid-game though.
The game's artwork is absolutely majestic, and watching the game is like watching a painting in motion. The praise continues to the characters and minimal setup for the "story" which is conveyed exceptionally well in the first few scenes.
However, the high quality of the first few moments does not hold up in the game's design and especially the difficulty level.
DIFFICULTY is the main factor for the negative review.
It's a brutally unforgiving game requiring pixel-perfect jumping and timing. This is one of the few games I've played recently when my hands have cramped up and hurt terribly after game sessions on the gamepad. Attempting to play for anything more than 30 minutes at a time is a recipe for controller-throwing frustration.
Enemy placement seems deliberately cruel where enemy behavior and firing arcs are very unpredictable. It's not uncommon to go through a very tough, difficult platforming areas only to be blinked out of existence in a fraction of a second by a powerful enemy. This is compounded by the fact that many enemies are tedious or, in some portions, impossible to kill.
And you will be blinked out of existence very, very often. Although health and attack upgrades are available, enemies remain difficult to kill and will usually take 65-75% of your health in a single hit. Most enemies are also ranged and leave behind explosive "residue" which makes platforming sections with enemies extremely unforgiving. You can technically save anywhere, but this costs valuable energy and many sections are designed to not give you a "break" to do so.
The platforming sections require immaculate timing, and after the mid-game, many of them rely on your ability to "jump" off of fired enemy projectiles. However, because enemies fire unpredictably, you will VERY frequently failed and instantly get killed by spikes whilst waiting for an enemy to fire a projectile right where you need to jump. As the game wears on, these sections get more elaborate and more "random" in the sense that you just have to hope this time the stars align and enemies fire where you need to go.
So the main qualifier is this, when considering whether you should buy Ori. Are you an exceptionally patient gamer willing to deal with extremely infuriating platforming? Are you okay with losing again and again not because you aren't skilled but simply because the game, at that moment, didn't reward you with a favorable situation?
Personally, I would recommend buying Rayman Legends, it's a far higher quality game with amazing artwork and gameplay that won't cause you to pop an aneurysm.

I've played for about 3 hours straight and feel that I've experienced suffiicient of the game to give a review. I'm at the bit with the shards, so I've played a good chunk so far.
TL:DR - overall I'm giving the game 8/10.
---------------------------------------------------
Pro's:
* Very well optimized. I've got the game maxed out and am running max fps constantly. Only very very few frame drops mostly when loading a new area.
* Absolutely gorgeous, I think Hellblade - Senua's Sacrifice must be one of the most beautiful games I have ever played in my life. I am playing everything maxed out on a 1080 Ti , on an Acer Predator X34a curved 3440x1440 Monitor.
* The story is intense and great so far, although not for everyone I think. Having worked with mentally ill people in the past myself (schizophrenia mostly) , I can relate to how the main character is feeling and the voices in the game. The story has not bored me and makes me want to continue playing.
* Combat is simplistic but intense. People have reported it being too easy, but this game would become very frustraing if you'd go game over all the time. I found the combat enjoyable and challenging enough to make me want to experience more. The difference in enemies could be a little more, but the boss fights have been great!
---------------------------------------------------
Cons:
* The character runs a bit slow. Some puzzles require quite a bit of running up and down which starts feeling like a drag.
* Puzzles are simple in the beginning but become more challenging throughout the game. What disappointed me was that the puzzles quickly become repetitive.
* Not really a con, but the story is a bit weird, definitely not for everyone!
---------------------------------------------------
Overall I am very happy with my purchase. It's definitely not for everyone, but it's a nice game changer. Lately I've been very bored and can't decide what to play, this game is nothing I have experienced before and is quite original. I feel there's a happy and good balance between challenging, storyline, combat, and narration.
I'm giving this game an 8/10 so far, with the main downside that the puzzles become a little bit repetitive.
I most definitely recommend buying this game, if you are into adventure games with simple but enjoyable combat, and if you don't shy away from an original, but weird storyline.

My enemy and I swing at exactly the same time, my enemies blow lands first and knocks me to the ground. In the little six hours I have played No Man's Sky, I can very safely say this has become of my favorite games. (hear me out) I never really followed this game or the hype that was built around it until the bad reviews started rolling in. At which point I decided to take a closer look at the reviews and what they had to say (lying, lack luster, and just overall a terrible game) blah blah so on.  It wasn't until yesterday, however, I decided to take the time and draw my own conclusions on "The worst game of 2016" or even to go as worst game ever!  I made sure to play a good while before writing this review to get a good understanding of how you do things, and what things there are to do.
Before going any further I will just say right now: If you're looking for an action packed space shoot 'em up, you will be let down!
I was aware of this before buying this game and I personally love games with a heavy emphasis on exploration which you sadly do not see more of. (Jurassic Park: Trespasser)
Off to the review now. When first I entered NMS I was very impressed with the landscape and overall scenery. It felt like I was really on another planet!  Noticing my first goal is to repair my heavily damaged ship, I head off to gather resources where I encountered many creatures both harmless, and hostile. Every creature I faced was unique and this greatly varies from planet to planet, where one may be thriving, while another can be completely baron. HOWEVER! This is not exactly a good thing, as it is so varied that some planets have laughable beasts that cannot be taken seriously and breaks the immersion. Almost like spore creatures made by a young child.. the algorithm for this is a little messy, but most times it makes some very interesting animals!  Which makes venturing out to other worlds very very fun for me.  But the interaction with player and the animals is almost non existent. This being said, this greatly hinders what NMS could be, seeing as interaction is one of the main keys to gameplay.
Moving on to resource gathering and base exploring.
Gathering resources for you or your ship is pretty average I must agree and I could see how this could get reptitive. But it is the way of getting to the materials you need that makes it fun. going in caves, climbing atop a vantage point to get a better view of your surroundings, exploring different parts of the worlds, and sometimes facing a dangerous run in with the beings that inhabit the world you are alien to or shooting down drones.
Base and ruin exploring is generally the same as resource gathering but you get the satisfying feeling of learning a new word, or obtaining a rare item!
Overall No Man's Sky is a very fun game for what it is and not what it was hyped up to be. If you have the time to explore distant lands and get the enjoyment out of doing so with tidbits of action, this is definately the game for you.
No Man's Sky has given me a very good memorable gaming experiance that no other game has given me. And for that I can't really complain.
I look forward to future updates on this flawed, yet amazing game

The three main characters in the game - a wizard, thief and knight become 'fused' together allowing you pick the relevant character for the task at hand. Along the way experience is picked up which you can apply to one of the three characters as you see fit. The only gripe I've yet comes across wih the game is the absurdly large gap between checkpoint saves - which can see you redoing literally several minutes of a stage if all three characters die.
Aside from that, I'd highly recommend Trine as an enjoyable, beautiful and quite cerebral game. 8/10.

This game get a NO from me for several reasons.
As a TL;DR here is a list
- No objective indicator/map/sense of direction whatsoever
- Extremely difficult to grasp system of functions etc
- Frustrating atmosphere in general coupled with clunky controls
As a more in depth version:
The fact that there is no objective indicator or map or something may seem like a modern gamers lazy complaint, but it really isn't. For a game as complex as this there really should be an objective indicator for those who want to progress the story. Those who want to fiddle about with any piece of code they can touch can do that if they want, but for those who want to go towards progression at all times, this game is very frustrating. I found myself wandering aimlessly several times with not a clue where to go until I looked up a guide, or simply stopped playing in anger. To be clear: I was not stuck on puzzles, I just had no idea where to go to get to the next puzzle etc.
The way the code is presented to you is very hard to understand. I am currently a computer science student at my university, so I know how to write code and make programs, mainly in Java, C, C++ etc, at the moment, and not Lua itself, but I know that no language looks like this game tries to make it look. Apparently it is based on the games Lua bytecode which FYI is not meant to be read by humans, it is meant for the computer to compile. If it were based on actual Source Code for the game, maybe it would be easier to grasp. But the implication of those weird crystals to represent hundreds of different things inside functions? Forget it. I can normally grasp programming ideas pretty quickly and easily, but in this game, I couldn't understand a thing during Act 5. This also links back to the previous point, if I was told perhaps what place to search in or maybe what function to investigate, not specifically what to do etc but at least a clue? Maybe then it would be easier to see what needed to be modified. Others may disagree with this one, but I personally found it very hard to grasp.
The entire atmosphere of this game is basically designed to be annoying. The sounds get extremely repetitve and annoying e.g going in and out of several functions in short amount of time. This also ties in with the first point, when wandering aimlessly not knowing where to go, I get frustrated a lot easier, so this may contribute to the fact that I'm complaining about this as well.
ALL IN ALL I think this game could have been great with different execution, and easier to understand interfaces/functions and such. As it is, I will not be completing it without a walkthrough of the (final?) Act 5, as I cannot progress on my own from here it seems.

I had thought I was buying another game.  I've been trying to play it, but upgrading the ship designs is a bit more complicated than it needs to be...I don't know why we have to keep the original design of every ship in the shipyard when it is so completely outdated.

Games are long, and without much action, especially if you use a relatively peaceful strategy-- and peaceful strategies, executed properly, are so massively overpowered that you'd be a fool not to use them. The ship design system incorporates a lot of meaningless cosmetic elements to try and disguise its fundamental shallowness. Ignore all of the aesthetic stuff and underneath you'll find a very basic system without any art to building a good ship. Just put on the defenses and weapons that counter what your enemy has and that's it. Due to the lack of tactical combat, ships will all fight the same way no matter what kind of weapons they're armed with.
Economic management is tedious and ultimately irrelevant in face of the fact that, if you're using a peaceful strategy, you can ultimately build whatever you want and then get the AI to pay for it using the diplomacy system.
I'd say skip this one and find yourself a more interesting 4x.

A very interesting concept, but I see several issues with this game.
Cons:
* It's absolutely NOT recommended for people with no programming/algorithmics knowledge. The first half of the game should be doable by almost anyone, but as soon as actual code is shown and modifiable (end of Act 4 and all of Act 5), it can be overwhelming.
* The code you can hack is displayed in a very hard to understand way. I heard it's based on the game's Lua bytecode. Why not let people see/modify the source code instead? Bytecode is not meant to be read by humans.
You can see the code as text, or there is a sort of visual representation with machines and crystals, but it's just too confusing. As a professional programmer, I grasped most of it, but I think most people won't.
* The graphics look mostly bad. The characters are OK but the backgrounds... The level design is meh, with many useless paths and dead ends.
* The music is forgettable
* A bit on the short side, with low replay value unless you just want to test how far you can go with the hacking. But then why not program your own game instead?
* The ending is surprising but weird, nonsensical and abrupt to me.
Pros:
* Awesome base concept
* Some of the puzzles are quite cleverly made
* The "Double Fine touch" is here, with quirky characters and dialogs, but it's a bit weak. Psychonauts is way better in that regard.
* It's challenging for your brain for those who like that.
Not really a pro nor a con:
* Near the end I think I skipped an important scene completely with hacking. That's pretty cool but I'm missing part of the story!
* It's only in English. I didn't really mind even though I'm French, but some people will. I think it would be really hard to translate such a game anyway (all the game's variables and functions would have to be translated)
Conclusion:
If you are a programming junkie, a bit curious, or just want to challenge your brain, buy this game when it gets cheaper. Otherwise I think it will just be a frustrating experience and you will not enjoy it.

HACKED:
~~~~~~~
Are you a fan of match three / puzzle games? If you are, you are going to be hooked when playing HACKED!
In HACKED you are in control of a canon which is located at the bottom your screen. This Canon shoots colour orbs and you can move it horizontally. Your goal is to eliminate all orbs in each level with a minimum number of shots. For example, you need to clear all orbs with eight shots; if you manage to do better or par you will earn a golden star. Some orbs have power up within them and it is very easy to recognize them as they have either an icon or an effect on them.
The ones with an icon have power up for your canon: the like of grenades, bullets, spike balls and ghosts. By using the grenade, it will destroy a large number of orbs. If you decide to shoot a spike ball, it will clear all orbs that come in contact with it but only from the direction of the shot and the other one you will have to play to find out what they do!
The orbs with the lightning effect on them will destroy all orbs of the same colour when you activate them. A total of ten power ups is available.
How do you die in this game, you may wonder? Well, on both sides of the screen there is a gauge. Each time you shoot an orb and miss a match three, or you move the canon too frequently, the gauge will go up and as soon as it reaches the top of the screen all orbs will be pushed down. If an orb reaches the bottom of the screen, you die!
Plenty of game modes in HACKED. The arcade has five different modes within it and the levels are progressively harder. You will have to earn a certain number of golden stars to unlock some of them, which gives you a fair bit of replay-ability. In the classic one, you can choose your level of difficulty (easy, normal or hard) as well as one of three types of modes you want to play. They are Standard, Marathon and Time Attack. You can also create your own level and share it with the entire Steam community.
The graphics are standard for this genre of game. The music is pumping but not to my liking, I must admit. Thank god we can turn it on and off.
Positives:
~~~~~~~

-	100 levels
-	Several modes of play
-	Create your own levels and share it with the community
-	Good price point
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Annoying soundtrack
-	No trading cards
HACKED is a fun, addictive casual puzzle game at a good price point!
7/10

It took me all of about 20 min playing this before I knew I was going to love it. And after about three hours I knew that it was going to be one of my favorite games of all time. The visuals and the audio are what stand out the most when you first get into the game.  The way that it throws you right into the game with Senua and her voices. As you get further into the game, it becomes quickly apparent that this is like nothing you've ever played before. The HUD is nowhere to be seen, but is replaced by a series of visual and auditory cues that really make the game feel less like a game and more like a lived experience (just you and the voices in your head fighting your way through the horrors of the North lands).
In combat, you feel less like a nameless badass like you might in some other games and more like a real person, fighting to survive - when you get knocked down for the third time it's harder to get up in time to dodge that kill strike that's coming for you. Out of combat, the game plays like a startlingly beautiful mash up of Silent Hill and Layers of Fear, where you try and work your way through puzzles that trick your eyes and your mind and force you to try and think the way Senua might, all the while having to deal with a barrage of voices bickering and offering suggestions from the corners of Senua's mind until you want to scream at them to shut up.
In short, this is already one of my favorite games I've ever played. It's not what you're expecting. It's not what you think it's going to be. It's so much more.

⭕️ If your looking for a good WW2 shooter I can safely say that Brothers in Arms: Earned In Blood is a great gem. It’s a shooter that excels in friendly AI and squad command systems. It may be an old game by the time of this review (2017), but it holds up well. However, you need to also remind yourself that your playing a game that came from a decade ago. This game can feel a bit clunky and the graphics are not super amazing as today’s standards, but give the game a chance. I'd give this game a resounding ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐/ 10. (8/10).
❤️Pros:
⚪Squad commands
- Not many games have AI that is actually helpful to you but EIB has perfected (at the time) helpful allies
⚪Tactics
- This game is primarily suppressing your foes and trying to look for ways to flank. It makes you think how to get around enemies to finish them off while your squad is suppressing them.
💔Cons:
⚪Story
- It's typically your run of the mill paratrooper story. You drop into Europe and get disorganized. Fight your way to your main objective.
⚪Controls
- The default key bindings are a little messy imo. With the addion of your squad commands you can be slightly overwhelmed on your button mapping. You can kind bind but I only wished they had a ADS hold rather than toggle, but thats just me.
⚪Graphics
- It's a game from a decade ago, I really shouldn't put this as a Con but just putting it out there. It's not SUPER amazing like the games we have now.

Brothers in Arms Earned in Blood wow what can I say...
Best damn WWII game I ever played period. As of now I have 50 hours, and have completed the game on Authentic the hardest difficulty. If I ever have children, and they are of the prerogative to play video games this is the♥♥♥♥♥♥I'd like them to play. Not mindless run, and gun Cod, or the SJW ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t of today. Brothers in Arms Earned in Blood puts the player in a Sargents position. You are in command of a fire team which lays suppression, and an assualt team which flanks. You must play this game tactically to win. Enemies have pinpoint accuracy which means you must use cover, and suppresion to your advantage. Timing, and positioning is everything. You have an overview mode which allows you to see enemy positions to plan your movements, and assualt.
Beautiful orchestral soundtrack which gives a vibe of patriotism,  honor, valour, and adventure in a time of war. Fun tactical gameplay that relies on strategy. The game does hinder your aim, by nerfing it with some shifting making it hard to hit enemies. Although with practice I never had a problem nailing nazis from a distance with the Garand, or spraying them down with a B.A.R, or Thompson.
Which brings me to the weapons. I love the sounds. I love how beefy the Garand sounds. I love spraying the Thompson. It sounds mean as hell. Brothers in Arms did the American armament justice in this game. However the German weapons are in fact better. The kar98 has a really good sight picture, and is very accurate. The Mp40 is the best SMG in the game. The STG44 ( Sturmgewehr 44 ) is easily the best gun in the game. You will find that the firepower, and accuracy of the STG 44 will soften enemy positions allowing you to make more bold power moves on the enemy. However late into the game there will be FG 42 machine guns even with scopes. And the scoped FG 42 is perhaps the best gun in the game. I give it to the St44 though for the ammo capacity over the FG 42. Still those guns are the best.
The German war machine throws everything at you, and the kitchen sink. As a U.S Paratrooper in the 101st you will land behind enemy lines on D-Day. You will come across Wehrmacht (Heer Soldiers) Waffen SS, Fallschirmjäger, Stugs, Panzers, Tiger Tanks, entrenched machine gun positions, motar teams firing in your direction, Halftracks with mounted machine guns maneuvering to your flank. 88's firing artillery at you. You must find your enemy, fix their position, and flank them to win. Standing your ground, and trading lead all day is not an option. In some cases enemy motars will fix your positions. You must use your head, and be fast.
There is so much enjoyment to be had from this game. The playstyle I developed was to supress, and fix enemies fast, hitting them hard with the assualt team up close while I try to flank. On authentic difficulty the key is to listen to your battle-buddies because they will indicate emeny suppresion. "They're scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ / We got em pinned ect" Because in authentic there are no suppresion indicators like in normal or easy modes.
Did I mention you command a Stuart tank, a Sherman, and a Hellcat tank destoyer in certian levels? Telling your tank where to go, and who to attack is a challenge in itself. 88's, anti tank guns, and German infantry with panzerfäust pose a threat.
This game is a classic, and you unlock history facts, and extras by completing missions. You get a feel of brotherhood by the character personalities in the story. ( I have played all three games of the BiA franchise) I must say out of all three games this one is my favorite.
Arcade games that are hard, and require repetition for skill are my cup of tea. On authentic the game punishes you by not including save points. So you must complete an entire mission flawlessly. A daunting, and challenging task. They don't make video games like they used to back in the day. But that is what I like about this game. Strategy, and skill is required.
All this to say I reccomend this game. But not to those expecting a mindless run, and gun like Cod. If you want a challenge, and a strategic, historical fps this game is for you. But if you want to mindlessly run around and spray while streaming, and drinking a starbuck coffee then move your♥♥♥♥♥ This game is not for you son.
I'll be fond of this game for many years to come... It's perhaps even one of my favorite video games of all time as of now. I love it. And that will conclude my review. Show this game some love it deserves it.

I'm a fast typist and have always wanted a challenging typing game. I bought this game on a whim and was pleasantly surprised with a great dramatic story dialogue, a mix of simple puzzle elements (mostly a hybrid of Legend of Zelda and Undertale-esque floor puzzles), cool upgrades, hidden-item secrets and thoughtful level design. The game is presented to you in a dungeon format and features an unlockable skill tree progression of your choosing. This is neat, because you can cater to your own play style for an easier or more challenging game early on (although you'll eventually unlock all skills).
Everything in the game is done through typing - including the ability to navigate the pause menu (opened with the Tab key, how clever), movement, attacking and changing skills. Enemies crawl towards you (on easier difficulties, they move slower) and if you're hit once, you have to redo the encounter from the beginning. If desired, you can change difficulty on the fly with no penalty. For achievement hunters, note that there are no achievements related to difficulty setting.
I used to play Typing of The Dead on my SEGA Dreamcast a lot and even picked up the new one, but it always lacked a challenge and isn't difficult to complete without dying if you're a good typist. With Epistory, the hard mode in combination with adaptive difficulty feels just right. Skills affect enemies in different ways and on harder difficulties, you need to use them effectively - being able to switch skills on the fly opens for really unique ways to tackle different situations.
As a learning tool for typing, I can see this game as being quite effective. The game itself has only cartoon monster violence and no explicit language in it's stock dictionary list (the author plans on implementing Steam Workshop support for community submitted dictionary lists, however). Multitasking is encouraged with skills, but you are only typing one word at a time - not sentences. Since the majority of the dictionary has short words, this has the benefit of reinforcing muscle memory quickly. The game would be best used for learning in combination with another typing tool or website utilizing full sentences, however.
My only complaint is that I do not feel in-game statistics (viewable at the title screen) of words per minute are accurately assessed. This isn't a huge deal and beginning typists should familiarize themselves with knowing where the keys are before chasing such numbers. I can only surmise this inaccuracy is due to the way words will slowly crawl onto the screen, as well as the typing of short bursts, but I don't know how the game timer calculates WPM. In other words, in a real world scenario, you will be typing full sentences and not waiting for words to crawl onto the screen at a varying pace.
During boss encounters, the game throws hordes of enemies at you. This is when the game gets very fun and tests your ability to type short bursts of words in as little time possible. Once you defeat the boss, however, you cannot replay that same boss battle again without starting the game over (normal dungeon and overworld enemies will continue to respawn upon re-entry, even after completion). At the time of writing, the multiplayer mode is not present, but it's my understanding the online multiplayer aspect will feature a boss battle sort of scenario - allowing you to continue practicing in this fashion.
Epistory took me about seven and a half hours to complete with all skills, unlocking all of the overworld and doing a lot of optional stuff on the hardest difficulty with adaptive on. Further replayability lies in multiplayer and achievements, which are mostly just replaying the game again to get more kills. Still, this is the best typing game I've ever played and worth it even at full price!

One question I see about this game is "Do I need to know how to program to play this game?"
Yes. Yes, you do. Or you need to be willing to sit down with a reference book for a few hours before having any chance of finishing the game, although the first half is totally doable with minimal programming knowledge.
The game does try to have a reasonable learning curve, but it is not meant to teach you programming. You will have to do that yourself.
I would say that 1-2 years of computer science background is ideal for this game. Less than that and it's going to be a huge chore. Much more than that and it's going to be pretty easy (although still very fun).
The short version:
Do you like programming? Do you like games? How does a game that involves tinkering with programs sound? Interesting? Buy it!

Trine is an excellent, gorgeous little game in the same vein as the old 2D side-scroller, The Lost Vikings.  Through a twist of fate, an unlikely trio (thief, mage, and knight) become soulbound to one another via a mysterious artifact known only as the Trine.  Now they must tolerate their newly-shared existences and put each of their unique skills to good use in order to break the spell - and perhaps discover something more in the process.
Gameplay consists of one on-screen character at a time, with the ability to switch between any of the three at any time.  Use the thief to swing across gaps and shoot enemies from afar, the mage to create weighted cubes to solve puzzles, and the knight to slay and defend against the undead who would try to stop the trio in their search. Victory and discovery yield EXP, and as the team levels up, their abilities expand and improve.  The game also has a wry sense of humor.

I bought this blindly to test out a new keyboard, so you can imagine my surprise when a "typing game" actually turns out to be an expansive RPG with a challenging and complex battle system and a touching story. In fact, the typing-game-connotations aren't doing this game any favors, since it has more in common with Bastion, Okami or Darksiders - it has a gradually expanding overworld, themed dungeons, elemental powerups that also act as gating abilities to access certain areas, secrets and collectibles, side activities like monster-nest removal, etc. The combat tests more than just your typing skills, asking you to switch between elements on the fly (by actually typing the element's name) and using the right elements on the right targets (by judging their size, the complexity of their words, and the speed they're approaching you) in the right order. It makes for some pretty nail-biting encounters, and more than a few deaths.
I was pleasantly surprised with how the story integrates into the gameplay. The game has no cinematics, and never leaves the isometric perspective, so storytelling falls to the voice-over narration and, more importantly, the level design. The girl-riding-a-fox-and-fighting-insects fantasy plot allegorically tells the biography of a woman, and every dungeon depicts a pivotal moment in her life. E.g., the "water temple" is a puzzle-filled greek ruin under constant threat of a flood, mirroring the woman's stressful college years. This is conveyed through visual design, subtle narration (occasionally in another voice, which always signifies the woman in question speaking outside of the fantasy plot), details like the enemies having academic terms as their "health bars," and that dungeon's collectibles, which together make a picture of a graduation ceremony. It's a really nice way to freshen up the classical Ocarina-of-Time level progression.

What a lovely game. What a lovely game! I'm only 1.5 hours in, but I want to type a couple of words here before I forget.
I can already say that it is well worth the money, and unless this game ends in like 30 minutes or less from where I am I'd even venture to say they should up it a bit, because 14,99€ seems like an absolute steal.
The typing feels great and thrilling - some encounters are really hectic, and pulling off a perfect spree when it's practically hailing words and letters at you makes you feel awesome. There is also a "dynamic difficulty"-setting which is hard to measure without knowing how it works, but it seems to me like the difficulty adapted pretty well. I feel that the challenge is just right to not be frustrating but still make me sweat a bit.
The world is very pretty with the crumpled paper look, and it's really sweet how it unfolds before your eyes.
The narration is stellar, well-paced and delivered in a way that befits a world that unfolds piece by piece as you explore it. Really draws me in and makes the experience feel really special.
The music is also great. I remember getting shivers down my spine when the music emphasized the sudden dramatic turn in the narration in the beginning. I feel like that sync between music and narration was lost a bit after the intro bit though, not as much well-timed changes that amplify the narration, but maybe I'm just a bit too focused on typing words like a raging lunatic to notice now.
One small gripe I have is that it becomes a bit tricky to follow the narration that happens during hectic fights because the audio seems to be overcome by the sound fx of magic being fired and enemies dying. Might be a setting to increase the volume of the narration, but I think the sound level is perfect out of combat, so not sure if that's a good solution for me.
As a final note, it takes a bit of getting used to the proposed control scheme(EFJI), but after a while it starts feeling natural and doesn't cause any noteworthy grief. I missclick from time to time, but no problem really, and it's getting earier all the time. If you really can't stand it they've enabled ordinary WASD-movement as well, so it shouldn't be a problem for anyone.
I absolutely, absolutely recommend this game if you even slightly enjoy typing-games. Even if you aren't a huge fan, this might be the title to win you over since the world and the narration draws you in.

Comparative review: Bastion meets Typing of the Dead with a touch of Zelda.
It tells its story in a very interesting way. Literally a storybook that's being created as you move about the world. The core mechanic is switching into a "typing mode" and quickly typing out words hovering over the environment, chests, and enemies. Typing quickly extends a combo meter and when the meter is finished, it adds XP to your level bar. The XP bar gates abilities and places you can go. As you unlock new areas, new dungeons are discovered. Within these dungeons are "tools" that grant you new special abilities. The two I've encountered so far is my attacks/typing are now Fire & Ice based. By entering "typing mode" I can switch between them by typing "fire" or "ice". Fire burns enemies after the first correctly spelled word (most enemies take two words to defeat) and Ice will stop an enemy for a period of time. Since your character dies after being touched by an enemy, combat consists of using your typing skills to pick the right targets and switching between your two attacks.
My only criticism is that the movement is a little clunky. It Tries to teach you an alternative control screen at the start of the game but I found myself naturally using WASD to move. It works well enough and you can quickly put points into movement speed (and a sprint skill) but traversing the world feels very rigid.
Apparently the difficulty adjusts as you play the game. The worse you are at typing, the easier the words are. I spend my entire day typing so I'm getting some very long and difficult words thrown at me. There have been a few occasions where part of a word was not inputted since I was typing too fast. This isn't a normal occurrence, however.
Did I mention you are a young girl riding around on a fox being narrated by a the author writing a book? I probably should have mentioned that.
I really recommend this. Despite it being very Bastion, it's incredibly unique.

A fun game with a lot of really poor design choices nevertheless... is what I said before playing it for a bit.  Now I just think it's awful.  It reminds me of the PS1 era in a lot of ways, both good and bad, like by having a big mysterious world with not a lot of direction, kind of like Soul Reaver - definitely a point in its favour.  Camera and combat are decidedly PS1 era with the many many flaws that plagued those games as well.  One of the earliest enemies in the game (the light/dark elemental) occurs in large numbers that like to hide outside your field of view and spam knockdown projectiles.  The target locking is terrible and will frequently work against you, which is especially aggravating when you've got enemy types that are invincible to one or the other character.
Everything I've encountered thus far uses knockdown attacks and nothing else, which makes combat choppy and severely lacking in flow.  You, on the other hand, are lucky if you even stun the things you hit.  Generally, they barely react to being struck at all.  Switching characters (largely pointless anyway) has a slight delay that makes doing it in combat an invitation to anyone who wants to pulverize you, a stark contrast to boasts about the character switching mechanic.  Boss arenas are overlarge, which will make you want to resort to projectile spamming, which is just about the most boring way to play when all of your interesting abilities are melee.  There is not one single enjoyable aspect to the combat.
Mechanically, Ergo and the Bearer might as well be the same person.  There are slight differences in their style, but not enough to make the character-switching in any way meaningful.  They have essentially the same basic abilities, with slight variances, like Ergo's dodge being terrible.  Ergo is, ultimately, just your second healthbar.
English voice acting is PS1 tier.  Ergo is decent, but the Bearer reads her lines, ESPECIALLY the story bits, like a highschool student being called on to read part of MacBeth.
Lastly, having played some of the tabletop game ... it's kind of a disappointing representation of THAT too, at least mechanically.  Which probably won't surprise you if you have much experience with the tabletop game's mechanics.  I'm not sure how you'd really do that.  Anyway, what I mean to say is don't expect to roll in and get to customize a character from Anima mechanics.

Despite some bugs, none game breaking, and some occasional balance issues, this is a good game, with a very appealing artistic direction, great soundtrack, and a story which does not start very strong but builds up pretty finely over the course of the game.
The game isn't all shiny though. The voice acting, overall, is quite weak, although some character do stand out of the bunch positively, and the gameplay can be a frustrating mess sometimes as you will be ganked a lot, and have to deal with quite a lot of projectile spamming.
The moves of the characters are pretty flashy and satisfying to use, although they do feel too similar until you unlocked the more high level skills. There is a certain lack of balance among those skills too, as some skills will be your bread and butter, while others are mostly useless.
The final areas of the game are a bit underwhelming in my opinion, however, if you are interested in lore and intrigue, you will want to keep going anyway.
In regard to gameplay, the game is more DMC than Dark Souls, and shares with both games a certain emphasis on boss battles. The game can be challenging at times, although a large part of said challenge depends on whether you managed to identify and unlock the most useful skills or not, You cannot count on invincibility frames a lot, the timing to dodge attacks isn't always intuitive, and bosses can get spammy and usually don't have much in the way of recovery frames, which means that if you are not careful, damage can add up very fast.
This does not mean that you can play too defensively either, though, as bosses have a dazzling amount of health points. Fights can drag on and on, which is a good thing since it encourages you to learn patterns rather than to rely on a lucky break, but can be gratting when you finally have have a boss' patterns down, and yet the fight drags on because their health lowers agonizingly slow. A certain boss, who likes to pay you a visit several times with little change to his move set, certainly must have a sore♥♥♥♥♥♥by now.
Another thing that I found disappointing, in regard to bosses, is that most of them, being very quick but also easy to combo, encourage you to throw your wide selection of skills out the window and beat them down with just dashes, dodges, and basic attack combos. Of course, the blame is less on the bosses themselves, and more on the wide range of skills which are just painfully slow, even when comboed. Definitely not a good fit for the "spammy attitude" of most bosses.
In the end, it is a pretty good game as it does most things decently, and a few things very good. It sure helps that it comes from an already fully developped and complex fantasy universe, that of Anima, the tabletop RPG.
If you come only for the gameplay, you might be disappointed, but if you like the Anima franchise, a good over the top fantasy universe, or, hu... "anime fantasy"?, you should have a good time!

I remember having no idea about any fighting game lingo or how to even play one at all. I then picked up Skullgirls as i had wanted something to play and only had 20 bucks. Here I learned everything I know from burst baiting to how to do a dragon punch. I understand frames, combo creation, and could even use this as a springboard for other fighting games. This is due to all the time they spent on the tutorials and extensive training mode. The game controls simply enough never getting too complex with stick movements, and once you begin to learn these and put them in combos, you feel great. The characters and backgrounds are all drawn which looks very nice and the game runs locked at 60fps. (Important for a fighting game.) Music and soundtrack fit the environment well and I enjoy Michiru's work. Online works well enough thanks to thier GGPO system. The best part honestly is how they handle thier DLC as when you purchase the game, you have access to the Endless Beta which has all the DLC characters inside and even the ones they are still working on. This creates interesting feedback on characters still in the works. You can also see which you may want to buy. Though too late for the others, Beowulf will be free for three months upon release. I recommend ten-fold.

Let me start by saying Ori and the Blind Forest is beautiful. The entire game is eye candy. Great animations and cutscenes. Enviroments are extremely colorful and diverse. Enemies are recycled a bit but I was happy enough with the variation.
Music is well done, but I have some problems with it. Most of it sounds quite similar. What I mean by that is lots of calm atmospheric tunes and very little stray from that genre. Despite all the songs sounding pleasant and relaxing, I wasn't really hooked by any of them. The music does not attempt to emulate classic metroid, castlevania, or even zelda tunes. It goes full orchestra-esque. You will not find anything funky like Super Metroid's Brinstar, or retro and catchy like Castlevania's main theme. It's all sort of background music that does it's job and fits the theme but I feel like the composer could have experimented a bit more. None of the music ever made me stop and just listen for a while. I suppose one could argue that the composer was not going for that angle, but with a metroidvania game I feel like emulating different styles to try and give that unique platformer feel to each level is better than just making a "one genre" album for the entire game. I want to hear music that makes me say "oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ I should download this." Again, don't get me wrong. The music was good, but personally coming from a platformer background with genre expansive tunes, I wasn't that interested in most of the songs.
Story is excellent. I don't want to spoil anything so I will leave it at that. I played this game drunk a couple times and that was a huge mistake. It's often very touching.
Gameplay is very patience demanding. If you start to tilt you will find yourself continuously dying. That said it is very skillful and rewarding when you get past a difficult part. I often found myself swearing when I'd be at an intense moment and mess up. Sort of like the newer donkey kong games. Some mechanics of the controls aren't quite 100%. The jumping is fluid but not as much as classic titles of this genre. Players familiar to the platformer genre will most likely find themselves slightly screwing up an important jump just because it handles ever so slightly off. It's not by any means huge, but it's noticeable sometimes. I kind of missed the fact that there were no boss battles, only boss "encounters." There were mini boss fights but they weren't that noteworthy. With all the great mechanics to this game I was hoping the developers would implement some interesting boss fights.
Game is awesome. If you like platformers you will enjoy this. If you like touching stories you will enjoy this. If you like a challenge you will enjoy this. I'd definitely recommend this game.

Seriously, try this game. I can guarantee you've spent more money on less enjoyable games this one.

Must play it if you know and enjoy programming logics. Not otherwise though.
As a teenager studying computer science, this game is everything I've dreamt for and beyond, and I'm saying this having progressed no longer than act 4. I have already seen and beaten every aspect of programming that I deal with on a daily basis, and yet I am not in any way bored. I am utterly entertained and challenged for every minute. I have even learned and gotten new ideas from this game alone. Thanks for that, Double Fine.
But let's face it, you're probably not a computer science student. And since you're not, don't expect to find the same entertainment as I did. This is not a ah-let's-chill-out-this-afternoon-with-a-nice-little-indie-game-kind of game. This is a game that will test your math- and logic skills to the max. And if you're never written any code, you're pretty much screwed.
Don't play it if you don't know a ♥♥♥♥ about programming; find some other game that fits your taste. Steam is vast.
Don't play it either if you aim to learn programming; go find and spend money on some proper education.
But if you know your way around coding and enjoy a challenge, you have no time or money to lose. Definetly worth 20 euros.
Why I have voted it down if I enjoyed it? Because the question is not 'Do you like this game?' but 'Do you recommend this game?'. 10/10 for computer geeks.

This game is...unique, to be certain. It scratched an itch I didn't know I had. While my playtime does show 7 hours, I effectively beat the game in about four, only getting stuck on the final inch of the last puzzle due to a technicality (and a large amount of second-guessing myself). The game is quite short, almost disappointingly so, and the features available to you advance at a breakneck pace, which is extremely disorienting at first. You gain new abilities faster than I would like, and oftentimes they are not explained or even required for advancement, leaving you with items in your inventory that you have no idea how to use.
Another issue I have with this game, while not necessarily a "bad thing", is that oftentimes you will solve a puzzle without even knowing how you've done it or indeed, what exactly you were solving in the first place. The game's interface, while allowing you to view the code in macroscale, only allows you to edit it inside "algorithm rooms", which, besides being clunky on larger scripts, obfuscate the code by only allowing you to see a small amount of the script at a time while editing it, necessitating backing out of the room to view your changes on the code, and even then the behavioral changes to the game will only be apparent once you leave the room entirely. If your solution doesn't work, it's back to square one.
Overall, an enjoyable game, but far from a polished experience.

A fun game when things go right. Suppressing and flanking your enemy in this game is really fun, and I haven't found a series like Brothers in Arms that does it as well.
This is an old game though, so there is some clunk to watch out for. Your squad's AI is mediocre, and will usually take a path that leads them into fire, so you'll need to shepherd them through the battlefield to the spot where you want them. Indeed, sometimes it's easier to just do everything yourself and just stow your squad away to keep them alive (you get a Perfect Victory for keeping them alive throughout the whole mission, which I aimed to do in my most recent playthrough).
Checkpoints are infrequent, and I had to replay many sections over and over (sometimes the game pairs two big engagements together, so you'll get stuck on the second and have to re-do the first each time). Fortunately, the game senses when you're having trouble, and allows you to heal yourself and your squad if you die too many times. Since your squad's health bars don't recharge over the course of a mission, this can be a helpful semi-cheat to avoid too much frustration.
I think the biggest thing this game could use is the ability to command your fireteams to go to parts of the map that aren't in your line of sight. You're given a tactical view that allows you to plan your flanking, but it isn't a free view --you instead dash the camera between certain points of interest. For instance, you can see your squad and enemy squads, but the game controls the camera, not you. So it's not too useful, since you can't command your troops from it, nor really see all the battlefield.
The storylines of the Brothers in Arms series never really appealed to me, they're usually overwrought and poorly-acted. I'm not even sure what the storyline of this game was; Road to Hill 30 and Hell's Highway are clearer, but still yawn-inducing. You come to the series for some great tactical gameplay, so don't expect Band of Brothers.
Again, this game can really frustrate, especially given its age. But there's a lot of satisfaction to be had when you succeed, so I recommend a playthrough of it.
If you ever wished they made a Band Of Brothers game, then this is it.

A nicely done sequel to Brothers in Arms: Road to Hill 30, instead of following Sgt. Matthew Baker, you play now as his squad member and best friend; Sgt. Joseph "Red" Hartstock as he reaccounts the events of DDay and beyond DDAY + 7. He was at first a fireteam leader under Baker, but after his promotion to being Sergeant, Red assumes command of 2nd Squad which was leaderless. The story focuses on how the US Paratroopers of both the 101st and the 82nd had to cooperate and share objectives because they were all scattered across Normandy on DDay. Red befriends a member of the 82nd Airborne on DDAY and he would find himself fighting alongside this other paratrooper occasionally.
The gameplay is exactly the same from the previous title, use fire and manuver tactics to outsmart and take out small, but smart enemy fireteams. They also added the ability to share ammo with your squad members if you began to run short. With a great and devoted research team at Gearbox, you also get to learn a lot on what the 101st Paratroopers had to do during the battle for Normandy. You learn that the 101st was only supposed to secure Carentan intially and be relieved from the frontlines, however, with the main American forces swinging towards Cherbourg and St. Lo, a gap is drawn out and the 82nd and 101st were recalled to plug the gap and prevent the Germans from breaking through and driving to the beaches in Normandy. The Paratroopers were expected to spend a minimal of at least three days fighting after DDay, but the fighting dragged on, and the paratroopers would spend nearly a full month fighting deep in Normandy just to protect the flanks of the the main American drives to secure the port city of Cherbourg and the key road junction at St. Lo.
Another 10/10 of this great game series. Gearbox had delivered another smart and challenging authentic WW2 tactical FPS. Each character is likeable and their deaths bring weight. The story is very strong and it also allows development for Red just as the previous title did for Baker.

Since I definitely recommend this game I'll start by listing the "cons" just to get straight to the point:
- The level design is weak. There's a lot of pointless walking in this game, with empty rooms and maze-like paths that ultimately serve no purpose. I haven't finished the game so maybe there's something later on that's supposed to make up for this, but they could have just as easily trimmed down the convoluted paths, or make them accessible only later on with new powers.
- The graphics are adequate, but messy. The walkable paths tend to blend into the background and get covered by stuff from the foreground. Seeing how this game take inspiration by Zelda they should have applied one of its most important lessons: don't clutter the screen. I know there's an item early on that clearly shows you the walkable areas, but it's no excuse.
- Everything resets as soon as you leave the current "room". This avoids getting stuck, but it also means that you'll have to do specific actions over and over again, and seeing how most of this involves hacking it can get a bit tedious.
From a purely mechanical standpoint I also have to say that:
- only having 5 quick buttons (the space bar and buttons 1 through 4) is just inexcusable, especially seeing the vast abount of items you get to use. Of all games I expected this one to be more flexible in its options section, and to be at least more accomodating towards people who play with a keyboard.
- The inventory only displays two rows of items at a time, despite clearly having room for a third one. This is a bit nitpicky, but it also caused me some confusion when I got an item that went in the third row of items, which I couldn't see at all until I scrolled down.
The pros are fewer in number, but ultimately redeem the game in my opinion:
- The mechanics are really a lot of fun to use, and very insightful when it comes to game development. You can speed up and slow down time, change the beaviour of enemies and traps - and even of your own character! - and see behind the curtain of the graphics.
- The puzzles can be really creative and complex, requiring you to think outside the box and make full use of your powers.
Overall my impression is that a simpler, cleaner graphic style and more concise level design would have served this game much better. Aside from that it's definitely worth a try.

I remember having no idea about any fighting game lingo or how to even play one at all. I then picked up Skullgirls as i had wanted something to play and only had 20 bucks. Here I learned everything I know from burst baiting to how to do a dragon punch. I understand frames, combo creation, and could even use this as a springboard for other fighting games. This is due to all the time they spent on the tutorials and extensive training mode. The game controls simply enough never getting too complex with stick movements, and once you begin to learn these and put them in combos, you feel great. The characters and backgrounds are all drawn which looks very nice and the game runs locked at 60fps. (Important for a fighting game.) Music and soundtrack fit the environment well and I enjoy Michiru's work. Online works well enough thanks to thier GGPO system. The best part honestly is how they handle thier DLC as when you purchase the game, you have access to the Endless Beta which has all the DLC characters inside and even the ones they are still working on. This creates interesting feedback on characters still in the works. You can also see which you may want to buy. Though too late for the others, Beowulf will be free for three months upon release. I recommend ten-fold.

Trine is an excellent, gorgeous little game in the same vein as the old 2D side-scroller, The Lost Vikings.  Through a twist of fate, an unlikely trio (thief, mage, and knight) become soulbound to one another via a mysterious artifact known only as the Trine.  Now they must tolerate their newly-shared existences and put each of their unique skills to good use in order to break the spell - and perhaps discover something more in the process.
Gameplay consists of one on-screen character at a time, with the ability to switch between any of the three at any time.  Use the thief to swing across gaps and shoot enemies from afar, the mage to create weighted cubes to solve puzzles, and the knight to slay and defend against the undead who would try to stop the trio in their search. Victory and discovery yield EXP, and as the team levels up, their abilities expand and improve.  The game also has a wry sense of humor.

- With a 5 ½ hour campaign (Hard difficulty in co-op) encompassing 12 short chapters, combined with little to no story at all, and topped off with unimaginative boss fights... there is zero replayability here outside of a forgettable arena mode.

It’s always a horrible feeling to have expectations for a product, and then have your experience with said product under-deliver. I’ve been itching for a good brawler and dungeon crawler, and Gauntlet falls directly into both of those fields.
 
Players are offered the classic quartet of heroes (Warrior, Valkyrie, Elf and Wizard), and surprisingly all play completely different from each other. This could have created a fun balance and provided a reason for multiple playthroughs, but after trying all options I don’t see any reason as to why you’d need to be anything but the Elf. He is a ranged beast, with a quick getaway move to maneuver around clusters of monsters, and has a charge shot and powerful bomb which can dispatch the armored foes and spawn huts that are encountered. The other heroes have somewhat comparable skills, but not nearly as efficient.
 
The levels are a bit too long and don’t offer much variance outside of the three main acts, and the item shop could actually be skipped entirely with no real negative side effects. I wanted to keep playing the game after the final boss, but in retrospect there wasn’t any specific goals left for me to work for. Dragging a friend over for a co-op experience is largely the same, though you may have some more fun busting down monsters with a partner (depending on how well you work together with co-op games).
 
If there was a bit more content to play through, or some extra gear or abilities to work toward, I could see Gauntlet being a title that I would keep installed for a long time. As it is, however, it was fine being a one-and-done playthrough. Not recommended - it can be skipped over for a different dungeon-crawling co-op game.

This is going to be a long one, so to save the trouble for those whose attention span is limited, I'll post a tl;dr here:
Uninspired and badly optimized game with no substance.
Now onto the in-depth criticism:
Music is tolerable and can even provide occasional atmosphere, but general sound direction is atrocious. There were numerous times when certain sound samples were playing at a ridiculously loud volume (to get what I'm talking about - try dying to one of the messengers and continuing, you'll hear that obnoxiously loud *CLUNK* as you respawn). You don't feel satisfaction as you land a hit on the enemy, because usually you are awarded with an ear-grating metal screech or muffled thump, taking away all the enjoyment from combat. Another issue is lack of voice samples. Every boss has a whooping total of 2 or 3 phrases on an endless cycle, prompting the player to turn off the sound at times. And sometimes you can get a speech box from the boss, but no voice whatsoever. Oh and don't get me started on protagonists calling out their attacks with no follow-up. "HEAVEN'S WRATH!"<animation><no sound><character awkwardly floats back onto the ground>. And I'm not even going to elaborate on inconsistencies, such as dashing along the grassy plain, dodging and hearing the sound of boots clacking against stone floor.
Right, I almost forgot the
, the worst offender of them all when it comes to sound. I have caught myself wanting to punch both the writer and Ergo's VA in the face on numerous occasions, because of how bad was the pacing and delivery for all of his lines. There is not a single instance of Ergo's VA being likable or sounding professional. The only bearable voice in the cast was, ironically, Bearer's VA, but that is probably because she is talking in a constantly
neutral tone. It's not "so bad that it's good.", it's "so bad that I want to buy me a pair of earplugs".
I'd like to wrap up this tirade (because there is actually way too much bad things that I want to say about this game) y talking about optimization. A:GoM can't handle open areas with objects in them (as apparent from one of the starting zones in the game, where you meet the Lady for the second time. I kept getting freezes on my PC and lowering the resolution changed nothing, because apparently it was just the game loading up assets as I progressed, deleting them once I move past a certain point, THEN loading them in again if I backtrack), instead sentencing the players to dozens of small loading screens. You can't make two steps before stumbling into one, all because of bad optimization, which would cause freezing issues. How is it possible to screw up this bad is beyond me.
4 years of development and a small budget, and yet you didn't even have time to rig the models for your cutscenes, instead resorting to static ones. For shame.
And yet I still have hope. After 10 hours of enduring this, I still expect to find at least one redeeming quality for this game. After all, if it's trying to rip off Nier, then there is just bound to be a plot twist that, while not fixing the whole mess, will make it a bit more tolerable.

Fun action gameplay

PRETTY AS ALL ♥♥♥♥

A good amount of time, I estimate I am 1/6th or 1/7th of the way through the game at almost 6 hours of playtime.

Occasional bugs - I have had two bugs that required me to revert to a checkpoint and one CTD.  That said, the game autosaves frequently, mitigating the effects of this
Needs optimization - The 'Pretty as all ♥♥♥♥' comes at a clear cost.  I was dropping frames regularily during my gameplay, though my graphics card is out of date (GPU: Gigabyte-made Radeon HD 6850) and I was also streaming at the time.  Still, it could use some work on that end probably.

Voice Acting - the voice actors seem to lack direction at times, or are unsure of context.  That said, much of the voice acting is very well done.  I simply got a sense that sometimes the tone used seemed out of context

NOTICE: Since the overall gameplay and graphical fidelity of BIA: EIB is more or less the same as Road to Hill 30, I will not be mentioning their detailed qualities here. Please refer to my review for the first game here:
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Prolouge: Brothers in Arms: Earned in Blood is the second installment in the BIA franchise. A series of World-War 2 themed tactical First Person Shooters that follow the exploits of US Army Paratroopers of the 101st Airborne division as they fight their way across Europe. Featuring some of Troy Baker's first works of video game voice acting. But, in all seriousness, BIA is my personal favorite WW2 themed franchise; and for good reason. But, we're here to talk about EIB specifically. So, let's get right into it.
Story: BIA: EIB takes place alongside, and after the events of BIA: Road to Hill 30. And this time around, you're not playing as the shy, poetic young squad leader that we know and love: Sgt. Matt Baker. Instead, you're put into the boots of Baker's friend and fellow squad leader, Sgt. Joe "Red" Hartsock. During the game's first acts, you'll be going back to Normandy; reliving the events of Road to Hill 30 through the eyes of our new protagonist. However, once that's done, you and your squad will be tasked with neutralizing the last remnants of Nazi resistance in Normandy in an attempt to liberate it once and for all. Pacing-wise, the story's more of the same with some new locales and set pieces. However, with a new main character, new squad members, and a new mission, it's kept fresh. Overall, if you're looking for a game that holds up to the level of storytelling from series like Band of Brothers, this is about as close as you're gonna get.
Graphics: Overall, the graphical fidelity in EIB hasn't changed all that much from Road to Hill 30, if at all. They still hold up, but it would've been nice to see some improvement over the previous installment.
Sound: Sound design in EIB is a bit of a mixed bag. While the ambience and voice acting are superb, things like weapon sounds and explosions leave something to be desired. That's not to say that they're all bad, though. I just feel like certain weapons could do with sounding a bit more meaty or sharp. As for explosions, they all sound the same. It's that one stock sound that you hear in lots of Hollywood productions, and it gets a bit strange after hearing the same sound for a grenade exploding being the equivalent to an artillery shell. Overall, it's good. But it's far from the best.
Gameplay: EIB's gameplay, as with it's graphics, hasn't changed that much from Road to Hill 30. Your character still waves his gun around like a monkey on LSD while aiming down sights, the squad command system is the same, and you still throw grenades like a pansy. However, there have been some features added that improve the movement mechanics. It seems as though your character moves a bit faster now to compensate for the lack of a sprint key, and you now have the ability to vault over low walls. It was a step in the right direction, but I can't help but think it would've been more productive just to fix what we had already. Other than that, there are a few new weapons in there, like the German FG-42, and the Gewehr-42 which are...cool, I guess.
Final Verdict: BIA: EIB gives us more of the same, but changes things for the better. Considering that this game didn't come out long after the first installment, Road to Hill 30, i'd say it's a worthy successor. And just based on how it's story flows much better, and how the movement system's been improved, I consider this game my favorite in the franchise. But you might be asking: "Why this one? What about Hell's Highway, the third installment?" The answer to that question is coming soon. But, for now, Brothers in Arms: Earned in Blood earns the highest possible 9/10 that I can give it. If you're into old-school tactical shooters, or just WW2 shooters in general, you can't go wrong.
Final Score: 9/10

Earned in Blood is the second installment of the Brothers in Arms series. In this game you play as Joe Hartsock, one of the members of Sgt. Backer’s squad. In this game, you fight parallel to the story of Road to Hill 30 and get to see the story form another angle.

When you can remember the names of the NPC's you were with the entire game, you know that you made a good story and characters. And that is exactly what this game does brilliantly. The charactisation of US paratroopers dropped into German-occupied Normandy, pushing to St Saveur. Being able to rely upon and command them is also paramount and very well displayed. Even if the AI gets stuck at times, but that is very rare.
This game also goes for a more realistic approach. Weapons aren't pinpoint accurate (with exception of the OP scoped Kar98k), so unlike in other FPS games, you cannot use a pistol to 360 no-scope a kraut in the head with a Colt .45. Cause if you are forced to use pistols, you probably got an MP40 up your♥♥♥♥♥cause you messed up. The enemy AI is unforgiving, especially the MG42's. Again, they go for realism. If you are in the open and the MG has a beat at you? One rattle is all you need to hear cause you are dead by then. Furthermore, if you an explosion goes of around you, you will be knocked back. Ringing in your ears, the inability to get up... your character needs to fix himself up mentally before he can get back into the action.
With realism, goes health and tactics. There's a health bar, but no health recovery, forcing you to plan your moves and work with your squad. As said earlier, you can command them. Send them to different positions, tell them to take cover, assault a German position, order them back to where you are, suppress the ♥♥♥♥ out of the Germans, distract tanks, MG's and artillery (advised to have them fire on them from behind cover or they will be picked off with ease) so you can grab a Panzerfaust or flank the enemy from the side or rear, shoving an M1 Garand up their♥♥♥♥♥ Haha!
Keep your men in check and close, cause together and when well commanded, you are an unstoppable force. You have two teams within your squad that help you accomplish that: Fire and Assault teams. Armed with the appropriate weaponary and functions. Fire teams have rifles and specialize in suppressing the enemy. A circle above the enemy is an indication whether they are gonna fire (red) or they are going to cover (grey) Assault teams have submachine guns or compact rifles so they can ASSAULT enemy positions. Used together, the Assault teams can safely flush out the Germans taking cover. This gives the game another aspect to it: every character is fully voiced and will give you clues, spout something about the Germans ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ bricks or call out to teammates getting shot. You want none of your team to die, cause they will be less effective. If you have only one member of the Fire team, suppresive fire will be a joke and the Germans can more easily pop their heads out and take a shot the last remaining member. Each member is vital to your survival.
Sometimes, you even get a tank! You can order it do to the exact same things as your squad with the obvious exception of taking cover, logically. You can even climb on top of it and use the .30 or .50 on the turret and ride along with the tank to be extra deadly! Now don't feel high and mighty, cause the German infantry has Panzerfausts, artillery and Panzer IV's or Stug III's which they will use. A few hits on your tank, and it's done. The first tank you got control over is an M5 Stuart light tank. Great against infantry, but so good against armor. The next one is the M4 Sherman medium tank. Your best friend against Panzer IV's. And finally the M10 Wolverine tank destroyer!
The game is quite brutal in that aspect, but there's gore too. Blood splatters when you hit an enemy or the other way around. Or maybe even dismemberment by means of an explosion, like missing legs or arms. Not on the World at War level, but it's notable.
So, great characters, moving story, well working mechanics, resistant and potent AI, tough enemies... anything to complain?
Little niggles here and there. The non-pinpoint accuracy can be a ♥♥♥♥♥. The artillery and enemy Panzerfausts on the contrary is relentlessly accurate, especially those ♥♥♥♥ing 88's. The MG's are a ♥♥♥♥♥ too but that's realism for ya. The command mechanic can sometimes be wonky, putting your squad in positions you don't want them to. The enemy AI has a mind of its own and is seemingly telepathic, knowing that you are about to flank them from the side so they shout "Sie kommen von die andere Seite!" and get in cover so you can't flank them. The tank AI seems to mostly focused on you, even when you have your own tank blasting it to pieces. You can sometimes see the enemy before they have even appeared in your own line of sight, by way of the red circle above their heads. The AI can get stuck on branches or walls but it's fixed quite easily by way of a new command.
Overall, this is a game Ubisoft should not have stopped making. I give it a 9/10, just because I love the story and characters. In memory of Allen, Garnett, Desola, Doyle, Corrion and Leggett
